To the first question, he says that according to the Philosopher in the fourth book of Ethics, all those things whose price can be compared to currency can be given and accepted in things; and therefore those acts that are exhibited in the succoring of another's misery, even when gifts are accepted, are spent toward the aforementioned end. To the second, he says that habits are distinguished by acts and acts by objects; therefore, sometimes names are equated to habits, acts, and objects, as is evident in the case of faith, which can signify the habit of faith, or the act of it, or the thing itself believed. And similarly, the name of alms sometimes signifies the thing itself given, and thus it is not defined here. Sometimes it signifies the giving itself, and thus the aforementioned definition is accepted. To the third, he says that even though clerics themselves may not need alms, they are given to them as ministers of the poor and dispensers of alms; and therefore, what is given to them as alms is transmitted by them to the poor. To the fourth, he says that just as it is said in the first book, distinction 26, the names of sensible passions are sometimes transferred by a certain similarity to acts of the will that are without passion. And thus, the passion that it imports is the passion of sadness concerning another's misery, and even concerning the very act of the will by which someone is displeased by another's misery; and without such compassion, alms should never be given, because one would not succor another's misery unless he wished for him not to be miserable. And such compassion is even in God, because our evils are displeasing to Him from a preceding will; and sometimes even from an antecedent one. In us also, sometimes a passion properly called compassion is joined, because the superior appetite is born to move the inferior appetite, whence this strong impression is made in the superior, and it will also be in the inferior unless something repels it. And according to this, mercy and modesty and certain other passions are praiseworthy insofar as they proceed from a due election of the good. To the fifth, he says that although one might not give the act of alms for the sake of God regarding its own being, still he gives to himself the ultimate complement of this, which is meritorious, and therefore it is placed last in the definition of it. To the second question, he says that to desist from sin is not of the essence of satisfaction, as is evident from the aforementioned; it is a preamble to satisfaction, it becomes the foundation of it. Whence, when someone sins by not doing what he is held to do, it is not of the essence of satisfaction; it is a preamble to it. Whence, when someone is held to the distribution of alms, sometimes one is and sometimes one is not, as will appear later; it stands that the distribution of those alms to which someone is held is not a part of satisfaction but a preamble to it. Those alms, however, to which one is not held can be satisfactory, as they are good and penal works, which were required for a satisfactory work. For one is punished not only by the affliction of the body, but by the subtraction of things. And through this, the solution to the first is evident. Some, however, say that even the former are satisfactory from the largesse of divine mercy. To the second, he says that that reasoning proceeds concerning an integral part; alms, however, is not such a part of satisfaction, but rather a subjective one, and therefore, even without it, satisfaction completes its perfection in itself, or otherwise in any of its species. To the third, he says that pain is called evil insofar as it subtracts some good, whereby it harms nature. Whence, there is a diverse reason for the good in riches, which the lust of the eyes covets, and the delights which the lust of the flesh covets, and the honors toward which the pride of life tends. Thus, there is a diverse reason for pain in alms, which subtracts riches, and in fasting, which subtracts delights, and in prayer, which depresses the height of the proud spirit through humility. And for this reason, they are diverse parts of satisfaction. Nor does it differ regarding the aforementioned goods whether they are simply good or estimated good regarding the reason for the pain, nor regarding the reason for the appetite; for pain is contrary to the will, as Anselm says. To the fourth, he says that alms does not consist only in the collection of money, but also in other services performed for the neighbor for the sake of God, as was said. Whence, even if this money of others is lacking, the ability to give alms is not lacking; and if the ability were entirely lacking regarding corporal alms because of the penury of things and bodily weakness, yet the ability would not be lacking regarding spiritual alms, because one could at least advise or pray for another. And if even that ability were entirely lacking, a complete will would suffice.
To the third question, it must be said that since virtue is a habit by which we are directed to act well, it is necessary that every act that imports rectitude in itself be reduced to some virtue, even if it does not express in its own reason all that is required for the perfection of the virtue. Thus, when it is said that giving when it should be given is an act of liberality, although this does not express all the due circumstances that are required for an act of liberality. Furthermore, if any person binds that instance to the assets about which the matter is concerned—namely, that if the experience of those who are called heirs is absent or non-existent, the judgment remains—we, therefore, wishing to obstruct such precautions and frauds, desire that the same thing be done in a case of this kind as is done in other cases in which there is no such free collusion and the truth can be known from many indications. Specifically, if the heirs or others who are called to the succession do not wish to put it to the test, or if they wish to desist after the suit is joined, or even appear to act through collusion, then another of those heirs may be admitted to such prosecution or defense. But if none of the heirs or others called to the succession wishes to pursue such a suit, then it is necessary for an inquiry to be made by the judge's office so that the truth may be elicited from other reasons and evidence, regarding the judgment of those who, in fraud and collusion, have made themselves to be accused, or have allowed themselves to be accused, for the disadvantage and loss of the heirs or others who are called to the succession.

Et licet Medicina quoque abuti possent Medici, quæ ob eandem caussam prohibenda etiam videtur, tamen alia est ratio Medicinæ, alia Magiæ; siquidem Medicina eiusque usus per se necessarius est mortalibus, & abusus manifestior, quàm vt omnindè celari queat, ideoque punitu atque emendatu facilior est: Magiæ autem nec vsus hominum Societati per se necessarius, & abusus occultus est, latet enim, per quas res & qualiter Magia operetur. Quam ob rem valdè timeri potest, ne quò est occultior in operando, eò magis fiducia impunitatis, lubrica fit ad nocendum, ait Perer. c. 14.

VIII. Magiæ diabolica & superstitiosa est ratio quadam siue ars operandi mira per signa ope dæmonum. Sicut enim Magia naturalis, vtitur caussis naturalibus, ita superstitiosa vtitur signis quæ sunt caussæ morales; his enim ex pacto allicitur dæmon, vt faciat, quod Magus petit, & sic ipsamet signa videntur aliquid præstare, vt innuit S. Aug. lib. 12. de ciuit Dei, c. 6. vbi etiam tradit hæc signa & totam disciplinam institutam esse primum à dæmonibus, qui tamen signis per se spectatis non delectantur, sed quatenus iis honorantur, vel quatenus ab eorum instituto pendent. At quisnam inter homines primus auctor, primumque instrumentum fuit, per quod diabolus mundo hanc pestem infudit? Greg. Turon. lib. 1. Histor. Franc. c. 6. ait Chus primogenitum Chami, diabolo imbuente, fuisse totius Magicæ artis inuentorem, quem Persæ se venientem Zoroastrem (quasi viuens astrum) nominarunt, & fulmine ictum pro Deo habuerunt. D. Clemens lib. 2. recog. putat etiam antè diluuium Magiam viguisse ac post diluuium à Chamo traditam filio Mizraim, à quo Aegyptii, Chaldæi, Persæ, qui maximè his artibus dediti fuêre.

IX. Porrò quàm certum est Philosophis Christianis dæmones esse, tàm certum est Magiam dæmoniacam esse, quæ neq; industria vel artificio hominum, neque caussis tantùm naturalibus, sed immateriali quadam & separata virtute seu actione, hoc est, ab immaterialibus, & separatis substantiis profecta, nititur, ac potissimum experientia demonstratur; nam responsa dare occultissimis de rebus, consequi repentè scientiam absque omni labore addiscendi, subtrahere corpora oculis intuentium, &c. ad nullam causam reduci possunt, quàm intellectualem aliquam separatamque naturam, hæc autem non est Deus, nec aliquis bonus genius (qui non se admiscent rebus vanis) ideòque solus Cacodæmon, vt rectè probat Delrius lib. 2. q. 2. ex quo discas, præter naturalem suprà expositam nullam esse Magiam Albam & licitam, quæ immediate à Solo Deo, vel mediate ab eodem per angelos bonos ad nos dimanet, sed omnem aliam esse Nigram & illicitam, vtpote à spiritibus malignis traditam, eorumque pacto explicito aut implicito nixam.

X. Cum ergò nulla sit Alba Magia, seu theurgia, vt vocant, patet omnem aliam (præternaturalem) esse damnandam fugiendamque, hoc est, vniuersim Magiam

translation:
**VIII.** Diabolical and superstitious Magic is a certain rationale or art of working wonders through signs by the aid of demons. For just as natural Magic uses natural causes, so superstitious Magic uses signs which are moral causes; for by these, according to a pact, the demon is enticed to do what the Magician seeks, and thus the signs themselves seem to perform something, as St. Augustine intimates in *The City of God*, book 12, chapter 6, where he also relates that these signs and the whole discipline were instituted first by demons, who nevertheless are not pleased by the signs viewed in themselves, but insofar as they are honored by them, or insofar as they depend on their institution. But who among men was the first author, and the first instrument, through which the devil infused this plague into the world? Gregory of Tours, in *History of the Franks*, book 1, chapter 6, says that Cush, the firstborn of Ham, the devil imbuing him, was the inventor of the whole Magical art, whom the Persians, seeing him coming, named Zoroaster (as if to say "living star"), and because he was struck by lightning, held him as a God. St. Clement, in *Recognitions*, book 2, thinks also that Magic flourished before the flood and after the flood was handed down by Ham to his son Mizraim, from whom the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Persians, who were most addicted to these arts.

**IX.** Furthermore, as it is certain to Christian Philosophers that demons exist, so it is certain that Demoniacal Magic exists, which relies neither on the industry or artifice of men, nor on merely natural causes, but on a certain immaterial and separate virtue or action, that is, one proceeding from immaterial and separate substances, and is most especially demonstrated by experience; for to give responses about most hidden things, to attain knowledge suddenly without any labor of learning, to subtract bodies from the eyes of beholders, etc., can be reduced to no cause other than some intellectual and separate nature, but this is not God, nor any good genius (who do not mix themselves in vain things), and therefore it is only the Cacodemon <note>i.e., evil spirit</note>, as Delrio rightly proves, book 2, question 2, from which you may learn that, besides the natural one explained above, there is no White and licit Magic, which flows to us immediately from God Alone, or mediately from the same through good angels, but all other is Black and illicit, as being handed down by malignant spirits and resting upon their explicit or implicit pact.

**X.** Since, therefore, there is no White Magic, or theurgy, as they call it, it is clear that all other (preternatural) magic is to be condemned and avoided, that is, Magic universally.

P. A.
What is: *He sowed in that year and found hundredfold barley*? <note>original: "Genesis 26:12"</note>

§. 189. A year is a perfect time consisting of all the seasons of the year; whence it is named <term>eniautos</term> <gloss>year</gloss> in itself and outside itself. Moreover, the hundred is the most sacred of numbers, the power of the most perfect ten. The letter is therefore a certain testimony that for one adorned with virtue, both those things which pertain to agriculture and those which pertain to the use of the life of the world go well, and that his latter things are found to be more manifold and fuller than his former. To the mind, however, barley is food for both men and brute animals; but in each of us, the man is the mind and the brute is the sense. When, therefore, a sterility of goods has not supervened, but the soul has exhibited itself as a fertile field, capable of conceiving the seed of virtue, it is rendered fruitful and, having been seen to generate according to individual virtues, it finds more than that which it generates, with God favoring and increasing, and beneficently transposing from the invisible to the visible and another form the rational and irrational part, with one and the same grace according to the number

<margin>In aquis mineralib. non inesse tincturæ spiritales.</margin>
Confutatur autem eiusmodi generatione opinio eorum, qui aquis mineralibus, veluti acidulis, &c. nil tribuere possunt, præter spirituaales commistiones, & immatura seminaria, seu prima entia, quę antequam coagulent & formam acquirant, ab aquis anticipata assumantur. Feri quidem hoc posse fatendum est: sed nec catholicum habendum, cum ipsa quoque ars non raro ex aquis mineralibus coagulando succos istos substantia sua perfectos, educat. Nolle vero tales aquas in mineralibus habere, angusti admodum est, & sua nimium amantis animi. Qui vero possunt aquam metallicam dicere, & monstrare, quæ primam metallorum materiam, antequam consistat, & nondum habeat vt formam, ita nec virtutes metalli perfecti, secum vehit? Quomodo aquam hanc serratam dicent, illam æratam, si nunquam primæ materiæ metallorum singulorum qualitates cognouerunt? Omnia reduci possunt in hydrargyrum, ex omnibus sal, & calcanthum elicitur, hæc qui dignoscent in suis primordiis & ruditate? Verisimilior est Philosophi nostri sententia, euenire nempe istiusmodi per resolutionem seu in spiritus, de quibus supra, seu in fuccos calcesve solubiles, cum ars contestetur metalla calcinata in liquores solui, & alias etiam alios succos ex iisdem educi, & per aquas elementares percolatas ablui: quin & acribus rebus (aquis acutis, cæmentis, coloritio, &c.) corrodi, corrosionemque ita misceri aquis, vt plane non appareant, nisi post coagulationes, quo pacto tantarum in limpidissimo inest vino, succi rerum decoctarum in decoctis depuratis, in aqua forti metallica ramenta, in solutionibus succi solubiles.

# CAP. XII.
## Mineralium analoga.

**A**D hanc de corpulentis mistionibus classem reuocari & illæ aquæ possunt, quæ in minera quidem, seu potius terræ cauernis nihil admodum acquirunt, sed vna secum afferunt virtutem iam mistione in terræ extimo facta. Ita si mare subiret hiatus terræ, alioque capite iterum prorumperet, pro minerali scaturigine haberi posset: ita si aqua cœli, fluuiatilis, stagnans, palus, &c. accepta vi ex plantarum succis, excrementis animalium, aliisve descenderet aliquo vsque, & iterum prodiret eodem modo affecta, aut saltem ex illo principio quadamtenus immutata. Notum est vbi greges animalium stabulant, loca excrementis perfusa kalinitri primordia accipere. Si iam ea combibantur à riuulo sparsim serpente, & tandem vno fonte prodeunte, euadet aqua prope mineralis dicenda. Computruere item in aquis stagnantibus varias res, potissimum animales & vegetales, posse notum est. Inde quoque origo mineralem repræsentans erit.

# CAP. XIII.
## Paracelsi sententia.

<margin>Prima materia metallorum.</margin>
**I**D edoctus etiam à suis præceptoribus & experientiæ euidentia Paracelsus est. Quanquam enim aliquando mineralibus aquis tribuat propriam primæuamque ab ortu mundi naturam, & dicat minerales aquas cum simplicibus vnum idemque fuisse, at ob salutem animalium & plantarum seiunctas, postea profluere separatim: tamen aut correxit sententiam, aut variaffe postea pro more suæ inconstantiæ, aut Scepticæ Socraticæque incertitudinis videri potest, dum scriptum reliquit, minerales frigidas oriri vel ex alumine sale, atramento, in sua vena immaturis, & non mistis: itane vt nulla aqua elementaris accedat, sed illa ipsa immatura, incongelata, & specie liquoris existentia syncere prodeant, & mineralem fontem fluxu perenni constituant? Quod si est immensam vim in conceptaculis spaciove vasto collectam esse necesse est, vt fluxus in multum tempus sufficiant, aut naturam in illu loco frustrari suo conatu, & nihil nisi abortus imperfectos in luce emittere) vel ex tribus principiis septē metallorū antequam consistant, si aquę catharactæ percurrit, & illa corrupit ne possint perfici, aut saltem ex prima materia istorum triū in vnoquoque, metallo tum simpliciter, tum miste: (quasi affluxu aquæ elementaris anteuerteretur naturæ operatio, dissiparetq; iam coagulandum salē, sulphur, & mercuriū auri, argenti, stanni, plūbi, ferri, æris & hydrargyri, quanquam illa res non potest dici prima materia, cum nihil sit aliud, quam sal solutus, sulphur incongelatū, & mercurius inconcretus: prima vero materia istorū vel vapor, halitusq; est seminalis potentiam ad illas res habens, vel principium viscosum spiritu tali fæcundum, quod si ante maturitatem suam rapitur & aquis diluitur, neutiquam metallicam naturam aquis imprimere potest, cum eam non actu, sed in potentia habeat, sicut nec qui gallinacei liquor discussus & aqua remissus, hanc natura viribusq; gallinæ induit, ne dū agnosci possit. Ridiculum autem est, tale principium et simpliciter profluere posse, cum constet in minera id concludi & maturescere in morem fructuū plantarū & animaliu: quod si confluit, tantum non est, aut iā formā in minera accepit, justa carens coagulatione, quam demum in lacuna sua acquirit. Facilius certe est tale quid fingere, q̄ ostendere. Non tamen negandum est, ex immaturis metallorum primordiis seu spiritus sint, seu liquores, p̄ aquaru ferarū commistionē euadere metallares aquas aliquo modo. Sin addas et̄, separatim illa tria principia intelligenda esse, vt sic <margin>Dubitatio de primordiis metallicis.</margin> viginti & vna mineralis fluxio inde possit existere, etiam amplius delirabis. Non n. existunt separatim, nec metalla fiunt compositione ex illis separatis, sed tanquam è semine progignuntur, in quo principia ista simul erant potentia, si quide sunt pro principiis veris habenda, & non potius pro Chymicū magisteriis, arte elicitis ex diuersimode affectis metallis, quo pacto possumus ex iisdem facere chalcanthum, flores, calces, liquores, &c. quæ tamen pro veris primordiis non habentur, &c.) vel ex spiritibus trium principiorum metallicorum: (Idem dicitur: Nihil enim refert, siue spiritus, siue liquoris appareant foris forma, si interiore sunt imperfecta. Possumus tamen etiam resolutorum halitus intelligere, & principia ista catachrestice accipere pro sale, fulphure, hydrargyro, non quæ sunt initia compositionis aut generationis rerū, sed quæ res in se perfectæ, quomodo & elementa in se consideramus, quatenus sunt corpora simplicia pe-

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the composition of mineral waters, transitioning from the idea of "spirits" or vapors to the physical resolution of metals and minerals into liquids, while critiquing the theories of Paracelsus regarding the "first matter" of metals.</meta>

Commentary on Alchemy, Part II, Book VI.

...you would not bring it forth by washing or boiling. Nor indeed can you extract salt by any fire from a thing in which there is naturally no principle of salt.

<margin>Spiritual tinctures are not present in mineral waters.</margin>
By this kind of generation, the opinion of those who can attribute nothing to mineral waters—such as <term>acidulae<note>original: "acidulis"; these are "acidic" or "sour" mineral springs, highly valued for their perceived medicinal properties in the early modern period.</note></term> and the like—except for spiritual mixtures and immature seeds, or "first entities," is refuted. These theorists believe that before these substances can coagulate and take on a form, they are prematurely taken up by the waters. It must be admitted that this can happen; however, it should not be held as a universal rule, since <term>the Art<note>original: "ars"; specifically refers to alchemy or the "spagyric art," which sought to replicate and accelerate natural processes.</note></term> itself often draws out these juices, perfected in their substance, from mineral waters through coagulation. To deny that such waters contain minerals is the mark of a very narrow mind, too fond of its own ideas. Truly, who can name and show a "metallic water" that carries the "first matter" of metals before it is solid—before it has a form or the virtues of a perfected metal? How can they call this water "iron-bearing" or that one "copper-bearing" if they have never known the qualities of the first matter of each individual metal? All things can be reduced to <term>mercury<note>original: "hydrargyrum"; quicksilver.</note></term>; from all things, salt and <term>vitriol<note>original: "calcanthum"; a term for metallic sulfates, often blue or green in color.</note></term> are extracted. Who shall distinguish these in their first beginnings and raw state? More probable is the opinion of our Philosopher: that these things happen through resolution, either into the "spirits" mentioned above, or into soluble juices or <term>calxes<note>original: "calces"; the powdery residue left after a metal or mineral has been roasted or "calcined."</note></term>. For the Art bears witness that calcined metals are dissolved into liquids, and other juices are drawn from them and washed away by percolating elemental waters. Indeed, they are even corroded by sharp things (strong waters, <term>cementing powders<note>original: "caementis"; refers to the alchemical process of "cementation," where metals are refined using dry mineral powders and heat.</note></term>, coloring agents, etc.), and this corrosion is mixed with the waters so thoroughly that it is not visible until after coagulation—just as the essence of many things remains in very clear wine, the juice of boiled things in purified decoctions, or metallic filings in <term>aqua fortis<note>original: "aqua forti"; literally "strong water," refers to nitric acid.</note></term> and soluble juices in solutions.

# CHAPTER XII.
## Analogies of Minerals.

**T**o this class of "corporeal mixtures" one may also refer those waters which acquire nothing at all within the mineral vein or the caverns of the earth, but rather carry with them a power already mixed at the earth's surface. Thus, if the sea were to enter a gap in the earth and burst forth again at another opening, it could be considered a mineral spring. Likewise, if rainwater, river water, stagnant water, or marsh water, having taken on power from plant juices, animal excrement, or other things, were to descend somewhere and emerge again affected in the same way, or at least changed somewhat from that original principle. It is well known that where herds of animals stable, the places soaked in excrement receive the beginnings of <term>saltpeter<note>original: "kalinitri"; refers to potassium nitrate or nitre.</note></term>. If these are then soaked up by a stream creeping here and there and finally emerging as a single spring, the water will turn out to be what should be called "nearly mineral." It is also known that various things, especially animal and vegetable matters, can rot in stagnant waters. From this, too, an origin representing a mineral will arise.

# CHAPTER XIII.
## The Opinion of Paracelsus.

<margin>The first matter of metals.</margin>
**P**aracelsus <note>The famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist (1493–1541) who pioneered the use of chemicals in medicine.</note> was also taught this by his teachers and the evidence of experience. For although he sometimes attributes a unique and primeval nature (existing since the beginning of the world) to mineral waters, saying that mineral waters were once one and the same as simple waters but were later separated and flowed apart for the health of animals and plants; nevertheless, he either corrected this opinion or changed it later (consistent with his usual inconstancy or Socratic uncertainty). He left written that cold mineral waters arise either from <term>alum<note>original: "alumine"; a specific type of mineral salt used in dyeing and medicine.</note></term>, salt, or <term>vitriol<note>original: "atramento"; literally "ink," but in an alchemical context, it refers to "atramentum sutorium" or ferrous sulfate.</note></term> that are immature and unmixed in their vein—does this mean that no elemental water is added, but those very immature, uncongealed substances existing in the form of a liquid emerge purely and establish a mineral spring with a perennial flow? (If this is so, an immense force must be collected in vast reservoirs or spaces for the flow to last a long time; otherwise, Nature is frustrated in her attempt in that place, emitting nothing but imperfect abortions into the light). Or, he says they arise from the <term>Three Principles<note>The alchemical triad of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which Paracelsus believed were the components of all matter.</note></term> of the seven metals before they solidify. If a rush of water runs through and "corrupts" them so they cannot be perfected—or at least from the first matter of these three in each metal, both simply and mixed—as if the operation of nature were overtaken by the influx of elemental water, dissipating the salt, sulfur, and mercury of gold, silver, tin, lead, iron, copper, and quicksilver that were about to coagulate. Yet that thing cannot be called "first matter," since it is nothing other than dissolved salt, uncongealed sulfur, and unsolidified mercury. The true "first matter" of these is either a vapor and seminal breath having the potential for those things, or a viscous principle fertile with such a spirit. If this is snatched away before its maturity and diluted by waters, it can in no way imprint a metallic nature upon the waters, since it possesses it not in act, but only in potential—just as if the <term>fluid of a chicken egg<note>original: "gallinacei liquor"; literally the "liquid of a hen." The author argues that a raw egg yolk mixed in water doesn't have the "nature" of a chicken yet.</note></term> were scattered and diluted in water, it would not take on the nature and powers of a hen, nor could it even be recognized as such. Moreover, it is ridiculous that such a principle could flow out simply, since it is established that in a mine it is enclosed and matures like the fruits of plants and animals; if it flows together, it is either not that principle, or it has already taken a form in the mine, lacking only the proper coagulation which it finally acquires in its pool. It is certainly easier to imagine such a thing than to show it. However, it should not be denied that metallic waters arise in some way through the mixing of "wild" waters with the immature beginnings of metals, whether they be spirits or liquids. But if you also add that those three principles are to be understood separately, so that <margin>Doubt concerning metallic origins.</margin> twenty-one mineral flows could exist from them, you will be raving even further. For they do not exist separately, nor are metals made by a composition of those separate parts, but they are brought forth as if from a seed, in which those principles were together in potentiality—if indeed they are to be held as true principles, and not rather as "chemical masteries" elicited by art from metals affected in different ways. In this way, we can make vitriol, flowers, calxes, and liquids from the same metals, which nevertheless are not considered true "origins." Or, they arise from the spirits of the three metallic principles. (The same is said: for it matters not whether they appear outwardly in the form of spirit or liquid, if they are imperfect within. We can, however, also understand the breaths of resolved things, and take those "principles" <term>figuratively<note>original: "catachrestice"; a rhetorical term for using a word in a forced or improper sense.</note></term> for salt, sulfur, and mercury—not those which are the beginnings of the composition or generation of things, but things perfected in themselves, just as we consider the elements in themselves, insofar as they are simple bodies per...

<summary>The author refutes the idea that mineral waters are merely "spiritual" seeds, arguing instead that they contain physically dissolved mineral substances. He critiques Paracelsus's theories on the "Three Principles" (Salt, Sulfur, Mercury) as the origin of mineral springs, suggesting these theories are more imaginary than observable.</summary>

translation:
...the Italian. Now, mild ones, from wherever they are brought, are not rejected as food. Paulus commended its use with vinegar and oil, because it both invites appetite and loosens the spleen, and drives out phlegm through the bowels. In pharmacies, it has retained its name; the common people, happy to abbreviate names, by wearing down two letters, bring forth *capres* as if *cappares*. Some of the Latins call it *inturim*, for the shrub is seen to be of a thorny kind, scattering itself in a circle on the ground. It has thorns like a bramble, curved into a hook, leaves like a quince, fruit like an olive, upon the bursting of which a white flower breaks out; when this falls, an oblong pod coalesces, which, finally unfolding itself, represents small grains that are red, such as are seen in the pomegranate, with large, branch-like roots. Small stems, leaves, flowers, seeds, and pods preserved in salt are brought to us in this appearance and shape which we have described. France now nourishes the shrub. In Cyprus, the caper grows in great abundance. It offers little nourishment to those eating, because it excels in the thinness of its parts, being born for medicine rather than for food. The fruit is preserved sprinkled with salt, otherwise it quickly senses corruption. Fresh [fruit] not having experienced salt nourishes more than that which has been aged in it, yet it moves the bowels more. Washed and soaked for a short time until it lays down the whole nature of the salt, it nourishes very little indeed, but invites a languishing appetite. It disperses the loathing of foods, casts down phlegm that had gathered in the belly, and clears out the obstructing blockages of the spleen and liver. But to perform these uses, it ought to be preferred to other dishes in honeyed vinegar or oil and vinegar. They eat the tender buds while they are green with vinegar and salt, and store them away for uses. They say that those who eat them daily are not endangered by the resolution of the nerves, nor by pains of the spleen. The root removes white vitiligo if they are ground and rubbed in the sun. It is beneficial to those with spleen ailments when drunk in wine, two drachms of the bark of the root, with the use of baths removed. And they say that in thirty-five days, the entire spleen is emitted through urine and the bowels. It is drunk for pains in the loins and for paralysis. The seed ground and boiled in vinegar, or the chewed root, soothes pains of the teeth. A decoction in oil is infused for pain in the ears. The leaves and fresh root with honey heal ulcers which they call phagedenas. In this way, the root also disperses swollen glands and parotids. Boiled in vinegar, it removes ulcerations of the mouth; it also cures ailments of the liver and kills worms of the ears. They give it in vinegar and honey for dandruff. It is agreed among authors that they are useless for the stomach. The stem and fruit are preserved for the sake of food. It disturbs the bowels, harms the stomach, and creates thirst. However, it is more useful for the stomach when boiled than raw. The seed itself, taken in two drachms in wine for forty days, consumes the spleen. It draws out urine and drives out bloody scrapings. It is beneficial for pains of the hips and resolution of the nerves; likewise for ruptures and convulsions. It moves the menses and elicits phlegm of the head. The seed boiled in vinegar soothes pains of the teeth if the mouth is rinsed. The dried bark of the root has the same effects. It purges all ulcers that are old, dirty, and that have become calloused. For those with spleen ailments, it is smeared on with barley flour. The root, seized bitingly with the tooth, relieves that evil. It removes white vitiligo when ground with vinegar. The ground root and leaves disperse swollen glands and hardness. The juice is infused against worms of the ears. The foreign caper which is brought from Marmarica in Libya excites great inflations. The Apulian causes vomiting; [as does] the very harsh African, and that which is conveyed from the Red Sea, for it raises pustules in the mouth and is an enemy to the gums, for it eats them away down to the bone, which is why it is condemned in foods.

### Lepidium. Chapter CV

The appearance of *lepidium* is not represented by Dioscorides. *Lepidium* was once foreign; now it is sown in many places by Fauonius; then, when it has grown into a shrub, it is cut close to the ground and harvested like cut leeks, but more rarely. It should not be cut after the Kalends of November, since it dies from being violated by the colds, especially if the severity of winter worsens, for it is most impatient of the cold: yet in two years, it extends its life up to ten years. It grows, as Pliny records, to a cubit's height, with laurel-like leaves, but soft. Its use is not without milk. Paulus Aegineta, in the third volume, in the mention of sciatica, says: "Lepidium which grows among us is shrub-like, with laurel leaves, [but] far larger; they are more efficacious in summer." If the time of year denies these, it will be appropriate to use the bark of the root in place of the leaves. It has provided wonderful experience for those with sciatica and long illnesses. This herb is cultivated among us, not unknown to the pharmacies, though under the borrowed name of another plant. For herbalists now call it not *lepidium* but *raphanus*, perhaps [because of the] root.

<header>VII.</header>

<note>A decorative blue initial O</note>Ummidia Quadratilla passed away at a little less than eighty years of age. She was vigorous and healthy right up until her final illness, even for an old woman, with a stout and compact body. She died having made a most honorable will. She left as her heirs her grandson, with two-thirds of the estate, and her granddaughter, with one-third. I am very fond of both the granddaughter and the grandson, who is a remarkable young man. He is a person to be loved not only by his blood relatives but also by those not related to him. From his early youth, he was notable for his beauty, and he avoided all the gossip of malicious people. He was married before his twenty-fourth year and, if God had willed, would have been a father. He lived with his grandmother in a refined manner, very modestly, and yet with the greatest obedience. She kept mimes, and she favored them more effusively than was becoming for a noble woman. Quadratillus did not watch these mimes at the theater or at home, nor did she require him to. I have heard her say herself, when she was commending to me her grandson’s studies, that as a woman in that leisure of her sex, she was accustomed to relax her mind with the game of dice and to watch her mimes; but whenever she was about to do either, she always instructed her grandson to leave and study. This seemed to me to be done not more out of love for him than out of reverence. You will be surprised, as I was, that at the recent priestly games, when the mimes were brought out for the opening, as Quadratillus and I were leaving the theater together, he said to me: "Do you know that today I have seen my grandmother’s freedman dancing for the first time?" This from the grandson, but by Hercules

# On My Own Books.

...it established the premise so that men might understand that a good and honest man cannot be unhappy. I am poor, sick, old, and now bereft of my excellent son, a young man of the best hope and most loving to me, lost through injustice. Another man, with little to no hope of good fortune or of propagating his lineage, has a daughter married for nine years who is sterile. I was once flourishing in every way: in friendship, children, profit, and good health. As a young man, I was raised to great hope and was accustomed not only to comforts but even to luxuries. Yet now, I am entirely wretched, despised, and burdened with many enemies. I do not consider myself unhappy; rather, I consider myself far happier than ever before. I am not insane, nor am I boasting; my actions show this. I profess this with a most steadfast mind, and for that reason, my auditorium is even more crowded. I manage all things better than before; if anyone compares the books I have recently completed with the earlier ones, they will understand that my mind is fuller, more vivid, and purer. 

But you, whoever you are, weep like a woman over a single misfortune, even a very slight one. We bear so many and such great ones. We have gained this one thing: that we do not regret life because of virtue and knowledge, nor do we fear death, the end of so many dangers and inconveniences, and a thing so necessary. Another man is tormented far more by a calamity that is not even a calamity. Because his horse limps due to the negligence of a servant, he exclaims and spends sleepless nights. All the many opportunities for happiness bring him no comfort, as if he were entirely invested in the foot of his horse. Another is miserable because he is despised; another because his son is his grandson; another because he fears for the chastity of his wife; another because he has lost his magistracy, and he attempts to end his life with a noose. Therefore, the more delicate senses and tastes of men, as well as their ignorance of the nature of things and our condition, and their despair of a future life, make men miserable even for the smallest reasons. Such men cannot be happy by any reasoning, nor can they be consoled in adversity. 

See what our life is like. There are two men, both of whom sleep for six consecutive months (as they report of Alpine mice). One of them dreams of prisons, chains, crosses, nooses, tortures, the slaughter of his children, fears, destruction, flights, storms, diseases, poverty, and hunger. At one moment, he is carried alone on a wandering sea, with the hope of safety abandoned; at another, he flees the cavalry of a tyrant through deserts, destitute of everything; at another, he is conquered and thrown into a foul pit; at another, he is led to punishment; at another, he is exiled by a crowd as a madman. Conversely, the other dreams of kingdoms, honors, banquets, games, associations, gardens, fortresses, pleasant journeys, mistresses, a beautiful wife, children, and he passes from one pleasure to another. Moreover, not content with these human delights, he is carried to heaven, where he sees most beautiful things, green fields, hunts, fowling, and fishing. Then both wake up at the same time. Who is so foolish as to say that one is happy and the other unhappy? But you reply that this is a short dream, it affects one less, and nothing is left behind from it. Yet life is longer with a true sense of things, and with greater pleasure and pain; and when we exit it, those things remain for others: children, honors, wealth. They do not vanish entirely as in a dream. You are talking nonsense. This time of six months
<column-break/>
of perpetual happiness, if one considers it correctly, no one in any long life ever equals. Regarding sense, cares, and pleasure, all things in dreams are, and appear, greater than in wakefulness. Reason persuades us of this, especially since we are not distracted by the senses. But as far as the true life is concerned, this is what we are arguing about. Indeed, the interval between the future life and this one is far greater than that between wakefulness and sleep. The things that are left behind, if they are referred to foolish hope, are something, and therefore one should grieve more that we are forced to leave them. If we look toward true opinion, if we look toward the outcome of things, we are deceived by a false image. Thus, anyone is free to imagine an immortal life, an immense and peaceful kingdom. But since these trifles cannot be moved, one must conclude about our life that it is truly a dream. 

But, as I said, if something greater had existed, I had raised my affairs to such a point that I could have been the happiest of men from the most unhappy, and from the poorest, through my own efforts and those of my son, we were earning two thousand golden crowns every year. There was no order of men, no princes, who were not in our hands. I had conquered envy, I had surpassed emulation, I had crushed conspiracies, I had penetrated into the inner circles. I had opened the ways; I had built an approach for myself and my son to everything. Moreover, the opportunity of foreign princes was not lacking to me any more than it was to anyone else. I was called first to the King of the Dacia <note>original: "Dacorum Regem"</note>, then to the French <note>original: "Gallorum"</note>, and soon after to allies. I will tell, however, a story that happened in the year 1551. 

John Hamilton <note>original: "Ioannes Amulthon"</note>, of the royal Scottish line, was the primary bishop among them, a man of remarkable faith, learning, and piety, and most liberal. He suffered from a difficulty in breathing so severe that those who had seen him in the illness itself did not think he would survive the day. Yet he had been enduring such a disease for a whole decade, although things were slipping into the worse day by day. He had not failed to try the service of any notable physician. But since he had tested both Royal and Imperial physicians, as well as the more illustrious professors of the art, by chance, a certain friend of his, William Cassanatus <note>original: "Gulielmus Cafanatus"</note>, his physician, had come upon our books *On Subtlety* and *On Wisdom*. As they were reading through them, they found me boasting that I had cured some who suffered from consumption <note>original: "phthificos"</note>. And certainly, I had cured very few of such a disease, though I had healed many suffering from a similar affliction. Thus, that boasting and the proclamation of my false praise profited the not-at-all-lying man not a little. For, incited by these and other arguments, they persuaded him that, since there was no hope of safety anywhere else, he should flee to the final anchor. The condition was pleasing, and he sent letters to us first, inviting us to Lyon <note>original: "Lugdunū"</note> or Paris <note>original: "Lutetiam"</note>. And although I inscribed a copy of his letter in the previous edition of this book, I thought it better, having omitted the superfluous parts so as not to delay the reader, to insert here what pertained to the matter, but in such a way that neither the sense nor the words themselves were changed. This, therefore, was the letter from his physician. 

The Most Illustrious Bishop of the city of Saint Andrews, and prelate of the whole kingdom, and brother of the Viceroy <note>original: "Proregis"</note>, and my Maecenas, for whom I have been the physician for four years, has been held for nearly ten years with a difficult breathing condition by a cyclical distillation, although without fever...

<vocab>etas argentea, aenea proles, Mars, Ditis, heroum, Iusticia</vocab>
translation: The rude beginning of nature, by which a fading age also led a rude heart in its own dwellings. Yet, after the age had grown and reached its peak, the space of living was shorter, and the anxious ardor of cares was present, which the wicked joys of the mind created. Alternating injury never ceased. And the silver age saw no reverence for the gods and no rites of sacred things. The god extinguished this race, inflamed in deserved anger, after the earth hid the silver ages of men. Yet, their life did not depart without a name; under the earth, they cultivated secondary seats of the gods. Third after that followed the brazen race, not at all similar to the silver, created from the blood of the dryads, indeed hardy and stretching out robust chests, it was all burning with the miserable love of wild Mars. There was no rest for it, no law. The age was harder than adamant itself, to be feared for its proud face. Its invincible strength and strong arms never failed its shoulders. Then, bronze were the weapons, and all labor was in bronze. The use of iron had not yet emerged. This race, however, consumed by its own madness, departed without honor to the dark places of cold Ditis <note>Pluto, god of the underworld</note>. And although it existed with invincible strength, it was nevertheless conquered by black death and left the light of the sun. After it was hidden and the brazen age collapsed, the fourth was an offspring, better and more just, to whose mind the precepts of revered justice clung. It was the divine race of heroes, first so called.

## XII.

Constat itaque Paracelsistarum, Weigelianorum, Mysticorum, Quakerorum & cæterorum, qui communi illuminatorum nomine vocari solent, opiniones fanaticas in eo conspirare, quod præter corpus & animam rationalem sit in homine substantialis quædam pars divinitus ipsi, &, ut plerique non dissimulant, ex ipsa divina essentia concessa. Eandem doctrinam de tribus partibus hominis satis prolixe explicat Felgenhawer im *Vorhoff/ im heiligen und Allerheiligsten am Tempel GOttes*: cujus fanatici libelli lectiones singulæ singularum partium rationes & Fanaticorum de iis somnia satis declarant. Conferri etiam meretur Bartholomaei Sclei *anständige allgemeine GOttes Lehre*/ nec non das *Buch des Zeugnisses des verborgenen Ackerschatzes*/ cujus Autor se ipsum vocat HIEL, das *einwesige Leben GOttes*/ ut & des von GOtt hocherleuchteten Matthes Weyer *gründlicher Unterricht*/ & similia a furiis illis conscripta librorum portenta, indigna sane quibus legendis quis bonas ac irrevocabiles horas perdat.

## XIII.

Cæterum hæc de triplici hominis parte doctrina principem in ipsorum Matæologia locum obtinet. Hanc enim non modo Christianismi totius, sed omnis in universum sapientiæ, quæ in cælo & terra est, fundamentum continere ineptissime jactitat Autor des *Vorhoffs* Cap. XII. At vero si quem forte lateat se quinque habere sensus, vel quæ sit visus vel auditus aut reliquorum natura, anne propterea statuendum, quod isti munere suo fungi nequeant? Non equidem puto. Interim Andreas Christophorus Rafelius hoc dogma tantis extollit encomiis ut non vereatur in *Der Neujahrs Posaune* hunc in modum de eo loqui: *Das ist eigentlich der rechte Grund-Fels/ und das gewisse Fundament/ darauff das Hauß unsers Christenthums soll gesetzet/ geleget und fundiret werden/ soll es bestehen: und daraus alles predigen/ lesen/ schreiben/ GOttes Wort hören/ singen/ beten/ gute Wers*

translation:
<meta>continues from previous page: the author is concluding the survey of various mystical groups' views on the divine essence in man.</meta>

### XII.

It is therefore clear that the fanatic opinions of the <term>Paracelsians</term>, <term>Weigelians</term>, <term>Mystics</term>, <term>Quakers</term>, and the rest—who are commonly called by the name "the Illuminated"—conspire in this: that besides the body and the rational soul, there is in man a certain substantial part granted to him by God, and, as most do not hide, granted from the very essence of God. <term>Felgenhauer</term> explains this same doctrine of the three parts of man quite at length in *The Forecourt, the Holy, and the Most Holy Place of the Temple of God*. The individual readings of this fanatic pamphlet sufficiently declare the nature of each part and the dreams of the Fanatics concerning them. It is also worth comparing the *Decent Universal Doctrine of God* by <term>Bartholomaeus Sclei</term>, as well as the *Book of the Witness of the Hidden Treasure in the Field*, whose author calls himself <term>HIEL</term> <gloss>The Uniform Life of God</gloss>. Also, the *Thorough Instruction* of the "highly enlightened by God" <term>Matthes Weyer</term>, and similar monstrous books written by those furies—truly unworthy of anyone wasting good and irrevocable hours in reading them.

### XIII.

Furthermore, this doctrine of the threefold part of man holds the chief place in their <term>Mataeology</term> <gloss>vain or useless discourse</gloss>. For the author of *The Forecourt* foolishly boasts in chapter 12 that this contains the foundation not only of all Christianity, but of all wisdom in general that exists in heaven and on earth. But truly, if someone were perhaps unaware that they have five senses, or what the nature of sight or hearing or the rest might be, should it therefore be concluded that those senses cannot perform their function? I certainly do not think so. Meanwhile, <term>Andreas Christophorus Rafelius</term> extols this dogma with such praises that he does not fear to speak of it in this way in *The New Year's Trumpet*: <note>original: "Das ist eigentlich der rechte Grund-Fels/ und das gewisse Fundament/ darauff das Hauß unsers Christenthums soll gesetzet/ geleget und fundiret werden/ soll es bestehen: und daraus alles predigen/ lesen/ schreiben/ GOttes Wort hören/ singen/ beten/ gute Wercke / sollen und müssen herfliessen."</note> "This is actually the right bedrock and the certain foundation upon which the house of our Christianity shall be set, laid, and founded, if it is to stand: and from it all preaching, reading, writing, hearing God's Word, singing, praying, and good works shall and must flow."

<summary>Wiedeburg dismisses the "threefold man" doctrine as "vain discourse" (Mataeology), despite its proponents—like Felgenhauer and Rafelius—claiming it is the bedrock of all Christian wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Felgenhauer, Bartholomaeus Sclei, Matthes Weyer, Mataeology, bedrock of Christianity, the Illuminated, Hiel</keywords>

# To the Dukes of Saxony, Jülich, Cleves, and
# Berg; to the Landgraves of Thuringia; to the
# Margraves of Meissen and of both Lusatias;
# to the Counts of Princely Rank in Henne-
# berg; to the Counts of Mark, Ravensberg,
# and Barby; to the Lords of Ravenstein, etc.,
# etc.; the most merciful Lords and Patrons 
# of this Academy:

Since the Professorship of Eloquence was entrusted to me not long ago by "letters of vocation" (as they are called), soon followed by the confirmation of the Most Serene and Powerful Elector of Saxony,

## JOHN GEORGE III,
## my most indulgent Lord,

I judged that I would be doing nothing foreign to the duty most mercifully enjoined upon me if, under his auspices and according to the custom received in this Academy, I should deliver a discourse concerning **THE MOST FRIENDLY COMPANIONSHIP WHICH EXISTS BETWEEN ELOQUENCE AND PHILOSOPHY**, this coming Friday, after the morning religious services, in the Lecture Hall <note>original: *Acroaterio*, a Greek-derived term for a place of listening or a lecture hall.</note> of the Philosophers. I ask and entreat, with all due respect, reverence, and kindness, that the Magnificent **RECTOR** of the Academy, the most distinguished leaders of both Republics <note>This likely refers to the "two-fold commonwealth" of Church and State, or perhaps the University and the State.</note>, the Doctors, Licentiates, and Masters of all Faculties, as well as the generous and most noble students, deign to make this event more illustrious by their splendid and benevolent presence. I solemnly promise that I shall compensate this notable token of favor by promptly offering my services and studies at any time. Publicly posted on the second Sunday after Epiphany, in the Year of our Redeemed World 1685.

---

most certain, that the Eugubine city, where it finally began to raise its head and flourish again, had to labor greatly to assemble the torn limbs of its territory and recover what was lost. This was the first concern of the Eugubini, after the form of the republic was introduced in the city, in the eleventh century, I believe. From that time, the country counts and other noble men, who had built camps, fortresses, towers, and fortifications on their lands and estates, or had occupied those built in ancient times, began to migrate into the city and be held in the number of citizens, with the surrender of the camps and fortresses having been made under fair conditions. If any resisted more stubbornly, they were subdued by arms: the castles and rights of many were also bought up by the commune at a just price. This was also done with the bishop and the abbots, for whom, after grave dissensions, it was necessary to abdicate the lordship of the castles they possessed in the Eugubine territory and grant them to the Eugubine commune, concerning which matter some things will be said in their proper place in the chronicle of the bishops, and even more in the second book of the Avellanensian antiquities.

II. In this way, following the example of other cities <margin>(a)</margin>, the Eugubine state was gradually restored, the number of citizens increased, the resources of the treasury grew, and the city seemed to flourish to the greatest degree. Under the Emperor Frederick I, the Eugubini held a not insignificant part of their territory by the best right, in which these places and camps were contained, some of which, however, still seem to have pertained to the bishopric and the monasteries of S. Peter and S. Donatus, namely: Mons Episcopi, otherwise the castle of Montis Episcopalis, Agnanum, Mons Ranaldi, Mons Lulianus, Monticellius, Sanvictorinum, otherwise Mons S. Mariae, Clefium, Petrorium, Sclizza (or Schiggia), and Collis Casalis, all of which are listed in Frederick's diploma indicated in the previous chapter. Frederick's diploma, as I said, was given in the year 1163. On Natural Questions.

I heard them narrating that they had performed a long journey when, provided with assistance from the King of Ethiopia and armed with letters of recommendation for the kings further on, they had reached the distant parts. "We arrived," they said, "at immense marshes, the exit of which neither the inhabitants knew, nor could anyone hope to find. For it was so entangled by waters and grasses that the waters were not navigable to ships—which the marsh, muddy and covered in vegetation, would not bear unless it were small and capable of carrying only one person." There, he said, we saw two rocks from which a huge force of the river fell. Whether that is the head of the Nile or an addition, or whether it is born there or returns into the earth after having been received from a previous course, do you not believe that whatever it is, it rises from a great lake of the earth? For it must have moisture scattered in many places and collected at the bottom so that it can erupt with such great force. Some judge that earthquakes are caused by fire, while others do not attribute it to the same cause. Primarily <term>Anaxagoras</term> <gloss>a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</gloss>, who believes that the earth is shaken by a cause almost similar to how the air is shaken, when, in the lower part, a spirit forces dense air and clouds together in the same way that clouds are accustomed to break among us. Fire flashes from this collision of clouds as the air is forced out. It rushes to meet this as it seeks an exit, tearing apart what opposes it until it finds a path to the sky through narrow spaces, or makes one through force or damage. Others do not judge that fire is the cause, but rather that it burns in many places it encounters and consumes everything nearest to it. If these places fall down because they have been eaten away, then a movement of those parts follows, which, deprived of the supports beneath them, slip until they collapse, with nothing occurring to intercept the weight. Then, calm is restored, and vast chasms open.

...therefore, for this requirement, the magnitude of Europe is... the length is 87,014,000. The length of Africa—if one takes a median computation from the whole variety of reporters—is 37,098,000; the breadth, where it is cultivated, nowhere exceeds 250,000. But since Agrippa made it 810,000 in its Cyrenaican part, encompassing its deserts as far as the Garamantes, where they were known, the entire measurement that will come into comparison makes 46,008,000. The length of Asia is, by general admission, 50,137,750; the breadth should certainly be computed from the Ethiopian Sea to Alexandria, situated near the Nile, so that the measurement runs through Meroe and Syene: 18,075,000. It appears, therefore, that Europe is a little less than half of Asia; that Asia is larger than Africa by another such amount and a sixth part of Africa. But if all the sums are mixed, it will be clearly evident that Europe is the third part of the whole earth and a little more than an eighth; Asia is the fourth and a fourteenth; and Africa is the fifth and sixty-first in addition.

(39) To these we will add one more bit of knowledge from Greek discovery...

<sig>NN iij</sig>

WITHOUT DOUBT: Do not doubt, for the truth of these things offends me. 180:

ABOUT THESE LETTERS: Which were delivered to me by Caesar; you wish me to write, so that he, when he hears that Caesar is not angry with me, might take joy from this comfort of mine. But, he says, I am not doing this: first, because those letters do not delight me, since they are both written meagerly and have suspicions of not being from Caesar; then, because I understand from a friend’s letter that Quintus himself is not well-disposed toward me. THAT HE IS WRITING TO YOU: Quintus. 180:

IF YOU THINK IT IS RIGHT, AND THAT IT CAN BE UNDERTAKEN BY YOU: A double consideration; whether it is right that Terentia be advised about the will at all; and whether she ought to be advised by Atticus. For that, "If you think it can be undertaken by you," as I believe, this is what it means: if you seem to be so intimate with Terentia that you can deal with her about the will. CAMILLUS: For he, no less than Pomponius, was taking care of Cicero’s affairs and business, as the fourteenth book of the letters which are called "Familiares" shows on pages 236 and 238; and of these, which are written to Atticus, book V, page 72, and book VI, page 88. ABOUT THE WILL: Cicero desired that a will be made by Terentia, so that she, when she settled her own affairs, might satisfy those to whom she owed money. For it seemed less honorable to Cicero that Terentia, his wife, should be in debt.

<header>PRINCIPIORUM PHILOSOPHIÆ</header>
<meta>in</meta>

tem. Visque illa debet æstimari tum à magnitudine corporis in quo est, & superficiei, secundùm quam istud corpus ab alio disjungitur; tum à celeritate motus, ac naturâ, & contrarietate modi, quo diversa corpora sibi mutuò occurrunt.

<margin>XLIV. Motum non esse contrarium, sed quieti & determinationem in unam partem determinationi in partem oppositam.</margin>
Atque notandum est, unum motum alteri motui æquè veloci nullo modo esse contrarium: sed propriè tantùm duplicem hîc inveniri contrarietatem. Unam inter motum & quietem, vel etiam inter motus celeritatem & tarditatem, quatenus scilicet ista tarditas de quietis natura participat: Alteram inter determinationem motus versus aliquam partem, & occurfum corporis in illa parte quiescentis, vel aliter moti, atque pro ratione partis, in quam corpus alteri occurrens movetur, hæc contrarietas est major vel minor.

<margin>XLV. Quomodo possit determinari, quantum cujusque corporis motus mutetur propter aliorum corporum occursum; idque per regulas sequentes.</margin>
Ex quibus ut possimus determinare, quo pacto singula corpora motus suos augeant vel minuant, vel in alias partes convertant, ob aliorum corporum occursus, oportet tantùm calculo subducere, quantum in unoquoque fit virium, sive ad movendum, sive ad motui resistendum, ac pro certo statuere, illud semper, quod valentius est, fortiri suum effectum. Hocque facilè calculo subduci posset, si duo tantùm corpora sibi mutuò occurrerent, eaque essent perfectè dura, & à reliquis omnibus fic divisa, ut eorum motus à nullis aliis circumjacentibus impedirentur, nec juvarentur; ea enim regulas sequentes observarent.

<margin>XLVI. Prima.</margin>
Primò, si duo illa corpora, putà B & C, essent planè æqualia, & æquè velociter moverentur, B quidem à dextra versus sinistram, & C illi in directum à sinistra versus dextram, cùm sibi mutuò occurrerent reflecterentur, & postea pergerent moveri, B versus dextram, & C versus sinistram, nullâ parte suæ celeritatis amissâ.

<image-desc size="small" type="diagram" significance="high">A diagram showing two rectangular blocks labeled B and C facing each other.</image-desc>

<margin>XLVII. Secunda.</margin>
Secundò, si B esset tantillò majus quàm C, cæteris positis ut prius, tunc solum C reflecteretur, & utrumque versus sinistram eâdem celeritate moveretur.

<margin>XLVIII. Tertia.</margin>
Tertiò, si mole essent æqualia, sed B tantillò celeriùs moveretur quàm C, non tantùm ambo pergerent moveri versus sinistram, sed etiam transferretur ex B in C, media pars celeritatis qua hoc ab illo excederetur: hoc est, si fuissent priùs sex gradus celeritatis

And that force must be estimated both from the magnitude of the body in which it resides, and from the surface area along which that body is separated from another; as well as from the speed of the motion, and the nature and contrariety of the mode by which diverse bodies mutually encounter one another.

<margin>XLIV. Motion is not contrary to motion, but to rest; and determination toward one part is contrary to determination toward the opposite part.</margin>
And it must be noted that one motion is in no way contrary to another motion of equal speed; but properly speaking, only two types of contrariety are found here. One is between motion and rest, or even between the speed and slowness of motion, insofar as this slowness participates in the nature of rest. The other is between the determination of motion toward a certain part and the encounter of a body resting in that part, or one otherwise moved; and according to the proportion of the part toward which the body encountering another is moved, this contrariety is greater or lesser.

<margin>XLV. How it may be determined, how much the motion of each body is changed due to the encounter of other bodies; and this by the following rules.</margin>
From these, so that we may determine how individual bodies increase or decrease their motions, or convert them into other parts due to the encounters of other bodies, it is necessary only to calculate how much force exists in each, either for moving or for resisting motion, and to establish for certain that the one which is more powerful always obtains its effect. And this could be easily calculated if only two bodies were to encounter one another, and they were perfectly hard, and so divided from all others that their motions were neither impeded nor aided by any other surrounding bodies; for they would observe the following rules.

<margin>XLVI. First.</margin>
First, if those two bodies, namely B and C, were perfectly equal, and were moved with equal speed, B indeed from right to left, and C directly from left to right, when they mutually encountered one another, they would be reflected, and afterward would proceed to move, B toward the right, and C toward the left, with no part of their speed lost.

<header>FESTUS AVIENUS</header>

Long-lived: among the glowing stars, only six
Lift themselves up. Ancient fable carries the names
Of seven sisters, yet six reveal themselves under a faint light:
Electra, Alcyone, Celaeno, and Taygete,
And Sterope, and Merope at once, and the famous Maia.
<margin>5</margin> Mynthis asserts in verse that only six are to be discerned
By the offspring of the god: he records that Electra departed from the deep sky
On account of having previously feared Orion.
Some say that, weeping for the fires of Idaean Troy
And lamenting the numerous deaths of her own race,
<margin>10</margin> Electra sadly hides her orb in gloomy clouds,
So that her head is more often encircled by dark shadows:
Sometimes, however, she rises from the waves of Ocean
Into the convexities of the pole, but lacks the seat of her sisters:
And she presents a face separated far off, abandoned,
<margin>15</margin> And torn by the ruins of her kin’s offspring in the chorus of sisters,
And she is seen with hair scattered, and the image of a loose tress
Is displayed: rumor commemorates these as dread comets
Rising from afar in a sorrowful form.
Her face burns for a long time, she drenches the ether with her hair,
<margin>20</margin> Reddening with thick, glowing gore.
Furthermore, they believe that after Merope accepted the chains of Sisyphus
And obtained the marriage-bed by the cruel omen of the gods,
She was thought less worthy of the aerial seat.
Thus the story of their number becomes uncertain, and custom maintains
<margin>25</margin> That six Vergiliae are seen through the ether, but at once they all
Tighten the globe: the angle exits three times into the breezes
Flaming, and the Atlantides burn with mingled fires,
Yet the vigor is not similar to the fame; a grand story
Ennobles the sisters: their manner is sparing, and their fire
<margin>30</margin> Is scarcely visible from afar with a thin torch
When twin twilights return to the world in turn.

Sed iccirco locis ipsis numerus datus est quia melius & tenentur sæpe præcepta nul lamque recipiunt confusionem fi ad memoria numeris col locentur quanquam indigna tionis primum locum recte su pserit quæ rebus omnibus a nu minibus traxit exordium: Sed ut diximus in hoc locorum nu mero rerum ordinem nullo q ramus fed ex more manifesto ris præcepti factum esse memi nerimus iam ipsi loci diligenter inspicientibus manifesti sunt: idest res quæ præcipiuntur faci le perspici possunt. Illud tame præceptum tenere debemus si ue in indignatione: siue in con questione nos locis omnibus uti non oportere: sed his quos causa suggerat: neque his om nibus sed quo ad iudicantium animi moueantur quod si etia uno aliquo loco factum uide rimus orationem continuo fi nire debemus. <header>BOOK</header>

the sixteen questions, and let not the order of the places themselves move us because they are arranged in certain numbers; for there is no step toward greater or lesser, nor any sequence. But a number has been given to the places themselves because precepts are held better and receive no confusion if they are arranged for memory by numbers, although it has rightly taken the first place of indignation, which drew its beginning from all things from the divine powers. But as we have said, in this number of places, let us not seek the order of things, but let us remember that it has been done according to the custom of the manifestation of the precept; the places themselves are now manifest to those who inspect them diligently, that is, the things which are prescribed can be easily seen. However, we must hold this precept: whether in indignation or in questioning, we ought not to use all the places, but those which the case suggests, and not even all of these, but only insofar as the minds of the judges are moved; for if we see that the oration has been achieved by even one place, we must finish it immediately. For in this way, even tears, while they begin and are fresh, have the most power. Questioning is an oration capturing the pity of the auditors. We have said that the work of questioning is this: to move the minds of the judges to pity. But for this, sixteen places of our own are to be sought in the order of things

<column-break/>

saying that it is foul, cruel, nefarious, and tyrannical, having been done by a rich hand and by force, a matter which is most remote from the laws and from equal right. The eighth place is that through which we demonstrate that it is not common, nor practiced, nor is that bad thing about which we argue done by the most audacious of men, and that it is remote from savage men, from barbarian nations, and from monstrous beasts. These will be the things said to have been done cruelly against parents, children, spouses, blood relatives, and suppliants, and subsequently, if anything is brought forward concerning those older in age, hosts, neighbors, friends, those with whom you have spent your life, those among whom you were educated, those by whom you were instructed, the miserable dead, those worthy of pity, famous and noble men who have used honor, those who were able neither to harm another nor to defend themselves, the young, the old, the women; from all of these it is compared, and thus through contention it is shown how atrocious and unworthy that is about which one argues. The tenth place is that through which we collect all things that were done in the execution of the business and what was done after the business, with the indignation and crimination of each, and we place the matter in words as much as possible before the eyes of the one before whom it is said, so that that which is unworthy may seem to him as if he himself had been present and had seen it. The eleventh place is that through which we show it was done by him by whom it was least fitting, and by whom another would be forbidden to do it. The twelfth place is that through which we are indignant that this has happened to us first, nor has it happened to anyone by use. The thirteenth place is if, when joined with injury and insult, it is demonstrated, through which place hatred is incited against pride and arrogance. The fourteenth place is that through which we ask from those who are listening that they refer our injury to their own affairs, if to the young, if to the old, concerning parents or fathers. The fifteenth is the place through which we say that even to enemies and foes, those things which have happened to us are accustomed to seem unworthy, and indignation will be taken most gravely from these places. It will be necessary to seek parts of such questioning from the things of this kind. Questioning is an oration capturing the pity of the auditors. In this, first it is necessary to make the mind of the auditor mild and merciful concerning the confirmation.

Corpus itaq[ue] humanum constitutum formatumq[ue] rebus naturalibus, non solùm per excrementorum expulsionem, quæ per concoctione[m] collecta sunt, uerùm etiam (quia corpus in continuo fluore est) per restitutionem illius quod effluxit, conseruatur.

causes, which we have said are necessarily efficient, altering, and changing our body.

IIX.

The human body is thus established and formed by natural things, and it is conserved not only through the expulsion of excrements, which have been collected through digestion, but also (because the body is in a continuous state of flow) through the restoration of that which has flowed away.

IX.

Who doubts that something is always flowing out from the human body? For if nothing flowed out from our bodies, but an equal mass of substance were always preserved, there would be no need for nourishment.

X.

Since it is true, therefore, that the entire mass of living creatures is in a perpetual state of flow, if a similar substance is not restored for that which has flowed away, it will certainly evaporate, and the whole will be dissipated.

XI.

Lest this happen prematurely, it is necessary for us to eat and drink.

XII.

This non-natural thing (of which we speak here) is so constituted that it always alters, changes, and moves the human body.

XIII.

It alters and moves in two ways: sometimes according to nature, sometimes contrary to nature.

translation:
<meta>This page continues the medical instructions for treating internal and external inflammations. It transitions from the pharmaceutical applications mentioned on the previous page to the theoretical and practical application of bloodletting (phlebotomy) and "humoral diversion," explaining how to draw diseased fluids away from afflicted organs like the liver, spleen, and womb.</meta>

...steep and infuse these things. Just as those suffering from <term>quinsy</term> <note>original: "sinancici"; a severe sore throat or peritonsillar abscess that obstructs breathing.</note> are accustomed to gargling usefully, that is, with the juice alone. Take dates and dried figs, boiled in bran with sweetness mixed in, so that you may drink it, or other such things which are gathered together in a singular pharmaceutical cause and described properly; let these be administered in their own time according to what you follow, so that they are applied to the places that suffer. 

Thus one may know when and why you ought to perform <term>antispasis</term> <note>original: "antispasis"; from Greek, meaning "revulsion" or "counter-traction." A medical technique of drawing blood or humors from a part of the body distant from the site of the disease to redirect the flow.</note> and <term>metocheuresis</term> <note>original: "metocheuresis"; from Greek, meaning "derivation" or "shifting." Drawing fluids from a site near the afflicted area to relieve pressure.</note>. For "antispasis" is a counter-diversion; for example, if <term>humors</term> <note>The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health.</note> flow into the thigh from some other part of the body, I should immediately open a vein in the arm to release them, and by directing the heat of the humors elsewhere, I may interrupt the rising cause [of disease]. Or, I might place <term>cupping glasses</term> <note>original: "cuebras"; medical vessels used to create a vacuum on the skin to draw out blood or humors.</note> upon the breast to provide warmth, have the hands rubbed, or bind the joints of the hands with bandages. 

"Metocheuresis" is the shifting of humors, as when I remove the cause by opening a vein in the calf or the sole of the foot or the ankle, and by leading it to a nearby part, I derive and purge the place and the matter, so that I may apply cupping glasses to that part and both warm and rub it, and bind it with bandages. 

Therefore, if the right side of the <term>womb</term> <note>original: "matrici"; the uterus.</note> or the body suffers, draw blood from the right arm or the right leg, striking the vein that is on the inside, or which is closer to the member that suffers. If, however, the left side suffers, the removal of blood ought to be done from the left arm or leg. Likewise, if the liver is inflamed below, I should take blood from the right arm. If it is the spleen, from the left, striking the inner vein. If any upper part of the body is afflicted by an attack from below, such as the throat in quinsy, or the heat and onset of eye pain, or any sudden pain, I draw blood from those same high parts, whether by "antispasis" or by "metocheuresis," and through a purging <term>clyster</term> <note>original: "elistere"; an enema used to clear the bowels and balance humors.</note>, diligently administering these by reason of their utility, just as the reason for the diet may require. 

If these beneficial things are applied immediately at the beginning [of the illness], they are useful. If, however, the cause has become <term>chronic</term> <note>original: "chronia"; a long-standing or deep-seated illness.</note>, that is, already long-established, then it is more effective to remove blood from the suffering place or member itself. Thus, for those with quinsy, we also cut the veins under the tongue, since at that time—as they say—the evacuation has been proven to help. Nevertheless, for the sake of the treatment, the diet should be maintained for a long time; we also place cupping glasses over the spleen and the liver themselves, and with a <term>scalpel</term> <note>original: "scalpello"; a small surgical knife.</note>, we purge any other place by <term>scarification</term> <note>original: "scarfando"; the practice of making small incisions in the skin to draw out fluids.</note>. This is done when the cause is already chronic and no humor is still flowing into it. Otherwise, if it is done differently, it will not be said to benefit the results, but rather to cause much harm. 

Above all, it must be considered that we should know the quality or the power of the medicines and the nature of the places or members themselves which suffer. For some of them are slow to feel [the medicine] and can endure the power of the medicines for a long time. Others feel it immediately and cannot endure it long. Those members that feel it quickly are harmed rather than healed by the application of forceful and sharp remedies, if they are applied harshly or beyond measure.

It emphasizes the importance of timing (acute vs. chronic) and the sensitivity of different body parts to various medicines.</summary>

Lactuca vt dicit Isidorus ex lactei humoris exuberantia est vocata. vel quia nutricientes mulieres lacte implet. hec in viris veneris motum arcet cuius duplex est species. scilicet domestica et agrestis qua feralia vocamus. quod dorsum eius aculeos habet duros ad modum ferre. vt dicit Isidorus libro. xvii. capitulo ultimo. de qua dicit Plinius in dietis. lactuca agrestis domestice in forma est similis. sed longiores habet frondes. subtiliores. asperiores. et minus virides. propter sue humiditatis paruitatem. et ideo multum est amaritudinis et ponticitatis respectu illius que domestica est. quia maioris est caloris et siccitatis. et ideo multi dicunt quod menstrua puocat et humores crudos expellit. vt dicit Dyascorides. lactuca pro domestica frigida est et humida secundum gradum et in neutra qualitate excedit modum. et ideo eius usus grauisui medicine. subtilibus subam et marie qui erit recens. et ideo cito digeritur et stomachi arsuram et morsuram et colera rubea sedat. sanguinis ebullitionem refrigerat. infomnietate placat. capitis dolorem et fumo colerico sanat. lac in mulieribus multiplicat et semen in viris generat augumentar. et accidit propter bonitatem sanguinis que gignit in pfecta quantitate. et in pfecta etate sed quando antiquatur et indurat minuitur eius humiditas et amaricat. et vsu eius sanguis pessimus generatur. virtus visina inde deficit et debilitatur. cuius causa est sensus animalis mortificatio. quod cum sua ponticitate ipsum suffocat naturale. et ideo talis lactuca generare voletib. maxime est nociua. nam materia gelat. coagulat seminale. et precipue semen eius si in cibo aut in potu sepe assumatur.
