translation:
### On Lettuce, Ch. XXII
Lettuce, as Isidore says, is so named from the exuberance of its milky humor, or because it fills nursing women with milk. This herb restrains the motion of lust in men. Its species is twofold: domestic and wild, which we call <term>feralia</term> <gloss>wild/brutish</gloss>, because its back has hard prickles in the manner of a wild beast, as Isidore says in Book XVII, in the last chapter. Regarding it, Pliny says in his *Diets*: "Wild lettuce is similar in form to domestic, but it has longer leaves, thinner, rougher, and less green because of the paucity of its humidity, and therefore there is much bitterness and astringency compared to that which is domestic, because it is of greater heat and dryness." And therefore many say that it provokes menses and expels raw humors, as Dioscorides says. Lettuce, as the domestic, is cold and moist according to the degree and in neither quality exceeds the mean. And therefore its use is of great medicine for subtle stomachs, and especially when it is fresh, and therefore it is quickly digested and calms the burning and biting of the stomach and red bile. It cools the boiling of the blood. It calms sleeplessness. It heals headache and choleric smoke. It multiplies milk in women and generates and increases seed in men, and this happens because of the goodness of the blood which it generates in perfect quantity and in perfect age. But when it becomes old and hard, its humidity is diminished and it becomes bitter, and by its use the worst blood is generated. The visine <note>likely visional</note> power fails and is weakened, the cause of which is the mortification of the animal sense, because with its astringency it suffocates the natural [spirit]. And therefore such lettuce is most harmful to those wishing to generate, for it gels and coagulates the seminal matter, and especially its seed if it is often assumed in food or drink. <note>Thus</note> Isaac in his *Diets*. Pliny, however, in Book XX, Ch. VIII, says about lettuce: "There is a species of lettuce born spontaneously which they call 'caprina' <note>goat-lettuce</note>, which, when protected in the sea, kills fish, and they are in the vicinity. Its stalk and leaves, crushed with salt, heal incised nerves. Another species of lettuce is that which is born in fields, whose leaves crushed with polenta heal ulcers, and this the Greeks call 'isopon' <note>good-hyssop</note>. The third species is that which grows in woods, which they call 'steraton,' whose leaves crushed with pus heal wounds. With the root and leaves, they mitigate the sacred fire <note>St. Anthony's fire/erysipelas</note>. There is also another species of this lettuce, round and short, which many call 'beratia,' whose juice hawks take by scratching the herb...

<column-break/>
...and there, dyeing their eyes, they dispel obscurity and dimness when they grow old. The juice of this herb heals the eyes and especially when mother's milk is mixed with it. It treats the bites of serpents and the stings of scorpions if its juice is drunk with wine and the crushed leaves are applied to the wound as a plaster. It also dispels and calms every inflation. The seed of lettuce, as much wild as domestic, calms the imaginations of lust in dreams and does not allow the body to be polluted if it is frequently assumed in food. However, its frequent and excessive use causes obscurity of the eyes." Pliny attributes many other praises to it in the same chapter, but let these suffice.

### On Burdock, Ch. XXIII
Burdock <note>or Lappa</note> is a herb having broad and thick leaves around the ground, having on the tips of the stalks certain thorny and prickly little heads, but recurved, which are accustomed to adhere to the clothes of passersby. Whence Isidore says in Book XVII: "Burdock is so called because it has a stalk disposed toward the earth, and it is called 'philanthropos' <note>lover of man</note> by the Greeks, because it adheres to the clothes of men on account of its roughness." And it is born near walls, and because of "philanthropos," i.e., "loving man," because it seems with a certain affection to adhere to the clothes of men. The species of burdock is twofold: sharp and round, disposed in the likeness of a horse's foot, wherefore it is called by many 'horse hoof.' The leaves of both are of horrible odor and taste alike, as Dioscorides says. But Pliny in Book XXVI says: "There are many species of burdock, and all are medicinal. For they treat the stings of scorpions, and they do not strike a man if he has been anointed with its juice. The decoction of its root aids the teeth and also firms them if held warm in the mouth. Its seed taken inside cures stomach ailments. To those vomiting blood, it assists in dysenteries. For its root with wine stops the flux of the belly, but given alone, it aids those with stones. The whole herb crushed with lard avails against scrofula." <note>Thus</note> Pliny. According to Platearius: Burdock or <term>lappacium</term> <gloss>dock/burdock</gloss> is a herb hot and dry, having the power of dissolving, relaxing, opening, and attenuating. And therefore it avails against scabies, itching, herpes, and impetigo, and it takes humors from under the skin. It dissolves the hardness and tumor of abscesses. It avails against cold dropsy and obstruction of the spleen. Its juice mixed with rue cleanses the brain and rheumatic superfluity if in a small quantity...

<summary>This page explores the medicinal uses and classical classifications of lettuce and burdock, detailing their efficacy in treating various bodily ailments including ulcers, eye afflictions, and digestive issues.</summary>

<header>IVN. LVD. PARISETI</header>

You will perform nothing worthy of the office of the supreme Pontiff unless you take care to have God stored and fixed in your mind, by whose imitation and example it is necessary that you moderate all acts. No one will rightly perform the divine office unless he uses divine counsels in acting, and associates God as the author in all matters being performed. After you have obtained divine rights on earth and have attained the office of God among mortals, it seems to be worth the effort that, as much as possible, you take care to compose yourself to God in your morals and in your manner of living. Whatever belonged to the affected man of the old self, it is fitting to banish and completely cast out, so that in you only religion and the care of virtue may remain. Much duty and much piety must be performed, and the reason for being innocent must be entered. Since the censure of all men pertains to you, and you stand over all as judge and censor, it is necessary that you conduct yourself in living such that nothing may be done by you that you could condemn if done by anyone else. You ought to protect divine matters with such a tenacious purpose and ardent mind that no loss should ever be avoided, and no danger should be shunned. You ought to pour out your soul and lose your life for Christ, for religion, and for the salvation of the human flock if there is need. Nothing should be so dear to you that you refrain from spending it for the reason of your office and for the sake of protecting the worship of God and piety. As I wish you, divine father, the greatest honor possible,

...but they can also assist in the great matters of national governance. Their benefits are infinite; students should recognize this for themselves.

Universal use is shared by all nations.

In a civilized nation, there is no place where tools are not used, and this is firmly established. Yet, in remote and desolate regions, such as the people of the Green-Headed Country located seventy degrees north of the equator—which can be called the most remote and wild of countries—they still know how to use leather boats to gather fish and bows and arrows to hunt birds and beasts. Thus, the public utility of tools is the same throughout the great earth. How vast it is!

Creation and transmission remain the same through the ages.

# Aristotelis

Here he says that Porphyry handed down the knowledge of the five universals, which are genus, species, difference, property, and accident, the knowledge of which is useful for having knowledge of the categories, as is evident at the beginning of his book. Without the knowledge of these universals, nothing can be known in logic. However, these universals according to the doctrine of Plato are monsters, because they fall short of their perfections, since according to him they are subsistent in themselves, and thus they cannot give essence, name, and definition to singulars, which nevertheless according to the truth belongs to them in many things—namely, to singulars or inferiors.

Prologus libri primi, & multa alia arguunt, non paucis scripsisse has fabulas Phaedrum, sed omnibus, neque tantum ad privatum dolorem leniendum, sed & ad famam publice aucupandam. Quorsum enim sollicitae illae <margin>aures</margin> ad lectorem, non in initio solum & fine, sed & in mediis libris, quibus nihil opus ad amicos? Quid? cum in Prologo libri III. fastidiose se in coetum recipi queritur, & in prologo libri V. desiderium suum declaret in litterarum plausum eundi, & Particulonem dicat
> *nomen chartis victurum suis,*
> *Latinis dum manebit pretium litteris.*

ex tacitis amicorum laudibus hanc gloriae immortalitatem eum sperasse putamus, an publicis virorum eruditissimorum suffragiis? Et fane cum coetum nominat, utique eum definit, quem Romae fuisse accepimus eorum virorum, quorum scripta Criticorum calculis probata erant. Porro qui illa conveniunt, nisi omnium manibus versatos hos Phaedri libellos existimamus, ex Prologo libri III.
> *Suspicione siquis errabit sua*
> *Et rapiet ad se, quod erit commune omnium,*
> *Stulte nudabit animi conscientiam.*
> *Huic excusatum me velim nihilo minus.*
> *Neque enim notare singulos mens est mihi,*
> *Verum ipsam vitam & mores hominum ostendere.*

Piget plura proferre, nullus enim Prologus est, epilogus nullus in fine librorum, quin editas publice a se fabellas doceat. Miror autem qui diverse a nobis sentiunt, in eam opinionem esse adductos, quod Sejani metum ostendit Phaedrus in prologo libri III. quasi ipse Aelius Sejanus hoc nomine, ac non potius homo, moribus ejus non dissimilis intelligatur. Nam si ipsum Sejanum intelligas, qui, quaeso, ausus est homo libertinus eum, sub saevissimo Principe crudeliter dominantem, tam acerbe perstringere in carmine publico? publicum enim fuisse ex iis perspicimus, quae modo ex hoc Prologo delibavimus. Aut si ausus est hoc est Phaedrus vitae suae prodigus, qui, quaeso, factum, ut tantam linguae licentiam impunitam tulerit? tulisse autem videtur, quod interposito tempore reliqui fabularum libri prodierunt. Nam non omnes simul esse editos facile largior Eruditissimo Auctori Epistolae Criticae, in qua Clarissimi Bentelii notae atque emendationes expenduntur; at vero nequaquam in eo adfentior, quod eodem in loco ad prologum libri III. monet, Sejano jam damnato eum librum esse scriptum. logue of the first book and many other things argue that Phaedrus did not write these fables for a few, but for everyone, and not only to soothe private grief, but also to hunt for fame publicly. For what purpose are those anxious <margin>ears</margin> directed to the reader, not only at the beginning and end, but also in the middle of the books, where there is no need to address friends? What of the fact that in the prologue of the third book he complains that he is received into the assembly <note>original: "coetum"</note> with disdain, and in the prologue of the fifth book he declares his desire to enter into the applause of literature, and says of Particulone:
> *A name that will live for his papers,*
> *As long as there will be value for Latin letters.*

Do we think he hoped for this immortality of glory from the silent praises of friends, or from the public votes of the most learned men? And indeed, when he names the "assembly," he certainly defines that which we have learned existed in Rome, consisting of those men whose writings had been approved by the calculations of critics. Furthermore, how do those things fit, unless we believe these little books of Phaedrus were in everyone's hands, from the prologue of the third book:
> *If anyone errs through his own suspicion*
> *And snatches to himself what is common to all,*
> *He will foolishly lay bare the conscience of his own mind.*
> *I would wish to be excused by him nonetheless.*
> *For it is not my intention to mark individuals,*
> *But to show the very life and morals of men.*

It is tiresome to bring forward more, for there is no prologue, no epilogue at the end of the books, without him teaching that his fables were published by him publicly. However, I wonder how those who feel differently from us were led to the opinion that Phaedrus shows fear of Sejanus in the prologue of the third book, as if Aelius Sejanus himself is understood by this name, rather than a man not unlike his morals. For if you understand Sejanus himself, who, I ask, being a freedman, dared to lash out so bitterly against him, who was cruelly dominating under a most savage Prince, in a public poem? For we perceive that it was public from those things which we have just sampled from this prologue. Or if he dared—that is, if Phaedrus was prodigal of his own life—how, I ask, did it happen that he bore such license of tongue with impunity? Yet it seems he bore it because the remaining books of fables were produced after an interval of time. For I readily grant the most learned author of the *Critical Epistle*—in which the notes and emendations of the most famous Bentley are weighed—that they were not all published at the same time; but I am by no means in agreement with him in that same place where he warns, regarding the prologue of the third book, that that book was written after Sejanus was already condemned. For if it was written after the condemnation, it was written after his death; for on the same day Sejanus was condemned in the Senate and dragged to his punishment; read Dio, book LVIII, page 628. But he had lived...

...with the rest of the living beings, since they <note>Beauty and Goodness</note> cannot be separated from God, they are never shared. If you seek God, you seek beauty itself. The only way that leads to this is piety <term>pietas</term> joined with knowledge <term>cognitio</term> <note>In Hermetic philosophy, "cognitio" refers to "Gnosis"—a direct, experiential knowledge of the divine rather than simple book-learning.</note>: for this reason, ignorant mortals, straying from the path of piety, do not fear to call a man "good" as well, although he can have no true knowledge of the good, but is instead entangled and ensnared in evils. He judges evil to be good and uses evils incurably; he even fears the loss and deprivation of these evils. Finally, he strives with all schemes and forces, not so much that he might be weighed down by a single evil, but so that these evils might increase in number and magnitude. Such are the "beauties" and "goods" of men, O Aesculapius, which we are neither able to flee nor to hate; for that is the most difficult thing of all, primarily for this reason: because we must use them and feed upon them, and deprived of them, we can in no way lead our lives.

---

->THE SUMMARY OF THE SEVENTH CHAPTER<-

*The seventh chapter laments the plague of ignorance <term>ignorantia</term>, which overturns all the earth and corrupts the soul that is enclosed in the bonds of the body. It exhorts the ignorant to come to their senses, and commands us to cast off the mortal body <term>corpus mortale</term> <note>The "mortal body" is often described in these texts as a "garment" or "cloak" that the soul must shed to return to the divine.</note> as if it were a garment, from which...*

<summary>Hermes explains that mortals mistake material evils for "goods" because they lack divine knowledge, and introduces a call to shed the physical body to escape this ignorance.</summary>

Gods, and says that all things can be dissolved by him who bound them. Again, you hear in the books of the Laws that the heaven and the stars are gods, and even the Sun itself, following those things which Hermes said before, is a very great god. You shall therefore interpret these things in the manner that Trismegistus, the prince of all philosophy and especially Platonic philosophy, taught. There is no need for refutations, since they declare themselves. He taught in the noble Platonic way that the Good, the eternal, the founder of all things, is unique, singular, and indivisible, of ineffable Goodness. The rest is fabricated, and either in name only, or a certain simulated and honored Goodness or Divinity. In the same sense, it will be necessary to understand Aristotle. Since all theology in his work flowed from the older Greeks and the Barbarians. Thus, he necessarily holds the divinity of the heaven in that place where those from whom he learned held it, retaining for himself the true piety and the truer Divinity, from which the divinity of the heaven came, in the manner the barbarians taught. It is not eternally hanging and generated, but made by the great Goodness and Divinity, the creator of other things, whose magnitude is so great that it alone could be, and alone deserved to be, everlasting. The other things, since they are at an immense distance from it, were gifted with a new Divinity and Goodness. Aristotle is certainly compelled to this, and indeed he confessed it, whether nature was dragging him here, or his mind was discerning truer things, looking back to those from whom that which he wrote himself was flowing. In another place, Trismegistus also confessed that the majesty is so great and so different from all things, that he says regarding its power: <note>original: "ὅτε τὰ ἀνθρώπινα, ὅτε τὰ θεῖα προβάλλει ἅμ τις μηδέποτε ᾄδῃ κἀντῶ..."</note> Neither human nor divine things are to be compared. Do not think that things below or things above are similar to God. Nothing is like to the unlike, the solo, and the one. From these things they prove what our theology cries out: that he is the one everlasting, truly immortal, unlike all things. But the gods and men were made by him, since he alone must be everlasting. Plato also reported these same things concerning the Goodness of God divinely in the Protagoras. In that book, following the opinion of Simonides, he asserts that a good man is very difficult to find. But it is possible to become so for a time. However, to have been good and to persevere in the habit of goodness, and to be a "virtuous good" as Pittacus said, is impossible and not at all human. But God alone is endowed with this honor; a man cannot be so when he becomes evil.

Plato says God is the creator of all things. Testimonies by which it appears he called him the founder of the universe. To Plato, the divine offspring is the author of the world, to whom he gives a Father in the Epistle.

CHAPTER X.

<note>A decorative initial E begins the chapter.</note> THAT THIS MIND was in Plato—that God, as he had heard from his elders, was the Creator of heaven and earth and of all things celestial and terrestrial which previously did not exist—which he had confessed so clearly in the Timaeus and in the tenth book of the Republic, other testimonies declare, shining like stars throughout his entire philosophy. For he spoke similar things in the book called the Sophist regarding God as creator, as he did in the tenth book of the Republic. There, when he was discussing true things and fictitious or simulated ones, he said this: Regarding all mortal animals, and plants, and whatever is produced in the earth from seeds and roots, and whatever inanimate things are held in the embrace of the earth, liquid and non-liquid bodies—shall we say they existed later, having not existed before, by any other than the creating and crafting God? <note>original: "μὴ ἄλλω τινὸς ᾄθεῦ δημιουργοῦ φύσωμεν ὕστερον γίγνεσθαι, πρότερον οὐκ ὄντα"</note> Or shall we follow the dogma and assertion of the many, that nature produced these very things from some fortuitous cause and without counsel? Or that they existed from God with reason and divine science? Thus spoke Plato. To this very deep question, Theaetetus, because he was a youth, does not respond, but turns his eyes to Zeno, or the guest, waiting for what he might pronounce. Although, he says, I think you will say these things existed from God, I think the same thing myself...

### §. 665.

<margin>
*Quomodo ex facto colligatur dissensus.*
</margin>
*Si quis facit, quod facere non poterat, nisi aliud quid fieri nollet; quoad hoc ipsum dissentit.* Patet non absimili modo, quo ante ostendimus (§. 663.), si quis facit, quod facere non poterat, nisi aliud quid fieri vellet, eum in hoc ipsum consentire.

Veritas propositionis per definitionem dissensus traditam (§. 659.) adeo manifesta est, ut ea jure axiomatum numero adscribatur (§. 273. *Log.*), atque adeo de ea demonstranda parum solliciti esse debemus (§. 267. *Log.*). Exemplo est venditor, qui pretio ab emtore oblato mercem aufert & reponit. Etenim si nollet mercem pro isto pretio tradere, nec eam auferre ac reponere poterat, cum mercem vendere velit. Hoc ipso facto sufficienter indicat, quod nolit pro isto pretio mercem tradere, immo dissensum suum magis declarat, quam si apertis verbis dixisset, sese pro isto pretio eam tradere non posse: etenim haud obscure simul indigitat, quod de justo pretio ab emtore dando desperet, immo quod aegre ferat, non majus pretium ab emtore afferri.

### §. 666.

<margin>
*Quomodo ex non facto colligatur dissensus.*
</margin>
*Si quis non facit, quod facere debebat, nisi aliquid fieri nollet; quoad hoc ipsum dissentit.* Patet hoc non absimili modo, quo paulo ante (§. 664.) ostendimus, si quis non facit, quod facere debebat, nisi aliud quid fieri vellet, eum consentire.

Quae modo de propositione praecedente annotavimus, ea de praesente quoque tenenda sunt. Exemplo veritas propositionis fit manifesta. Si emtor, qui mercem jam ante viderat, redit & pretium paulo majus offert, quam ante obtulerat, venditor vero mercem non depromit, quod hoc non faciat, ex eo abunde intelligitur, quod pro pretio isto mercem tradere nolit, consequenter quod in eodem adhuc dissentiat (§. 659.), etiamfi ne verbulum quidem dicat.

<header>Part I. Chap. VI.</header>

### §. 665.

<margin></margin>
*How dissent is gathered from an act.*
</margin>
*If anyone does that which he could not do, unless he were unwilling for something else to be done; he dissents in regard to that very thing.* This is evident in a manner not unlike that which we showed previously (§. 663), that if anyone does what he could not do unless he willed something else to be done, he consents to that very thing.

The truth of the proposition is so manifest from the definition of dissent handed down (§. 659), that it may rightly be added to the number of axioms (§. 273 *Log.*), and thus we ought to be little concerned with demonstrating it (§. 267 *Log.*). An example is a seller who, when a price is offered by a buyer, carries away and puts back the merchandise. For indeed, if he were unwilling to deliver the merchandise for that price, he could not [do otherwise than] carry it away and put it back, since he wills to sell the merchandise. By this very act he sufficiently indicates that he is unwilling to deliver the merchandise for that price; indeed, he declares his dissent more than if he had said in plain words that he could not deliver it for that price: for at the same time he indicates quite clearly that he despairs of a just price being given by the buyer, and even that he takes it ill that a greater price is not offered by the buyer.

### §. 666.

<margin></margin>
*How dissent is gathered from an omission.*
</margin>
*If anyone does not do what he ought to do, unless he were unwilling for something to be done; he dissents in regard to that very thing.* This is evident in a manner not unlike that which we showed a little before (§. 664), that if anyone does not do what he ought to do unless he willed something else to be done, he consents.

What we have just noted concerning the preceding proposition must also be held concerning the present one. The truth of the proposition becomes manifest from an example. If a buyer, who had already seen the merchandise before, returns and offers a slightly higher price than he had offered before, but the seller does not bring forth the merchandise, it is abundantly understood from his not doing this that he is unwilling to deliver the merchandise for that price, and consequently that he still dissents regarding the same (§. 659), even if he does not say a single word.

translation:
<meta>Shelfmark: 171 G 93. This page continues the Layman’s discourse on the soul’s relationship to Divine Wisdom. Following the previous discussion of the "foretaste" and the magnet-like attraction of the soul toward its source, the Layman now explains how the soul, as a living image, finds its true being only in its eternal Exemplar.</meta>

...becomes the life of the life of truth, and not its own. From this, it is moved toward its Exemplar <term>exemplar; the divine original or "blueprint" of a thing</term> as toward the truth of its own being. **I**f, therefore, the Exemplar is eternal, and the image has a life in which it foretastes its Exemplar, then it is moved toward it with longing.

**A**nd since the motion of a living thing cannot find rest except in the infinite, which is eternal Wisdom, that spiritual motion—which never attains infinite life infinitely—can never cease. **F**or it is always moved by a most joyful desire to reach it, because it is never weary of the delight of that contact. **E**ternal Wisdom is the most savory food, which, while satisfying, does not diminish the desire for consuming it, so that in that eternal feeding, one never ceases to find delight. 

**O**rator. **I** hold that you have spoken excellently, without a doubt. **B**ut I see that there is a great difference between the taste of Wisdom and those things which can be expressed about that taste.

**I**diota. **Y**ou speak well, and it pleases me to have heard these words from you. **F**or just as all knowledge about the taste of a thing is empty and sterile for one who has never tasted it—until the sense of taste actually reaches it—**s**o it is with this Wisdom, which no one tastes through hearing, but only he who receives it in his internal taste. 

<margin><unclear>knowledge through experience...</unclear></margin> **H**e bears witness not of the things he has heard, but of what he has tasted within himself by experience <term>experimentaliter; knowledge gained through direct personal experience rather than abstract reasoning</term>. **T**o know many descriptions of love which the saints have left to us, without having the taste of love itself, is a kind of vanity. **W**herefore, to seek eternal Wisdom, it is not enough to know what can be read about it; rather, it is necessary that after the intellect has discovered where it is, it should make Wisdom its own through the affection <note>original: "affectu"; the emotional or volitional capacity of the soul, distinct from the pure intellect</note>...

<summary>Nicholas of Cusa describes the soul's eternal journey toward Wisdom as a "joyful desire" for a food that satisfies without causing satiety. The passage emphasizes that true spiritual understanding comes through "tasting" or direct experience rather than merely reading descriptions written by others.</summary>

<keywords>Wisdom, Exemplar, experiential knowledge, eternal life, spiritual desire, Nicholas of Cusa, intellect vs. affection</keywords>

Thomas in 2.2. quaest. 11. art. 2. ad tertium argumentum. nam Ecclesia in his quae pertinent ad fidem, non potest errare, vt habetur & notatur. 24. quaest. 1. cap. à recta ergo fide. & cap. Memor sum. & hoc quia dominus pro ea rogauit ne deficeret fides eius. Lucae. 22. cap. dixit dominus: Ego rogaui pro te vt non deficiat fides tua. & ponitur 21. dist. §. 1. in vers. Ego pro te.

<margin>21</margin> Notandum tamen est, quia ad hoc quòd aliquis proprie dicatur haereticus, quatuor requiruntur, primum est error in intellectu, ita quòd male sentiat de veritate, vnde si aliquis conculcet corpus Christi, credens tamen ibi esse verum corpus Christi, & quòd hoc sit malum, sed hoc facit vt placeat diabolo, iste non dicetur haereticus, quia non habet errorem in intellectu, nec male sentit de sacramento altaris.
Secundum est, quòd talis error sit circa ea quae pertinent ad fidem, vel contra determinationem Ecclesiae, in his quae pertinent ad fidem & bonos mores, & necessaria sunt ad consecutionem vitae eternae.

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological definitions of heresy, specifically addressing the poverty of Christ, the infusion of grace in infants, and the psychological requirements for an individual to be formally classified as a heretic.</meta>

# OF THE INQUISITORS.
<header>INQUISITORUM.</header>

...[common] even as to right and ownership, is a heretic, as is clear from the *Extravagant* <note>A collection of canon laws that circulated "outside" the main official codifications like the Decretals.</note> of John XXII, which begins: *Cum inter nonnullos* <note>original: "Since among several." This refers to a famous 1323 decree regarding the poverty of Christ.</note>.

<margin>17</margin> The opinion which holds that baptized infants are not infused with virtues and informing grace <note>term: <term>Informing grace</term> refers to the theological concept of "gratia informans," the grace that gives "form" or spiritual life to the soul.</note> as a habit—even if not at that time as to use—is rejected by the Church, indeed condemned, as is clear in the single *Clementine* decree <note>Part of the *Clementinae*, a collection of canon law.</note> regarding the Most Holy Trinity, at the end. Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> also rejects this opinion in the third part, question 69, article 6.

<margin>18</margin> Likewise, to stubbornly assert that Christ and his Apostles, in those things which Holy Scripture testifies they possessed, had no right of use over them, nor had the right to sell or give them away, or to acquire other things from them—since such an assertion concludes that their use and actions in the aforementioned matters were not just—is erroneous and heretical. This is clear through the said *Extravagant* of John XXII, which begins: *Cum inter nonnullos*. <note>This ruling specifically targeted the "Spiritual" Franciscans who argued that Christ and the Apostles owned absolutely nothing, neither individually nor in common.</note>

<margin>19</margin> There are, however, many other heresies or sects of heretics, which Isidore enumerates in the eighth book of the *Etymologies*, chapter 5; they are also placed in Question 24, point 3, in the chapter *Quidam autem haeretici* <note>original: "certain heretics however."</note>.

<margin>20</margin> Many other heresies are found as well, which are collected from the sayings of Blessed Thomas in various places, and are also listed in the table of the Reverend Father Master Peter of Bergamo <note>A 15th-century Dominican scholar who created the *Tabula Aurea*, a massive alphabetical index to the works of Thomas Aquinas.</note>, under the word "heresy." See them there: for whenever anything is said or held stubbornly that is against the determination of the Church regarding those things pertaining to the faith, that is always heretical. This is proven in Question 24, point 1, in the chapter *Haec est fides* [This is the faith], and the final commentary on the chapter *Cum Christus* [Since Christ] regarding heretics, at the end; and the commentary on the word *docuit* [he taught] in the single chapter regarding the Most Holy Trinity in the sixth book. For it belongs to the Church to determine doubts if any should occasionally arise concerning the faith, as is clear in the chapter *Quotiens* [Whenever], Question 24, point 1; regarding baptism, the chapter *Maiores* [The ancestors] at the beginning; regarding the Most Holy Trinity, chapter 2 at the end; and the single *Clementine* decree under the same title, in the section "We therefore." This is supported by Distinction 22, the chapter *Omnes* [All]. Blessed Thomas agrees in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, question 11, article 2, in the response to the third argument. For the Church, in those matters pertaining to the faith, cannot err, as is held and noted in Question 24, point 1, in the chapter *A recta ergo fide* [From the right faith therefore] and the chapter *Memor sum* [I am mindful]. And this is because the Lord prayed for her that her faith might not fail. In the 22nd chapter of Luke, the Lord said: "I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail." This is also placed in Distinction 21, section 1, in the verse *Ego pro te* [I for you].

<margin>21</margin> It must be noted, however, that for someone to be properly called a heretic, four things are required. The first is an error in the intellect, such that one holds a wrong opinion regarding the truth. Thus, if someone were to trample upon the body of Christ <note>The consecrated host or Eucharist.</note>, yet believing it to be the true body of Christ and knowing this act to be evil, but doing it to please the devil, that person would not be called a heretic; for they have no error in the intellect, nor do they hold a wrong opinion regarding the Sacrament of the Altar. <note>This distinguishes the crime of sacrilege or devil-worship from the crime of heresy; heresy requires a doctrinal disagreement, not just bad behavior.</note>
The second requirement is that such an error must concern those things which pertain to the faith, or be against the determination of the Church in those things pertaining to faith and good morals, which are necessary for the attainment of eternal life.

<meta>The catchword "Te" indicates the next page will begin with "Tertium," the third requirement for defining a heretic.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Topic VI (On Humanity), specifically examining the Ethiopian theological view of Adam’s creation. It transitions from refuting Pre-Adamite theories to analyzing the "four elements" theory found in Ethiopian liturgical texts.</meta>

<meta>catchword: three</meta>

However, the Ethiopians seem to me a bit too bold <note>original: *audaculi*</note> here in determining the creation of the first man, when they imagine that God mixed the four elements and formed the first man from their mixture. Concerning this matter, the Author of the *Organ* <note>original: *Organi*; likely referring to the *Arganonä Maryam* (Harp of Mary), a major work of Ethiopian Marian and creation theology</note>, *Lecture I, otherwise 2,* hands down the following, saying: *“God performed a miracle when He created our father Adam and formed him from four elements; He mixed the elements, yet in such a way that they would not disagree with one another. He mixed the first with the second, and the third with the fourth, the moist with the dry and the hot with the cold, the invisible with the visible, the tangible with the intangible.”* (As if these things could truly be mixed, which is a property only of matter.) *“He made two from the tangible and two from the intangible; He made three from the dry and one from the moist; He made three from the cold and one from the hot. The Architect knew where the inner sanctuary was to be established, and He founded the corners of the house upon the four elements. And since He knew that a clay vessel could not move itself nor speak without the mixture of the spirit proceeding from Him, He therefore breathed into his face and made him rational and self-moving.”* On this occasion, let us note at the same time that the **Abyssinians** assert at least two essential parts of man, and they have no dealings with the **Fanatics** (see the dissertation by the late <term>HENRICUS WIDEBURGIUS</term> <note>Heinrich Wideburg (1641–1692), a German Lutheran theologian who wrote on the "trichotomy" of body, soul, and spirit</note>, *On the Three Parts of Man*), who...

<summary>The author critiques Ethiopian theology for its specific claims that Adam was created from a precise mixture of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water). He cites the Ethiopian "Organ" to describe the architectural metaphor of the body as a house for the spirit.</summary>
<keywords>Adam, creation, four elements, Ethiopian theology, Arganonä Maryam, Heinrich Wideburg, anthropology, body and soul</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of metallurgy, moving from the "red metals" (copper) discussed on the previous page to the nature, properties, and purification of gold. The text cites authorities like Hermes Trismegistus, Plato, and Empedocles to explain why gold is the "most perfect" metal.</meta>

<sig>a iij</sig>

# **B**ut it must be objected by those concerning the nature of gold that, according to **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origins of alchemy.</note>, it is the only metal in which no "sickness" <note>imperfection or impurity</note> appears. For neither part of its matter is infected or out of balance. Since, like other metals, it is composed of **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>, its sulfur is most lucid and pure, brought to a state of purity through the strongest washings so that it has no combustible oiliness at all, nor any phlegmatic, watery moisture that might evaporate. Perhaps in hollow places where the solid surface is frequently sublimated and "digested" <term>digestio; a natural ripening process similar to slow cooking within the earth</term> by a temperate heat, a process called **pepansis** <note>original: "pepansis"; a Greek term for the ripening of fruit or the "cooking" of humors/minerals</note> occurs. Its earthy substance, which is incorporated into the sulfur, is pure, extremely subtle, and suspended like a vapor throughout the entire substance of the sulfur's radical moisture. For this reason, it remains that the heat of that sulfur is balanced in its temperament, receding from nothing; and this acts as the **masculine power** in the composition of gold.

Similarly, its quicksilver has two substances purified to the extreme. For a third quality within its own heat is refined—not merely divided materially, but most subtle in a vaporous way—frequently sublimated in the cavities of the earth by the life-giving heat of the sun and stars. Likewise, the watery part is refined in the same way through repeated purification; and since it contains "glass-like" qualities <note>clarity or transparency</note>, it is refined most delicately. It is established that when these are mixed together by heat and the disposition of a place that stifles and reflects the vapor back into itself, they are bound together by the strongest bond of mixing. 

<margin>Why gold is heavy.</margin>
<margin>Why gold is not burnt.</margin>

Sulfur, however, does not enter into the composition of gold merely through its quality, but through its substance; and since it is of a subtle substance, it penetrates everywhere through the quicksilver and colors it by coagulating it. Since both are brought by sublimation to the form of the "superior elements" <note>the celestial or pure elements</note>—which agree in their transparent nature with the "perpetual body" <note>referring to the incorruptibility of the heavens</note>—both will possess a great deal of transparency. And when many parts of the matter are thickened together, they will stand firm. For this is a property of a subtle substance: that when it stands firm through coagulation, it will contain many parts in a very small space. Therefore, contracted transparency produces a **yellow color**, and its subtlety produces the greatest solidity. The constancy of many parts together in a small space and position produces **weight**, as is proven by those things reasonably demonstrated in the book *On the Heavens and the World* <note>referring to Aristotle's "De Caelo et Mundo"</note>. 

It also follows from its solidity and temperament together that gold evaporates little or not at all; therefore, it has almost no smell. For although a smell is not essentially a smoky evaporation, a strong smell often accompanies smoky evaporation. Because of this, it further follows that gold is more incorruptible than any other metal and withstands fire better due to the extremely strong mixing in its composition. For smoky evaporation indicates a certain corruption of bodies, which is less in silver and greater in copper. From these facts, we find the reason why things that do not burn gold, such as sulfur, arsenic, and certain others, do burn silver. For the cause of this—

---

—kind of mixture is that all of its earthy part is defended from burning by its moisture, and all of its moisture is held back by the earthy part so that it does not fly away through evaporation. This connection **Plato** calls a "covenant," and **Empedocles** calls the "glue of siblings" <note>original: "collam germanorum"; a metaphor for the strong chemical/alchemical bond between related elements</note>. 

<margin>The virtues of gold.</margin>

Because of the balanced temperament of gold, it is considered "hot and moist." It is beneficial for **trembling of the heart** <note>palpitations</note> and for **melancholy** which makes a person sad; and because of this, it helps those whose condition makes them talk to themselves. Gold provides relief against these passions whether it is rubbed on the body in its specific form or even taken internally when ground up. 

<margin>Why gold does not stain.</margin>

Due to its solidity, it does not easily affect the bodies it touches. Therefore, it is worn in rings and other ornaments. Silver, however, stains a little, and other metals stain a lot because they "touch" what they contain <note>they rub off on the skin</note>. This is because their oily moisture is entirely separated from them, mixed with burnt earthy matter, and this stains like the soot of an oily body. 

<margin>Grains.</margin>

The great purity of gold's matter means it is very rarely found mixed with other bodies, but almost always pure; for when it is mixed with others, it cannot retain such purity and thus degenerates into copper. Conversely, it is very rarely found unless it is incorporated into stones. Furthermore, it is often found as grains of sand, because such great purity must exist in small amounts, elevated from and almost expelled by that matter, and thus distinct. However, a grain is sometimes found together with **marcasite** <note>iron pyrites, often called "fool's gold"</note>.

From these facts, it is clear why these two metals—namely gold and silver—were chosen by the wise men of old as the material for **coinage**. For they have this special benefit of aiding and comforting the human temperament, and they are more durable and noble than the rest. 

<margin>The purification of gold.</margin>

The things that purify gold are sharp and very dry, such as salts (especially sea salts), the soot of oily but dry bodies, and crushed brick. When gold is to be purified, a clay vessel is made in the shape of a **cucurbit** <note>a gourd-shaped alchemical flask</note> or a small dish. Over this vessel, another similar one is placed and sealed at the joints with a tenacious clay which alchemists call the **Lute of Wisdom** <note>original: "lutum sapientie"; a specialized sealant used to make vessels airtight</note>. In the upper part, there are many small holes through which vapor and smoke may escape. The gold is then thinned into short, thin plates and arranged in the vessel so that every layer of plates has a powder of mixed soot, salt, and flour-like brick above and below it. It is cooked in a strong fire until it is most pure and the ignoble substances within it are consumed. 

The "Lute of Wisdom" from which these vessels are made is itself created from crushed pottery shards, mixed again and fired. For this vessel, when placed in the fire, is not diminished by the sensible consumption of the fire. However, the Lute of Wisdom is prepared in another way in alchemical works, but let that which the goldsmiths use suffice here. Thus is gold purified, and nothing in it is burnt away except the ignoble substance. Because of this, Hermes elegantly says in his alchemical works: 

> "Sulfur itself, by a certain subtle affinity of sulfur to which all metals are related, burns through and incinerates all their bodies—but gold it does not. For its pores are tight and indissoluble." 

However, gold which is found more abundantly in our times...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mechanics and benefits of vomiting. It addresses common misconceptions about the nature of the matter expelled and argues for the superior efficacy of emetics over standard laxatives for specific internal organs.</meta>

# CHAPTER I. ON VOMITING.

<margin>From where this common error arose.</margin>
...while the main reason for distinction must be observed to this extent: in some conditions, milder remedies should be given. These disturb nothing beyond the stomach. Only those things that float in its cavity or stick to its linings are gently led out. In other cases, stronger remedies are suitable. These impart a spasm to other internal organs as well. By doing so, whatever waste stagnates in them or is gathered anywhere may be stirred from its source <note>original: "è minera"</note> and immediately eliminated upward or downward. Sometimes, a viscous and seemingly <term>Phlegmatic: pertaining to phlegm or thick mucus</term> matter is primarily excreted. This occurs because the "ballast" <note>original: "faburra"</note> of the stomach is purged almost entirely without shaking the receptacles of the bilious humor. However, when the <term>bile ducts: the vessels that carry bile from the liver</term> <note>original: "vafa choledocha"</note> are drained, the excretion turns out for the most part to be bilious. The vomiting of black humor mostly depends on the tint of the medicine. For <term>vitriolic: substances containing sulfates, often metallic</term> materials stain the expelled matter with blackness.

<margin>If emetic medicine is suitable, it is more effective than any other.</margin>
Evacuation through vomiting is more violent than through bowel movements. However, if it is performed within the patient's strength, it is often ten times more beneficial in some conditions than a repeated purgation. In this way, heavy phlegm clotting in the folds of the stomach is swept out as if with brooms. Any other laxatives would simply slide past this matter. Furthermore, neighboring parts are stirred by a powerful shaking. These include the <term>Pancreas: an organ that aids digestion</term>, the <term>Mesentery: the membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall</term>, the <term>Spleen: an organ involved in blood filtration</term> <note>original: "Lien"</note>, and the <term>Liver: the organ that produces bile</term> <note>original: "Jecur"</note>. Consequently, obstructions formed in these organs are most easily removed. Even stagnations of blood and humors are cleared by this kind of remedy. Foreign ferments produced anywhere in the body and the deeper seeds of diseases are rarely uprooted without the use of emetics. The use of emetics is found to be very beneficial, especially in conditions of the brain and the nervous system. By this kind of medicine, the filth of the stomach and organs is wiped away. This filth would otherwise pollute the <term>chyle: a milky fluid of lymph and emulsified fats</term> and the blood. Not only is this cleared, but also the glands,

It transitions from the previous discussion of a mystical experience of the Passion to a scholastic inquiry into Christ's foreknowledge and his physical appearance.</meta>

# THE ANT-HILL, BOOK I.

...showed to his followers through frequent expression, gesture, and word. Third, whether he ever laughed.

<margin>Response to the first point.</margin>
**THEOLOGIAN.** To the first point I say: he was a martyr, so to speak, in the knowledge of his infused wisdom, but not in the feeling of pain and experience. For from the moment of his conception, he had knowledge of all future things in the higher powers of his blessed soul, where he saw the Word <note>The Logos, or the Second Person of the Trinity</note> most clearly and through infused knowledge; but foreknowing these future things did not move his physical senses to feelings of sadness and pain, except when the time of his passion approached.

<margin>Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on the Sentences, Book 3, Distinction 17, final question, article 5.</margin>
This is what the Holy Doctor <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas</note> means when, in the third book, distinction 17, final question, he says: "Although death was foreseen from the beginning of conception, it was not foreseen as imminent; therefore, it did not cause a disturbance—that is, a dread of the emotions—but only when it was already hanging over him." For this is how we experience fear or pain in ourselves.

<margin>Aristotle, Ethics, Book 3, Chapter 6.</margin>
For a young student of life knows that the end of all terrifying things is death, according to the saying of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the third book of the *Ethics*, and that he himself will die; but because he does not imagine it as near, but as distant, it moves him little or not at all toward sadness. However, it does move a person of feeling if he is old and it is near, if it is forethought in that way.

<margin>To the second point.</margin>
To the second point: I find that Christ was most beautiful in his face and in all the limbs of his body; for the greater part of his life, while living among others, he walked with a cheerful and joyful countenance, and in his words, he perfectly displayed the virtues of affability and <term>pleasantness</term> <note>original: *eutrapelia*; the Aristotelian virtue of social grace, wittiness, or being "well-turned" in conversation</note>. The first is evident from Holy Scripture, from the doctrine of the saints, from approved history, and is proven by the diligence of reason.

<margin>Psalm 44.</margin>
For according to the Hebrew and Latin commentators of Holy Scripture, that verse of the Psalm is interpreted literally regarding Christ's humanity: *You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips* <note>Psalm 45:2 in modern Bibles; Psalm 44:3 in the Vulgate</note>. Upon this, Blessed Jerome, in his letter to Principia...

->*******************<-

### *PREFACE.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'A'. The interior of the letter contains a landscape scene featuring a classical building with a dome or rounded roof, set among trees and rolling hills under a sky with light clouds.</image-desc>

We call those "acoustic instruments" by which we represent remote sounds to the ears—sounds otherwise hidden from the sense of hearing. Just as with optical instruments <note>original: "opticis instrumentis"</note> we bring remote objects that are entirely inaccessible to the sense of sight before the eyes as if they were nearby and close (about which we have treated extensively in the last book of the *Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Arte magna Lucis & Umbræ"</note>), so with acoustic instruments, sounds are narrowed and channeled <note>original: "coarctatos"</note> within organs manufactured with wondrous industry and skill according to nature’s own model.

This section contains, *First*, the construction of Halls, Private Rooms, and Porticos disposed with such ingenuity that within them, at a certain and determined point, Princes <note>referring to rulers or patrons</note> may be able to hear every utterance of words, no matter how whispered. *Second*, it covers the construction of acoustic instruments for the use of the hard of hearing <note>original: "surdastrorum"</note>, together with *Acoustic Cryptology* <note>The study of secret communication using sound</note>, or the hidden communication of mutual concepts through sounds, and other new and most secret inventions. But before we approach the matter, we have thought it necessary to set forth the properties and experiments of the Tubes and Trumpets themselves, which we shall use in the architecture of the work.

Signum hoc (inquiunt) quod propheta dedit, liberationis futurae Regis Achaz à duobus Regibus, qui contra eum venerant, signū fuit. Christus autem vester post Achaz vltra annos quingentos, natus est. Signum igitur hoc conceptionis eius ex virgine esse non potuit.

<margin>Solutio.</margin>
B GAL. Facile nobis erit huic argumento respondere, si prius pro veritatis propheticae intellectu, historia summatium notauerimus. Tempestate igitur qua Achaz in Iudā regnabat, cum reges potentes duo, Syriae scilicet & Israel Ierosolyma copioso exercitu obsedissent, vt scribitur apud Isaiam 7. cap. & 4. ...and that he might preserve the unconsumed substance of humanity within the very flame of divinity. We also read in the sixth chapter of the Book of Judges that Gideon said:
**"If there be dew on the fleece only, and dryness on all the earth, then I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said."** <note>original: אם טל יהיה על הגזה לבדו ועל כל הארץ חרב וידעתי כי תושיע בידי את ישראל כאשר דברת; Judges 6:37</note>
And it was done so. In this passage, the fleece—which is the garment of the lamb—signifies human nature, which the dew of divinity took upon itself. The "dry earth," however, represents the Virgin’s womb, which was not moistened by human seed. Regarding what is said afterward—that the fleece alone was dry while the whole earth had dew—this signifies that the nature of Christ was not merely "infused" <note>meaning his humanity was not a separate addition but fully united with his divinity</note>; rather, the "whole earth" of the Virgin’s body was imbued with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

The virginity and integrity of the Mother of God was also signified by the rod of Aaron. Without any external moisture, by the power of God alone, it flowered, grew leaves, and bore fruit that was equally sweet and useful to both the healthy and the sick. For thus we read of it in the seventeenth chapter of Numbers:
**"And behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi had blossomed, and brought forth a flower, and sprouted a bud, and produced almonds."** <note>original: והנה פרח מטה אהרן לבית לוי ויצא פרח ויצץ ציץ ויגמול שקדים; Numbers 17:8</note>
It does not hinder our argument that the text says Aaron’s rod flowered "for the house of Levi." For the Messiah was destined to be born not only from the tribe of Judah, but also from the tribe of Levi, and even for the sake of the Gentiles. Therefore, against all laws of nature, Aaron’s rod produced what could be supplied neither by seed nor by root. If a rod was able to produce nuts against the course of nature, could the Virgin Mother of God not generate a Son beyond the laws of nature by the command of God? Let the unbelieving Jews tell us: by what means did a dry rod flower, leaf, and bring forth almonds? Then we shall tell them how a Virgin conceived and gave birth to the Son of God. But the Jews will not be able to explain the "conception" of the rod to us, nor can we explain the birth from a Virgin to them. Since they furthermore believe that Eve was formed from the body of Adam—claiming this happened by a miracle of the divine will—then they must be answered in the same way regarding the conception and birth of the Messiah from a Virgin. For the divine will has no need for the usual course or order of nature.

## CAPNIO.
<note>Capnio is the Greek-style pen name of Johann Reuchlin, a famous Christian Hebraist and character in this dialogue.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a man's face and leafy vines.</image-desc>ALTHOUGH these things are so, the Jews of our time, desiring to attack the virginity of the Messiah’s mother, do not cease to contradict in various ways that wonderful sign given by Isaiah concerning the virginal conception and birth, which you have introduced. They deem it impossible for a virgin to conceive and bear a son. Therefore, they assert that these words of Isaiah, when he said, "A virgin <term>Alma</term> <note>Isaiah 7:14 uses the Hebrew word 'Almah,' which Christians translate as 'virgin' and Jewish commentators often translate as 'young woman.'</note> shall conceive and bear a son," should not be understood as referring to the mother of the Messiah, as their ancient predecessors explained, and as the Catholic faith affirms those words were spoken concerning the glorious Virgin Mary. On this point, they are accustomed to make many arguments against us.

<column-break/>

<page-num>418</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN</header>

<margin>The first argument of the Jews.</margin>
To ensure that their "barking" against the mother of the Messiah may be silenced, I desire you to answer them using their own scriptures. First, they argue as follows: This sign (they say) which the prophet gave, was a sign of the future liberation of King Ahaz from the two kings who had come against him. However, your Christ was born more than five hundred years after Ahaz. Therefore, this could not be a sign of his conception from a virgin.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
GALATINUS: It will be easy for us to answer this argument if we first briefly note the history for the sake of understanding the prophetic truth. In the time when Ahaz reigned in Judah, two powerful kings—namely, those of Syria and Israel—besieged Jerusalem with a massive army, as written in Isaiah chapter 7 and 2 Kings 16. Then the Lord God sent Isaiah to Ahaz to warn him not to fear the army of those kings. But he, being wicked and unbelieving (for he was a worshiper of idols), refused to believe the prophet’s words. For this reason, the prophet urged him,

since he did not believe, to ask for some sign of his liberation to be performed, saying: *Ask a sign for yourself, or a miracle from the Lord your God. Ask it in the depths or in the heights above.* That is: Ask for a sign of your liberation to be made, whether from the depths of hell through the resurrection of some dead man, or from heaven by the stopping of the sun, as was done in the time of Joshua. But he, being impious and unwilling to ask for a sign from God, offered an excuse, saying that this would be tempting God. Whence he said: *I will not ask, and I will not tempt.*

Since Isaiah knew that Ahaz had not said this in good faith, but rather because he had no fear of God, he judged him unworthy of such a sign. He refused to give the sign to him personally, but gave it to the House of David, saying: *Hear then, O House of David; is it a small thing for you to weary men, that you weary my God also? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and she shall call his name Emmanuel.*

From this it is clear that the sign of the virgin’s conception and birth was not given to Ahaz himself, but to the House of David, from whose seed the Messiah was to be born according to the flesh. Therefore, we must deny what is said in the argument—namely, that this sign was given to Ahaz. Furthermore, to the point that Christ was born more than five hundred years after Ahaz, and thus his virginal conception could not be a sign of liberation from those two kings, we say that two types of signs are found in Holy Scripture: one is <term>prognostic</term> and the other is <term>rememorative</term>.

<margin>The two types of signs: prognostic and rememorative.</margin>
A **prognostic** sign is one regarding a future event. An example is the one given to Gideon (as said in Judges chapter 6) regarding the fleece, which indicated a future victory. A **rememorative** sign, however, is one regarding the past [or confirming a promise]. Such was the sign that the Lord gave to Moses in Exodus chapter 3, saying:
**"And this shall be a sign to you that I have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall worship God upon this mountain."** <note>original: וזה לך האות כי אנכי שלחתיך בהוציאך את העם ממצרים תעבדון את האלהים על ההר הזה; Exodus 3:12</note>
That is: you shall give thanks to me for this mission which is imposed upon you. Therefore, the sign of the virgin’s conception and birth was rememorative, not prognostic. Nor does the great distance of time stand in the way...

164 APPLICATION OF THE HISTORY OF MELCHIZEDEK
if this Melchizedek, the first of his kind, as far as is evident from Moses, and the last Priest, born of neither a priestly father nor mother; much less belonging to the priestly family of Aaron itself, nevertheless was a Priest of the most high God; it follows that Christ also, from whatever parents he was eventually born, and from whatever tribe he descended, could have been a Priest according to the order of this Melchizedek, truly and properly so called, and also much greater than all the Aaronite priests, who were bound to those rules and required conditions. Therefore, nothing stands in the way of our Lord's priesthood from the fact that it is established he was born not from Levi, but from Judah, as Paul specifically says in verses 12 and 14 <note>referring to Hebrews chapter 7</note>. The entire weight of the Apostolic discussion serves to prove this thesis against the Jews.

<margin>Which Schmidius himself saw and acknowledged: although he does not settle on this explanation himself.</margin>

§. XIV. By way of an <term>epimetron</term> <gloss>supplementary addition</gloss>, I will now add here what the famous Sebastian Schmidius <note>a prominent 17th-century Lutheran theologian and biblical scholar</note> commented on this passage. Because I had only looked into his work after these pages were already sent to the press, I had previously warned in the Dissertations—from which I have now formed this small work—that I had placed his comments in a less convenient location at that time. For he, even if he does not embrace this interpretation of ours himself, but prefers to take these words as being said of Christ himself, understands that being <term>agenealogēton</term> <gloss>without genealogy</gloss> refers to the manner of production, by which different essences constitute different persons and are numbered in them <note>Schmidius is likely referring to the internal relations within the Trinity</note>. Whether this is well or poorly reasoned I will not inquire now, yet he candidly writes as follows: *This opinion seems the best of all those held by Interpreters: not so much because it belongs to Epiphanius (to whom Justinian also writes it belongs in this passage, as we already noted in section 11), as because it is most suitable to our text, and can be supported by good reasons.* Nor is it tedious to add them here, since they greatly contribute to both the clarification and confirmation of those things we discussed in the preceding sections. For 1. the Apostle, he says, *does not want to simply deny that Melchizedek had any kin or genealogy; but in a certain respect, that his kin is not described when he is called Priest.* Nor do we doubt 2. *that an opposition is made between Melchizedek the priest and the Levitical priests: which opposition the Apostle soon explains in more detail. Now, the status of the Levitical priests—*

<page-break/>

165 TO THE PURPOSE OF PAUL. CHAPTER V.
—was so arranged that all were required to demonstrate their priestly lineage, and <note>rather than being</note> <term>agenealogētoi</term> <gloss>without genealogy</gloss>, they had to have their genealogy ready at hand. *For if they did not have it, they were removed from the altar, Ezra 2:62-63.* Therefore, a <term>hiereus agenealogētos</term> <gloss>priest with a genealogy</gloss> was one who could show his priestly lineage; whereas one who was <term>agenealogētos</term> <gloss>without genealogy</gloss> did not have a priestly genealogy. 3. *The matter is clearly explained this way in our chapter, both when in verse 6 Melchizedek is said <term>mē agenealogēton ex autōn</term> <gloss>not to have derived his genealogy from them</gloss>, namely the sons of Levi, as all Levitical priests were from the sons of Levi; and because in verse 13 it is expressly said that Christ is from another tribe, from which no one served at the altar: and in verse 14 he is clearly assigned to the tribe of Judah. Here now the comparison of the <term>type</term> <gloss>symbolic precursor</gloss> and <term>antitype</term> <gloss>fulfillment</gloss> will be clear: for just as Melchizedek was a Priest <term>agenealogētos</term> <gloss>without genealogy</gloss>, who did not have a priestly lineage, or to whom the priestly office did not descend through lineage and blood; so the priesthood ought not to descend to Christ through lineage and blood, but was conferred upon him from a more sublime principle.* From which it also follows, *that Christ ought not to have been born from the tribe of Levi, but from the tribe of Judah, lest he be a Priest <term>agenealogētos</term> <gloss>possessing a genealogy</gloss>, obtaining the priesthood from lineage.* Thus far Schmidius reasons, as you see, Reader, with a most accurate logic in all parts, especially notable through this last observation. By this he concludes not only that Christ, in order to be a Priest, did not necessarily have to have a genealogy from the tribe of Levi—which I also showed extensively enough in section 13—but that he even ought not to have had one. For in this way, Paul clearly demonstrated to the attentive Hebrews that it was far from the case that the priesthood of Jesus should be suspect to them because he lacks the priestly genealogy they desire in him; on the contrary, if he had it, he could not be a priest. He later warns of this in plain words regarding the earthly priestly dwelling in Hebrews 8:4. Nevertheless, what he says—that Christ ought not to have been born from Levi, or that the priesthood ought not to have descended to him through lineage and blood—was not necessary by the nature of the thing, or <term>a priori</term> <gloss>from first principles</gloss>. For why, if it had so pleased God, could Christ not have been born from the lineage of his typical ancestors, as

<summary>This page argues that Melchizedek's lack of recorded priestly genealogy serves as a model for Christ's priesthood. Because Melchizedek was a priest without belonging to the Levite bloodline, Christ's descent from the tribe of Judah validates rather than disqualifies his superior priestly status.</summary>

unum CORNERI NOSTRI de me judicium, me non tantum, uti Teucrum clypeus Ajacis facilè tuebitur, ne à malè feriatis hominibus, quorum plena terra, plenum mare, vel invidiæ morSibus, vel maledicentiæ latratibus infons adpetar; verum etiam hoc mihi apud Vos, AUDIT. benevolentiæ conciliabit, hoc audientiæ faciet, ut cujus rei gratiâ hanc in scenam prodierim, æqué atque animis atque auribus, pro singulari vestrâ humanitate sitis accepturi: Et ita hîc pedem figo, hôc unô sum contentus, ut si nihil amplius dicam, multa a. & alias esse quæ facto huic meo favent sciatis, Audit. caussam omnem locutionis meæ dictam existimem, & nihil sit, si quis aliam anxiè, sed frustra scrutetur.

Neque verò hâc in panegyri Philosophicâ, de PHILOSOPHIA in genere, quæ verè DEI donum & dulcissimum animi est pabulum, longam comparabo orationem; nec de ejusdem partibus & adminiculis in specie dicere constitui; neque ejusdem utilitates & encomia persequi habeo; ne actum agere & post Homerum ingeniorum fontem Iliada scribere censear.

De ANTIPATHIA sive fastidio, nauseâ, abstinentiâ & odio cibi & potus quorundam mirabili antiloquij caussâ & nè prorsus sim ἀσύμβολος aliquid dicam.

Videmus namque, quod non pauci in mensa nobis adsidentes Carnibus, Piscibus, prorsus abstineant: Videmus, quod Vinum, Cerevisiam, Lac, Mel non gustent, Caseum, Butyrum, Poma non tangant. Et sunt qui Fraga, qui Allium, qui Ova non possunt concoquere, nec ROSÆ, nec POMI odorem perferre; Videmus, inquam, Audit. videmus hæc omnia; Sed qui hîc caussam expedierint, caussam dico adæquatam, necessariam & sufficientem dederint, rari sunt: & si dixero fermè nulli, nihil certè mali nec contra veritatem, dixero.

translation:
<meta>This page follows the speaker’s humble apology for his own inadequacy, where he explained that he is standing in for the high-ranking official Johannes Cornerus. He now transitions into his defense against critics and introduces the specific topic of the dissertation: the strange phenomenon of physical antipathies toward food.</meta>

<header>Lipsius’s singular dissertation on food & drink.</header>
<sig>A 3</sig>

The single judgment of our **CORNERUS** <note>Johannes Cornerus, the official mentioned on the previous page who was unable to attend due to illness.</note> concerning me will easily protect me—just as the shield of **AJAX** protected **TEUCER** <note>original: "Teucrum clypeus Ajacis." In the *Iliad*, the archer Teucer often stood behind the massive shield of his half-brother Ajax for protection while shooting. The speaker implies Cornerus’s endorsement acts as his protective shield against critics.</note>—so that I am not attacked as an innocent man by idle people (of whom the earth and sea are full) either by the bites of envy or the barks of slander. Furthermore, this will win me favor and a hearing among you, **LISTENERS**, so that you will receive the reason for which I have come onto this stage with both mind and ears, in accordance with your singular kindness. And so here I fix my foot; I am content with this one thing: that if I say nothing more, you should know that there are many other things favoring this action of mine. I consider the whole cause of my speech to be told, and it would be nothing if anyone anxiously but fruitlessly searched for another.

Nor indeed in this philosophical assembly will I prepare a long speech about **PHILOSOPHY** in general, which is truly a gift of **GOD** and the sweetest food for the soul; nor have I decided to speak specifically about its parts and aids; nor am I here to pursue its benefits and praises, lest I be judged to be **doing what has already been done** <note>original: "actum agere," a Latin legal and theatrical idiom for repeating a finished task needlessly</note> and writing an **Iliad after Homer** <note>original: "post Homerum... Iliada scribere," a proverb meaning to undertake a task that has already been perfected by a master</note>, the source of geniuses.

Concerning **ANTIPATHY** or loathing, nausea, abstinence, and the miraculous hatred of food and drink in certain people, I shall say something for the sake of an introduction, and so that I may not be entirely **without a contribution** <note>Greek original: ἀσύμβολος (*asymbolos*). In ancient Greek social gatherings, a "symbolon" was a contribution to a communal meal; to be "asymbolos" meant to enjoy the feast without bringing anything to the table.</note>.

For we see that not a few sitting at the table with us abstain entirely from **Meat** or **Fish**. We see that they do not taste **Wine**, **Beer**, **Milk**, or **Honey**, and do not touch **Cheese**, **Butter**, or **Apples**. And there are those who cannot digest **Strawberries**, **Garlic**, or **Eggs**, nor endure the scent of a **ROSE** or an **APPLE**. We see, I say, **Listeners**, we see all these things. But those who can explain the cause here—I mean an **adequate, necessary, and sufficient cause** <note>These are technical terms from Scholastic logic used to define a complete scientific explanation</note>—are rare; and if I were to say there are almost none, I would certainly say nothing wrong nor against the truth.

<summary>The speaker defends his right to speak based on the endorsement of Cornerus and introduces his topic: the mysterious medical and philosophical causes behind "antipathies," or intense physical revulsions to common foods and scents.</summary>
<keywords>antipathy, food loathing, Cornerus, Ajax and Teucer, philosophy, nausea, medical causes, strawberries, roses</keywords>

translation:
## ON MARK

<margin>The Apostles used this word several times: it is derived from <term>praetore</term> <gloss>praetor</gloss>, which itself takes its name from <term>prae</term> <gloss>before</gloss> and <term>eundo</term> <gloss>going</gloss>. Among the Romans, the <term>praitōr</term> is called <term>stratēgos</term> <gloss>general</gloss>, as Suidas indicates, under whom are the military tribunes. The Praetorium is the tent of the praetor, and the house where he pronounces judgment. But the houses of kings, princes, and the highest magistrates are also called praetoria; as are the more magnificent buildings on country estates.</margin>

<term>Prasiai</term>.

Suidas interprets <term>prasion</term> as <term>lachanon</term> <gloss>vegetable/herb</gloss>. Likewise, <term>prasiai</term> are <gloss>the vegetable beds in a garden</gloss>. These are areas, or little plots, or mounds in gardens, in which vegetables and other garden plants are sown. By <term>catachresis</term> <gloss>misuse of a term</gloss>, unless I am mistaken, the grassy areas of meadows are meant here.

<term>prasiai prasiai</term> <gloss>in part</gloss>. Reference: 6.f. Erasmus: <gloss>They collapsed in garden-beds</gloss>, or <gloss>they reclined divided into greenery in groups of hundreds and fifties</gloss>. Valla reads, <gloss>In parts</gloss>, and corrects it to <gloss>in bundles</gloss>.

<term>Prattō</term> <gloss>I sell</gloss>.

<term>prathōsi</term> <gloss>to be sold</gloss>. Reference: 14.a.

<term>Presbys</term> <gloss>old man</gloss>.

It is also a title for those who excel not only in age, but also in wisdom, dignity, and power. Just as among the Greeks <term>presbys</term> is used for an <gloss>ambassador</gloss>; and <term>presbeion</term> is <gloss>dignity</gloss>, especially that of old age. Among the Romans they are called <term>senatores</term> <gloss>senators</gloss>, among the Hebrews <term>zekenim</term> <gloss>elders</gloss>.

<term>presbyteroi</term> <gloss>elders</gloss>. Reference: 11.d, 14.f. Formerly, bishops and elders, or presbyters, were the same. And Peter indeed calls himself a <gloss>fellow-elder</gloss>.

<term>presbyterōn</term> <gloss>the tradition of the elders</gloss>. Reference: 7.a, b. To the elders. Reference: 8.d, 14.e, 15.a.

<term>Prin</term> <gloss>before</gloss>.

<summary>This page discusses the etymology of "Praetorium" and "elders," noting that early church leaders were synonymous with elders and comparing them to Roman senators and Hebrew zekenim.</summary>
<keywords>Praetorium, garden beds, selling, elders, presbyters, tradition, philology</keywords>

Thom. in Cath. fup. 13. Marci. Ecclefiam montem appellat, propter eminentiam, & firmitatem. S. Aug. in pf. 2. Sanctus mons ejus fancta Ecclefia ejus.
