translation:
<meta>This page continues an alphabetical list of metaphors and "figures" (symbolic representations) of the Christian Church. The previous page ended with titles for St. Augustine; this page transitions into the letter M, focusing on the Church (Ecclesia) described through biblical women, nature, and objects. The catchword "rum" at the bottom suggests the next page begins with the end of the word "Presbyterorum" (of the Priests).</meta>

(82)

Christ — Likewise, the sphere of the Moon is half bright and half dark: so in the Church, some members are bright and others are dark. St. Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> on Psalm 10: *Fair as the Moon:* she who is illuminated by the Sun of Justice <note>Christ</note> lights up the night of the World. St. Isidore on the Song of Songs: The Church is the Moon, which suffers eclipse in certain of its members. St. Thomas on Revelation 6.

*The Maccabean.* The Church is prefigured in the Mother of the Maccabees <note>A Jewish martyr who encouraged her seven sons to die for their faith rather than break God's law</note>. St. Isidore in the Book of Maccabees: The Church is the Maccabean mother. St. Augustine, Discourse 2 on Psalm 68.

*Magdalene, — Martha* signifies the Church in this life, — Mary demonstrates the same Church resting in the future age. St. Isidore in his *Allegories*. Mystically, Simon the Leper signifies the world, first unfaithful and later faithful; however, the woman with the alabaster jar signifies the faith of the Church. — The house filled with fragrance is heaven and earth; the broken jar is carnal desire, which is broken when Christ reclines (that is, when He humbles Himself) so that the faith of the sinful woman might touch Him. St. Jerome, cited by St. Thomas in the *Golden Chain* on Mark 14. Mary Magdalene bore the figure of the Church. St. Augustine, Sermon 150 *On the Season*.

*Great.* The Church is "Great" in its expansion, power, and dignity. St. Thomas on Psalm 21. *In the great Church,* that is, in the Catholic Church; which is great in power and firmness. Matthew 16: *The gates of hell, etc.* — And great in its spread. Malachi 1: *From the rising of the sun even to its setting, etc.* St. Thomas on Psalm 39. What is it that adds "great"? Except that it was previously not great? What is great, if not that which is gathered from all parts of the whole world? St. Isidore on Psalm 39.

*The Pomegranate* <note>original: "Malogranatum"</note> is the Church, having within itself a multitude of peoples through the number of its seeds. St. Isidore, chapter 11 on Numbers.

*Pomegranate* <note>original: "Malum punicum"</note> is the Church itself: because while it nourishes many peoples in the unity of faith, it binds many seeds together under one rind. St. Gregory the Great on Song of Songs 4.

*Mary* signifies the Church: who, since she is betrothed to Christ, as a Virgin conceived us by the Holy Spirit, and as a Virgin also gives birth. St. Isidore in his *Allegories*. These women (the Marys in John 20) hold the feet of Christ; they hold the pattern <note>original: "typum"</note> of Gospel preaching in the Church; and they earn this by their haste. St. Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 76. Finally, the same Mary later both goes and announces; but now carrying the image not of a woman, but of the Church: so that there, like a woman, she may keep silent, but here, as the Church, she may proclaim.

*Martha and Mary;* the Church and faith are understood. Arnobius, Annotations on John 4.

*The Table* placed in Exodus 43 <note>likely referring to the Tabernacle instructions</note> bore the pattern of the peace and faith of the Church. St. Isidore, chapter 43 on Exodus.

*The Noonday.* *Where do you dwell at midday?* <note>Song of Songs 1:7</note> You know the "Noonday" to be the Church, which holds Christ; and do you seek Him in the nights? — To me you were as the morning, when I still believed; but I did not believe fully. St. Ambrose, Sermon 2 on Psalm 118.

<column-break/>

*The Mountain.* Why did the Scripture call her a mountain? Because she cannot be overturned. Why does it call the same a rock? Because she cannot be shaken or corrupted. St. John Damascene, *Parallels*, book 2, chapter 14. Mystically, in the mountain and the tabernacle, the present Church or the heavenly Church is designated. St. Thomas on Psalm 42. The Mount of Olives designates the fruitful height of the Holy Church. Venerable Bede, cited by St. Thomas in the *Golden Chain* on Mark 13. He calls the Church a mountain on account of her eminence and firmness. St. Augustine on Psalm 2. His holy mountain is His holy Church. That is the mountain which grew from a tiny stone in Daniel 2, so that it filled the entire face of the earth. St. Augustine on Psalm 42.

*The Woman.* The Canaanite woman herself bears the figure of the Church from the Gentiles <note>non-Jewish people</note>. St. Isidore in his *Allegories*. Like a dog, she sought crumbs from the table of the Masters, that is, to be satisfied by the doctrines of the Apostles and Prophets. Ibid. The woman who found the lost silver coin <note>original: "drachmam"</note> is the Church. Ibid. The woman who had an infirmity for 18 years and was cured by the Lord is a pattern of the Church. Ibid. The adulterous woman, who is offered by the Jews to the Lord to be stoned, is the Church from the Gentiles: which previously, having abandoned God, had committed "fornication" with idols. Ibid. The woman who anointed the head of the Lord with ointment is the Church. Ibid. The woman with the flow of blood is the Church — moreover, His garment, which she touched, is the Body of Christ. The twelve years <note>of her illness</note> demonstrate the number of the Apostles. Arnobius, chapter 13 on Matthew. *The woman clothed with the Sun,* that is, the Church clothed or adorned by the illuminating Christ. She is called a woman because the knowledge of the Divine Word generates children for her Spouse. St. Thomas on Revelation 12. This woman who takes the leaven and hides it <note>Matthew 13</note> seems to me to be the Church, gathered from diverse nations. She takes the leaven, namely the understanding of the Holy Scriptures. St. Jerome, cited by St. Thomas in the *Golden Chain* on Matthew 13. *A woman clothed with the sun.* Revelation 12. This authority is understood literally as the Church. She is clothed with the Sun, that is, with Christ from the clarity of the faith which He Himself preached — *The Moon,* that is, the science of Philosophy, *is under her feet,* and not upon her head: because in matters of faith no one ought to guide themselves by Philosophy — because Philosophers are like servants who do not know the secrets of the King, or like advisors. — *And on her head a Crown of twelve Stars,* that is, fashioned from the twelve articles of faith. 2 Timothy 4: *I have fought the good fight... there is laid up for me a Crown.* St. Vincent Ferrer, Sermon 13 on the 5 Crowns. I think this woman in John 4 <note>The Samaritan woman</note> is the Church gathered from the nations; who, having passed through five thousand years, when she was subject to the fornications of idols in the sixth millennium, purged all her ignominy at the coming of the fountain of Christ. St. Ambrose, Sermon 31.

*The Ship.* The Christian Church is like a ship with three decks: 1. The lower is for the Religious <note>those in monastic orders</note>, just as the lower deck is hidden; so the religious person ought to be hidden in the cloister. 2. It signifies the state of the Priest...

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Pythagoras's education under Thales of Miletus. The previous page established Thales's great age and reputation. This page describes the transition of Pythagoras from a student of Thales to a traveler seeking deeper wisdom in Egypt.</meta>

Our subject had devoted himself <note>The author uses "noſter" or "our man" to refer to Pythagoras, indicating a close biographical focus.</note> to these studies, as he was inflamed by the greatest desire for learning, more than perhaps anyone else at any time. He could not remain hidden for long, but soon became especially dear to the teachers he studied under. They discovered that he surpassed even his already widespread reputation, leaving his fellow students many parasangs <note>A parasang is an ancient Persian unit of distance, roughly three to four miles. Here it is used metaphorically to mean he was far ahead of his peers.</note> behind, and they were amazed by him. Indeed, Thales himself, having imbued the youth with various doctrines, did not hesitate to prefer this young man to his own elderly self. He felt that he was neither provided with such great natural gifts nor could he match him in disciplined practice <note>original Greek: *askēsei*, meaning rigorous training or exercise</note>.

For this reason, Thales urged him to travel to Egypt and to connect himself with the greatest possible familiarity with the priests of Memphis and the priests of Jupiter <note>The author refers to the Egyptian god Amun, whom the Greeks and Romans identified with Zeus or Jupiter.</note> in particular. For in this way, he would acquire the greatest wisdom among mortals and would rise even above the human condition. One might believe that these praises, with whatever intention Thales bestowed them upon his disciple, were more harmful than beneficial to Pythagoras, since nothing is more effective for inspiring self-love <note>original Greek: *philautian*, often implying vanity or excessive self-regard</note> and that which constantly follows it...

# BOOK THREE #

...from whom my purpose might be guided, not to mention the many types of exercises which, because they have fallen out of use in our times and the ancients' method of performing them is no longer maintained, we must guess at how they were done or what they were like, rather than affirm anything with certainty. This is what happens regarding the *Cricilasia* and the *trochus* <note>The *trochus* was an iron hoop or wheel used for exercise, often driven by a rod.</note>. For although Oribasius <note>A 4th-century Greek medical writer and personal physician to the Emperor Julian.</note> seems to have explained the method and form of *krikēlasia*—which in Latin means "hoop-driving"—based on the writings of Antyllus, the matter itself is so shrouded in darkness that it is very difficult for any learned person to distinguish the exact form and conditions of such an exercise. But lest anyone justly mark us with the crime of thick ignorance, rashness, fear, or arrogance, I will bring forward the Greek words of Oribasius himself, copied from a Vatican codex, as read in the 6th book of his *Medical Collections* addressed to Julian.

<margin>Chapter 26.</margin>
> The hoop should have a diameter smaller than the height of the person, so that its height reaches as far as the chest. It should be driven not in a straight line, but in a winding path. The driver <note>The "driver" (elater) was the rod used to push the hoop.</note> should be made of iron with a wooden handle. Some people thought the thin rings attached to the wheel were unnecessary, but this is not the case; rather, the noise they make creates a sense of relaxation and delight for the mind. <note>original Greek: Ἐλλάσσονα δὲ χέτω ὁ κρίκος... καὶ ἡδονὴν τῇ ψυχῇ</note>

> That is: Let the hoop have a diameter smaller than the man's height, so that its height reaches up to the breasts, and let it be driven not lengthwise, but crosswise; let the driver be iron with a wooden handle. Some have thought the thin rings placed around the wheel were superfluous: but this is not the case at all; rather, the sound produced by them generates relaxation and pleasure for the mind.

From these words it is clearly evident that in this exercise, men were accustomed to drive a large hoop—to the circumference of which small rings were fixed—using a specific iron rod with a handle, pushing it sideways. From this practice, Marcus Cicero <note>The famous Roman orator and statesman.</note> drew a metaphor in his 9th letter of the 2nd book to Atticus, where he wrote: "Believe me, it happened quite charmingly, and this wheel of state <note>original: "orbis hic in repub."; Cicero uses the hoop as a metaphor for a political cycle or shift.</note> has turned with less noise than I expected." But since it is not used in this age, we can certainly guess at it, but it is not possible to fully know its form and conditions. As for the fact that it was a Greek wheel, about which Horace wrote in the 3rd book of his *Odes*:

-> *Or if you bid him play with the Greek hoop,* <-
<note>original Latin: "Seu Graeco iubeas trocho"; Horace is contrasting traditional Roman virtues with the "softness" of Greek sports.</note>

this may indeed be so; but for this reason, nothing more certain will be established, since that is equally unknown to us. Similarly, someone might perhaps imagine in their mind what the *petaurum* <note>A specialized acrobatic device, sometimes resembling a see-saw or a high-swinging balance beam.</note> was; yet they will very easily see that the matter is otherwise once they realize it was a wooden machine by which men were tossed into the air by certain wheels...

# CRITIQUE OF CELEBRATED AUTHORS

...not with slow steps, but hurrying toward the ultimate goal of Sacred Theology. While he had already continued this long course of study with some success, a certain desire seized his mind to dedicate a <term>History of English Affairs</term> <gloss>Historia Rerum Anglicarum</gloss> to posterity. Therefore, with good omens, taking his beginning from William the Norman down to the times of Edward, second of that name, that is, from the year of Christ 1066 to the year 1308, he wrote the deeds of the English with the greatest care. <note>From John Leland's manuscript On Illustrious Men.</note>

Walter of Hemmingford describes the deeds of the English in a style that is not inelegant, with great care and equal faithfulness. <note>From William Horman in his collections.</note>

Love of his Fatherland impelled him to read the histories of England, to select from them things worthy of note, and to hand them down to posterity with an accurate method. <note>From John Pits, On the Illustrious Writers of England.</note>

In the territory of the Brigantes is Gisburgh, now a small town, which brought great glory to itself while it stood. It was a very beautiful and wealthy monastery, which produced Walter of Hemmingford, a historian who was not unlearned. <note>From Quenstedt.</note>

Several copies of this History exist. Two are kept in Trinity College at Cambridge. A third is held by the Office of Arms, or the Heralds. A fourth is in the Cottonian Library. A fifth is in my possession. I remember seeing others, though their locations do not come to mind now. <note>From Thomas Gale.</note>

---

### ARNOLD OF VILLANOVA

<margin>Famous in the year 1260.</margin>
The Aragonese, I know well, still try to claim Arnold of Villanova for Catalonia today, but in vain, since he was born in Narbonnese Gaul, in the town of Villanova, in the year 1300. He taught medicine in France. He was a man skilled in the Greek language, and also in Hebrew, as can be seen in his explanation of the booklet on the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <gloss>the four-letter name of God</gloss>. He was also not ignorant of Arabic. Furthermore, he searched into the secrets of Nature so deeply that almost no one after his time penetrated further. <note>From Paul Colomiès, Oriental Gaul.</note>

Arnold of Villanova was most skilled in medicine at that time. However, he had greater fame than praise, because he seemed to defile his noble genius and great erudition with perverse superstitions and perverse opinions about religion. For this reason, he was marked with ignominy by the Inquisitors some time later, and the books which he had published in great number were rejected. I have an author who affirms that he formed a human body from human seed using certain medicines in a vessel. <note>From the Jesuit Juan de Mariana, Book 14, Chapter 9, On Spanish Affairs.</note>

Arnold of Villanova was a Spaniard, an exceptionally learned man. He was most skilled in the Hebrew, Greek, Arabic, and Latin languages, as well as in Philosophy and Theology. He flourished 300 years ago. He is counted by the Pope and his supporters among the heretics because he reproved their errors. This Doctor had many listeners and followers even after death, especially in Spain, whom the papists called Arnoldists...

Charles, having been called and requested, began his journey toward Italy so that he might restore the Roman Church—which had been thrown into disorder by warring factions—to its former security. Once Italy and the remaining shores were pacified, he finally set out for Rome.

There, after several days, an investigation was conducted regarding the crimes that had been alleged against Pope Leo <note>Pope Leo III, whose papacy was marked by conflict with the Roman nobility</note> by his enemies. The rebellious Roman citizens—some of whom were leaders of the city and who had treated the Pope quite poorly—numbering three hundred in total, were ordered by Charles to be beheaded on a single day in the Lateran Field <note>original: "Campo Lateranensi," the area surrounding the Lateran Palace in Rome</note>. # CHEMICAL DICTIONARY

<page-num>162</page-num>

->## LEXICON CHYMICUM ##<-

*Phoenix*, the fifth essence <note>the most purified "quintessence"</note> of fire is so called; likewise that most celebrated Stone of the Philosophers.

*Physiognomy*, that art is so called by which the property and nature of humans is known from the face down to the chest, so that a judgment may be made from one's appearance regarding their character and readiness.

*Pulpezia*, or *pulpelxia*, is a stupor, a state of being stunned, apoplexy, or "sideration" <note>original: "syderatio"; a sudden stroke or paralysis once believed to be caused by the influence of the stars</note>.

*Presage*, is some notable sign preceding the history of a future event, from which a prophecy is sometimes derived.

*Preservatives*, are medicines defending life from its enemies and corruptions.

*Press*, is a wine-press or an instrument by which crushed species <note>raw medicinal materials</note> are squeezed out.

*Primales*, deceptive bodies are so called, placed before our eyes by the stars, about which *Paracelsus* <note>a famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</note> discusses more at length in the same place through *Matthew*; they are called *Pruma* elsewhere.

*Pruinum*, is called the first species of tartar <note>the potassium bitartrate crust that forms in wine casks</note>.

*Pusta*, is the digestion of gore <note>original: "saniei"</note>, named after pus.

*Putrescence*, is the first matter of generation; but it is better said that *Putrefaction* is taken for corruption in the process of alteration <note>the alchemical idea that something must rot to be transformed into a new life or substance</note>.

It is easy to see the difference between this man and that true and genuine Metellus of the Numidian line. The latter would not help L. Lucullus, his sister’s husband—with whom he got along very well—by his own praise; while this man forces cities to provide praise through violence and fear. When I realized that recent messages and tribute records—not letters of recommendation—had carried much weight with him, I acted on the advice of the Syracusans themselves and made an attack on those registers in which each item was recorded. 

But behold, a new disturbance and brawl—so that you do not think him entirely naked and deserted in Syracuse, without friends or guests. A certain Theomnastus began to hold onto the records—a man ridiculously insane, whom the Syracusans call "Theoractus." He is the kind of person whom boys follow around and everyone mocks as soon as he starts to speak. Yet his insanity, which is laughable to others, was quite annoying to me at that time. For as he foamed at the mouth, with burning eyes, and shouting at the top of his lungs that I was using violence against him, we reached the court together. 

Here I began to demand that I be allowed to seal the records and take them away; he argued the opposite. <header>HISTORY OF PHILOSOPHY.</header>

Xenophon provides an example of this in a dialogue with the Sophist Hippias (*Memorabilia*, Book IV, Chapter 4, sections 12 to 16, and 25). In that passage, Socrates asserts that the just man is the one who obeys the law, and that these laws are divine. Xenophon shows Hippias replying by asking how Socrates could declare it an absolute duty to obey the laws. Hippias points out that the people and the governors often reject laws by changing them, which proves that they are not absolute. 

But Socrates responds by asking if those who conduct war do not also eventually make peace. He argues that making peace does not condemn the war, because each state of affairs was just in its own turn. In short, Socrates says that the best and happiest state is the one in which the citizens share the same mind and are obedient to the law. This represents one side of the argument, where Socrates ignores the potential contradictions and treats laws and justice as they are accepted by each individual as the positive content of morality. 

However, if we ask what these laws actually are, we find they are simply those that are valued at a specific time. They appear in the state and in the minds of the people as they happen to exist. At another time, these laws cancel themselves out as they are redefined. Therefore, they are not held to be absolute.

B. We see this other, negative side of the issue when Socrates brings Euthydemus into the conversation. He asks Euthydemus whether he strives after the virtue that makes a private man or a citizen useful to himself, his people, or the state. Euthydemus declares that this is undoubtedly true. Socrates replies that this is not possible without justice. He then asks whether Euthydemus has achieved justice within himself. 

Euthydemus answers that he has, saying he believes he is no less just than any other man. Socrates replies that just as craftsmen can show the products of their labor, the just man should be able to say what his works are. Euthydemus agrees and says he could easily do so. Socrates then proposes that if this is true, they should write down a list. Under the letter Delta <note>original: "$\Delta$"; the first letter of the Greek word *Dikaion*, meaning "Just"</note>, they would list the actions of the just.

<summary>Socrates argues that while a just man obeys the laws of his state, those laws are often temporary and subjective rather than absolute. He begins a dialogue with Euthydemus to define the specific actions that constitute justice.</summary>

# 460 THE BORROWED DAYS.

They have, however well intended, greatly favored the cause of vice and dissipation without doing any essential service to rational religion. Complaints appear to have been made in almost every synod and council regarding the licentiousness introduced by keeping vigils. Nor will the philosopher wonder at this, for it has its foundation in the nature of things.

---

->THE BORROWED DAYS.<-

THERE is a singular old proverb preserved in Ray's Collection: "April borrows three days of March, and they are ill."

"April" is pronounced with an emphasis on the last syllable, so as to create a jingling rhyme with "ill," the last word in the line.

I have taken notice of this because I find in the ancient Calendar of the Church of Rome, to which I have so often referred, the following observations on March 31st:

"The rustic fable concerning the nature of the month."

"The rustic names of six days which shall follow in April, or may be the last in March<margin>a</margin>." There is no doubt but that these observations in the ancient calendar, and our proverb, are derived from one common origin; but for want of more evidence, I am unable at present to trace them any further.

"You know that Monday is Sunday's brother;
Tuesday is such another;
Wednesday you must go to church and pray;
Thursday is half-holiday;
On Friday it is too late to begin to spin;
The Saturday is half-holiday again."

Hooker says: "Holy-days were set apart to be the landmarks to distinguish times."

<margin>a</margin> "Rustic fable concerning the nature of the month."

A striking instance of this is recorded by Dr. Moresin: "And it happened in the year 1582, at Lyons, during the Christmas Eve vigils, that two people were caught in adultery dancing after mass between midnight and one o'clock, when, apart from one or two altar candles, there was none other in the church..." (*Papatus*, p. 177.)

<summary>This page introduces the "Borrowed Days" of March and April and discusses the tendency for vigils and holy days to devolve into immoral behavior.</summary>

### HUMAN NATURE

builds up new structures upon the ruins created by that Quality. In persons of the <term>Motive temperament</term> <note>In phrenology, a physical type characterized by a strong bony and muscular frame, associated with energy, action, and physical leadership.</note> it inclines toward mechanical invention, creation and construction; while in persons of the <term>Mental temperament</term> <note>A type characterized by a large brain and nervous system relative to the body, associated with intellectual work, sensitivity, and thought.</note> it manifests in creating and constructing ideas, thoughts, theories, scientific classification, literary productions, etc., and in persons of the <term>Vital temperament</term> <note>A type characterized by well-developed internal organs and a rounded physique, associated with physical vigor, sociability, and a love of comfort.</note> it manifests in creating and improving upon things calculated to appeal to persons of that class. It manifests outer form in the lower and frontal part of the temples, backward and upward from the outer corner of the eye-brow (see group figure). Prof. O. S. Fowler <note>Orson Squire Fowler (1809–1887) was a leading American phrenologist who wrote extensively on character reading and social reform.</note> says:

> “In broad-built and stocky persons it causes this part of the temples to widen and bulge out, but in tall, long-headed persons it spreads out upon them, and hence shows to be less than it really is.”

It is directly below <term>Ideality</term> <note>The faculty associated with imagination, taste, and the appreciation of beauty.</note> and in front of <term>Acquisitiveness</term> <note>The drive to acquire, possess, and accumulate property or wealth.</note>.

<summary>This page describes how the faculty of Constructiveness expresses itself through different physical temperaments—mechanical for the Motive, intellectual for the Mental, and sensory for the Vital—while providing its specific cranial location.</summary>

Magnus, that was King of Norway, held his fee by wrong and tyranny, whom Edward sent away anon in great array with lords and knights and squires, fresh and gay, with archers fell. By craft he gained his land of Norway, whole, and seized it in his hand.

Earl Eustace of Boulogne, that had wedded Edward’s sister on his mother’s side, came to Edward at Dover, sore beset, where his men slew the townspeople that tide. Wherefore Earl Godwin, set full of pride, asked the King to have deliverance of the Earl’s men to abide his ordinance.

Notwithstanding, the townspeople slew his knight, for the same cause wherefore he denied it, but made peace than as he felt he had the light of Boulogne allied to his brother-in-law. For which Earl Godwin replied, and warred sore upon the King each day with his five sons in right foul array.

Not considering that the King had wed his daughter, and his treason had pardoned and hidden, concerning his brother Alfred whom he had murdered—whom the King then summoned, commanded, and bid to answer in his court, and advised definitely all that by them might be known.

At whose summons he would not then appear, but warred foul, both he and his five sons, for which the King exiled them all clear. But soon after, that land was arrived at Sandwich, so the King met him willingly, where lords had treated and accorded, and afterward no more discorded.

<margin>How Duke Siward of Northumberland in battle killed Macbeth, King of Scots, and crowned Malcolm at Scone by the precept of Saint Edward the Confessor, which Malcolm made homage to Saint Edward by his letters patent.</margin>

Duke Siward was then of Northumberland, in battle against King Macbeth, of Scotland, who was false of his bond. Which to the King he made, who takes heed, wherefore the King in charity, as I read, by his letters charged Duke Siward to take on hand to crown Malcolm, that was of Cumberland.

Which he did full mightily anon at Scone Abbey, where kings were all crowned.

*Hamzah’s Precepts:—* The first precept of <term>Ḥamzah</term> enjoins veracity in speech; the second, protection and mutual aid to the brethren in faith; the third, renunciation of all forms of former worship and false belief; the fourth, repudiation of the devil (<term>Iblīs</term>) and all forces of evil; the fifth, confession of the unity of the <term>Ḥākim</term>-God; the sixth, acquiescence in his acts no matter what they be; and the seventh, absolute submission and resignation to his divine will in both secret and public.¹

*Sources and Operation:—* The first two precepts enunciated by the founder of <term>Druzism</term> are ethical in their nature and therefore difficult to trace back to their origin. The genealogy of the third and fourth is likewise difficult to ascertain. The fifth is the dogma we treated before, and the rest are corollaries from that dogma. The operation of the first precept is, of course, circumscribed by the already established law of <term>dissimulation</term>.

Of these principles the second has perhaps been the most potent force in the life and history of the <term>Druze</term> people. It has made of the <term>Druze</term> community one compact social body, presenting more the aspects of a religious fraternal order than a sect. This fraternal feature is one of the distinctive characteristics of the <term>Druze</term> people and has, in a large measure, contributed to their survival to the present day. It has enabled them at the time of crisis to act in unison and as one body moved primarily by motives of self-interest and by the instinct of self-preservation.

*Hamzah’s Precepts:*—The first commandment of <term>Hamzah</term> <note>The primary author of the Druze scriptures and leader of the movement</note> commands truthfulness in speech; the second requires the protection and mutual assistance of fellow believers; the third calls for the rejection of all previous forms of worship and false beliefs; the fourth demands the rejection of the devil (<term>Iblis</term> <note>Arabic: the name for the primary devil or Satan</note>) and all forces of evil; the fifth is the acknowledgment of the oneness of the <term>Hakim</term>-God; the sixth is the quiet acceptance of his actions, whatever they may be; and the seventh is total submission and surrender to his divine will, both in private and in public.¹

*Sources and Operation:*—The first two commandments proclaimed by the founder of <term>Druzism</term> are ethical in nature and are therefore difficult to trace back to a specific single source. The origins of the third and fourth are likewise difficult to determine with certainty. The fifth is the core belief we discussed previously, and the remaining precepts are logical conclusions drawn from that belief. The practice of the first commandment (truthfulness) is, of course, limited by the already established law of <term>dissimulation</term> <note>The practice of concealing one's true faith to avoid persecution, known as *taqiyya*</note>.

Of these principles, the second—mutual aid—has perhaps been the most powerful force in the life and history of the <term>Druze</term> people. It has transformed the <term>Druze</term> community into a single, tight-knit social group, appearing more like a religious brotherhood than a mere sect. This brotherly characteristic is one of the defining features of the <term>Druze</term> people and has, in large part, contributed to their endurance to this day. It has enabled them, in times of crisis, to act together as a single unit, driven primarily by the need for self-preservation and the protection of their own interests.

---

The architecture is of an unique and ancient type, antedating most of the Rājpūt civil building now extant, and on the whole of a simple character; the interiors are coloured plain red or green, the walls are without decoration. The colouring is extremely rich, and much play is made with notes of black, particularly in the form of tassels; the use of gold and silver is very restricted.

It will be seen subsequently that many of these peculiarities connect these works very closely with those of Jammu.¹ The significance of this will be clearly expressed if we point out that the mannerisms of Rājasthānī and Hill Rājpūt painting cannot have been much differentiated previously to the consolidation of the Mughal Empire, which divided the Rājpūts of Rājasthān from those of the hills by the wide strip of the Pañjāb plains, where now runs the railway from Delhi to Lahore. The local peculiarity of the 18th century Kāngrā style is to be explained as a post-Mughal local development, while the common and archaic features of Jammu and early Rājasthānī paintings point to their early date, when free intercourse between the Rājpūts of Rājasthān and of the Hills was not yet interrupted.

The subject of night scenes may also be referred to here, as a good example occurs amongst the twenty-three *rāginīs* (Plate I). The representation of such scenes, where brightly illuminated figures are set against a dark background is most likely a very old motif in Indian art, for some such indications are essential to the representation of certain *nāyakās* (*Utkā* and *Abhisārikā*) and certain *rāginīs*; and such representations are vividly suggested in the visual character of many of the poetical descriptions. Mughal painters, on the other hand—possibly affected by European suggestions—developed night scenes in a more picturesque and realistic manner, often representing firelight and cast shadow;² and this method again reacted on the later schools of Rājpūt painting, as exemplified in Plate LXX, B.

Another beautiful work of the latter part of the 16th century is the *Gaurakarī Rāginī*, reproduced on Plate IV. Many of the same motifs are repeated, but the conventions are less violent and the drawing more refined. This work is closely related to the two *rāginīs* reproduced on Plates V and VI, and these again with all those of the British Museum MS. Or. 2821, which may be as late as the middle of the 17th century. They seem to form a local group, but there is nothing to indicate their exact source. It may be mentioned that at this time Orchā, as well as Amber, was a great centre of Rājpūt culture and art patronage; and the architecture in these pictures strongly recalls that of the early 17th century palaces at Orchā and Datiya. In all these works the architecture is represented with unusual care, paralleled only in some of the later Kāngrā works, where, however, it is of a very different and more feminine character.

Two other Rājasthānī works of the late 16th century are reproduced: the delicate fragment of Plate XVII, A, too much damaged for much remark; and the larger example of Plate VII, a fine work of a hieratic character.

Rājpūt mural painting of the early 17th century is preserved in the old palace at Bikāner, but I am not able to reproduce anything more than the excerpt given on Plate VIII; this is a copy admirably executed for me by a modern Bikāner craftsman, commissioned by the Mahārājā. This is a remarkable

The narrow strip of dark sky filled with ragged cloud is characteristic of Rājasthānī and Pahāṛī works alike, and may be regarded as archaic, for it occurs also in Jaina art of the 15th century (*Notes on Jaina Art*, ‘Journal of Indian Art’, Oct. 1914, Figures 1, 7, 13, 29, &c.; also Plate LXXVII, D, of the present work), and in Ceylon (*Mediaeval Sinhalese Art*, Plate XIX).

# RĀJASTHĀNĪ

[...continued from previous column] representation; but notwithstanding its more or less Chinese appearance, it differs from the clouds and lightning of the picture reproduced on Plate IV only in the stronger convention appropriate to mural art; there also the lightning is a red and gold snake. The falling rain is also repeated in many other works, conspicuously, for example, in the late Kāṅgṛā example of Plate LVIII. The lightning of most of the late Kāṅgṛā paintings (Plates LVIII, LXXI, B, LXXIII, A) is, however, much more realistic, and so are the clouds (Plate LV).

The suggestion of Far-Eastern art in the Bīkāner mural fragment is one that occasionally becomes conspicuous in Rājasthānī art,<note>These Chinese motifs are referred to by Sir George Watt, *Indian Art at Delhi*, 1904, pp. 170, 180, etc.</note> particularly at Bīkāner, where true Chinese clouds are painted on the lacquered shields, and at Udaipur, where the wall-painting of the island palaces, perhaps by an 18th-century hand, evidently repeats a Chinese model. Among Pahāṛī drawings, also, one occasionally meets with a copy of some Chinese motif. The Chinese element in Rājput art, however, is purely sporadic and cannot be traced as an integral factor, as it became in Persian painting and, to a smaller extent, in Mughal painting. In Rājput art, I am inclined to trace the Chinese motifs to sea-borne commerce. There has long existed an extensive importation of Chinese embroidery into Gujarāt, which continues today, while fragments of Chinese embroidery several centuries old are often found in Western India, associated with purely Indian work.

The most familiar Rājasthānī painting is that of Jaipur in the 18th century.<note>This art continued to flourish during the 19th century and is scarcely yet extinguished, notwithstanding that pupils in the local "School of Art" may now be seen laboriously studying from mural diagrams of English farm animals.</note> Its most impressive examples are the large cartoons represented on Plates IX and X, selected from a number of the working drawings (mostly pricked for reproduction by pouncing) designed for two large paintings on cloth now preserved in the library of the Mahārāja of Jaipur, and probably executed in the latter part of the 18th century. In these works, and another large picture reproduced on Plate XI, we see the persistence of ancient art, not merely as a miniature adaptation, but on its true scale.<note>See also *Indian Drawings*, ii, Plates I-V, and the *Burlington Magazine*, March 1912, Plate IV. Very slightly Mughalized versions of this type also occur; an example from Bodleian MS. Ouseley Add. 167, f. 2 is reproduced in *Indian Drawings*, i, Pl. XV. See also Plate XX of the present work (small in scale, but like in physiognomy).</note> These large works are in the purest idiom of Hindū art, handed down from century to century with a certainty and loyalty only paralleled in the transmission of sacred texts. We wonder at the persistence of tradition in the art of Egypt; it is scarcely less remarkable that the Hindūs, through centuries of religious evolution and warfare, should have been able to preserve almost to our own time so much of the grandeur that belongs to the art of the period of their supreme achievement.<note>"Asia has been called the cradle of mankind. What confirms this title of honor is that the old civilizations in the heart of Asia, with wonderful self-reliance, have remained true to a primitive art which is linear, decorative, and founded in handicraft. We Westerners have greatly prided ourselves on a 'progress' from stiff and primitive art to an art of realism; we have wearily pursued nature; and today we are face to face with an aesthetic bankruptcy which regards a Böcklin or a Klinger—as who should say, the type of the Royal Academy—as rather to be approved than condemned. And laboriously we are feeling our way back to those sources of art from which the more fortunate Asiatics have scarcely departed." H. Hieber, *Die Miniaturen des frühen Mittelalters* [The Miniatures of the Early Middle Ages], Munich, 1912, p. 72.</note> These works alone are sufficient proof of the authentic and indigenous character of Rājput painting.

These works are an immediate expression of the Hindū view of life. Here is that distinct, sharp, and wiry bounding line that William Blake—the most Indian of modern Western minds—regarded as the golden rule of art and life. A line so deliberate, so self-confident, so full of wonder at the beauty of the world (especially the beauty of women), and at the same time so austere, could not be a sudden achievement, nor depend on the brilliance of a single personality. It is the product of a whole civilization and of aristocratic traditions protected by priestly sanctions. In this work there is no room for cleverness; too haughty to admire ingenuity, too distinguished to affect a calligraphic elegance, or to feel the smallest interest in any attempt to create an illusion of modeling, it is an art both proud, passionate, and very reserved. It is sometimes said that the Indians have left no history; but what else than history is any work of traditional art? Of such art, we can at least say that it is not a product of chance, but is determined by antecedent racial *karma* <term>the sum of a person's actions in this and previous lives</term>, and cannot...

<summary>This page explores Chinese influences on Rājput art, the persistence of traditional Hindū art in Jaipur, and the character of Rājput painting as a deeply traditional, aristocratic, and proud reflection of Hindū life and civilization.</summary>
<keywords>Chinese influence, Jaipur, Rājput painting, Hindū art, William Blake, karma, tradition, aesthetics</keywords>

->AESAR INTELLECTUAL FIRE OR LOGH.—CHAP. V. SECT. XII.<-

The first, beginning at the bottom of the series, is Aesar.* He is called God; or fire intelligent, Dia or Logh: Mr. Vallencey says, the word Logh means the spiritual flame, and identifies itself with the Λογος of the Greeks. In a vast number of languages the word Logh, standing for some idea relating to fire, is to be found. The word Aesar, in Irish, literally means to kindle a fire. In Chaldean, אזה aza, to illuminate, אשא asa, fire. Sanscrit Osch,† fire or heat. By many of the ancient philosophers fire was considered as the primitive element, and it is unnecessary to say any thing of the fire of the Magi, or of the numerous examples of the appearance of God as a fire to Moses, the sacred fire of the Israelites, &c.

Mr. Selden says, “Although you may truly say with Origen that, before our Saviour’s time, Britain acknowledged not one true God, yet it came as near to what they should have done, or rather nearer than most of others, either Greek or Roman, as by notions in Cæsar, Strabo, Lucan, and the like discoursing of them, you may be satisfied. For although Apollo, Mars, Mercury, were worshiped among the vulgar Gauls, yet it appears that the Druids’ invocation was to one all-healing or all-saving Power.”‡ <margin>the Sun.</margin>

As fire was supposed to be the first principle of all things, it was also supposed, by a peculiar refinement, to be the destroyer, whence, probably, first arose the idea of the Creator and the Destroyer being identified. The primitive fire was supposed to have an insatiable appetite for devouring all things. According to Maximus Tyrius, the ancient Persians threw into the fire combustible matters, crying, Devour, O Lord!§ It is remarkable, that in Irish, easam or asam signifies to make or create. Aesar, then, would be the creator. Aesar was also connected with the power of magic, and he was called a magician. The word אָסַר asr, in Hebrew, has the meaning of ligavit, obligavit, with the signification of incantare. According to Schelling,|| the Eastern words which have the signification of binding, have generally the signification of incantation. He attempts to explain the meaning of the word Osiris by אָסַר asr, ais, ¶ incantator ignis. He founds this interpretation on the Samaritan text of the 18th chapter and 11th verse of Deuteronomy, which renders חבר חבר hbr, hbr, ligans, ligationem, by אָסַר asr, asr, which puts out of doubt the signification of magic. The first god, beginning at the bottom of the series, is Aesar.* He is called God, or "intelligent fire," *Dia* or *Logh*. Mr. Vallencey says the word *Logh* means the spiritual flame and identifies itself with the *Logos* <note>original: Λογος</note> of the Greeks. In a vast number of languages, the word *Logh* is found, standing for some idea relating to fire. The word *Aesar* in Irish literally means "to kindle a fire." In Chaldean, *aza* (אזה) means to illuminate; *asa* (אשא) means fire. In Sanskrit, *Osch*† means fire or heat. By many of the ancient philosophers, fire was considered the primitive element; it is unnecessary to say anything regarding the fire of the Magi, or the numerous examples of the appearance of God as a fire to Moses, the sacred fire of the Israelites, and so on.

Mr. Selden says, "Although you may truly say with Origen that, before our Savior's time, Britain did not acknowledge the one true God, yet it came as near to what they should have done—or rather nearer than most others, whether Greek or Roman—as you may be satisfied by the notions in Caesar, Strabo, Lucan, and similar authors discussing them. For although Apollo, Mars, and Mercury were worshipped among the common Gauls, it appears that the Druids' invocation was to one all-healing or all-saving Power."‡ <margin>The Sun.</margin>

As fire was supposed to be the first principle of all things, it was also supposed, through a particular refinement, to be the destroyer; from this, probably, the idea of the Creator and the Destroyer being identified first arose. The primitive fire was supposed to have an insatiable appetite for devouring all things. According to Maximus Tyrius, the ancient Persians threw combustible matters into the fire, crying, "Devour, O Lord!"§ It is remarkable that in Irish, *easam* or *asam* signifies "to make" or "to create." *Aesar*, then, would be the creator. *Aesar* was also connected with the power of magic, and he was called a magician. The word *asr* (אָסַר) in Hebrew has the meaning of "he bound" or "he tied," with the secondary meaning of "to enchant" or "to cast a spell." According to Schelling,|| Eastern words that have the meaning of binding generally also mean incantation. He attempts to explain the meaning of the word *Osiris* by *asr* (אָסַר) and *ais* (אִישׁ),¶ meaning "enchanter of fire." He bases this interpretation on the Samaritan text of the 18th chapter and 11th verse of Deuteronomy, which renders *hbr, hbr* (חבר חבר), "binding a binding," as *asr, asr* (אָסַר אָסַר), which puts the meaning of magic beyond doubt. # SEVENTEENTH SUGGESTION.

# I LISTEN.

# SEVENTEENTH MEDITATION.

I go into the silence and open my inner hearing to the "still, small voice." The sanctuary of the soul is the "Holy of Holies," the meeting place of the divine and the human. The tribunal of God is at the soul-center of man. The divine likeness is unveiled here. It is the "manger" where the <term>Christ-consciousness</term> is born, while external discords are only the animals in the stall. It is the angel who brings "good news of great joy." Here the resurrection takes place, when the stone of the lower self-consciousness is rolled away. Here is the divine affinity which feels its oneness with God. "The kingdom of God does not come with outward observation; neither will they say, 'Look, here!' or 'There!' for look, the kingdom of God is within you." That kingdom includes wholeness, harmony, and health. The sun of righteousness arises with "healing in his wings."

The Lord was not in "the wind," "the earthquake," nor "the fire," but in the "still, small voice." As we feel the <term>Presence</term>, we receive an impression of its beauty and perfection.

### CHAPTER IX

#### THE MONASTERY ARCHITECTURALLY CONSIDERED

The disposition of the monastic buildings naturally varies according as the site is an open or a restricted one, but certain governing principles are constant. The notable difference between the Eastern and Western monastery plans is the position of the church. Whereas our monastic churches usually occupy one side of a court, the Orthodox make it, where conditions allow, the central building of the whole: it normally stands free in the court, and in a cramped site it is always the court, never the church, which is curtailed, though the actual size of the church is small by Gothic standards. But that which is useless to them, and beneficial to us, will be the reward which we receive from them [of our attention to their concerns]. In sacrifices, therefore, we should abstain from animals. For, though all things are in reality the property of the Gods, yet plants appear to be our property; since we sow and cultivate them, and nourish them by other attentions which we pay to them. We ought to sacrifice, therefore, from our own property, and not from the property of others; since that which may be procured at a small expense, and which may easily be obtained, is more holy, more acceptable to the Gods, and better adapted to the purposes of sacrifice, and to the exercise of continual piety. Hence, that which is neither holy, nor to be obtained at a small expense, is not to be offered in sacrifice, even though it should be present.

14. But that animals do not rank among things which may be procured easily, and at a small expense, may be seen by directing our view to the greater part of our race: for we are not now to consider that some men abound in sheep, and others in oxen. In the first place, therefore, there are many nations that do not possess any of those animals which are offered in sacrifice, some ignoble animals, perhaps, excepted. And, in the second place, most of those that dwell in cities themselves, possess these but rarely. But if some one should say that the inhabitants of cities have not mild fruits in abundance; yet, though this should be admitted, they are not in want of the other vegetable productions of the earth; nor is it so difficult to procure fruits as it is to procure animals. Hence an abundance of fruits, and other vegetables, is more easily obtained than that of animals. But that which is obtained with facility, and at a small expense, contributes to incessant and universal piety.

<header>ON ABSTINENCE FROM [ANIMAL FOOD.—BOOK II.]</header>

However, what is useless to the plants but beneficial to us—such as their fruit—will be the reward we receive from them in exchange for our care for them. Therefore, in our sacrifices, we should refrain from using animals. For while everything in reality belongs to the Gods, plants seem more like our own property because we sow, cultivate, and nurture them with our own labor.

We should offer sacrifices from our own property, not from the property of others. Offerings that are inexpensive and easy to obtain are more holy, more pleasing to the Gods, and better suited for the purpose of sacrifice and the practice of constant devotion <note>original: "piety"</note>. Therefore, anything that is not holy, or that cannot be obtained at a small expense, should not be offered as a sacrifice, even if it is available.

14. We can see that animals are not among the things that are easy or cheap to obtain by looking at the majority of the human race; we should not only consider the few wealthy men who have plenty of sheep and oxen. First, there are many nations that do not even possess the types of animals usually offered in sacrifice, except perhaps for some lowly <note>original: "ignoble"</note> species. Second, most people who live in cities rarely own such animals.

Someone might argue that city-dwellers do not have an abundance of cultivated <note>original: "mild"</note> fruits. Even if that were true, they do not lack other plant products from the earth; it is never as difficult to find fruits as it is to find animals. Thus, an abundance of fruits and other vegetables is much easier to obtain than an abundance of animals. Since these items are easy and inexpensive to get, they encourage a lifestyle of constant and universal devotion.

15. Experience also shows that the Gods take more pleasure in these simple gifts than in lavish <note>original: "sumptuous"</note> offerings. For instance, when a certain man from Thessaly <note>Thessaly was a region in ancient Greece.</note> sacrificed oxen with gilded horns to the Pythian deity <note>The God Apollo at the oracle of Delphi.</note>...

<summary>Porphyry argues that sacrifices should consist of plants rather than animals because plants are the product of human labor and are inexpensive, making constant devotion possible for everyone. He suggests that the Gods prefer these simple, accessible offerings over the costly and rare sacrifice of animals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the union between God and "eternal Nature," focusing on how this bond is rooted in an unchangeable love that exists beyond the reach of divine anger or judgment.</meta>

# God's Union with Eternal Nature

...perceive the effects of God's love and hatred, mercy and justice, sweetness and severity. Yet in pure nature—into which God has introduced himself, and which we are discussing here—nothing can ever be found except the effects of an unchangeable love. This unchangeable love is the bond <note>original: "band"</note> that creates the inseparable union between God and pure nature, and between the Deity and humanity. 

This love passes through and penetrates every part of eternal Nature in a living <note>original: "vital"</note> way, and eternal Nature, in turn, presses into this love. This makes the union of them both most intimate, living, and inseparable. Thus we may ask: who shall, or who can, separate God and pure nature? Or who can cancel <note>original: "disannul"</note> the eternal covenant between them? 

*But despite everything that has been said regarding this union between God and the principle of pure nature, we must understand that this union exists without confusion. God is not pure nature, nor is pure nature God. For although one exists within the other, nature cannot fully contain or understand <note>original: "comprehend"</note> the Deity; rather, God contains and understands nature.*

<summary>This page explains that the union between God and pure nature is defined by an all-penetrating, unchangeable love. It clarifies that while God and nature are intimately united, they remain distinct entities; God encompasses nature, but nature cannot fully contain God.</summary>

Lastly, they say she is a middle nature between thick and thin, neither altogether earthy nor altogether fiery but a mean aerial substance—to be found everywhere and every time of the year.

The liberal mind naturally experiences a difficulty in disbelieving where, a possibility being granted, the testimony in support of a matter is fair and honourable. And though sensible evidence and more than this sometimes is required to silence negative assertion; yet reason, supported by her witnesses, may enervate it, and induce that strict investigation and thought which should always precede experiment, but which the multitude have never yet been found willing to undertake; and are consequently led astray in progress, and learn as it were by chance. It is said that Lord Bacon instituted certain experiments with a view to the discovery of the philosopher's stone, and in the *Advancement of Learning* he faithfully recognises the possibility, as does also Sir Isaac Newton in his works; while Leibnitz devoted his early life to the pursuit: nor did either of these great men, though they were practically unsuccessful themselves, condemn the ancient tradition or deny its validity. Yet it would seem to be more ordinarily natural to the human mind to reject those things, which it has neither been early imbued in the belief of, nor instructed to understand; besides individual research into mere possibilities, and because facts only are alleged, is too hopeless and arduous for this short life, which requires a definite assurance of success, and fruit even from the smallest labour.

# Theophrasti Paracelsi

Vermes externi compositum ex colocinthide attingentes si moriantur / detur vermibus laboranti : Liquore ex centaurea moriuntur anguillae serpentis : Oleo ex semine hypericonis bufones : Stelliones / Lacertae . Semine harmelli aranea / Agarico muscae .

Omnis medicina vermes interimens Venenum est . Omnes autem purgationes in vermibus vanae sunt / nisi ea vermes occidantur . Pulvis lignorum medetur vermibus . Ex pinu pulvis maxime medetur recentibus vermibus ex nutrimentis natis . Pulvis ex ligno quaiacum tollit lumbricos / sed adduntur hisce carbones / et maxime de turbith et silere montano / et etiam ex agarico . Hoc idem praestat nigredo ex aere / quae se recolligit in imo .

In cura so man will vermes curieren / das die stuck so ausswendig die würm tödten / die tödten die würm auch inwendig / man darff nit auff purgation gehen / die würm die auß dem Holtz wachsen tödten alle würm de nutrimentis im leib / also das man ein wurm neme auß dem fleisch / vnnd thüt es zuo dieser nach compositum cum coloquintida / das die würm daran rüren oder essen / wann dann die würm sterben aussen / so sterben sie auch innen mit
translation:
# Theophrasti Paracelsi

External worms, a compound from <term>colocinth</term> <gloss>bitter apple</gloss>, if they are touched, they die; let it be given to those suffering from worms: by the liquor from <term>centaury</term>, snake-eels die: by oil from the seed of <term>hypericon</term> <gloss>St. John’s Wort</gloss>, toads: geckos, lizards. By the seed of <term>harmel</term>, the spider: by <term>agaric</term>, flies.

Every medicine killing worms is poison. But all purges are vain in worms unless the worms are killed by them. Powder of woods heals worms. From pine, the powder most heals recent worms born from nutrients. Powder from <term>guaiacum</term> wood removes roundworms, but coals are added to these, and mostly of <term>turbith</term> and <term>silere montanum</term> <gloss>mountain laserwort</gloss>, and also of <term>agaric</term>. This same thing is provided by the blackness from the air, which collects itself at the bottom.

In the cure, when one wants to cure worms, the pieces that kill worms on the outside, they also kill the worms on the inside; one does not need to go for a purge. The worms that grow from the wood kill all worms <note>original: "de nutrimentis"</note> in the body; thus one takes a worm from the flesh and adds it to this compound with <term>colocinth</term>, so that the worms touch or eat it; when then the worms die on the outside, they die also on the inside with

translation:
By all means, however, one should pay attention to the spring, especially to April and May, and in the summer to the month of August, etc. In short, in my opinion, this year will not pass without a particularly great dying in many lands.

The most certain and excellent cause of the pestilence and all diseases, as well as other punishments, is our sin, along with the immoderate, disorderly life, the excessive gluttony and drunkenness, which (alas) is far too common, etc.

<center>Deuteronomy 28</center>

If you will not obey the voice of the LORD your God, the LORD will attach the <term>pestilence</term> <gloss>original: "Sterbdrůsse," literally "dying-glands" or buboes</gloss> to you (because of your evil behavior) until He consumes you. The LORD will strike you with swelling, fever, heat, inflammation, drought, poisonous air, and <term>jaundice</term> <gloss>original: "Geelsucht"</gloss>, and will pursue you until He destroys you.

<center>Jeremiah 14</center>

I will visit their sins upon them and consume them with the sword, famine, and pestilence.

<center>Ezekiel 6</center>

Woe to all the abominations of wickedness in the house of Israel! Therefore they must fall by the sword, famine, and pestilence. He who is far off shall die of the pestilence, and he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who remains shall die of hunger, etc.

<center>Sirach 38</center>

Too much eating makes one sick, and an insatiable glutton gets the colic. Many have eaten themselves to death, but he who is moderate lives all the longer.

<center>The prognosis of Leopold of Austria from the Kalends of January.</center> <note>Leopold of Austria was a 13th-century astronomer whose work was popular in the Renaissance.</note>

If the <term>Kalends of January</term> <gloss>the first day of January</gloss> fall on a Friday, the winter will be troublesome and dry, there will be an abundance of grain, pains in the eyes, infants will die, and much hail will fall.

<center>The End.</center>

<center>Printed in Nuremberg by Valentin Fuhr, located on St. Lawrence Square.</center>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of motifs involving the awakening of the soul or its resuscitation by a divine figure, shifting from Zoroastrian and Manichaean examples to Babylonian parallels that validate previously skeptical readings of early Christian and Gnostic texts.</meta>

# Babylonian Concept of Awakening [Regarding Page 38]

---

...what seemed strange in the *Odes of Solomon* <note>A collection of 42 odes traditionally attributed to Solomon but actually early Christian or Gnostic hymns from the 1st or 2nd century AD, noted for their mystical and personal imagery.</note> and appeared unbelievable in the so-called *Hymn of the Soul* in the *Acts of Thomas* <note>A famous Gnostic poem, also known as the "Hymn of the Pearl," describing the soul's journey from a heavenly home to the material world and its eventual "awakening" and return.</note> has now found confirmation. We need not lament too much that fate has begrudged us the continuation of that wonderful song; its entire content is secured in its basic outlines.

[Recently, a Babylonian mystery of revivification has also become known to us through Zimmern, *Reports of the Saxon Society of Sciences* 70, 5, p. 45 ff. Certainly, it is not the <term>hieros logos</term> <note>original: "ἱερὸς λόγος"; literally "sacred word," referring to the foundational narrative, myth, or liturgy of a mystery religion.</note> or the liturgy itself; the sacred act seems to be used only as an image. A person saved from grave misfortune praises his savior Marduk <note>The patron deity of the city of Babylon and the head of the Babylonian pantheon, often associated with justice, healing, and creation.</note> and compares his rescue to an awakening from the grave. All Babylonians have recognized in this with astonishment the miraculous power of Marduk, who, after all, first created man. The conclusion is formed by the descriptive hymn of praise:

> "[I who h]ad descended into the grave, | I have re-
> ->turned to the gate of the liv[ing].<-
> [In the gate] of the fullness of life | I was gifted with the fullness of life,
> [In the g]ate of the great guardian spirit | my guardian
> ->spirit approached [me] again,<-
> [In the] gate of well-being | I beheld well-being,
> 5 In the gate of life | life was granted to me,
> In the gate of the sunrise | I was numbered among the
> ->living,<-
> In the gate of bright omens | my omens became bright,
> In the gate of absolution | my ban <note>A ritual or spiritual curse or restriction.</note> was released,
> In the gate of oral inquiry | my mouth made inquiry,
> 10 In the gate of the release of sighs | my sighing was released,
> In the gate of purification by water | I was sprinkled with
> ->purification water,<-
> In the gate of well-being | I was seen at the side of Marduk,
> In the gate of the pouring of abundance | I was laid at the
> ->feet of Sarpanitu.<- <note>The consort of Marduk, associated with pregnancy and birth.</note>
> In prayer and supplication | I sighed before them,
> 15 Good incense | I laid down before them."]

<summary>Reitzenstein links the "awakening" motifs in the Odes of Solomon and the Hymn of the Pearl to Babylonian traditions, specifically a hymn where a survivor compares his recovery to rising from the grave through the gates of Marduk's temple.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the bibliographic review of historical sources that documented or illustrated Gnostic gems. In the previous section, Bellermann discussed the seven images from Origen's diagrams; he now lists the 17th-century scholars who first categorized these artifacts, often confusing their symbolic elements.</meta>

*Ecclesiastical Annals* <note>original: "Baronii annales eccl."</note> Vol. II. Cologne 1624. folio.
P. 72.

*Claude Saumaise’s Discourse on Climacteric Years and Ancient Astrology.* <note>original: "Cl. Salmasii de annis climactericis et antiqua astrologia diatribe." Saumaise (1588–1653) was a renowned French classical scholar.</note> Leiden 1640. 8vo. Of the single stone appearing on page 573, a very similar one, if not the very same, can be found in Chiflet, No. 7, among others. Out of a rooster’s comb <note>A common feature of the Abraxas figure, which typically has the head of a rooster.</note>, Saumaise has—humorously enough—created a stag’s antlers.

*Athanasius Kircher’s Egyptian Oedipus.* <note>original: "Athanas. Kircheri Oedipus aegyptiacus." Kircher was a Jesuit polymath who attempted to decipher hieroglyphs.</note> Vol. II. Part II. Rome, 1653. folio. pp. 461 and 462. Seven *Abraxas* gems, numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 14. These appear again in Chiflet and others.

*John Macarius’s (Jean l'Heureux) Abraxas, or an Inquiry into Basilidian Gems.* <note>original: "Jo. Macarii (Jean Heureux) Abraxas, seu de gemmis Basilidianis disquisitio." Basilides was a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher in Alexandria.</note> Edited by Jean Chiflet. Antwerp 1657. 4to. In *Chiflet’s Miscellany.* <note>original: "Miscellanea Chifletiana."</note> Vol. VI. Among the 120 illustrated gems, only fifteen are true *Abraxas* <term>Abraxas|In Bellermann's classification, a 'true' Abraxas gem specifically depicts the creature with a rooster's head, human torso, and serpent legs</term>; the rest are *Abraxoids* <term>Abraxoids|Gems that resemble Abraxas stones in style or spirit but lack the specific central figure</term> and *Abraxasters* <term>Abraxasters|Stones that Bellermann considers lesser imitations or those containing only fragments of Gnostic motifs</term>.

*Lorenzo Pignoria’s Isiac Table.* <note>original: "Laur. Pignorii mensa Isiaca." A work discussing the "Bembine Tablet," an Egyptian-style bronze plate.</note> Amsterdam 1669. Large 4to. On the third plate stand five *Abraxas*, figures 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, and on Plate V, one figure 7, following Chiflet.

*Jacob Spon’s Miscellany of Learned Antiquity.* <note>original: "Jac. Sponii Miscellanea eruditae antiquitatis." Spon was a pioneer of archaeology.</note> Lyon 1679. folio. A single inscription from an *Abraxas*.

*The Roman Museum, or a Treasury of Learned Antiquity,* <note>original: "Romanum Museum, sive thesaurus eruditae antiquitatis"</note> in which gems, idols, etc. are recorded in 170 plates, through the care, study, and expense of *Michel-Ange de la Chausse.* Rome 1690. folio. Little of relevance here, though a particularly large *Abraxas* is included among them. (Montfaucon, Plate 145.)

*The Cabinet of the Library of Saint-Geneviève* <note>original: "Le cabinet de la Bibliotheque de St. Gèneviève"</note> by *Molinet.* Paris, 1692. Large folio. Relevant here are copperplate 29, figures 7, 8, 12, 14; Plate 30, figures 13, 15, 17, and others.

<summary>This page provides a chronological bibliography of major 17th-century scholarly works that cataloged and illustrated Gnostic gems, noting errors in their interpretation of symbols.</summary>
<keywords>bibliography, Claude Saumaise, Athanasius Kircher, Jean Chiflet, John Macarius, Abraxas, Abraxoids, Abraxaster, Gnostic gems, Michel-Ange de la Chausse</keywords>

Es entsteht dadurch ein ähnliches Verhältniss der begünstigten und nicht begünstigten Töne, aber alles eine Duodecime tiefer. <header>First Part. Fifth Section.</header>

One notices this clearly on both the violin and the cello, at least for the lowest natural tone, when one produces the corresponding notes on the strings. They sound particularly full, and the fundamental tone of these sounds emerges particularly strongly. I believe I have heard the same thing to a lesser degree for the a' of the violin, which corresponds to its higher natural tone.

Since the lowest tone of the violin is G, only the higher octaves of its three lowest notes can be somewhat strengthened by the resonance of the higher natural tone of its air mass. In general, however, the fundamental tones, especially of its higher notes, must be favored over the overtones, because the aforementioned fundamental tones lie closer to the natural tones of the air mass than the overtones. This produces an effect similar to that on the piano, where the construction of the hammers also favors the overtones of the deep notes and weakens those of the higher ones. In the cello, whose lowest string produces C, the stronger natural tone of the air mass lies, just as in the violin, a fourth to a fifth higher than that of the lowest string. This creates a similar ratio of favored and non-favored tones, but everything is a twelfth lower. In the viola, on the other hand, the most favored tones, corresponding roughly to b', do not lie between those of the first and second string, but between the second and third, which seems to be related to the changed timbre of this instrument. Unfortunately, this influence cannot yet be expressed in figures. The maximum of resonance for the natural tones of the air mass is not exactly very strongly pronounced; otherwise, it would cause a much greater inconsistency in the scale of the aforementioned string instruments as soon as one passed the part of the scale in which the natural tones of their air masses lie. Accordingly, it is to be suspected that the influence on the relative strength of the individual partial tones of the sounds of these instruments is not very prominent.

### 5. Sounds of flute pipes.

In the instruments belonging to this class, the tone is produced by driving a stream of air against the opening of a cavity filled with air, which is usually provided with sharp edges.

# CAPVT IIII.

### Erkennung von Stichen/ Pfeilschuß/ Fall/ vnd Knütschung.

<margin>A</margin>Nun weiter von andern gschlechten der Wunden/ als von Stich/ Pfeilschuß/ Fall/ vñ dergleichen. Zwischen diesen vnd den Wunden ist kein vnderscheid irs wesens/ als allein in dem/ daß ein solcher Stich/ oder Pfeil dem Anfall/ seiner Enge halben/ nicht mag statt geben/ darumb er weiter in das Fleisch vnd Adern gehet/ dann ein Wunden. Dann es ist eines jeglichen Anfals art/ daß er vil Höle vmb sich haben wil/ vnd Weite. Darumb die offnen Wunden/ so nit verhefft/ mit weniger Anfalls vnd Sorgen beladen seind als die verhefften. Vnd je mehr ein Wunden oben zusamen getrungẽ wirdt/ je sorglicher sie vnden am Boden ist. Also ist es mit den Stichen vnd Pfeilschuß/ so sie aussen verschwellen/ der Anfall einwertz dringt/ denselbigen Lacerten/ meatibus vnd Adern nach: Darumb sie mehr zum todt vnd sorglicher als offen Wunden/ so außwendig weit sind.

Auch ist in solchem zumercken/ daß ein Stich oder Pfeil von stund an soll außgezogen werden/ ehe daß die Geschwulst vnd Anfall zugehet. Wo solches aber nit geschicht/ mehr zum Tod ist/ dann zum Leben. Vnd wo solche sorg vor Augen were/ mit genugsamen Zeichen/ da soll dasselbig Instrument inen bleiben/ vnd lassen durch die Mumia herauß gehen. Dann sein Heylung hat ein andern Griff/ vnd das in zween wege: Der ein/ daß ein Wunden neben Pfeil gehawe werde/ oder durch den Mumia, der zu attrahiren gemischt ist/ außgezogen/ vñ nit von der Hand. Was also die Artzney außzeucht/ das ist dem Leben nit nachtheilig. Also ist es auch mit den Knütschchen oder Fall/ daß am selbigen ort auch Wunden gemacht werden/ auch daß der Anfall ein außgang habe/ vnd nit ihn hinwertz nach dem Leben gehe/ Oder durch den Mumia außwendig gestillet vnd vertriben. Dann an ein jeglichen: Stoß oder Knütschung/ sey wie hart vnd streng es wölle/ blau oder schwark/ so vermags der Mumia in sein erst Wesen zubringen/ ohn Auffschneidung oder Eyterung. Wann solche Inflationes seind nit verbrechung/ oder von zerbrochner Natur/ sonder ein Geschwulst in guten dingen/ <margin>B</margin> Darumb sie also hingehn/ ohn weiter Zufall.

So sichs aber begebe/ daß ein Fall/ Stich/ oder dergleichen in die inwendigen regiones gangen were/ Adern/ oder etwas gebrochen hette dardurch den regionibus ein frembder Gast zu fiel: Am selbigen ort soltu geflissen sein/ solches zuvertreibe/ wie von den Zufällen geschrieben wird/ Aber so ein solch Eisen sich anglettet/ oder widerhecket/ da wisse/ daß es hindersich nit außgehet/ sonder durchgestossen soll werden: Oder aber in ein Geschwer gebracht/ vnd herauß gefeilt/ so dieselbige statt dem Leben nit nachtheilig were. Aber ob solchs fürgenomen werde/ mit Mumia attractiva verbunden/ welcher die Geschwulst dermassen niderlegt/ vnd den Anfall nimpt/ daß der Hacken wider zurück gehet den weg/ da er hin ist gangen. Du solt auch gewarnet sein/ daß du in keinem wege mit Zangen oder Instrumenten dich vnderstehest etwas zumachen. Dann du äffest das Glied: Es were dann so nahe bey der Haut/ oder an ein flachen ort/ da es ohn sorg anzunem̃en were: Wiewol ohn Mumia ist es selten möglich. Dergleichen auch begibt sich vil/ dz Kuglen also in Leib geschossen werden/ vnd durch den Mumiam attractivam, durch sein art vnd natur/ widerumb herauß gezogen werden: Es were dann sach/ daß die Kugel in ein ander Region fiele. Darinn merck/ daß der Mumia in frembden regionibus nit gewalt hat: darumb so ein Kugel geschossen wird in Leib/ vnd fiele zwischen die Intestina nider/ oder käme ausserhalb oder vnderhalb dem Diaphragma, am selben ort ist es nicht möglich herauß zuziehen. Dergleichen/ so in ein Röhre geschossen wird/ vnd die Kugel suncke im Rohr vndersich/ so ists auch ein ander Region. Vnd ob schon der Mumia so starck were/ die Kuglen herauß zuziehen/ so gibts die Rewe/ so inwendig am Rohr ist/ nit zu. Darumb in solchen stücken gut acht zu haben ist/ war mit einer vmbgehe.

# CAPVT V.

### Von Heylung der obgemelten/ vnd was darzu gehört.

<margin>C</margin>Nun ist die Heylung solcher Wunden/ gleich dem Proceß von gemeinen Wunden: Scheidt sich allein in dem/ daß der Mumia soll mit attractivis gespeist sein/ vnnd sollen attractiva sein/ die da nicht humores an sich ziehen/ noch liquores, oder dergleichen/ sonder allein/ das sie Metallen/ Holtz oder Bein/ rc. annemen: Wann solten die gemeinen attractiva gebraucht werden/ so stünden Flüß hinzu.

Wiewol es sich auch manchmal begibt/ daß ein Kugel oder solch Eisen/ in den lacertis verheylen/ auß vrsach des guten Mumia, der in kein Anfall gefallen ist/ oder nit starck erzörnt ist worden. Etwann nach vil jaren mit der zeit sich entert vnd wider außfellt: Solchs wird der Natur zugelassen/ vnd nit vnderstanden zunemen. Dann so es die Natur verheylet/ wer wils ihr wider nenen?

Von den attractivis zu reden/ seind etliche die Holtz ziehen/ Fäsen vnd solch ding/ als Asphaltum vnd Carabæ: Etliche Eisen/ als Magnes: Etlich Kupffer vnd Zinn/ als die gefärbten Amethisten: Etlich Bley vnnd Stein/ als der Alabaster. Etlich Lumpen vom Fleische/ Beinschrot/ als die Gummi/ Terpentin/ vnnd Asphaltum. Etlich in allen stücken/ als die Serpentina. Wie solche Krafft all seind/ soll von ein Artzet nicht gescheiden sein. Wann in wirckung der Natur/ so sie den Wunden vbergelegt werden/ attrahierens alle gleich/ also/ was hauffen Stroh vnd Holtz zeucht/ das zeucht in Wunden Eisen/ Bley/ Stein/ vnd Beyn: Hinwiderumb auch/ was allein Eisen zeucht das zeucht in Wunden was ledig darinn ligt. Darumb ein Artzt nit soll den außwendigen kräfften nachgehen/ sondern den inwendigen/ wie sie sich mit der Natur vereinigen.
