<page-num>345</page-num>
<header>FIRST BOOK.</header>
<sig>Gg iij</sig>

# CHAPTER IV.

### Recognition of Puncture Wounds, Arrow-Shots, Falls, and Bruising.

<margin>A</margin>Now, we shall proceed to other types of wounds, such as punctures, arrow-shots, falls, and the like. Between these and common wounds, there is no difference in their essence, except that such a puncture or arrow-shot—due to its narrowness—cannot allow the <term>Anfall</term> <note>original: "Anfall." In this context, it refers to the sudden onset of inflammation, congestion, or the "rush" of vital humors to a site of injury.</note> to escape; therefore, it penetrates further into the flesh and vessels than a common wound. For it is the nature of every such inflammation that it requires much hollow space and width around it. Therefore, open wounds that are not stitched are burdened with less inflammation and concern than those that are closed up. And the more a wound is compressed at the top, the more dangerous it is at the bottom. So it is with punctures and arrow-shots: if they swell on the outside, the inflammation forces itself inward, following the <term>lacerten</term> <note>From the Latin "lacertus," referring to the muscles or fleshy parts of the limbs.</note>, the <term>meatibus</term> <note>Latin: "passages" or "canals" within the body.</note>, and the vessels. For this reason, they are more deadly and worrisome than open wounds which are wide on the outside.

It should also be noted in such cases that a puncture or arrow-head should be pulled out immediately, before the swelling and inflammation set in. If this is not done, there is more hope for death than for life. And where such danger is evident by sufficient signs, the instrument should be left inside and allowed to be expelled by the <term>Mumia</term> <note>The innate healing power or "internal balsam" of the body.</note>. For its healing requires a different approach, and that in two ways: one, that a wound be cut next to the arrow, or that it be drawn out by the Mumia when mixed with <term>attractives</term> <note>Medicines designed to "draw" foreign objects or toxins out of the body.</note>, and not by the hand. Whatever the medicine draws out in this way is not detrimental to life. So it is also with bruising or falls: a wound should be made at that same spot so that the inflammation has an exit and does not move inward toward the life-centers, or it should be stilled and driven away from the outside by the Mumia. For in every blow or bruising—no matter how hard or severe it may be, or how blue or black—the Mumia is capable of bringing it back to its original state without cutting or suppuration. For such <term>inflationes</term> <note>Latin: "swellings" or "puffiness."</note> are not a breaking or a destruction of nature, but rather a swelling in otherwise healthy tissue; <margin>B</margin> therefore they pass away without further complication.

But should it happen that a fall, puncture, or the like has reached the internal <term>regiones</term> <note>Latin: "regions" or internal cavities of the body.</note>, or has broken a vessel or something else whereby a "foreign guest" falls into those regions: in that place, you must be diligent to drive it out, as is written concerning complications. But if such an iron [arrowhead] has smoothed itself in or is barbed, know that it will not come out backward, but must be pushed through; or else, it must be brought into a sore and filed out, provided that location is not detrimental to life. But if this is undertaken, it should be bound with <term>mumia attractiva</term> [drawing Mumia], which lays the swelling down to such an extent and takes away the inflammation that the hook may go back the same way it entered. You should also be warned that you should in no way attempt to do anything with pliers or instruments. For you will only harass the limb, unless it is so close to the skin or in a flat place where it can be taken hold of without worry; though without Mumia, this is seldom possible. Similarly, it often happens that bullets are shot into the body and are drawn out again through the "drawing Mumia" by its art and nature—unless the bullet falls into another "region." Note here that the Mumia has no power in foreign regions; therefore, if a bullet is shot into the body and falls down between the <term>intestina</term> <note>Latin: "intestines."</note>, or comes above or below the <term>diaphragma</term> <note>Latin: "diaphragm."</note>, it is not possible to draw it out from that spot. Likewise, if one is shot in a "tube" <note>likely referring to a bone cavity or a major vessel</note> and the bullet sinks down within the tube, that is also a different region. And even if the Mumia were strong enough to draw the bullets out, the <term>Rewe</term> <note>A difficult term, likely referring to the internal friction, "roughness," or the natural narrowness/obstruction within the anatomical structure.</note> inside the tube would not permit it. Therefore, in such matters, one must take good care of what they are dealing with.

# CHAPTER V.

### On the Healing of the Above-Mentioned, and What Belongs Thereto.

<margin>C</margin>Now, the healing of such wounds is similar to the process for common wounds. It differs only in this: the Mumia should be "fed" with attractives, and these attractives should be those that do not draw <term>humores</term> [fluids] or liquids to themselves, but only those that take hold of metals, wood, or bone, etc. For if common attractives were used, fluxes <note>Pathological discharges of fluid.</note> would persist.

Although it also sometimes happens that a bullet or such an iron heals within the <term>lacertis</term> [muscles] because of a good Mumia that has not fallen into inflammation or been severely provoked. Perhaps after many years, with time, it shifts and falls out again. This is permitted by Nature and should not be interfered with. For if Nature heals it, who would want to take it away from her again?

To speak of the attractives: there are some that draw wood, fibers, and such things, like <term>Asphaltum</term> [asphalt/bitumen] and <term>Carabæ</term> <note>An old term for amber.</note>. Some draw iron, like the <term>Magnes</term> [magnet/lodestone]. Some draw copper and tin, like colored amethysts. Some draw lead and stone, like alabaster. Some draw scraps of flesh or bone-shards, like gums, turpentine, and asphalt. Some draw all things, like the <term>Serpentina</term> <note>Likely referring to "Serpentine" stone or a specific compound believed to have universal drawing power.</note>. How all such powers work should not be unknown to a physician. For in the operation of Nature, when they are placed over wounds, they all draw equally; thus, that which draws a heap of straw and wood will, in a wound, draw iron, lead, stone, and bone. Conversely, that which draws only iron will draw whatever lies loose in a wound. Therefore, a physician should not follow the external powers, but the internal ones, as they unite with Nature.

<summary>This chapter discusses the dangers of deep puncture wounds and arrow-shots, emphasizing that their narrowness traps inflammation. Paracelsus advocates for using "drawing Mumia" to remove foreign objects like iron and lead rather than invasive surgical tools.</summary>

...I say that two kinds of visions can occur in the intellect. Some are of bodily substances, and others are of separate, bodiless substances. The bodily ones involve all material things found in heaven and on earth. A soul can see these through a certain light proceeding from God, in which all distant things of heaven and earth can be seen. The other, non-bodily visions of bodiless substances require another, more excellent light. These visions of bodiless substances, such as angels and souls, are not very common, nor are they proper to this life. Much less common is the vision of the Divine Essence, which belongs only to the "beholders" or those already established in the state of blessedness, unless it were communicated to someone only in passing. Let us now deal with those visions of bodily substances that are received in the soul in a spiritual way, which are like bodily visions. For just as the eyes see bodily things by means of natural light, so the soul, with its intellect, sees these same natural things and other things pleasing to God internally by means of the aforementioned supernatural light. However, there is a difference in the way and manner. The spiritual visions arising in the intellect appear much clearer and more delicate than the bodily ones. When God wishes to grant this grace to a soul, He bestows that supernatural light we have mentioned. In this light, the soul sees heavenly or earthly things quite easily and clearly, as God wills, without their presence or absence being any hindrance. This occurs as if one were to open a very clear door, through which one sees things clearly, much like a flash of lightning suddenly shining in a dark night.

<meta>This page follows the narrative of the Crusader intervention in Egypt. While King Amalric I and the Templars were occupied in the south supporting the Vizier Shawar, the northern frontiers of the Crusader States were left vulnerable to Nur ad-Din’s counter-attacks.</meta>

-># Bertrand de Blanchefort.<-

Shortly thereafter, however, Nur ad-Din <note>Nur ad-Din Zengi, the Sultan of Aleppo and Damascus and a major adversary of the Crusaders</note> made the Christians feel the folly of having stripped their land of manpower and having moved the war into Egypt. He attacked the castle of Harem <note>also known as Harenc, modern-day Harim, Syria</note> or Hasrenk, and would have taken it by surprise if Thoros, Prince of Armenia, Raymond, Count of Tripoli, Bohemond III, Prince of Antioch, along with the Knights Templar, had not rushed to the scene and forced him to lift the siege. The Sultan withdrew toward Artesia <note>modern-day Artah</note>, and the Christians dared to attack his right wing. This wing pretended as if it wanted to flee; however, while the Christians pursued them with great heat, the remaining Muslims fell upon the Christians and carried out a great massacre i). Almost all of the Templar soldiers and the <term>Turcopoles|Light cavalry units, often consisting of locally recruited soldiers, who fought alongside the Crusader orders</term> remained on the field, and out of sixty knights, only seven escaped with their lives. Both sides fought like desperate men; ten thousand of the Christians remained on the field, and the number of prisoners was even greater. Raymond, Bohemond, Joscelin, and Hugh of Lusignan were taken as captives to Aleppo, while Nur ad-Din pursued his victory, returned immediately, and captured the castle of Harem. These two events, which William of Tyre <note>original: "Wilhelm von Tyrus," the primary historian of the early Kingdom of Jerusalem</note> places in the years 1165 and 1167, actually belong to the second year of Amalric's reign, and consequently to the year 1164. It has been claimed, entirely without foundation, that Blanchefort <note>Bertrand de Blanchefort, the Grand Master of the Templars</note> was present at this defeat.

We must assume an analogous turn in the plant, following analogous outward appearances, only that everything which in humans falls into clear self-consciousness will here fall more into feeling and instinct, though these may nonetheless be definite and lively enough. A kind of turning inward of the plant’s feeling into itself <note>original: "Einkehr," a term often used in German for spiritual reflection, retreat, or a traveler stopping at an inn.</note> may begin, while its susceptibility to external stimuli decreases—just as we indeed see the organs for these stimuli gradually wither—and a kind of instinct may develop that urges it to reflect or reproduce its own life in the formation of the young plantlet within the seed, looking both backward and forward. (Let us remember that the plantlet is truly already preformed according to its entire plan within the seed, in the little roots <note>term: "Würzelchen" (radicle); the part of a plant embryo that develops into the primary root.</note> and little leaf-feathers <note>term: "Blattfederchen" (plumule); the primary bud of a plant embryo, which often has a feathery appearance.</note>.) One might say that the formation of the young plantlet in the seed represents the first and only real thought in its head <note>The "head" here refers to the seed-bearing part of the plant, continuing the anthropomorphic analogy.</note>, in which the memory of its entire past life is darkly summarized, and at the same time expresses the care for the future of another being similar to itself. Our own thoughts, too, are attached to physical processes in the head, which leave behind something altered within it. Gewöhnlich bedient man sich bey Saiteninstrumenten nur der erstern Schwingungsart, wo eine Saite ganz schwingt; nur selten macht man auf der Geige und dem Violoncell bey dem Solospielen Gebrauch von den höhern Tönen, wo sich die Saite in aliquote Theile eintheilt. Man nennt sie Flageolet-Töne, (sons harmoniques, oder sons flutés), sie klingen besonders auf der Saite des Violoncells, wo man noch wenigstens das 4 gestrichene a oder das 5 gestrichene cis sehr bequem dadurch erreichen kann, weit sanfter, als wenn man eben so hohe Töne auf die gewöhnliche Weise greifen wollte. Es giebt eine Saite, wie schon bemerkt worden, auf diese Art nicht alle Töne, z. B. die d Saite nur die, welche gegen den Ton d, die a Saite nur die, welche gegen den Ton a in Verhältnissen der natürlichen Zahlenfolge stehn; man kann aber auch alle andere hohe Töne auf diese Art erhalten, wenn man die Saite durch ein gewöhnliches Greifen mit dem Daumen verkürzt, und sodann mit einem andern Finger, irgend einen Schwingungsknoten dieser verkürzten Saite gelinde berührt, indem es ganz einerley ist, ob der Schwingungsknoten, welcher der nächste am Stege ist, oder der, welcher der entfernteste ist, berührt wird. Diese Art, durch ein doppeltes Greifen jeden beliebigen hohen Ton als Flageolet-Ton hervorzubringen, lehrt la Grange in den Recherches sur le son §. 51. in Miscellan. Taurinens. tom. I, es wird meines Wissens auch von einigen Violoncellspielern ausgeübt. Auf der sogenannten Meertrompete (trompette marine) welche ein sehr unvollkommenes Instrument ist, aber doch vielleicht könnte mehr vervollkommnet werden, macht man Gebrauch von den verschiedenen Eintheilungen der Saite in gleiche Theile. Es besteht dieses Instrument aus einem langen hohlen, oben schmalen, nach unten sich erweiternden, und am untern Ende offenen hölzernen Körper, auf welchen nur eine Saite aufgespannt ist, die unterwärts auf einem Stege ruht, welcher auf der einen Seite nur locker auf dem Resonanzboden aufliegt, wodurch der Klang etwas schnarrend und dem Klange einer Trompete ähnlich wird. Die Saite wird oberwärts an einem Schwingungsknoten mit dem Finger berühret, und zwischen dem obern Ende, und dem berührten Schwingungsknoten mit dem Violinbogen gestrichen. Die Töne der Aeolsharfe, wo die Saiten durch einen Luftzug in Bewegung gesetzt werden, beruhen ebenfalls auf solchen Transversal-falschwingungen der Saiten, wobey sie sich, nachdem sie von dem Winde auf verschiedene Art getroffen werden, in eine größere oder kleinere Zahl von gleichen Theilen abtheilen. Sehr gute Bemerkungen darüber finden sich in Matthew Young's Enquiry into the principal phaenomena of sounds and musical strings P. II. sect. V. Hieher gehört auch die sogenannte Wetterharfe oder Riesenharfe des Hauptmann Haas in Basel, welche aus gespannten sehr langen Eisendrähten bestand, und bey Veränderung des Wetters auf sehr mannigfaltige Art zu tönen anfieng. Daß die Eisendrähte tönten, wenn sie in der Richtung der Mittagslinie, nicht aber, wenn sie von Ost nach West gespannt waren, rührt wohl nicht, wie man vermuthen wollte, von einer Einwirkung des Magnetismus her, sondern die Ursache mochte wohl theils in Localumständen, welche mehr der einen, als der andern Richtung einen Luftzug bewürkte haben, theils auch meines Erachtens darin liegen, weil die meisten Winde West- oder Ostwinde sind, welche also die Drähte, wenn sie in derselben Richtung gespannt waren, nicht genug seitwärts treffen konnten, um sie hinlänglich in Bewegung zu sehen. Note: On string instruments, one usually makes use only of the first mode of vibration, where a string vibrates as a whole; only rarely, when playing solos on the violin or cello, does one make use of the higher tones where the string divides into aliquot <note>proportional or fractional</note> parts. These are called flageolet tones (<term>sons harmoniques</term> <gloss>harmonic sounds</gloss>, or <term>sons flutés</term> <gloss>flute-like sounds</gloss>). They sound much softer, especially on the cello string—where one can still very conveniently reach the four-times-accented a or the five-times-accented c-sharp—than if one were to finger such high tones in the usual way. As has already been noted, a string does not produce all tones in this manner; for example, the d-string only produces those that stand in ratios of the natural numerical sequence to the tone d, and the a-string only those that stand in such ratios to the tone a. However, one can also obtain all other high tones in this manner if one shortens the string by conventional fingering with the thumb and then lightly touches any vibrational node of this shortened string with another finger, since it is entirely immaterial whether the vibrational node nearest the bridge or the one furthest from it is touched. This method of producing any desired high tone as a flageolet tone by means of a double-fingering is taught by la Grange in the <term>Recherches sur le son</term> <gloss>Researches on Sound</gloss>, §. 51, in <term>Miscellan. Taurinens.</term> <gloss>Miscellanea Taurinensia</gloss>, vol. I; to my knowledge, it is also practiced by some cello players.

On the so-called <term>trompette marine</term> <gloss>marine trumpet</gloss>, which is a very imperfect instrument but perhaps could be further perfected, one makes use of the various divisions of the string into equal parts. This instrument consists of a long, hollow wooden body, narrow at the top and widening toward the bottom, which is open at the lower end. Only one string is stretched over it, resting below on a bridge that lies only loosely on the soundboard on one side, which makes the sound somewhat rasping and similar to the sound of a trumpet. The string is touched with the finger above at a vibrational node and bowed with a violin bow between the top end and the touched vibrational node. The tones of the Aeolian harp, where the strings are set in motion by a draft of air, also depend on such transversal vibrations of the strings, in which they divide themselves into a greater or smaller number of equal parts depending on how they are struck by the wind in various ways. Da in (74.) $y$ nur in $\frac{\quad}{\quad} F(x)$ vorkommt, so kann bei der Ersetzung des $y$ durch den deutschen Buchstaben $\mathfrak{a}$ die Höhlung diesem Ausdrucke nach § 11 unmittelbar vorhergehen. Man kann (81) übersetzen:

> *Wenn $x$ eine Eigenschaft $F$ hat, die sich in der $f$-Reihe vererbt, und wenn $y$ in der $f$-Reihe auf $x$ folgt, so hat $y$ die Eigenschaft $F$.*)

Es sei beispielsweise $F$ die Eigenschaft, ein Haufe Bohnen zu sein; es sei das Verfahren $f$ die Verminderung eines Haufens Bohnen um eine Bohne, so dass
-> $f(a, b)$ <-
den Umstand bedeute, dass $b$ alle Bohnen des Haufens $a$ ausser einer und sonst nichts enthalte. Dann würde man durch unsern Satz zu dem Ergebnisse gelangen, dass eine einzige oder selbst gar keine Bohne ein Haufe Bohnen sei, wenn die Eigenschaft, ein Haufe zu sein, sich in der $f$-Reihe vererbt. Dies ist jedoch nicht allgemein der Fall, weil es gewisse $z$ giebt, bei denen wegen der Unbestimmtheit des Begriffes „Haufe“ $F(z)$ unbeurtheilbar ist.

Since in (74.) $y$ only occurs in $\frac{\quad}{\quad} F(x)$, when replacing $y$ with the German letter $\mathfrak{a}$, the concavity <note>a symbol in Frege’s notation indicating universal quantification over a variable</note> can immediately precede this expression according to § 11. One can translate (81) as:

> *If $x$ has a property $F$ that is inherited in the $f$-series, and if $y$ follows $x$ in the $f$-series, then $y$ has the property $F$.*<note>original: "Wenn $x$ eine Eigenschaft $F$ hat, die sich in der $f$-Reihe vererbt, und wenn $y$ in der $f$-Reihe auf $x$ folgt, so hat $y$ die Eigenschaft $F$."</note>*)

Let $F$, for example, be the property of being a heap of beans; let the procedure $f$ be the reduction of a heap of beans by one bean, such that
-> $f(a, b)$ <-
signifies the circumstance that $b$ contains all the beans of the heap $a$ except for one, and nothing else. Then, through our theorem, one would arrive at the result that a single bean, or even no bean at all, is a heap of beans, if the property of being a heap is inherited in the $f$-series. However, this is not generally the case, because there are certain $z$ for which $F(z)$ is undecidable due to the indefiniteness of the concept "heap."

Johannes de Lasnioro: Many, torturing mercury with various punishments, wishing to make it fixed, but when they cannot effect it, say that it is a fugitive thief. Jodocus Greverus: Into this work there does not enter the gold of the crowd, nor the mercury of the crowd, nor the silver of the crowd, nor anything else common, but that of the philosophers, etc.

ἔδοξέ τε ἡμῖν λαχεῖν τοῦ κλήρου κατ’ ἀγχιστείαν, καὶ ἐλάχομεν τὸ μέρος ἕκαστος. μελλόντων δ’ ἡμῶν αὐτομυᾶσαι διεμαρτύρησε Λεωχάρης οὑτοσί, μὴ ἐπίδικον εἶναι τὸν κλῆρον ἡμῖν. ἐπισκηψαμένων δ’ ἡμῶν, ἡ μὲν λῆξις τοῦ κλήρου διεγράφη. ἡ δὲ τῶν ψευδομαρτυριῶν δίκη εἰσήει. ἐν δὲ τῷ δικαστηρίῳ πάντα μὲν ἡμῶν εἰπόντων ἅπερ νυνί, πολλὰ δὲ Λεωχάρους αὐτὰ ἀπολογησαμένου, ἔγνωσαν τὰ ψευδῆ μαρτυρῆσαι Λεωχάρην οἱ δικασταί. ἐπειδὴ δὲ τοῦτο φανερὸν ἐγένετο ἐξαιρηθεισῶν τῶν ψήφων, ἃ μὲν τῶν δικαστῶν, καὶ ἡμῶν ἐδεήθη Λεωχάρης, ἢ ὅσα ἡμῖν ἐξεγένετο διαπράξασθαι τότε, οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅ τι δεῖ λέγειν. ἃ δὲ ὡμολογήθη ἡμῖν, ταῦτα ἀκούσατε. συγχωρούντων ἡμῶν τῷ ἄρχοντι μὴ συναριθμεῖν, ἀλλὰ συγχέαι τὰς ψήφους, ἀφίστατο μὲν Δικαιογένης τοῖν δυοῖν μεροῖν τοῦ κλήρου, τοῖς δικαιογένους ἀδελφαῖς. καὶ ὡμολόγει ἀναμφισβήτητα ποιήσειν ἡμῖν ταῦτα τὰ μέρη. καὶ ταῦτα ἐγγυᾶτο αὐτῷ Λεωχάρης οὗτος. καὶ ὡμολόγει ποιήσειν οὐ μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ Μικίωνι τὸ βαλανεῖον, καὶ τούτων ὑμῖν τοὺς μάρτυρας παρέξομαι.

->μάρτυρες.<-

ἡμεῖς τοίνυν ταῦτα παθόντες ὑπὸ Λεωχάρους. καὶ ἐγγυώμενον ἡμῖν αὐτόν, ἐπειδὴ εἵλομεν ψευδομαρτυριῶν ἀτιμώσου, οὐκ ἐβάλομεν. ἀλλ’ ἐξήρκεσε τὰ ἡμέτερα ἡμῖν κομισαμένοις, ἀπηλλάχθαι. γινομένοι δὲ γενόμενοι περὶ Λεωχάρην καὶ Δικαιογένην, ἐξηπατήθημεν ὑπ’ αὐτῶν ὦ ἄνδρες. οὔτε γὰρ Δικαιογένης τὰ δύο μέρη ἡμῖν τοῦ κλήρου παρέδωκεν, ὁμολογήσας ἐπὶ τοῦ δικαστηρίου, οὔτε Λεωχάρης ὁμολογεῖ ἐγγυήσασθαι αὐτὸν τότε. καίτοι εἰμὶ ἐναντίον μὲν τῶν δικαστῶν, πεντακοσίων ὄντων. ἐναντίον δὲ τῶν περιεστηκότων ἐγγυᾶτο, οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅτι ἂν ἐποίησεν. ὡς μὲν τοίνυν πεφανερῶς ψεύδονται, μάρτυρας ὑμῖν παρέχομαι τοὺς παρόντας, ὅτε Δικαιογένης μὲν ἀφίστατο τοῖν δυοῖν μεροῖν τοῦ κλήρου, ᾑ ὡμολόγει ἀναμφισβήτητα παραδώσειν τοῖς Δικαιογένους ἀδελφαῖς. Λεωχάρης δὲ ἐγγυᾶτο αὐτὸν ἃ ὡμολόγησε καὶ ποιήσειν. οἰόμεθα δὲ καὶ ὑμῶν ὦ ἄνδρες εἴ τις ἔτυχε παρὼν τότε, ἀναμνησθῆναι ἃ λέγομεν ἀληθῆ καὶ βοηθῆσαι ἡμῖν. ἐπεὶ ὦ ἄνδρες εἰ Δικαιογένης ἀληθῆ λέγει, τί ἡμεῖς ὠφελούμεθα νικήσαντες, ἢ τί οὗτος ἐζημιώθη ἡττηθείς. εἰ γὰρ ἀπέστη μόνον ὡς φησὶ τοῖν δυοῖν μεροῖν τοῦ κλήρου, ἀναμφισβήτητον δὲ μὴ ὡμολόγει παραδώσειν, τί ἐζημιοῦτο ἀφιστάμενος ὧν τι μὴ εἶχεν. οὐ δὲ γὰρ πρὶν ἡττηθῆναι τὴν δίκην εἶχεν ὧν ἡμεῖς λαγχάνομεθα, ἀλλ’ οἱ παρὰ τούτου πριάμενοι καὶ θέμενοι οἷς ἔδει αὐτὸν ἀποδόντα τὴν τιμήν, ἡμῖν τὰ μέρη ἀποδιδόναι. διὰ ταῦτα γὰρ καὶ τὸν ἐγγυητὰς παρὰ αὐτοῦ ἐλάβομεν. οὐ πιστεύοντες αὐτῷ ἃ ὡμολόγησε ποιήσειν. πολλῷ γὰρ δυοῖν οἰκειῶν ἔξω τείχους, ἣ οὐ περὶ ἑξήκοντα πλέθρων, οὐδὲν κεκομίσμεθα. ἀλλ’ οἱ παρὰ τούτου θέμενοι καὶ πριάμενοι. ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐξάγομεν. δείσαντες γάρ, μὴ ὄφλωμεν δίκας. ᾑ γὰρ Μικίωνα κελεύοντος Δικαιογένους, καὶ φάσκοντος μὴ βεβαιώσειν ἐξάγοντες ἐκ τοῦ βαλανείου, ὤφλομεν τετταράκοντα μνᾶς διὰ Δικαιογένην ὦ ἄνδρες. ἡγούμενοι γὰρ οὐκ ἂν αὐτῷ βεβαιώσειν οὐδὲν ὧν ἡμῖν ἀπέστη ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ, διὰ τοῦτο ἔθετο πρὸς Μικίωνα ἐναντίον τῶν δικαστῶν ἐθέλοντες ὁτιοῦν πάσχειν, εἰ βεβαιώσειεν αὐτῷ Δικαιογένης τὸ βαλανεῖον. οὐκ ἂν ποτε οἰόμενοι αὐτὸν ἐναντία οἷς ὡμολόγησε πρᾶξαι. οὐ δι’ ἄλλ’ οὐδέν, ἢ διὰ τὸν ἐγγυητάς. ὅτι καθεστήκεσαν ἡμῖν. ἀποστὰς δὲ Δικαιογένης ταῦτα τὰ μέρη ὧν καὶ νῦν ὁμολογεῖ ἀφιστάναι ἡμῖν, ἐβεβαίωσε Μικίωνι τὸ βαλανεῖον. καὶ ἐγὼ μὲν ὁ ἄθλιος, οὐχ ὅπως τί ἐκ τοῦ κλήρου εἰληφώς, ἀλλὰ προσαπολωλεκὼς τετταράκοντα μνᾶς, ἀπέρχομαι ὑβρισμένος ὑπὸ Δικαιογένους, καὶ τούτων ὑμῖν μάρτυρας παρέξομαι.

it seemed best to us to sue for the estate according to the rights of kinship, and each of us sued for our portion. When we were about to swear the preliminary oath, this man Leochares filed a protest <note>original: "διεμαρτύρησε" — a legal maneuver to block a claim</note>, claiming the estate was not subject to litigation by us. When we contested this protest, the claim for the estate was struck down, and the lawsuit for perjury was brought to court. In the courtroom, after we said everything we are saying now, and after Leochares made many defenses, the judges decided that Leochares had given false testimony. When this became clear after the votes were counted, I do not know what I need to say about what Leochares begged of the judges and us, or how much we were able to achieve then. But listen to what was agreed between us. 

We agreed with the <term>archon</term> <gloss>presiding magistrate</gloss> not to count the votes but to mix them together <note>effectively nullifying the formal verdict in favor of a private settlement</note>. Dicaeogenes then withdrew his claim to two-thirds of the estate in favor of Dicaeogenes' sisters. He promised to deliver these portions to us free from any third-party claims. This man, Leochares, stood as his surety for these things. He promised to do this not only for us but also to return the bathhouse to Micion. I will provide the witnesses for these matters.

->**Witnesses.**<-

Now, although we suffered these things at the hands of Leochares, we did not cast him out <note>perhaps meaning they did not press for the full penalty of disenfranchisement</note> even though he stood as surety for us after we caught him in perjury. Instead, it was enough for us to recover our own and be settled. But though we were fair toward Leochares and Dicaeogenes, we were deceived by them, men. For Dicaeogenes did not hand over the two portions of the estate to us as he agreed in the court, nor does Leochares admit that he stood as surety then. And yet he stood as surety in front of five hundred judges and in front of the bystanders; I do not know what else he could have done. To show that they are clearly lying, I provide as witnesses those who were present when Dicaeogenes withdrew from the two portions of the estate and agreed to hand them over to Dicaeogenes' sisters without dispute, and when Leochares stood as surety that he would perform what he promised. We think that if any of you, men, happened to be present then, you will remember that what we say is true and you will help us. 

For, men, if Dicaeogenes is telling the truth, what did we gain by winning, or what did he lose by being defeated? For if he only withdrew, as he says, from the two portions of the estate, but did not agree to hand them over free from claims, what did he lose by withdrawing from things he did not even possess? For even before he lost the case, he did not hold the items we were suing for; rather, they were held by those who had bought or taken mortgages from him. He should have paid them their price and returned the portions to us. This is why we took sureties from him, because we did not trust him to do what he promised. For we have recovered nothing of the two houses outside the walls, nor of the sixty <term>plethra</term> <gloss>about 15 acres</gloss> of land. Instead, those who took mortgages or bought from him still hold them. We do not evict them, for we fear we might lose subsequent lawsuits. Indeed, when we tried to evict people from the bathhouse at Dicaeogenes' command—even though he said he would not guarantee the title—we were fined forty <term>minae</term> because of Dicaeogenes, men. We thought he would guarantee nothing of what he gave up in court, so he made an agreement with Micion in front of the judges, saying he was willing to suffer anything if Dicaeogenes did not guarantee his title to the bathhouse. We never thought he would act contrary to what he promised. This was for no other reason than the sureties we had established. But although Dicaeogenes withdrew from these portions—from which he even now admits he is withdrawing—he instead guaranteed the title for Micion's bathhouse. And I, wretched as I am, not only have I received nothing from the estate, but I have lost an additional forty <term>minae</term> and I leave the court insulted by Dicaeogenes. I will provide witnesses for these matters.

->**Witnesses.**<-

These are the things we have suffered from Dicaeogenes, men. But Leochares, who stood as his surety and is the cause of all our troubles, says he did not stand as surety for the things testified against him. He claims that in the document we handed up on the <term>bēma</term> <gloss>speaker's platform</gloss>, only certain things were written. But men, when we handed it up on the <term>bēma</term>, we wrote down some things and made others the subject of witness testimony. These men claim that whatever parts of the agreement benefit them are valid, even if not written down, but whatever does not benefit them is not valid unless written. I wonder, men, that they deny what was agreed. For not even the written... <note>sentence continues on next page</note>

He was taken prisoner in 407 BCE, but was later released <note>original: "Xen. Hell. i. 5. 19"</note>. According to Androtion, <term>apud</term> <gloss>in the works of</gloss> Pausanias <note>original: "Paus. vi. 7. 6"</note>, when the revolt of Rhodes from Sparta with which we are concerned took place, Dorieus was near the Peloponnese, and was arrested and put to death by the Spartans. Their conduct is now much more intelligible in view of the fact that the <term>Diagoridae</term> <gloss>a powerful aristocratic family in Rhodes</gloss> had clearly taken the lead in expelling the Spartan <term>harmosts</term> <gloss>military governors</gloss>.

καθάπερ ἂν παρόντι, τῷ γεγραφότι χαρίσασθαι τὸ μὴ
ἐρήμην καταψηφίσασθαι τοῦ βιβλίου, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἐν ἡμῖν
ἐκ Θεοῦ λόγον καὶ τὴν τῆς ἀληθείας συνείδησιν δικαστὰς
καθίσαι τῇ τε γνώμῃ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ τῇ σπουδῇ, καὶ
οἷ ἂν ἄγοιεν ἕπεσθαι, καὶ ὅπως ἂν ψηφίσαιντο πράττειν.
Εἰκὸς γὰρ ἴσως αὐτὸν ἐπιγεγονότα τοῖς ἄλλοις ὅσοι περὶ
τῶν τοιούτων ἐσπουδακότες εἰσὶν, ἀμείνω τινὰ τῆς θρη-
σκείας συνηγορίαν εὐρεῖν, καὶ λόγοις καινοτέροις ὁμοῦ καὶ
ἀξιωτέροις ἐντυχόντα πεισθῆναι, οὓς δέοι γ’ ἂν μὴ περι-
ιδεῖν· τοὐλάχιστον γὰρ, οὐ πόρρω συγγνώμης ἂν εἴη, λό-
γοις ἰσχυροτέροις ἐνδοὺς, οὔπω μὲν ὑπὸ τῶν τῆς Ἐκκλη-
σίας διδασκάλων ἐξητασμένοις, αὐτοῦ δὲ πάνυ κεκρα-
τηκόσιν οὐκ ἔχοντος ἀντιλέγειν. Καίτοι συνῄδειμεν ἐκείνῳ
τὴν πονηρὰν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ὑποστάντι πρόληψιν. Ἀλλ’ ἐχρῆν
ἀπαθὲς καθίζειν τὸ δικαστήριον· ἡμᾶς δὲ μὴ δια-
φυγεῖν ἂν, οὔτ’ εἰ τὰ αὐτὰ ἢ καὶ χείρω τῶν ἄλλοις
ἐξευρημένων, οὔτ’ εἰ βελτίω τε καὶ καινότερα εἴη τὰ
τὴν ψυχὴν ἐκείνου θηρεύσαντα. Ἱερᾶς μὲν γὰρ θεολογίας,
ἧς πλεῖστα ἡμῖν ἐμέλησεν ἐν παντὶ τῷ βίῳ, καὶ προῦρ-
γου μηδενὶ ἂν συγχωρῆσαι τῶν νῦν ὄντων ἁπανταχοῦ
καὶ ἴσα ἡμῖν εἰδέναι· Ἑλληνικῶν δὲ βιβλίων καὶ λόγων,

The book is full of such calamities. From the very titles and topics, knowing this, we wished immediately not to proceed further. But since it was absolutely necessary that such a thing be destroyed, it seemed just to us, as if he were present, to grant the author the grace of not condemning the book in his absence, but to seat the reason from God within us and the conscience of truth as judges of the man's opinion and effort, to follow wherever they might lead, and to act as they might decree. It is likely, perhaps, that having come after others who have been zealous about such things, he found some better defense for his religion, and having encountered arguments that were both newer and more worthy, he was persuaded, which one should not disregard. At the very least, it would not be far from forgiveness to have yielded to stronger arguments, not yet examined by the teachers of the Church, while he himself, having been thoroughly conquered, had no way to contradict them. Yet we were aware that he had harbored a wicked prejudice from the beginning. But it was necessary to seat the court without passion; and we would not have escaped, whether the things that ensnared his soul were the same or worse than those found by others, or if they were better and newer. For of sacred theology, which we have cared for most throughout our whole life, and for which we would grant to none of those now living anywhere to know as much as we do, and of the Greek books and arguments to which he refers himself, nothing has remained hidden from us, when we were able to reasonably judge them to be such, even before coming to such a state,

Based on the surviving traces, the author appears to be addressing the <term>prolepsis</term> <gloss>preconception or innate idea</gloss> concerning the gods. It is argued that these beings exist in a state of <term>ataraxia</term> <gloss>untroubledness or imperturbability</gloss>, removed from the concerns of human affairs. 

<margin>Regarding the divine nature</margin>

The fragment suggests that <unclear>if one considers</unclear> the movement of the atoms, one must conclude that the <term>kosmos</term> <gloss>ordered universe</gloss> is not governed by providence but by necessity and chance. <note>The original Greek text here is heavily damaged, making a definitive reconstruction of the argument impossible.</note>

<warning>The manuscript displays significant ink bleed-through from the verso of both pages, making some portions of the Greek minuscule script difficult to read. There are numerous ligatures and abbreviations typical of 14th-16th century Byzantine hands.</warning>
<meta>Vaticanus graecus 283. This spread continues the manuscript's transition from folio 2 to folio 48. While the previous page examined the internal harmony and virtue of a "decent man" through an Aristotelian lens, these pages shift into a theological discourse on divine love and spiritual purification. The text on folio 2 heavily paraphrases the New Testament (specifically 1 John and 1 Corinthians) to define the relationship between God and the believer.</meta>

<column-break/>

...of love toward God, and of love toward one’s neighbor. The grace of the Spirit teaches us both in this present age and in the future life, and in the enjoyment of eternal glory. For this very love toward God and toward neighbor makes a person spiritual in this present age. For he who loves God and keeps His commandments is the one who loves God <note>A reference to John 14:15: "If you love me, keep my commandments."</note>. And he who loves God loves his neighbor also. He who loves his neighbor fulfills the law. For he who loves another has fulfilled the law. <unclear>For love works no evil toward the neighbor;</unclear> therefore love is the fulfillment of the law. Wherefore the Apostle <note>Likely referring to the Apostle Paul, specifically citing Romans 13:10.</note> also says that love toward the neighbor is nothing other than the <unclear>fulfillment</unclear> of the law. 

For this <unclear>love cleanses a person and enlightens them and leads them up toward God and makes them His own.</unclear> <unclear>For the demons do not hold power over such a person, but rather they withdraw, because he is the light of God.</unclear> <unclear>And the Christian who possesses love is always with God.</unclear> <unclear>For God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him</unclear> <note>original: ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστι (ho theos agape esti) — a direct quotation from 1 John 4:16.</note>. <unclear>And what shall we say concerning love? That this is the first and great commandment.</unclear> <unclear>For on this commandment hang all the law and the prophets.</unclear> <unclear>For even if someone possesses all faith, so as to move mountains, but has not love, he is nothing.</unclear> <unclear>And if he gives away all his possessions, and delivers his body to be burned, but has not love, he gains nothing</unclear> <note>A paraphrase of the famous "Hymn to Love" in 1 Corinthians 13.</note>. 

<unclear>For love never fails.</unclear> <unclear>Because of this, we also, beloved ones, ought to remain in this love, so that in the future life we may obtain eternal glory.</unclear> <unclear>For love is the sum of all good things.</unclear> <unclear>For through this, God is known.</unclear> <unclear>For he who does not love has not known God.</unclear> <unclear>Therefore, brothers, if we love one another, God remains in us; and His love is perfected in us.</unclear> <unclear>In this we know that we remain in Him, and He in us: because He has given to us from His Spirit.</unclear> <unclear>Therefore, we also ought to love one another, just as Christ loved us.</unclear> For if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. <unclear>And if we love one another, God remains in us...</unclear>

<meta>Catchword: for we seek (ζητοῦμεν γὰρ)</meta>

<column-break/>

<unclear>...in the light of divine grace... with boldness</unclear> <note>original: παῤῥησίας (parrhesia) — a technical term for the confidence or "freedom of speech" a believer has before God.</note> <unclear>he approaches God. Therefore, brothers, in love and harmony...</unclear> <unclear>toward the salvation of the soul. So that we also, the humble servants of God, may obtain eternal life. Because of this, always...</unclear> <unclear>God with all our mind.</unclear> <unclear>For God promises to those who love Him the kingdom of heaven...</unclear> <unclear>And through time and endurance, love toward God is shown.</unclear> <unclear>For he who loves God always rejoices in afflictions, and in trials...</unclear> <note>The text suggests that suffering is a "proving ground" for the sincerity of one's love.</note> <unclear>so that he may appear approved</unclear> <note>original: δόκιμος (dokimos) — a term for a person or metal that has been tested and found genuine.</note> <unclear>before God. ...the return toward God... and through repentance...</unclear> <unclear>Therefore, brothers... let us cleanse our souls from every defilement...</unclear> <unclear>so that we may become worthy of the divine promise. For God... always helps those who love Him... in the present age and in the future... Amen.</unclear>

<summary>This page presents a theological argument that love (agape) is the primary means of spiritual purification and union with God. It heavily utilizes Johannine and Pauline scripture to assert that love is the fulfillment of the law and the only protection against demonic influence.</summary>
<keywords>Agape, Love, Neighbor, Divine Grace, Fulfillment of Law, Holy Spirit, Repentance, Eternal Glory, Trials, Parrhesia</keywords>

to correct what was erroneously exposed in it. But he first asks us to direct our attention to the exposed diagram of the proposition, to see how the propositions of the impossible are ordered, and how those of the necessary, so that we might also be able to see what it is that is erroneous in this, which is why he adds these words:

> "The impossible, then, and the not impossible, follow the contingent, and the possible, and the non-contingent and the non-possible, contradictorily, but inversely. For the negation of the impossible follows the possible to be, <note>which is</note> the not impossible to be. And to the negation, the affirmation <note>follows</note>. For to the not possible to be, <note>there follows</note> the impossible to be. For the impossible to be is an affirmation. And the not impossible to be is a negation. And how the necessary stands, must be seen. But it is clear that it does not stand in this way. Rather, the opposites follow. But the contradictions are separate. For the not necessary to be is not the negation of the necessary not to be. For it is possible for both to be true of the same thing. For the necessary not to be <note>and</note> the not necessary to be."

Through these, he says that the propositions of the impossible, both affirmative and negative, are set out accordingly, and are placed under the affirmative and negative propositions of the possible and the contingent, with the negations being drawn in a direct line with their own affirmations. And the entire simple contradiction of the impossible is placed under the simple contradictions of those. And the entire <note>contradiction</note> by transposition <note>is placed</note> under those by transposition. translation:
### ON THE SAME DAY, THE MEMORY OF THE HOLY WOMEN XANTHIPPE AND POLYXENE:

Saint Xanthippe lived during the time of Claudius Caesar <note>original: "Κλαυδίου καίσαρος"</note> of the Romans, being the wife of Probus, the governor of Spain. She had a virgin sister named Polyxene. When the holy Apostle Paul came to the country of Spain and preached Christ, Xanthippe approached him and was catechized by him, being initiated into the faith of Christ by him. Afterwards, together with her, her husband Probus also became a Christian. Likewise, her sister Polyxene was taught by the same Apostle at that time. After his departure, having heard the blessed Apostle Andrew <note>original: "ἀνδρέαν τὸν μακάριον ἀπόστολον"</note> preaching the truth of the faith in Patras of Achaia, she went to him. Having learned the matters of religion more perfectly, she was baptized. And returning again to her own country, she found her own sister Xanthippe, shining with every virtue, and she received her with joy. And both, having taught many to believe in Christ, passed away.

...established, as it were, within the barriers that hinder the enterprise; for to be always fashioning hopes through procrastination is as something belonging to the gloom of Erebus, while those things which stand fast appear before the eyes of those who take courage. For we do not realize that on account of our disorders and ingratitude—having betrayed our nature and our ancient glory—we are in danger not only regarding present circumstances, but also the ultimate ones. And some attempt to snatch away no small fruit from the very many, and they do nothing other than count our misfortunes, as if over some brotherly inheritance of which he partakes. Grievous are the matters of the Savior, when even expectation is more difficult, which does not desire to labor, nor to exact tribute from the hope of things to come, but rather to extend benefits over things that exist and are present. Wherefore, over all that has been lost and all who have lost, along with the incense and the prayers, there is nothing else than the hope of the restoration from evils, and the deliverance from terrors, together with peace and concord, which no one and nothing else but the Divine might dispense to us; so that, having been delivered from shivering, and delivered from evils, with one mind, in one judgment and one impulse, our affairs might tend toward salvation. For there is no other way to be delivered from evils, unless we are of one mind toward the same end.

And that it is necessary to do these things as is fitting, regarding both the present and the future, both toward misfortunes and toward the hope of salvation, we are taught not only by words but also by facts; and these things are not in secret, but even in the open, and among all nations and places, wherever one might wish—not only now, but for a long time past, and they have not yet reached their peak so as to cease. For the fleeing from misfortunes and the seeking of salvation are not fluid and fabricated things, but are true and certain, based upon the words of God. And who does not know that the majority of evils are the inventions of our own lack of honorable ambition? For we have been eager to come not only toward nothing of the Savior, but even toward that which is evil and difficult; like a certain golden chain—not that of Homer, but that of the devil—through which he promises a hope that is golden, but an enjoyment that is bitter. And he does not cease until he declares all our abundance with the acclamations of the Macedonians, and toward the honor of friends, and the goods of the many—both theirs and ours, and those of people near and far—and whatever one might say, he draws all things toward himself, not in doing well, but in doing ill, making the things of others his own, and the things of others alien. And instead of icons he procures words, and instead of truth, idols, and instead of glory, dishonor; because he not only carries the money-box and deceives with the things collected there, but he also draws and compels their bodies, like certain instruments, toward his own vainglory.

There are, therefore, as it were, many dramas of evils, some upon the earth, some in the sea, and some in the air; and nothing seems to be a cause of wonder to those in the world, nor even to those in this life; since in these matters we the pious—who have Christ within ourselves and the light of truth—endure not only things no less or smaller, but even more and greater things than the nations. And we are examined in nothing else but in evils, and we introduce a reputation that is notable but evil and unholy. And we are in nothing else than in the paths of some enemy and wicked one: the passages of the seas, the loss of regions, the men within them, the expenditures at sea, the falls upon the earth, the sufferings in the air, the evils in life, the dangers in death, the things hoped for after these, the enemies in the present, and the punishments in the future. And nothing is lacking of evils, but all things together, and all things come upon us; and nothing else than the hope which we held before our eyes, as in a mirror and in a riddle, even this we lose; and nothing else than destruction, like an ancestral inheritance, do we draw upon ourselves.

And the lingering but wicked hope, and that which is not good, nor even saving; and all future expectation that is with fear and trembling, and the hopes of things to come; cheerfulness over things present and things following; and after the despair which we know to be against nature, toward the apparent glory, and the delight toward present things, and the evils within them, and the passions within them, and the abundance within them, and the wicked and unrestrained desire, and the pleasures within them, and the desires within them, and the profligacies within them, and the evils within them. And all those things not only throughout the cities, but also in the deserts, and in the roads, and in the houses, and in the places, and in the regions, and in the harbors, and in the seas, and in the mountains, and in the glens, and in the hollows, and in the caves, and in the plains, and in the mountains, and in the plains, and in all other things, and in all things, and in all things.

And nothing else than the wrath and the threat of God, and the desire over our evils, and the gladness over our evils, and the joy over our evils, and the good pleasure over our evils, and the cheerfulness over our evils, and the prosperity over our evils, and the happiness over our evils, and the good reputation over our evils, and the renown over our evils, and the acclamation over our evils, and the thanksgiving over our evils, and the blessing over our evils, and the piety over our evils, and the good order over our evils, and the lawfulness over our evils, and the propriety over our evils, and the seemliness over our evils, and the good condition over our evils, and the rhythm over our evils, and the melody over our evils, and the refinement over our evils, and the fruitfulness over our evils, and the good offspring over our evils, and the good life over our evils, and the good death over our evils, and the happiness over our evils, and the happiness over our evils, and the happiness over our evils.

Truth of Zeus. With an upright hand, restrain the blame of those who betray guest-friendship.
<margin>Antistrophe</margin> For the coming time, arriving from afar, puts my deep debt to shame. Yet it is possible to dissolve sharp blame, as the interest of mortals is now like a wave, which washes over the turning pebble. And where we shall pay the common debt for the sake of dear grace.
<margin>Epode</margin> For truth dwells in the city of the West-dwelling Locrians; and Calliope and brazen Ares are a care to them. For they tell of the Cycnean battle and the overbearing Heracles. And let Agesidamus, winning in the Olympiad as a boxer, carry grace, as Patroclus did for Achilles. Sharpening the man with virtue, he hastened to reach colossal glory, a man with the hand of a god.
<margin>Strophe 2</margin> Few have received effortless joy, work before all things is the light of life. The ordinances of Zeus awakened the chosen contest; which Heracles established by the ancient monument of Pelops, the six-numbered altar.

translation:
<meta>This page continues Psellos’s exploration of the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being. Having established the role of virtues and archetypes on the previous page, the text now moves into a technical distinction between the body and the mind, specifically focusing on the "Intellect" (Nous) and the "Soul" (Psyche) and their respective capacities for self-knowledge and divine participation.</meta>

Similarly, regarding the body, it is clear that the soul thinks of itself and **returns to itself** <note>original: "pros heauto epistrephei." In Neoplatonic thought, this "return" or "reversion" is the act of a conscious being looking inward to its own source rather than outward at material things.</note>. For no body thinks of itself. How is this evident? Because its thinking is not divided, whereas everything in a physical place is divisible. For this reason, those who study these matters do not consider them material. Since every individual substance possesses a share of the **immaterial intellects** <note>original: "nois aulois." These are "mind-beings" that exist without physical matter.</note> which are unparticipated. Nor is it fragmented. For those things which subsist for the sake of the world remain **unchanging**; and these are distinct from those things which change. And it was necessary that form not be the same as that which is below it, but rather that it transcend it. The entire order of things there does not descend from its own rank; its unique character merely proceeds forward, while remaining in its own forms and identities. Some things exist according to their nature, others according to their connections.

### + On the Intellect +

Because the **unparticipated intellect** <note>original: "amathekton nous." This refers to a "pure" Mind that exists independently and is not "shared out" or diluted by being joined to a physical body.</note>, and that which is unparticipated in the primary form, holds itself within itself. It possesses the measure of its own essence, both in its primary aspects and in those that transcend it. Hence, even the unparticipated intellect thinks in a "formal" way. For even if it is unparticipated, a certain manifestation is given to those things that come after it from its own existence. And it thinks of the **soul** and the **forms of nature**. It does not think of them merely as they exist in nature, for it does not know lower things in a lower way, nor higher things in a higher way; rather, it knows both "formally" (according to their ideal patterns). It does not change along with the things it thinks about. For it has the power to look toward the better, and it wills to look toward the lesser. Therefore, as its nature is, so it thinks both of itself and of the things after it. It does not possess things as they are in their changing states, but rather as their causes, knowing even the lower things through their higher forms.

<column-break/>

<margin>ai</margin>
...in a sensory formation. 

### + On the Soul +

Every soul is divine. One type is **self-complete** <note>original: "autotelos," meaning it is perfect in itself and doesn't need a body to function.</note>, while another is directed by the Intellect <margin>o</margin> toward a diversity of things that always remain, specifically the divine souls. Every divine soul acts in a "soul-like" manner. Every soul that is formed we hold to be eternally moving. Every change is a movement of the soul. Every soul is, in part, an essence that exists apart from the body, **unchanging and imperishable**. It is a **middle life** <note>original: "zoē mesē." Neoplatonists viewed the Soul as the "horizon" or bridge between the eternal, indivisible divine realm and the temporary, divisible material realm.</note> between the indivisible beings and those beings divided among bodies. Every soul that can be participated in also possesses an eternal activity, making use of what is immediately above it and being made like that which is primary. From all these things, souls exist as the **paradigms** (models) of the essences and the living substances mentioned.

### + On the Soul +

Concerning the "passions" (affections) of the soul: the highest part of the soul is united only with the **intelligible** <note>original: "noētois," the realm of pure thought/forms.</note> and is capable of "seeing" them. The lowest part of the soul communicates with **sensible** (physical) things, known through the senses and through opinions. The middle part is **discursive reason** <term>Dianoia: the type of logic that moves step-by-step, like a mathematician, rather than the instant "seeing" of the higher Intellect.</term>. Up to this point, it is similar; reasons and opinions belong to the "living being" (the human). For this multi-faceted nature of ours consists of divine portions. For **desire** is a "multi-headed beast." **Spirit** (or anger) is a "lion-like crowd." But the **true part** of us is the Intellect and something even more divine within us. The truest part of us is the friend of the **uniform** <note>original: "monoeidous," meaning simple, single, or monadic, as opposed to the complex and messy material world.</note>, which gazes upon sacred things.

<summary>This page defines the hierarchy of Intellect (Nous) and Soul (Psyche), explaining how the Mind remains unchanged while thinking of changing things and how the Soul serves as a bridge between the divine and material worlds. It concludes with the Platonic tripartite division of the soul using the imagery of the beast, the lion, and the divine intellect.</summary>

<keywords>Intellect, Soul, Neoplatonism, Self-Reflexion, Unparticipated Mind, Discursive Reason, Multi-headed beast, Lion-like spirit, Michael Psellos, Proclus</keywords>

translation:
And if you yourself, knowing nothing such [evil] about yourself, must bitterly rebuke those who sin, both in letters and in tongue; become much more fearful when the things of anger come to you according to the mark, do not spare anything of injustice; but rather, even going beyond the faults; for so it is necessary for those in charge to [ensure] that those who are ruled do not sin at all; but when, after time has passed, you yourself also feel by conscience that you have suffered something badly as if having sinned, or someone else of those under you has done well what is necessary, it would not then be unreasonable to admire repentance; if indeed toward the commands [it is] by part, it is necessary, but one would not overstep; and the things regarding anger [are] advantageous, as there is not where it is necessary to rebuke much for the one wishing to rule; nor to show forgiveness harshly to all; for not to the temperate, and by word, and simply to those who will not allow anything hurtful, do they sin similarly; for because of seeking nothing nor doing absurd things, and besides to the irrational and senseless is this word, the being conscious; but if they should seem to signify things not consonant with the law, let the laws [treat] such people not with horses and brilliant and commanding a private citizen; for it is a custom, as if from a machine, to stand by to bear and hold; whence not even to incline easily to be angry; for if indeed by nature the harsh [things are], but from another nature; these things, therefore, it seems to me, [are] about becoming self-control; wherefore it is necessary for those punishing those who sin, not with some anger and some harsh [manner] being harsh, for such ones stumble before God, [this] it is necessary to confess; for for all the transgression is wicked; but after these it is necessary to know that as toward an irrational [one], it would be to act by the base of own faults; but it is necessary to calculate the sins of the neighbors, so that even living, not to be ignorant; do not become by a temperate law and defend beyond what is necessary; for this reason one might escape being harsh to another, but if not [so], such; for such a one would not wish, to whom it might be better; but not in the magnitude of this, nor in the wishing to make the servants senseless; rather, to all the laws and according to mind, bring the charges; so that it would not be to wish, nor with self-control, nor irrationally, and through sin; for through such an admirable law he serves; but also to do irrational and senseless [things].

<summary>The author provides counsel on the proper conduct of those in authority, emphasizing the need for temperance, the avoidance of uncontrolled anger, and the importance of self-reflection when judging the faults of others.</summary>
<keywords>self-control, sin, law, anger, repentance, judgment</keywords>

# I #

...in ancient times it was perhaps fortified (just as Homer said, "and well-walled **Gortyna**"), but later it lost its wall from the foundations and has remained unfortified for all time. For **Ptolemy Philopator**, having begun to fortify it, only advanced about eighty stadia. At any rate, the settlement once filled a remarkable circle of about fifty stadia. It is ninety stadia distant from the Libyan Sea at **Lebena**, its trading port. It also has another seaport, **Matalum**, which is one hundred and thirty stadia away. The **Lethaeus** River flows through the entire city.

From Lebena came **Leukocomas** and his lover **Euxynthetus**, whose story **Theophrastus** records in his discourse *On Love*. He says that one of the tasks Leukocomas assigned to Euxynthetus was to bring back the dog from **Prasus** for him. The inhabitants of Prasus are neighbors to these people, being seventy stadia from the sea and one hundred and eighty from Gortyna. It has been mentioned that Prasus belonged to the Eteocretans and that the temple of **Dictaean Zeus** was there. For Mount **Dicte** is nearby, not as **Aratus** says, "near the Idaean mountain." For Dicte is a thousand stadia away from Ida, lying to the east of it, and it is a hundred stadia from Samonium. Prasus was situated between Samonium and the **Chersonese**, sixty stadia above the sea. <margin>C. 479</margin> The people of Hierapytna razed it to the ground. They say **Callimachus** is also incorrect in saying that **Britomartis**, fleeing the violence of **Minos**, leaped from Dicte into the nets of fishermen, and for this reason she was called **Dictynna** by the Cydonians and the mountain was called Dicte. For **Cydonia** is not at all in the neighborhood of these places, but lies toward the western limits of the island.

<meta>This page continues the Lamentations of Jeremiah, beginning with the conclusion of verse 11 where the city’s inhabitants trade treasures for food, and continuing through the destruction described in the first five verses of the second chapter.</meta>

## Column 1

They gave her precious things for food to restore the soul; see, O <term>Lord</term>, and look, because I have become dishonored.

<margin>MEM</margin>
All you who pass by the way, turn and see if there is any pain like my pain, which has happened to me; the <term>Lord</term> spoke through me and humbled me in the day of His fierce anger.

<margin>NUN</margin>
From His height He sent fire into my bones and brought it down; He spread a net for my feet, He turned me back, He made me desolate and grieving all the day.

<margin>SAMEKH</margin>
He watched over my impieties; they were entwined in my hands, they went up upon my neck; my strength failed, for the <term>Lord</term> gave pains into my hands, and I will not be able to stand.

<margin>AYIN</margin>
The <term>Lord</term> has taken away all my strong men

### CCXXXV. — HIERACI DIACONO.
<margin>Cavendum ne specie utilitatis decipiaris. Non videmus manticam in tergo.</margin>
> Decipis forsan teipsum putans te cernere quod in rem sit tuam. Cernere quidem videris, non cernis tamen, sed plerumque in tuis rebus cæcutis. Si enim quod ambiguum incertumque putatur, honorificum opinaris, neque mihi, neque tibi judicium permittas, sed communicans cum judicio prudentiaque præstantibus, sententiam ab illis mutuare.

### CCXXXVI. — JACOBO LECTORI.
<margin>Malos esse fugiendos. Consuetudo enim altera natura.</margin>
> Fuge, o charissime, improbos: quippe noxiam quemdam habitum animæ usu et consuetudine sua sensim ingenerant. Plerique enim fallentes seipsos quasi optimi sint et fortissimi, quasique tales casus lædere non possint, clam in mala se lenteque velut in barathrum præcipitant. Consuetudo enim quid magnum, et in naturam paulatim abit; alteramque esse naturam quidam affirmant. Alii etiam a consuetudine superari naturam, illud veteris poetæ adhibentes, asserunt.
>
> Gutta cavum reddit saxum, dum decidit usque.
> Et vero quid saxo durius? quid aqua mollius? attamen ictu assiduo naturæ vincitur durities.

### CCXXXVII. — HIERACI DIACONO.
<margin>Temperantia sanitatis mater.</margin>

(63) In place of "to be established" [*katastēnai*], both of the same codices write "to be transformed" [*metastēnai*]. Possinus.

(64) This is a proverbial verse of the poet Choerilus, who was not as inept as he seemed to Q. Flaccus. It is praised by many and invoked by Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius in Book IX of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, and by Simplicius in Book VIII of Aristotle's *Physics*. The passage was likewise expressed by Latin poets, by T. Lucretius and P. Ovid. The former in Book IV of *On the Nature of Things*, at the end:
> Do you not also see drops of moisture falling on rocks,
> In a long space of time, pierce the rocks?

And in Book I:
> The falling of a drip hollows out stones.

Naso [Ovid] indeed in Book IV *From the Pontus*:
> A drop hollows a stone, a ring is worn away by use;
> And the curved plowshare is worn by the pressed earth.

As for what Isidore adds here: *What is harder than a rock? What is softer than water?*, the poet Ovid expressed the same elsewhere thus:
> What is more hard than a rock? What is softer than a wave?
> Yet hard rocks are hollowed by soft water.

And Isidore himself in Book III, Epistle 284: *But I would wish to be persuaded of that,* he says, *which someone has asserted: that waters smooth the stones.* Tibullus, Book I, Elegy 4:
> Time itself eats away rocks with soft water.

And Plutarch in the treatise *On the Education of Children*: "Drops of water hollow a rock." Concerning the word *entelecheia* in the definition of the soul, I have discussed it abundantly in the *Tusculan Disputations*, Book IV, chapters 21, 22, and 23. Other verses of Choerilus were cited by Hadrianus Turnebus in Book IX of the *Adversaria*, chapter 9, and by M. Antonius Muretus in Book XII of the *Variae Lectiones*, chapter 14.

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the Eighth Homeric Hymn (To Ares) before transitioning into the introduction and commentary for the Ninth Hymn (To Artemis). The previous page established the late, "Orphic" character of the Hymn to Ares.</meta>

# 324

...brave men. Cf. *Orphic Hymn* 55, 11. — "turning the bright circle" <note>original Greek: *paraugea kyklon elissōn*</note>. According to Preller (*Mythology* I, p. 269), the sun is meant here, though this is hardly correct. According to the usual explanation, which finds strong support in line 10, "beaming down a mild light" <note>original Greek: *prēy katastilbōn selas*</note>, the text refers to the planet Mars, which is famously known to glow with a reddish light. Cf. Bergk, as cited above, p. 752.

7. **"Among the seven-pathed stars of the ether"** <note>original Greek: *aitheros heptaporois eni teiresin*</note> was already explained by Matthiae through Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher from the 5th century AD whose commentaries often touch on celestial mechanics.</note>, *Hymn* IV, 7: "whether you dwell in the ether above the rims of the seven circles" <note>original Greek: *eite kai hepta kyklōn hyper antygas aithera naieis*</note>. Bergk noted that one cannot think of celestial spheres <note>The ancient Greek concept that stars and planets were fixed to rotating crystalline shells.</note> before the time of Anaximander <note>An early Greek philosopher (c. 610–546 BC) credited with the first mechanical model of the world.</note>. However, no one would likely date this hymn as far back as Anaximander's time.

8. **"Above the third arch"** <note>original Greek: *tritatēs hyper antygos*</note> is explained by the passage from Proclus just cited.

9. **"Hear me, beaming down"** <note>original Greek: *klythi katastilbōn*</note> is supported by *Orphic Hymns* 3, 9; 27, 11; and 33, 27. Hemsterhuys and Ilgen wrote "beam down" <note>original Greek: *katastilpson*, the imperative form</note>. — "Courageous" <note>original Greek: *eutharseos*</note> in manuscripts D and M is an obvious improvement over "flourishing" <note>original Greek: *euthaleos*</note> found in manuscript E and some of the Paris class, which usually has a short *a* but occasionally appears with a long *a*. Jacobs already wrote "well-blooming" <note>original Greek: *euthēlē*</note> in *Palatine Anthology* 9, 247.

10. **"Life"** <note>original Greek: *biotēta*</note>—perhaps "youth" <note>original Greek: *neotēta*</note>? "The word *biotēta* points to a very late period," according to Bernhardy, *History of Greek Literature* II, I, p. 417.

16. **Ares as a bringer of peace?** This is based, as A. Matthiae already recognized, on the view that the one who brings the harm can also heal it.

17. Wolf and Ilgen followed Barnes in writing "violent" <note>original Greek: *biaias*, feminine form</note>, but Baumeister correctly defended "violent" <note>original Greek: *biaious*, masculine form</note> by citing Plato's *Republic* 3, 399 A. and *Laws* 10, 885 A.

<header>PREFACE</header>

Most recently, G. Koertius initiated a study on that part of the *Cynegeticus* <note>On Hunting</note> which is called technical, though he was cut short by death before he could bring it to completion. He first set forth that not only is the arrangement inconvenient, but the instruction itself is so incomplete and obscure that it could hardly be useful to hunters. It must be admitted that he argued this point correctly; yet, it confirms our conjecture regarding the origin of this little book. For the heir of Xenophon, a man certainly not unversed in rhetorical studies but little skilled in writing, preserved the series of events whole, just as he had found them written down in the volume handed to him, and he did not dare to add anything from his own knowledge that might clarify the rules or organize them into a suitable order.

"But," says Koertius, "many precepts in this part of the work are so false that they could in no way have been written by a man truly skilled in the art of hunting." The Fates prevented him from explaining and establishing this opinion with a full number of examples. But I would say that some things, at least, which he criticized or was about to criticize, are controversial rather than false. For the writer of the *Cynegeticus* advises that when a hare has been caught by the dogs, the hunter should hand it over to them to be torn apart. Koertius criticizes this advice as entirely absurd. Yet Blanius, a man no less knowledgeable in the art of hunting than Koertius, recommends the very same thing. What of it? In his book *On Horsemanship*, Xenophon praises Simon for teaching that the quality of a horse's feet is revealed by the sound; yet Bourgelat and Berenger declare this to be clearly false. Learned men struggle against one another over these and such matters, and no one could easily judge what is right or true in any given art. Therefore, not for this reason would I deprive Xenophon of the *Cynegeticus* simply because some who are hunters today attack part of its precepts. Nor, even if we grant that the author of the *Cynegeticus* often speaks nonsense, can it be understood why Arrian, especially since he disagrees not infrequently, never leveled such an objection against him.

For the purpose of reviewing the most corrupt text of all, the manuscripts known as Vindobonensis A and Vaticanus B are by far the most useful, regarding which, if you please, see what I have already stated in the preface to the book *On Horsemanship*. However, since the Vatican manuscript begins mutilated, starting from the word <term>παιδεύματα</term> <gloss>trainings/teachings</gloss> (ii. 1), and since the Vienna manuscript exhibits many more peculiarities in the first chapter than in the others, the prologue must be treated separately. Therefore, let us begin with the word <term>παιδεύματα</term> <gloss>trainings</gloss>:

**νιφοσιβεῖς** δίνυροι· <gloss>S Ai. 669</gloss> "καὶ γὰρ τὰ δεινὰ καὶ τὰ καρτερώτατα τιμαῖς ὑπείκει. τοῦτο μὲν νιφοσιβεῖς χειμῶνες ἐκχωροῦσιν εὐκάρπῳ θέρει."

**νόημα** ἐφεύρεμα· <gloss>A Eq. 1203</gloss> "τὸ μὲν νόημα τῆς θεοῦ, τὸ δὲ κλέμμ' ἐμόν." οὕτω γὰρ οἱ δημαγωγοὶ ἀσεϊζόμενοι ἔλεγον τὰς ἑαυτῶν ἐπινοίας τῆς θεοῦ, ὅτι ἡ μὲν θεὸς ὑπέβαλεν, ἥρπασα δ' ἐγώ.

**Νοήμονος**.

**νοητά** τὰ μὴ αἰσθητά, τὰ ἀόρατα.

**νοθεία** ἡ λαθραία γέννα, ἡ πορνεία.

**νοθεῖα**. τὰ τοῖς νόθοις ἐκ τῶν πατρῴων διδόμενα οὕτω καλεῖται, ἦν δὲ μέχρι χιλίων δραχμῶν. οὕτω *Λυσίας* καὶ *Ἰσαῖος* καὶ *Ἀριστοφάνης* <gloss>Av. 1643</gloss> καὶ *Ὑπερίδης* καὶ *Δημοσθένης* ἐν τῷ κατὰ *Ἀριστοκράτες* <gloss>213</gloss>. Harp.

**νοθεύει** ἀπατᾷ, ἀπαλλοτριοῖ.

**νόθος** ὁ ξένος.

**νοιδίων** διανοημάτων. παρήγαγε δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ πληθυντικοῦ τοῦ οἱ νοῖ τὸ νοιδίον ὑποκοριστικόν. τινὲς δὲ οὕτως, ὀνειδισμῶν καὶ λοιδοριῶν ἀπὸ τῇ οἴνε καὶ τῆς μέθης. *Ἀριστοφάνης* <gloss>Eq. 100</gloss> "ἐγὼ δὲ πάντα καταπάσω βουλευματίων γνωμιδίων νοιδίων."

**νομάδες** βοσκόμεναι ἀγέλαι. καὶ ἔθνη Σκυθικά· "νομάδεσι γὰρ ἐν Σκύθαις ἀλᾶται *Στράτων*" *Ἀριστοφάνης* <gloss>Av. 942</gloss>. ἐπὶ τῶν παρενοχλούντων καὶ ἐπιμενόντων, ἐπειδὴ οἱ Σκύθαι τῷ χειμῶνι διὰ τὸ ἀφόρητον αὐτοῦ ἐφ' ἁμαξῶν τὰ πράγματα βάλλοντες ἀπαίρουσιν εἰς ἄλλην χώραν. ὁ δὲ μὴ ἔχων ἐκεῖσε ἅμαξαν ἄτιμος παρ' αὐτοῖς κρίνεται.

**νομαδίτης** ὁ ἰδιώτης βίος.

**νομάδων** ἀγρίων, βαρβάρων, οἱ λεγόμενοι ἁμαξοφόρητοι ἢ ἁμαξόβιοι.

**νομαί** μερισμοί.

**νομαία** ἡ ἐκ τῆς νομῆς· ἐν ἐπιγράμμασι <gloss>AP 6 157</gloss> "καί σοι ἐπιρροέξει χιμάροιο νομαίης αἷμα."

**νομάρχαι** οἱ κατὰ τέλη τῆς χώρας ἄρχοντες παρ' Αἰγυπτίοις· οἳ ἦσαν ἐπὶ Πτολεμαίου τοῦ μετὰ *Ἀλέξανδρον* τὸν Φιλίππου.

**Νομᾶς** ὄνομα κύριον, ὁ Ῥωμαίων νομοθέτης.

**νομεύς** ποιμήν, βοσκός.

**νομή** ὁρμὴ πυρός· "τὴν νομὴν τοῦ πυ-

<column-break/>

ρὸς ἐνεργὸν συνέβη γενέσθαι καὶ πρακτικήν" <gloss>Polyb. 1 48</gloss>.

**νομιζόμενα** νόμιμα, ἢ ὑπολαμβανόμενα· *Ἀριστοφάνης* <gloss>Plut. 1186</gloss> "οὐκοῦν τὰ νομιζόμενα σὺ τέτων λαμβάνεις." ἐπειδὴ νόμος ἦν τὰ ὑπολειπόμενα τῆς θυσίας τὸν ἱερέα λαμβάνειν. δέρματα καὶ κωλαῖ. cf. v. κωλακρέτης.

**νομίζουσιν** ἀντὶ τοῦ νομίσματι χρῶνται. καὶ νομίζουσιν ἀντὶ τοῦ ἡγοῦνται· "ἥνπερ μεγίστην τιμὴν παρὰ βασιλέως ἐς ἰδιώτας νομίζουσι."

**νόμιον** δίκαιον. καὶ νόμιον μέλος τὸ ἐν τῇ νομῇ ᾀδόμενον.

**νόμισμα** δύο σημαίνει, τὸ νόμιμον ἔθος, ὡς *Ἀριστοφάνης* ἐν *Νεφέλαις* <gloss>249</gloss> "ἡμῖν νόμισμ' οὐκ ἔξι," καὶ τὸ κόμμα τᾶ τετυπωμένου χαλκοῦ. λεπτῷ δὲ νομίσματι ἐχρῶντο οἱ Βυζάντιοι.

**νομιζομένων** νομίμως διοικουμένων· "ἐνέβαλε δὲ χρυσοῦς ἐπισήμους, εἴς τινας δὲ τετράδραχμα τῶν ἐπιφανῶς νομιζομένων." καὶ αὖθις "χαλκοῦ τοῦ ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ νομιζομένου τάλαντα τετρακισχίλια."

**Νομίτωρος** ὄνομα κύριον.

**νομογράφοι**. παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις τριακοσιοσῷ πρώτῳ ἐνιαυτῷ μετὰ τὸν συνοικισμὸν τῆς πόλεως, παραλυθείσης τῆς τῶν ὑπάτων ἀρχῆς, ί νομογράφοι τὴν τῶν κοινῶν ἐπιτρέπονται προστασίαν· οἳ χρόνον δή τινα πρὸς τὸ λυσιτελὲς καὶ ἡδὺ τῶν πολιτῶν ἐξηγούμενοι μέτριοί τε ἐδόκουν καὶ ἄρχειν μάλισα πάντων ἐπιτήδειοι. οὗτοι γάρ πε καὶ τὰς ί δέλτους ἐπιχωρίοις τε καὶ Ἑλληνικοῖς νόμοις ἀναγράψαντες ἐς τὰς καλουμένας κύρβεις ἀνέθηκαν. δευτέρῳ δὲ ἔτει τῆς ἡγεμονίας, βαρύτητος τυραννικῆς αἰτίαν ἀπενεγκάμενοι διελύθησαν, *Ἀππίου* μάλισα τὸ πλῆθος εἰς ἀπέχθειαν τῆς δεκαρχίας κινήσαντος, ὃς *Βεργινίᾳ* τινὸς ἀνδρὸς οὐκ ἀσήμε τὰ πολεμικὰ θυγατέρα φθεῖραι παρθένον ἐπενόει, ἔρωτι γεγονὼς θερμῷ τῆς κόρης κατάσχετος· ἣν ὁ πατὴρ αὐτοχειρὶ διεχρήσατο, δείσας τὴν τοῦ *Ἀππίου* δυναστείαν, αἰσχῦναι τὴν κόρην πρὸς βίαν ὡριμημένε. ἐφ' ᾧ κινηθὲν τὸ στρατιωτικὸν ἅπαν ἀφείλετο τοὺς ί τὰ τῆς ἐξουσίας, δίκας τε ἀποτίσαι τῶν κατὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν πεπλημμελημένων ἠνάγκασε.

**νομοθεσία** θέσις νόμου.

**νομοθέται** τὸ πάλαι *Μωυσῆς*, μετέ<sig>α</sig>πειτα δὲ ὁ *Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς*.

<header>νιφοσιβεῖς — νομοθέται a</header>

**niphosibeis** <gloss>snow-lashed</gloss>, stormy; (Sophocles, *Ajax* 669) "For even terrible and most powerful things yield to honors. Snow-lashed winters give way to a fruit-bearing summer."

**noēma** <gloss>thought/idea/invention</gloss>; (Aristophanes, *Knights* 1203) "The thought was the goddess's, but the theft was mine." For this is how the demagogues used to play tricks, attributing their own schemes to the goddess, saying that the goddess suggested it, but I snatched it up.

**Noēmonos** <gloss>a proper name</gloss>.

**noēta** <gloss>intelligible things</gloss>, the non-sensible, the invisible.

**notheia** <gloss>illegitimacy</gloss>, secret birth, prostitution.

**notheia** <gloss>illegitimate share</gloss>. That which is given to illegitimate children from their paternal inheritance is called this, and it was up to one thousand drachmas. Thus Lysias, Isaeus, Aristophanes (*Birds* 1643), Hyperides, and Demosthenes in the speech against Aristocrates (213). Harpocration.

**notheuei** <gloss>adulterates/falsifies</gloss>, he deceives, he alienates.

**nothos** <gloss>bastard</gloss>, the stranger.

**noidiōn** <gloss>thoughts/notions</gloss>. He derived *noidion* as a diminutive from the plural *hoi noi* <gloss>the minds</gloss>. Others say it comes from reproaches and abuse, from *oinē* <gloss>wine</gloss> and drunkenness. Aristophanes (*Knights* 100): "I will sprinkle everything with little plans, little maxims, little notions."

**nomades** <gloss>nomads</gloss>, grazing herds. And Scythian tribes; "For among the nomadic Scythians wanders Straton" (Aristophanes, *Birds* 942). Used of those who disturb and persist, since the Scythians, because of the unbearable cold of winter, pack their belongings onto wagons and depart to another land. He who does not have a wagon there is judged dishonored among them.

**nomaditēs** <gloss>nomadic life</gloss>, the private life.

**nomadōn** <gloss>of nomads</gloss>, of wild, barbaric people, those called wagon-carriers or wagon-dwellers.

**nomai** <gloss>divisions/distributions</gloss>.

**nomaia** <gloss>from the pasture</gloss>; in epigrams (AP 6.157): "And the blood of the pasture-fed kid shall flow over you."

**nomarchai** <gloss>provincial governors</gloss>, the rulers of the districts of the land among the Egyptians; they were in power under Ptolemy, the one after Alexander son of Philip.

**Nomas** is a proper name, the lawgiver of the Romans.

**nomeus** <gloss>herdsman</gloss>, shepherd.

**nomē** <gloss>impulse/spread of fire</gloss>; "The spread of the fire happened to be active and effective" (Polybius 1.48).

<column-break/>

**nomizomena** <gloss>customary things</gloss>, customs, or things supposed; Aristophanes (*Plutus* 1186): "Do you not receive your customary portions from these?" Since it was the custom for the priest to receive what was left over from the sacrifice: hides and thighs. Cf. the entry *kolakretēs* <gloss>collector of public funds</gloss>.

**nomizousin** <gloss>they use</gloss>, instead of "they use as currency." And *nomizousin* instead of "they consider"; "Which they consider the greatest honor from the king for private citizens."

**nomion** <gloss>just/lawful</gloss>. And a *nomion* melody is that which is sung in the pasture.

**nomisma** <gloss>coin/custom</gloss> signifies two things: the lawful custom, as Aristophanes in *Clouds* (249), "We have no currency <note>original: "νόμισμα"</note>," and the stamping of minted bronze. The Byzantines used a small coin.

**nomizomenōn** <gloss>lawfully managed</gloss>; "He threw in stamped gold coins, and in some, tetradrachms of those clearly accepted as currency." And again: "Four thousand talents of the bronze accepted as currency in Alexandria."

**Nomitor** is a proper name.

**nomographoi** <gloss>law-writers/decemvirs</gloss>. Among the Romans, in the three hundred and first year after the foundation of the city, the office of the consuls having been abolished, ten law-writers were entrusted with the protection of public affairs. For a certain time, as they interpreted the law for the profit and pleasure of the citizens, they seemed moderate and most suitable of all to rule. For these men, having written the ten tables in both local and Greek laws, set them up on the so-called *kyrbeis* <gloss>three-sided tablets</gloss>. But in the second year of their leadership, having incurred the charge of tyrannical weight, they were dissolved, after Appius especially stirred the multitude to hatred of the decemvirate, for he intended to ruin the virgin daughter of a certain man—who was not obscure in military affairs—being gripped by a hot desire for the girl. The father killed her with his own hand, fearing the tyranny of Appius, as he was rushing to ravish the girl by force. At this, the entire military was moved, stripped the ten of their authority, and forced them to pay penalties for the crimes committed during their rule.

**nomothesia** <gloss>legislation</gloss>, the setting of a law.

**nomothetai** <gloss>lawgivers</gloss>. In olden times Moses, and afterwards Christ Jesus.

<summary>This page defines terms related to the letters N and the early Greek alphabet, specifically focusing on comic poets, historical figures (Nicostratus, Nicon), and the development of legal terminology (nomisma, nomothetai).</summary>
