In the time of the emperor Theophilus, Scholasticius the door-keeper was chamberlain, and in the time of Michael, son of Theophilus, the patrician Damian was chamberlain and after him, in the same reign, Basil, the Christ-loving emperor, was chamberlain. In the time of Basil, the Christ-loving sovereign, there was no chamberlain during all his reign. In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Samonas was chamberlain, and after him, in the time of the same emperor, the patrician Constantine. In the time of Alexander the emperor, the patrician Barbatus was chamberlain; and in the time of Constantine, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Constantine, mentioned before in the time of the sovereign Leo, was chamberlain again; and in the time of the sovereign Romanus, the patrician Theophanes; and in the second reign of Constantine, the patrician Basil.

In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving and ever-memorable emperor, lived the late Ktenas, an aged cleric of great wealth, who was precentor of the New Church and was skilled in singing as was no other at that time. This same Ktenas besought the patrician Samonas, who was at that time chamberlain, to intercede for him with the emperor so that he might be made protospatharius and wear the shirt and go in procession to the Lausiacus and take his seat as protospatharius and receive a stipend of one pound, and in respect of this remuneration might give the emperor forty pounds. But the emperor could not bring himself to do this, saying that it was out of his power, and «to the great disgrace of my imperial majesty if a cleric becomes protospatharius». On hearing this from the patrician Samonas, this same Ktenas added to the forty pounds a pair of ear-rings valued at ten pounds, and a silver table with animals on it in gold relief, also valued at ten pounds. And the emperor, besought by the request of the patrician Samonas, the chamberlain, took the forty pounds of gold and the pair of ear-rings and the table with its gold on silver relief work, so that the total gift of the same Ktenas amounted to sixty pounds. Then the emperor made him protospatharius, and he received a stipend on that occasion of one pound. After being honoured with the rank of protospatharius this same Ktenas lived two years and then died; and he received a stipend of one pound for each of the two years.

by the gods, it was for two reasons: they both thought that I had suffered terrible things and they wished at the same time to take vengeance for what they had seen him do to others, as he is bold and disgusting and <margin>3</margin> no longer even controllable. Since things are this way, all things that it was proper for me to guard have been justly kept for you, and I am here to accuse as you see since someone is bringing the case in. I have refused much money, O men of Athens, which I might have taken on the condition that I would not accuse him, and I have <margin>4</margin> endured many petitions and favors and, by Zeus, threats. But for what remains among you after this, the more this man has troubled and sent around messages (for I saw him just now before the courts doing such things), the more I hope to have justice. For I would not think so poorly of any of you, neither that you will neglect those things about which you yourselves were zealous toward me, nor that, so that Meidias might outrage others without fear in the future, any of you will vote, having sworn an oath, anything <margin>5</margin> other than what he thinks is just. If, therefore, O men of Athens, I were going to accuse him of illegalities or of a corrupt embassy or some other such charge, I would not think it right to ask anything of you, thinking that it belongs to the accuser regarding such things only to prove them, and to the defendant to ask for mercy. But since he corrupted the judges, and because of this the tribe was unjustly <margin>6</margin> deprived of the tripod, and I myself received blows and was outraged in such a way as I do not know if any other <term>choregos</term> was ever outraged, and I come into court following the vote of condemnation which the people made because they were indignant and shared in my anger over these things, I will not hesitate to also make a request. For if it is possible to say this, I am now the one on trial, if indeed for an outraged man to meet with no justice is a kind of calamity. <header>CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA</header>

<note>The text begins with a fragment of Julius Cassianus, an ascetic who advocated for the rejection of marriage and the body, followed by Clement’s rebuttal.</note>

> ...Isaiah. For if such a structure were from the God toward whom we hasten, He would not have blessed the eunuchs; nor would the prophet have said that they are not to be a barren tree, taking it from the tree and placing it on the free will of men who make themselves eunuchs for such a concept. And, struggling for his holy opinion, he adds: "For everyone..." And would one not reasonably praise the Savior if He transformed us and liberated us from error and from the communion of parts and appendages and genitals? 

This man teaches things similar to Tatian. He came from the school of Valentinus.
<margin>188</margin> For this reason, Cassianus says, when Salome asked when the things she asked about would be known, the Lord said: "When you trample upon the garment of shame, and when the two become one, and the male with the female, neither male nor female."

First of all, we do not have this saying in the four gospels handed down to us, but in that according to the Egyptians. Furthermore, he seems to me to be ignorant of the fact that "anger" hints at the male impulse, and "female" hints at desire; for those who act on these, repentance and shame follow. When, therefore, we do not indulge in anger or desire—which, having grown from habit and bad nourishment, overshadow and cloak the intellect—but having cast off the gloom from these, being put to shame through repentance, we unite spirit and soul according to the obedience of the Word; then, as Paul says, "There is neither male nor female among you." For when this soul, which has been distinguished by the appearance of male and female, departs, it is transferred into unity, no longer being one or the other. 

This noble man assumes, in a more Platonic manner, that the soul, being divine from above, was feminized by desire and came down here into generation and corruption. Immediately he struggles to claim that Paul says generation is constituted from deception, through these words: "For I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve, your minds might be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ." 

But the Lord also came explicitly for the sake of those who had strayed. And they had not strayed from above into this generation here; for generation is a creation of the Almighty, who would never bring a soul down from better to worse. But the Savior arrived for those who had strayed in name, for us; we who were corrupted by the disobedience of the commandments, having been lovers of pleasure. Perhaps the time of the first creation encompassed us, and we reached out for the grace of marriage before the proper time, and missed the mark. For "everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart," not having waited for the time of the will. The same Lord, even then, judged the desire that surrounded marriage. 

When, therefore, the Apostle says, "Put on the new man, which is being created according to God," he speaks to us, who have been fashioned according to the will of the Almighty as we have been fashioned. He does not read "old" in relation to generation, but in relation to the life in disobedience, before obedience. And Cassianus considers the "garments of skin" to be the bodies, regarding which we shall later prove both him and those who teach the same things as he does to be straying, when we handle the explanation of the creation of man consistently for those who need to be refuted. For, he says, those who are ruled by earthly things both marry and are given in marriage; but our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await a Savior. He spoke well, and we know these things; for we ought to live as foreigners and sojourners: those marrying as if not marrying; those acquiring as if not acquiring; those begetting children as if begetting mortals, as those who will leave behind their possessions, as those who will live without a woman if need be; using the possession with which they have been entrusted with thanksgiving in all things, and being high-minded. 

And again, when he says: "It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of sexual immoralities, let each man have his own wife"—as if explaining it again, he says, "So that Satan may not tempt you." For he does not say this because of incontinence to those who use marriage strictly for procreation alone, but to those who desire to proceed beyond procreation, so that the one who opposes, not having bent them much, might not stir up the appetite toward strange pleasures. Perhaps he opposes those living righteously out of jealousy and rivalry, wishing to lead them into his own rank, and wishes to provide them with occasions for grievous abstinence. Rationally, therefore, he says: "It is better to marry than to burn," so that the husband may render the debt to the wife, and the wife to the husband; and they should not deprive one another of the help given by God for generation. 

"Whoever," they say, "does not hate father, or mother, or wife, or children, cannot be my disciple." It is not that he commands to hate; for "Honor your father and mother," He says, "so that it may go well with you." But, "Do not be led away," He says, "by irrational impulses, nor be joined to political customs." For a household is not constituted by marriage, but cities are from households. Just as Paul said that those who are busy with marriage seek to please the world. Again, the Lord says: "He who has married, let him not cast out; and he who has not married, let him not marry." He who has confessed for the sake of pleasing God not to marry,

translation:
### PHYSICS, BOOK VIII

to judge in the same way as those who are older, for the confusion and motion surrounding them are great. <note>original: "πολλὴ γὰρ ἡ ταραχὴ καὶ ἡ κίνησις"</note> One is established and settles into a state of rest—sometimes by nature itself, and at other times by other things—yet in both cases, some things within the body undergo alteration, just as in the case of waking and of activity, when one becomes sober and awakens. It is therefore evident from what has been said that being altered and <term>alteration</term> <gloss>a change in quality</gloss> take place in sensible things and in the sensitive part of the soul, and in nothing else except by accident.

One might puzzle over whether every motion is comparable to every other motion or not. If all are comparable, and if that which moves an equal amount in an equal time is of equal speed, then some curved line would be equal to a straight line, and furthermore, a greater one and a smaller one would be equal. Moreover, alteration and <term>locomotion</term> <gloss>motion in space</gloss> would be equal when, in an equal time, one thing is altered and the other is moved. Thus, a change in quality would be equal to a length. But this is impossible. Is it then the case that whenever something is moved by an equal amount in an equal time, it is of equal speed? But a change in quality is not equal to a length. Thus, there is no alteration equal to a locomotion, nor even a smaller one. Therefore, not everything is comparable. And how will it happen in the case of a circle and a straight line? For it is absurd if one cannot move in a circle in the same way as in a straight line, but there is an immediate necessity to move either faster or slower, just as if one were moving downhill and the other uphill. Furthermore, it makes no difference in the argument if someone claims that there is a necessity to move faster or slower immediately; for the curved line would be greater and smaller than the straight one, and consequently also equal. For if in time A, one thing 

<column-break/>

traversed B and the other traversed C, then B would be greater than C; for let it be said that this was the faster. It is no different if the same amount is traversed in less time, it is faster; thus there will be some part of A in which it traverses the equal amount of the circle, and in the whole of A it traverses C. However, if they are comparable, the result just mentioned occurs: that a straight line is equal to a circular one. But they are not comparable; therefore, neither are the motions. But all things that are not <term>homonymous</term> <gloss>having the same name but different definitions</gloss> are comparable. For example, why is it not comparable whether a stylus, wine, or the <term>nete</term> <gloss>the highest-pitched string of a lyre</gloss> is sharper? Because they are homonymous, they are not comparable; but the <term>nete</term> is comparable to the <term>paranete</term> <gloss>the string next to the highest</gloss>, because "sharp" signifies the same thing in both. Is it therefore not the same "fast" here and there? It is even less so in alteration and locomotion. Or is this first point—that non-homonymous things are comparable—not true? For "much" signifies the same thing in water and in air, yet they are not comparable. And if not that, "double" signifies the same (for it is two to one), and they are not comparable. Or is the same account true for these as well? For "much" is also homonymous. But in some cases, the definitions themselves are homonymous, as if one were to say that "much" is "that amount and something else." "That amount" and "equal" are homonymous, and even "one," as it happens, is immediately homonymous. If this is so, then "two" is also; for why are some things comparable and others not, if there were one nature? Or is it because they are in a different primary receptive subject? A horse and a dog are comparable as to which is whiter; for the subject in which it primarily resides—the surface—is the same. And the same applies to magnitude. But water and sound are not; for they are in different subjects. Or is it clear that in this way one could make everything one, in another...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the taxonomy of fear. It transitions into the physical manifestations of grief and introduces the physiology and categorization of anger.</meta>

<header>NEMESIUS</header>

The organ of grief <note>original: λύπη (lypē). While "pain" is a general translation, in this context of emotions, "grief" or "distress" is more appropriate.</note> is the mouth of the stomach. For this is the part that feels the "biting" sensation during times of grief. As 
> **Galen** says in the sixth book of his *Demonstrations*: 
> In those who are grieving, a considerable amount of yellow bile flows down into the stomach; this is what causes the biting sensation for them, and they do not stop grieving and feeling "bitten" until they have vomited the bile. 
For this biting occurs just below the middle of the chest at the cartilage called the **xiphoid** <note>The xiphoid process is the small cartilaginous extension at the lower part of the sternum.</note>. However, the heart lies much higher up. Relative to the diaphragm, the stomach is located lower down, while the heart is higher. Yet, the ancients commonly called both the heart and the mouth of the stomach by the name *kardia* <term>kardia: καρδία</term> <note>In ancient medicine, "kardia" referred to both the heart and the upper opening of the stomach. This is why we still use the term "cardiac" in relation to the stomach's upper sphincter.</note>. This is seen in **Hippocrates** and also **Thucydides**, who, when describing the Great Plague, says: 
> "And whenever it settled in the *kardia* [the stomach], it upset it, and discharges of bile—all those named by doctors—followed." 
For that which is "upset" or overturned is the mouth of the stomach, which is forced to vomit, and not the internal organ we call the heart.

### ON ANGER. CHAPTER 21.

**Anger** <term>thymos: θυμός</term> is a boiling of the blood around the heart, caused by the evaporation or the agitation of the bile. For this reason, it is also called *cholē* <note>original: χολὴ (bile/gall)</note> and *cholos* <note>original: χόλος (bitter anger or bile)</note>. Sometimes anger is also defined as a desire for retaliation. When we are wronged, or believe we are being wronged, we become angry; in such cases, the passion becomes a mixture of desire and anger. 

There are three types of anger: **wrath** <term>orgē: ὀργὴ</term>, which is also called *cholē* or *cholos*; **rage** <term>mēnis: μῆνις</term>; and **resentment** <term>kotos: κότος</term>. For while anger at its beginning...

The nature of a good thing arises from external sources. Nor should these things be prepared against the enemy, or, when acting with other neighbors, failing in the agreement of the neighbors. Therefore, when it is reported that the enemy is preparing against us, it is necessary first to set [our position] in safety, such as the previously mentioned cities and lands. Then, one must aim to reach a state of desperation while observing the rest, and clearing out one's own places through which they intend to pass, so that the agreement back to us may be a clear trap for the enemy and profitable to us. As for what we give, whether we eat—for example, if we are campaigning with others and it is reported that the enemies are with us—it brings profit to us to be annoyed at those warring, and likewise if others are campaigning against them. Whether it is a civil war or [a war] of neighbors, one remains quiet, for the one warring often makes peace with himself while watching the foreigners, but one must be a neighbor. Those who have descended should each give back to those who are aware of the initiation <note>original: "μυσάγωγία"</note> what is proper. Both neighbors must have acted safely, as it is necessary for all of them to deliberate, and in what manner, and within what place—only the marketplace, through which many of our people and foreigners come up, while looking toward the trade. For in this, they will be more able to take the enemies. Hence, as the day progresses, again the same things of others [are returned] to them, and [one is] returning wars and showing us what is said among our own—the enemies and how their things are hostile. It is necessary for all those who command not to be of the same race as the opponents, nor to have suffered any great evil <margin>others kill</margin> from us, such as wives, children, parents, or brothers being there because of us, the longing for whom might make them wish for the enemies to be allowed into any place, not otherwise plotting against their own. It is necessary for them to be wise by nature, and those who are said to be warring well, <margin>fifth plaque</margin> having chosen those who are prepared. Furthermore, they must be experienced in the places through which they will pass. They must also be personally arriving.

translation:
But from the place where this excavated material is carried away in equal portions, they also collect the rubble according to the laws established previously in those places. This material they consider among the worthless things, having handed it over. The elders, who are most observant of the laws, transport the stone. These men are considered great by those called overseers <term>epopousin</term> <gloss>those who watch over or inspect</gloss>. For those within thirty years of age bear witness to the others. Likewise, having received it with courage, they strike it with iron tools upon silver-like surfaces. And they perform the greatest grinding in a similar manner, at the same hour, using thick pieces in part. In this way, the law honors the women who have been trained together after the watches. To the men and the leaders, there are a multitude of mills in a row. Upon these, they perform the treading of the stone just like the others, and all the women from the market are present. In this way, they describe the process. My breath <note>or perhaps "the scent"</note> exists as a captive of the body. They grind, and they continue grinding until the whole measure is reduced to dust, which is the portion handed over. All these people are those who have come to the number of captivity, facing death, even this very death. But for those who are entreating, the refinement <term>katargasmon</term> <gloss>working down or processing of ore</gloss> succeeds. Those called the "hares" <note>likely a technical term for a specific class of laborer or a specific tool</note> say all these things, having undertaken the royal service for the whole task. The labor is of such a kind: they cover the strength of the marble with woolly coverings. Upon flat boards, there is a spreading and an inspection as if we were burying someone. It is not upright. The exhausted land has flashed forth the name of gold. While carrying water, they rub it with their hands; at first lightly, then more vigorously. I am purified <note>original: "agnooumai", likely a scribal error for "agnizomai"</note>. For that which is exhausted flows away together with the influx of the boarding.

<summary>This page describes the labor-intensive process of gold mining and refining, involving the transport of ore, the use of mills by men and women, and the final washing of the crushed material on boards.</summary>

translation:
<meta>This page transitions from the general discussion of material elements to the specific metaphysical principles—Providence and Analogy—that Proclus believes the Demiurge (the Creator) used to bind the cosmos into a unified "icon" of the divine. It expands on the mathematical ratios discussed previously, applying them to the immortality of the soul and the structure of the world as a "living being."</meta>

# Commentary on Plato’s Timaeus

<page-num>130</page-num>

Those who hypothesize the cause of the **dissolution** <note>original: "lyseos" (λύσεως). In Platonism, this refers to the breaking apart of a composite being into its constituent elements.</note> for each of the beings give the power to those prior things, which the one who divides has set to be divided. Therefore, the subsequent thinkers say that from these we have the causes of those things that are coming into being, which is the object of our inquiry. Consequently, the world appears to have been generated from **ungrudging bounty** <note>original: "ex aphthonon" (ἐξ ἀφθόνων). This refers to Timaeus 29e, where Plato explains that the Creator, being good and lacking any envy, desired all things to be as like himself as possible.</note> and is revealed to those being educated, having been awakened from every side. Indeed, he named that which succeeds it, and having naturally generated the cosmos, it is not as a whole for each part of the discursive intellect. For this indicates that which is generated itself, as well as the being and the continuity of those things under **Providence** <note>original: "pronoia" (προνοίᾳ). The divine foresight or care that maintains the order of the universe.</note>, setting himself outside the very process of generation. 

He named, therefore, the two of them to fit all things together, and we complete this for each thing. In another way, it is not entirely easy in both cases for one who is thinking to grasp how it holds. Let this be one thing, and the other be another part of them, for the whole is not what it ought to be in this regard. But all things are greater, and everything seemed to be so. We have this itself for them, for its very existence is the being of the **substances** <note>original: "hypostaseis" (ὑποστάσεις). The underlying realities or essential natures of things.</note>; the form is with and within it, and we learn this through change. Our aim there is how it seems to complete the fitting things, and there is a continuity and a sense of what is proper through its own nature, and this is what we complete. 

Because of his easy and ungrudging **imparting** <note>original: "metadosin" (μετάδοσιν). The act of the higher principle sharing its essence or goodness with the lower.</note> to it, he says that this imparting exists, and through it, we complete the **immortals** <note>original: "athanatous" (ἀθανάτους). Likely referring to the "younger gods" or the immortal part of the human soul.</note>. Generation and the earth and the whole undergo natural changes, and everything is becoming. And naturally, no part has its being after generation, but rather as that which is becoming. And this same continuity seems to come from learning; for it exists for it, and in a way that is perishable in the two or more elements. By this, we mean the first element and that which is becoming, and one part belongs to numbers; for it is similar to the **Cause** <note>original: "aitia" (αἰτίᾳ). The primary principle (the Demiurge or the Good) that sets the universe in motion.</note> that is moved. 

One part belongs to itself. Therefore, that which is according to the **analogy** <note>original: "analogoun" (ἀναλογοῦν). Mathematical proportion used as a cosmic glue to bind disparate elements like fire and earth.</note> makes these things become a kind of likeness. For its being belongs to itself, and we call this "analogies." This, then, we call nature: the ordering of things toward one another. It is equal because it exists by **participation** <note>original: "methexei" (μεθέξει). The central Platonic concept where material things "share in" the reality of the immaterial Forms.</note>. Since there is an ease and a consistency, it is impossible to be without them. For everything is its being. Its being is the same for both of them. How does it act toward that which is there by its power? Because of the cause, that which is becoming is itself one thing, and another is another part of them. For this is the greater cause. Because of the things of the cosmos, this is the cause for it: that even this is a **wanderer** <note>original: "planetes" (πλανήτης). Often refers to the planets, but here perhaps to the "wandering" or unstable nature of material existence.</note> among that which is established. And so it reveals the nature of physical theory. There is no need to give way to the established order or to be drawn there; rather, it exists in a certain **ratio** <note>original: "logo" (λόγω). In this context, a mathematical ratio or a rational principle of organization.</note>, and is thus itself established otherwise. Because of the easy cause, Timaeus says that **harmony** <note>original: "harmonias" (ἁρμονίας). The fitting together of parts into a musical or mathematical whole.</note> belongs to the composition of the cosmos, and symmetry is upon it through this.

<column-break/>

<page-num>131</page-num>

The aim for the Maker is a **cosmic icon** <note>original: "eikon kosmike" (εἰκὼν κοσμική). The physical universe is viewed as a "statue" or "image" of the eternal, intelligible Living Being.</note>, as those things are to that analogy. This indeed produces **procession** <note>original: "proodon" (πρόοδον). The Neoplatonic movement where reality flows out from the One into multiplicity.</note> and remains. For it is clear from the name that it has one reference toward that which is becoming; hence Timaeus rightly says this regarding the whole of this subject. And then, after an interpolation, he named it two equalities which he uses: the **bond** <note>original: "desmos" (δεσμός). Plato calls proportion the "most beautiful bond" because it creates unity.</note> is equal, and the bond is most sovereignly created by analogy. He holds this as more demonstrative, and being upon the very thing sought, it was not entirely easy to see it dissolved by one who is not at all a specialist. For it acts as twelve to twelve. 

Nothing is dissolved by the dissolution... in the higher part of the genus, to be left behind at a sign, but rather wherever the whole is. According to which the universe is a **living being** <note>original: "zoon" (ζῷον). Plato describes the cosmos as a single, visible living being that contains all other living beings within it.</note>, two parts of the cosmos, the whole; whence in the making of it, he says, there is still the Same and the Other of them. Because the living being is eternal from all things, and they will be so even in perishable forms, and in the two or more where such a thing exists, as is likely. Not since it is not possible for these things to be held after he made them, but again toward this, these things are a certain reality. And indeed, from this, it comes to be, from which those who learn are shown what is likely; and it might be possible, in another way, in their analogy and in its likelihood. And we see many things by learning otherwise, because of seeking among the "easinesses" <note>Note: Proclus uses "easiness" (eukolia) to describe the effortless way the divine acts.</note> that one thing is not, and how it is, and it is the beginning of number. But always for him there is a continuity and a sense of his own affairs from learning, but always continuity and likelihood. And so it reveals the nature of physical theory. 

For the parts are limited even with him, and in order as toward a similar thing that is to be. In terms of numbers and oneself, we are able, because it is not otherwise, to first say that **geometry** <note>original: "geometrian" (γεωμετρίαν). The study of continuous magnitudes, essential for understanding the structure of space.</note> is necessary for the response, though not in the *Timaeus*. Regarding numbers, then, it is so. See how these things are also an icon. Since he himself wishes to show that **Being** <note>original: "to on" (τὸ ὄν). True, unchanging reality as opposed to the "becoming" of the physical world.</note> is properly beyond these, and to provide them as the two principles of the cosmos, we call these analogies the "likely." This, therefore, is indicated in that which is becoming, for there the learning of the part is to be similar through one's own nature. 

Therefore, he gives him help from divine, canonical, and political positions, since he is about to become that which Timaeus set him to be; and he did not say this was a wanderer, at least in the cause of what was seen. And in the whole and in such things. This is also because with him there is hope where there is difficulty. To those who compose the things of the cosmos and the whole as this, and as an icon, this is in a certain ratio; this is the cause of the difficulties being the whole itself. It is a ratio; and if it is the most **paradigmatic** <note>original: "paradeigmatikotaton" (παραδειγματικώτατον). Relating to the eternal Archetypes or Forms that the physical world copies.</note> number, it is so by participation. It is clear that the same thing becomes the analogical, not according to each part, for one must not nowhere move that which is similar to this from its established place!

<summary>This page discusses the metaphysical "bond" of analogy (proportion) that the Demiurge uses to unify the cosmos. Proclus explains that the world is an "icon" or image of eternal reality, held together by mathematical ratios that ensure its continuity and prevent its dissolution.</summary>

**Astronomy**, all rational <unclear>teaching</unclear>. That which is <unclear>according to</unclear> <unclear>the stars</unclear>.
To become. That which is becoming, a restoration <note>original: *apokatastasin*; a term often used in Stoicism to describe the cyclical restoration of the universe</note>. Wandering and those who wander, and the planet, and the rest is error <note>original: *planēn*; the Greek word for "planet" literally means "wanderer," which the author here links to moral or intellectual error</note>, to use the law in all things. **Goodwill**, that which comes from <unclear>upright</unclear> laws to leave to men who speak <unclear>rightly</unclear>: to **disown**, not through riddles, someone being cast out of the house.
From poverty, good health sets things right: **shaggy** <note>original: *dauloi*; can also refer to thickets or dense growth</note>. Those who perhaps <unclear>not</unclear>... like two: turned away, by an impulse from it. Empty **nonsense**. An impulse through hopes. Through straight lines. To have all rational things.
Of a **tunic**. One defiled in blood. Twice for <unclear>water-serpents</unclear> it was necessary. The "must." But "it is necessary" means the <unclear>useful</unclear>. And **vocally**: commonly, the opportune. That of the king in subtle talk—this month he shall be—to obey this in the **Prytaneum** <note>original: *prytaneion*; the seat of government in Greek cities where the sacred fire was kept and where distinguished citizens or victors were fed at public expense</note>: the palace, according to merit.
In the Prytaneum. Whence also with an uproar. And to select the things in the Prytaneum. And no one mentioned food in the Prytaneum.
Laying down. Things established by measures. Being burdened.
Before, and before someone. **Enclosure**: at the gates. **Might**, a child outright. Child. And instead of "on the ground." In from the future: **crush**, admittedly. In that which is crushed: to take. The spirit of no one. Having thought. Before someone: a **prophetic utterance**, to know. Of the **monastic** things for him: yes indeed, for him entirely. For friendship it is well remembered.
Double: intensity: upon all such things. Of a **bird**, the divine part of it. A **diviner by birds**: these differ. The outward-looking, together with these. Otherwise on subjects. We are transformed. **In order that**, and indeed.
**Over-piped** <note>original: *hyperaulos*</note>: **overdue** <note>original: *hyperēmeros*; specifically a legal term for a debtor who has failed to pay by the appointed day</note>. Public matters, therefore toward us but coming. A sign of preceding things.

<column-break/>

<header>41</header>
**Asserting**, to speak according to choice. Longing for riddles.
Toward receiving, to receive is rather to be. To **undertake**, to take, the "reception" is the wanting to receive something into oneself.
**Paltry** <note>original: *phlauros*; a word frequently used by Marcus Aurelius to describe things of no moral value, like fame or wealth</note> is the small, and light, and bad. But you **belittle**; he hates: **he said**: blood. Whence also "earthly." And the brothers.
**Kinship**. **Sons-in-law**: double from the "reception"... sitting, something laid aside. To cast through.
To withdraw, the opportune. That which is for nothing under the season, indeed the season: he gives to some.
But the "must" is necessary: it is applied. In nothing: of such a size.
Most manifest. Such a kind. Upon quantity. That which is upon many. Whence. From where. Whence: how. Of whom. How. The "how."
The things of one's own. To meet. From the... to meet.
In **lawsuits**: of perfect things, those of **fingertip-touching** <note>original: *akrolabēseōs*; a rare term likely referring to a specific legal gesture or a light physical contact used in rituals</note> by women or a nurse. Wretched of equals, memory before: in **frames**: in bodies. The **omen**, those dreaming, a sign from Zeus <note>original: *diosēmeion*; an omen appearing in the sky, such as thunder or a lightning strike</note>. And to those there: **hair-cut**, the circumcision. In the "six" to be guards. For the **sold-by-the-public**. To rule. Setting. **Spear-point**, the "nothing."
From the father. To place the head upon: by a change of nature.
By **customs**. To live **impiously**, regarding the gods.
According to the only, regarding the irrational: **eyelids** <note>original: *blephara*</note>. The skins of the eyes. For "eyelids" is of the eyelids: **herdsman**: a herdsman for the mature. For calves, the young.
To **roar**. The sound. To **weigh down**. And to bring back.
**Water**. To **mutter** <note>original: *gryzein*</note>. To speak frequently in life.
A **shore** <note>original: *aktion*</note> for the houses. They have looked down upon those who live in the houses.

translation:
# Epiphanius

They handed them over to be worshipped as gods by their subjects under a wicked pretext, <note>interpolated: "as if they were gods"</note>, just as Antinous, who was buried in the city of Antinous, was ranked as such by Hadrian, lying in a pleasure boat. Then there is Timogenes in Asia, and Canobus, the pilot of Menelaus, and his wife Enmenouthis, who are buried and honored in Alexandria by the seashore, twelve miles away. There is also Marnas, the slave of Asterius the Cretan, among the people of Gaza, and Casius the shipmaster among the people of Pelusium.

### 107
When you accurately explain all these things in the midst of the church, you <note>unclear: "show a bad example of a deadly path"</note> to those who have been thus led astray, and you lead others from adultery to chastity. Do not only free them from "stealing marriages," but <note>interpolated: "teach them"</note> to look down even upon their own <note>interpolated: "wife"</note> for the sake of <term>egkrateia</term> <gloss>self-control</gloss>, since "the time is shortened," as the holy apostle says. Instruct the fornicators so that they are not punished for committing an unlawful act before God and men. And when you have handed down all these things, toiling through both speech and deeds, you will persuade them to accept everything from you.

<note>Scholarly note: The author identifies historical figures who were deified, such as Hadrian's favorite Antinous and the pilot Canobus. The passage then transitions into moral and pastoral exhortation, urging church leaders to teach their congregations to avoid the "deadly path" of paganism and to embrace Christian virtues like self-control, citing the Apostle Paul (1 Corinthians 7:29).</note>

translation:
### True Dimensions of the Athanor, or Secret Furnace of the Philosophers.

The large Tower, marked **A** <note>shown on the following page,</note> must be constructed as its Figure demonstrates: The Bricks of this tower, <note>and those of the Towerlet, where the cooking of the Compound must take place,</note> must be half a Foot wide, but not of the same length; For this large Tower must not be wider in its cavity than half a Foot and four fingers; And from the Grate, marked **C**, up to the Lid, marked **B**, <note>meaning up to the top of the Lid,</note> it should be more than four feet in Height.

<header>ON PAINTING</header>

# ON PAINTING

Of lines, some are straight and some are curved. A straight line is a mark drawn directly along its length from one point to another. A curved line is that which is drawn not directly from one point to another, but instead forming an arc. If many lines, like threads in a cloth, are joined together, they will create a surface. Indeed, a surface is that outermost part of a body which is considered not in terms of any depth, but only in terms of width and length, which are its proper qualities. Of these qualities, some are so inherent to the surface that, unless the surface is completely altered, they cannot be moved or separated from it in any way. And some other qualities are such that, while the face of the surface remains the same, they fall under the view in such a way that the surface appears altered to those looking at it. The permanent qualities of surfaces are two: one is truly that which comes to our knowledge by means of that outer circuit by which the surface is enclosed, which circuit some call the horizon. We, if it is permitted, by way of a certain similarity, will call it by a Latin term, *Ora* <note>original: "Ora." Meaning a border, edge, or rim.</note>, or if it pleases us more, the **Outline** <note>original: "Il d’intorno." Literally 'the around,' referring to the contour or perimeter of a shape.</note>. And this outline will be bounded by a single line or by several. By a single line, such as a circular one; by several, such as by one curved and one straight, or even by several straight lines, or several curved ones. A circular line is that which embraces and contains within itself the entire space of a circle. And the circle is a type of surface surrounded by a line in the manner of a crown. In the middle of which, if there is a point, all the rays that depart in length from this point and go directly to the crown or circumference will be equal to one another.

---

And this same point is called the center of the circle. The straight line that cuts the circumference twice and passes through the center is called by mathematicians the diameter of the circle. We shall call this same line the **centric line**. And let us be persuaded in this place by what the mathematicians say: that no line which cuts the circumference—

En 1889, nous avons fondé à Paris le *Groupe indépendant d'études ésotériques*, destiné à contrôler les expériences concernant les forces encore inconnues en action dans l'homme et dans la nature.

Les premiers mois furent consacrés à la propagande et les travaux purent être fructueusement poursuivis dès le début de l'année 1891. ### THE MAGICAL EXPERIMENTS OF THE INDEPENDENT GROUP FOR ESOTERIC STUDIES.

In 1889, we founded the *Independent Group for Esoteric Studies* <note>original: "Groupe indépendant d'études ésotériques"</note> in Paris, intended to control experiments concerning the forces still unknown in action within man and in nature.

The first months were devoted to propaganda, and the work could be fruitfully pursued from the beginning of the year 1891. Barlet; but these experiments needed a control that only the continuation of studies could provide. Delfosse. In the middle of the year, facts reported in the <term>grimoires</term> <gloss>books of magic spells</gloss> were submitted to experimental control and M. We shall also be able to go much further through the restoration of the **Primitive Language** & **Knowledge**, & by the entirety of our research.

The sacred **Books of the Hebrews** will not be the only ones upon which we shall shed light through our progress. It will be much the same for most ancient **Books**, especially those we indicated in the article on compared **Cosmogonies** <note>Theories regarding the origin of the universe.</note> & **Theogonies** <note>Accounts of the origins and genealogies of the gods.</note>.

We shall be in a position, for example, to provide a **Translation of the EDDA** <note>The *Edda* refers to the primary collections of Old Norse literature; Gébelin treats them as a northern counterpart to Greek mythology.</note>, that **Mythology of the Children of the North**, written in old **Runic**, clearer than those that have been given to us in various Languages, & to accompany it with a **Glossary** that will explain many of those allegorical words which could not be understood, & which will present the striking relationships between the Language in which the **EDDA** was written and other Languages, just as we shall have shown the relationships of this Mythology with those of other Peoples.

A great number of passages from the Poems of **ORPHEUS**, **HESIOD**, **HOMER**, etc., & from ancient **Historians**, will thereby become easier to translate, clearer, and more interesting.

plus difficiles à rendre les uns que les autres ; on est pour lors obligé de les ajuster en plaçant des lévres sur une plus grande ou plus petite corde du trou de la Flute, en donnant un vent plus ou moins fort, ce que fait l'homme dans les mêmes tons, où il est obligé de ménager son vent, & de tourner la Flute plus ou moins en dedans ou en dehors.

On conçoit facilement que toutes les lames placées sur le cilindre font plus ou moins longues, suivant le tems que doit avoir chaque note, & suivant la différente situation où doivent se trouver les doigts pour les former : ce que je ne détaillerai point ici, de crainte de passer les bornes d'un Mémoire concis, que je me suis proposé de donner.

Je ferai remarquer seulement que dans les enflemens de son, il a fallu, pendant le tems de la même note, substituer imperceptiblement un vent foible à un vent fort, & à un plus fort, un plus foible, & varier conjointement les mouvemens des lévres, c'est-à-dire, les mettre dans leur situation propre pour chaque vent.

Lorsqu'il a fallu faire le doux, c'est-à-dire, imiter un écho, on a été obligé de faire avancer les lévres sur le bord du trou de la Flute, & envoyer un vent suffisant pour former un tel ton ; mais dont le retour, par une issuë aussi petite, qu'est celle de son entrée dans la Flute, ne peut frapper qu'une petite quantité d'air extérieur : ce qui produit, comme je l'ai dit ci-dessus, ce qu'on appelle écho.

Les différens airs de lenteur & de mouvement ont été mesurés sur le cilindre, par le moyen d'un lévier, dont une extrémité armée d'une pointe pouvoit, lorsqu'on frappoit dessus, marquer ce même cilindre.

A l'autre bras du levier étoit un ressort, qui faisoit promptement relever la pointe.

On lâchoit le mouvement, qui faisoit tourner le cilindre avec une vîtesse déterminée pour tous les airs.

Dans le même tems une personne joüoit sur la Flute l'air qu'on vouloit mesurer ; un autre battoit la mesure sur le bout du lévier qui pointoit le cilindre, & la distance qui se trouvoit entre les points, étoit la vraie mesure des airs qu'on vouloit noter ; on subdivisoit ensuite les intervales en autant de parties que la mesure avoit de tems.

more difficult to render than others; one is then obliged to adjust them by placing lips on a larger or smaller string of the Flute hole, by giving a more or less strong wind, which the man does in the same tones, where he is obliged to manage his wind, and to turn the Flute more or less inward or outward.

One easily conceives that all the plates placed on the cylinder are more or less long, according to the time that each note must have, and according to the different situation where the fingers must be found to form them: which I will not detail here, for fear of passing the limits of a concise Memoir, which I have proposed to give.

I will only remark that in the swells of sound, it was necessary, during the time of the same note, to substitute imperceptibly a weak wind for a strong one, and to a stronger one, a weaker one, and to vary jointly the movements of the lips, that is to say, to put them in their proper situation for each wind.

When it was necessary to perform the soft <term>doux</term> <gloss>a musical term for piano or soft volume</gloss>, that is to say, to imitate an echo, one was obliged to make the lips advance to the edge of the hole of the Flute, and send a sufficient wind to form such a tone; but whose return, through an outlet as small as that of its entry into the Flute, can only strike a small quantity of exterior air: which produces, as I have said above, what one calls an echo.

The different airs of slowness and movement were measured on the cylinder, by the means of a lever, of which one extremity armed with a point could, when one struck upon it, mark this same cylinder.

At the other arm of the lever was a spring, which made the point rise again promptly.

One released the movement, which made the cylinder turn with a determined speed for all the airs.

In the same time a person played on the Flute the air that one wished to measure; another beat the measure on the end of the lever which pointed the cylinder, and the distance which was found between the points, was the true measure of the airs that one wished to note; one then subdivided the intervals into as many parts as the measure had beats.

<meta>This page continues the catechism of the Apprentice degree, moving from the symbolic "three steps" to the physical posture of the candidate during the taking of the "Obligation" (the Masonic oath). It details the specific ritual arrangement of the body and tools used during the initiation ceremony.</meta>

**Q.*** What does this gait signify?
**A.*** The zeal that we must show in walking toward the one who enlightens us. <note>In the ritual, the "one who enlightens" is the Worshipful Master, who sits in the East and represents the sun or the source of wisdom.</note>
**Q.** What did the **Worshipful Master** <note>original: "Vénérable"</note> do with you?
**A.** As he was certain of my sentiments, after having obtained the consent of the **Lodge**, he received me as an **Apprentice Mason** with all the required formalities.
**Q.** What were these formalities?
**A.** I had my left shoe down at the heel <note>original: "en pantoufle." This ritual state of being "neither barefoot nor shod" symbolizes humility and a detachment from worldly status.</note>, my right knee bare on the **square**, my right hand on the **Gospel**, & with my left I held a **compass** half-open over my left breast which was bare.
**Q.** What were you doing in this posture?
**A.** I was contracting the **obligation** to forever keep the secrets of **Masons** & of **Masonry**.
**Q.** Do you remember this obligation well?
**A.** Yes, **Most Worshipful Master** ( 1 ).
**Q.*** Why did you have your knee bare & your shoe down at the heel?
**A.*** To teach me that a **Mason** must be humble.

---

( 1 ) There are **Lodges** where the **obligation** is repeated; but this is not a generally accepted law: it depends on the will of the **Worshipful Masters**. This is why every good **Mason** must remember it, as well as the **sacred words**, the **gait**, & the **signs**, given that these must never be printed. <note>This footnote reflects the 18th-century tension between printed "exposés" and the traditional Masonic rule of oral transmission. The author is reminding the reader that while the catechism is printed here, the most sensitive secrets should be kept in one's memory.</note>

<summary>This page describes the physical requirements for taking the Masonic oath, including the symbolic exposure of the knee and breast, and the use of the square and compass. It emphasizes the internalizing of Masonic secrets and the virtue of humility.</summary>
<keywords>initiation ritual, Masonic oath, square and compass, humility, Apprentice Mason, Worshipful Master, secrecy</keywords>

In opposition to these two classes of ignoramuses, other people—learned in other respects, but not at all in the high sciences <term>high sciences: likely referring to hermeticism, alchemy, or occult philosophy which sought deeper spiritual truths beyond mere physical observation</term>—have tried to persuade me that divination was a chimera <note>original: "chimere," meaning an impossible or foolish fancy.</note>; their sophistry did not stun me: look, I concluded by replying to them, here is what has happened to you.... here is what is happening to you.... and tomorrow, what will happen to you.

Astonished by the truth of the divinatory science <term>divinatory science: the systematic study of predicting future events or uncovering hidden knowledge, which the author treats here as a rational, interconnected discipline</term>, they tried to retreat through vague sounds and empty words: chance, habit, professional knack, or omens with multiple meanings. — But I have told you positive facts — That is true — Scholars, there is no such thing as chance, and there is no destiny except in the general masses of the universe; everything is linked, everything is interconnected; study the science of this chain, and you shall be a diviner.

Without expanding further, I say: men, you are in this low universe to contemplate the works of the Creator, and to imitate his divine art, his science, and his wisdom; and just as his will to procreate was his labor, let your labor be the principle of the will you have to create wonders.

sition du livre VIII du *Speculum naturale* de Vincent de Beauvais, afin de préciser l’état des connaissances effectives en chimie de son temps, et de fournir des termes exacts de comparaison avec les auteurs que nous analyserons tout à l’heure.

Le livre VIII du *Speculum naturale* parle d’abord des matières minérales, partagées en quatre genres, savoir : corps fusibles ou métaux, pierres, matières sulfureuses, sels. Les pierres précieuses et minéraux proprement dits n’y sont pas décrits, étant réservés au livre IX.

L’histoire de chaque métal est présentée séparément, en suivant une marche systématique; le compilateur résume d’abord les textes anciens de Pline, d’Isidore de Séville et autres; puis vient pour chaque corps un chapitre alchimique : *De operatione auri in alchimia*; *De operatione argenti, cupri, stanni, plumbi, ferri*, etc., chapitre où l’auteur reproduit des textes tirés de l’*Alchimiste*, des *Météorologiques* d’Aristote et de leur prétendue suite, de Rasès, d’Avicenne, etc., conformément à ce qui a été dit plus haut.

Aux chapitres <term>lx</term> et suivants commence l’étude des quatre esprits minéraux et du traitement (*operatio*) de chacun d’eux en alchimie.

Cela fait, l’auteur traite, au chapitre <term>lxxiii</term>, des autres minéraux, intermédiaires entre les corps et les esprits, et d’abord des aluns, des vitriols (*atramenta*), etc.

Il aborde ensuite la génération des minéraux, d’abord dans la nature, en exposant un mélange de chimères et d’observations réelles, tirées en grande partie des écrits latins d’Avicenne. Puis il examine leur génération artificielle, c’est-à-dire la pierre philosophale, ou élixir tinctorial, sous sa double forme : blanche pour l’argent, jaune (ou rouge) pour l’or. Suit une dissertation sur la réalité de l’alchimie, empruntée également au même auteur. L’indication des noms des principaux alchimistes (chap. <term>lxxxvii</term>) est prise également dans la traduction latine de l’ouvrage attribué à Avicenne.

Suivent des chapitres d’ordre pratique sur les procédés (*claves*) et instruments; sur les variétés de feux employés dans les préparations; sur la calcination et autres opérations; sur la soudure des métaux; sur

<header>TRANSMISSION OF ANCIENT SCIENCE.</header>

of book VIII of the *Speculum naturale* <gloss>Mirror of Nature</gloss> of Vincent of Beauvais, in order to specify the state of effective knowledge in chemistry of his time, and to provide exact terms of comparison with the authors whom we shall analyze in a moment.

Book VIII of the *Speculum naturale* speaks first of mineral matters, divided into four types, namely: fusible bodies or metals, stones, sulfurous matters, salts. Precious stones and minerals properly so-called are not described therein, being reserved for book IX.

The history of each metal is presented separately, following a systematic approach; the compiler first summarizes the ancient texts of Pliny, Isidore of Seville, and others; then comes for each body an alchemical chapter: *De operatione auri in alchimia* <gloss>On the working of gold in alchemy</gloss>; *De operatione argenti, cupri, stanni, plumbi, ferri*, etc. <gloss>On the working of silver, copper, tin, lead, iron, etc.</gloss>, a chapter where the author reproduces texts taken from the *Alchemist*, the *Meteorologica* of Aristotle and their supposed continuation, from Rhazes, from Avicenna, etc., in accordance with what was said above.

In chapters LX and following begins the study of the four mineral spirits and the treatment (*operatio*) of each of them in alchemy.

This done, the author treats, in chapter LXXIII, of the other minerals, intermediate between bodies and spirits, and first of alums, vitriols (*atramenta*), etc.

He then approaches the generation of minerals, first in nature, by exposing a mixture of chimeras and real observations, taken in large part from the Latin writings of Avicenna. Then he examines their artificial generation, that is to say the philosopher's stone, or tincturing elixir, in its double form: white for silver, yellow (or red) for gold. There follows a dissertation on the reality of alchemy, borrowed also from the same author. The indication of the names of the principal alchemists (ch. LXXXVII) is taken also from the Latin translation of the work attributed to Avicenna.

There follow chapters of a practical order on the procedures (*claves* <gloss>keys</gloss>) and instruments; on the varieties of fires employed in the preparations; on calcination and other operations; on the soldering of metals; on...

# Michaelis

Thomas de Hathewey, regarding the fact that he does not show the presentation in his own person: he was not on the same day one and the same person, for the presentation was made to one who was parson of the same church of Westcombe, to him and his successors; this John, who is now vicar, cannot be said to be a successor to the parson, by which it seems that this is a thing outside, or that which is outside their point. Wherefore he says that the Bishop of Norwich, neither in the writ of right nor in the [matter] of the parson John de Grendon and him, cannot be [held] by right of his church of Westcombe, for the vicarage is one, and the plaint is in the plaint <term>sicut vobis facit</term> <gloss>as it does to you</gloss> concerning that which you suppose to do; wherefore, concerning that which is a plaint, you ought not to proceed by another. John, although he is vicar, in a plea of trespass, the plaintiff shall not have [damages] by maintaining his plaint, but rather where the defendant pleads in the right of his vicarage, as the defendant does here, in such a case the plaintiff shall have aid of his parson. The plaintiff must, at the present time, [state] his plea in his plaint to the court that he had to do; the same proof is the cause of that, for he wishes to have the writings to him, by which the writings must be put to the court. [He] pleads in the writ of trespass to an issue of plea, for [himself] of right of the parson; for because the plaintiff is vicar, this is an issue to which he cannot be a party. He had aid, but [it did] nothing; wherefore <term>ad iudicium</term> <gloss>to judgment</gloss> of John, they go to say, and [as to] his tort of trespass, [it is] nothing by any word of this day. ### OF PYTHAGORAS.

some little spark of that life which animated, they say, the pebbles of Pyrrha <note>according to Greek myth, Pyrrha and Deucalion threw stones behind them which turned into humans to repopulate the earth after a flood</note>, I would make it a duty to repeat to them what I have just told you about Thales."

I replied to the man from Priene: Mandraite, I conceive and share your enthusiasm; only the fanaticism of virtue and truth is not to be feared. Go! your story adds to the veneration I already held for the name of Thales. Your delirium is quite natural, and his also. One does nothing great, one invents nothing sublime, if one does not have the measure of his genius, and the feeling of his strengths. Thales is right to be jealous of his discovery; it is his property; it belongs to him more than the conquests of Semiramis belonged to that woman. One must hold onto the good action of which one was capable, to a strong and bold thought that one knew how to produce. Modesty is the virtue of mediocrity. Why not do oneself justice, and claim it for oneself as for others?

We left each other at Myus, a small Ionian city halfway from Priene to Miletus. It is there that the Meander, after so many detours, finally falls into the sea, and regrets not having made even more in such an agreeable country.

Fatigued by the weight of the heat, I went to take refuge in an old temple that was standing open, because the <term>neocore</term> <gloss>temple warden</gloss> was cleaning it at that moment. In the back of the sanctuary, I distinguished, not without difficulty because of the little light, the seated statue of an old man, covered with a long, very dirty cloak. His shoulder was burdened with a dusty axe.

### SCENE III.

#### THE INFANTA, LEONOR, Page.

#### THE INFANTA to the Page.

Go find Chimene, and tell her for me,
That she should wait a little late to see me today,
And that my friendship complains of her laziness.

->*The Page leaves.*<-

#### LEONOR.

Madame, the same desire presses you every day,
And I see you pensive and sad every day,
Informing yourself with care how her love is going.

#### THE INFANTA.

I must indeed take care of it; I almost forced her
To receive the blows with which her soul is wounded.
She loves Don Rodrigue, and holds him from my hand,
And through me Don Rodrigue has vanquished his design.
Thus, having formed the chains of her lovers,
I must take an interest in the end of their pains.

#### LEONOR.

Madame, however, amidst their good success,
One sees in you a sorrow that goes to excess.
Does this love that fills both of them with joy
Cause the profound sadness of this great heart?
And does this great interest that you take for them
Make you unhappy when they are happy?
But I go too far, and become indiscreet.

#### THE INFANTA.

My sadness redoubles by keeping it secret.
Listen, listen at last to how I have fought.

translation:
<header>BOOK XII.</header>

giving signs of changing. Regarding the gardens, I beg you, conclude it. That is the principal reason, which you know. To which is added that in a certain way, necessity pushes me there; not being able to accustom myself to such a multitude, nor to distance myself from you. For this thought of mine, I find nothing more suitable than this place. And I am sure of what your opinion is, and even more so, as I see that we are in agreement that Balbus and Oppius bear great love for me. I would like you to discuss with them the great desire I have to buy the gardens, and for what reason; but that I cannot achieve the result if Faberius does not pay me. Because only then will you realize if there is hope or not, and how they are disposed to favor my thought. If they want to, their help will be great; if not, let us try by any other way. That which you think, as you write, that I should have for rest in old age, consider that it should be my burial in death. As for that place which is in the Ostiense <note>original: "Ostiense"</note>, there is no need to think about it, unless it happens that we get this one. I presume it is not possible to have it from Lamia. And it is necessary to try if those of Damasippus can be had.

I look for subject matter to write to you, but I have nothing, and I write to you the same things every day. You do me a great pleasure by going to see Lentulus. Give him those slaves, and as many as you think best. I have understood what you write to me about the will of Silius regarding selling, and about the fear you hold, primarily that he may not want to, and secondarily that he may not want to at such a low price. Sicca

He was accompanied to San Zorzi Maggiore, and afterwards, having been lifted <note>honored</note> with a beautiful company, he was accompanied to San Marco at vespers, where Messer Michiel Sten, Doge of Venice, at the high altar gave him the banner of Messer San Marco, confirming him Captain General of the whole army, with very great authority. Prima, ch' un'altra d'un cerchio la chiuse;
Et moto a moto, et canto a canto colse;
Canto, che tanto uince nostre Muse,
Nostre Sirene in quelle dolci tube;
Quanto primo splendor quel, che rifuse.
Come si uolgon per tenera nube
Du' archi paralelli et concolori,
Quando Iunon a su ancella iube,
Nascendo di quel dentro quel di fuori
A guisa del parlar di quella uaga,
Ch' amor consunse, come sol uapori;
Et fanno qui la gente esser presaga
Per lo patto, che Dio con Noe pose
Del mondo, che giamai piu non s'allaga;
Cosi di quelle sempiterne rose
Volgensi circa noi le due ghirlande,
Et si l'estrema a l'ultima rispose.
Poi che'l tripudio et l'altra festa grande
Si del cantar, et si del fiammeggiarsi
Luce con luce gaudiose et blande
Insieme a punto et a uoler quetarsi;
Pur come gli occhi, ch' al piacer che i moue
Conuien insieme chiuder et leuarsi;
Del cor dell'una de le luci noue

translation:
<header>PAR.</header>

As soon as the last word
The blessed flame took to say;
To rotate began the holy millstone:
And in its circuit it did not turn
Before another enclosed it with a circle;
And motion to motion, and song to song it gathered;
Song, that so much overcomes our Muses,
Our Sirens in those sweet tubes,
As primary splendor that which reflects.
As they turn through a tender cloud
Two arcs parallel and of the same colors,
When Juno gives orders to her handmaid,
Being born from the inner one the outer one,
After the fashion of the speech of that wanderer,
Whom love consumed, as the sun vapors;
And make here the people to be presaging
By the pact, that God with Noah placed
Of the world, that nevermore is flooded;
Thus of those sempiternal roses
Turn around us the two garlands,
And so the outer one answered the inner.
After the jubilation and the other great feast,
Both of singing, and of flaming
Light with light, joyous and bland,
Together at the point and at the will to quiet themselves;
Just as the eyes, that to the pleasure that moves them
Must together close and lift themselves;
From the heart of one of the new lights
Moved a voice; that the needle to the star
Made me seem in turning to its where:

translation:
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Canto I of the Paradiso. The previous page discussed the invocation to Apollo and the myth of Marsyas, establishing the transition from earthly knowledge to the divine heights Dante is about to explore.</meta>

# PARADISE

...rejoice in the Lord <note>original: "re in dño [Domino]"</note> with the first light and to know Him without being dazzled: [he is like] the figure of the eagle because he discerns the divinity above all others.

And just as a second ray
is wont to issue from the first and mount upward again,
like a pilgrim who wishes to return,
So from her action, infused through the eyes
into my imagination, my own was made;
and I fixed my eyes on the sun beyond our wont.
Much is permitted there which here is not
to our powers, thanks to the place
made as the proper home for the human race.
I did not endure it long, yet not so little
that I did not see it sparkling round about,
like molten iron coming out of the fire.
And suddenly it seemed to me that day to day
had been added, as if He who has the power
had adorned the heaven with another sun.

...suspended wonder: And to look into the sun: this is nothing else than that, illuminated by divine grace, one can look into the sun, that is, into the speculation of the divinity. Nevertheless, he did not endure it long: because if the eyes, that is, the sharpness of the intellect, had endured the light for a longer time, he would have been able to discern the entire solar body, that is, he would have had true knowledge of the divine essence. But he did not have so powerful an eye. Nevertheless, for the little that he endured, he saw the sparks and flashes that were born from the solar body, in the same way that they are born from a glowing iron. The allegorical sense is that the purified soul can contemplate God: but not in a way that it knows His essence: but it has knowledge of the sparks that come from the sun, that is, of the effects that proceed from God; seeing that we know the cause through the effects, and not the effects through the cause. And that the sun had so much greater light that it seemed doubled signifies that theological contemplation illuminates the intellect much more than philosophy does, because it is not without the infusion of the Spirit, as you will see a little further down.

Beatrice was standing with her eyes fixed
entirely upon the eternal wheels, and I on her
fixed my eyes, removed from those above.
In her aspect I became such within
as Glaucus became upon tasting the herb
that made him a peer in the sea among the other gods.
To <term>transhumanize</term> <note>original: "trashumanar" - to pass beyond the limits of human nature</note> could not be signified
by words; therefore let the example suffice
for him to whom grace reserves the experience.

Whether I was only that part of me which You created
last, O Love who governs the heavens,
You know, who with Your light raised me up.
When the wheel that You make eternal
by being desired, made me intent upon You
with the harmony that You attune and distinguish,
So much of the heaven then seemed to me kindled
by the sun's flame, that no rain or river
ever made a lake so widespread.
The novelty of the sound and the great light
kindled in me a desire for their cause,
never felt before with such sharpness.

<column-break/>

This same reason causes the Evangelist John to be represented in the figure of an eagle <note>The eagle is the traditional symbol of St. John the Evangelist because his Gospel "soars" to the heights of Christ's divinity.</note>.

Just as a ray of the sun, reflecting itself, returns upward from whence it had come, like a man who returns home from a pilgrimage; so the fixed act of Beatrice in looking fixedly at the sun entered into my "imagination" <note>original: *imagine* – in medieval psychology, the faculty that receives sensory impressions</note>, and disposed me to look similarly at the sun. Because when the rays of the divine sun strike back into theological doctrine—which alone can sustain their gaze—it illuminates us: it strengthens and corroborates our eyes so that we too can look at the sun. Therefore rightly writes Augustine: "The good of God is known through theology which perfects the intellect and directs the affection" <note>original Latin: *Bonum dei cognoscitur per theologiam que perficit intellectum: & dirigit affectum*</note>. And so that we do not wonder that he could look fixedly at the sun beyond our custom, he adds: that the power of that place is such that we can do many things there that we cannot do here. Because that place is made specifically for the human species; and Earthly Paradise was created by God so that man might inhabit it for a longer time in a state of innocence; and then, when it pleased Him, he would be assumed to his beatitude. Therefore, since through the purgatorial virtues we have returned to the state of innocence, it is no wonder if in that place—that is, in such a state—it is permitted for us to look into the sun, which is not permitted here—that is, in the state of sin. **I DID NOT** endure it long. The meaning of the poet is that once the sun rose, he began to rise toward heaven, that is, to contemplate; for "contemplation is the free and clear gaze of the mind into the speculation of wisdom with suspended wonder."

The Poet wishes to express something else by demonstrating that Beatrice held her eyes fixed on heaven, and he held his on the eyes of Beatrice; which means nothing other than that sacred theology contemplates nothing but divine things, and whoever wishes to understand them must place their entire mind in theology and in its doctors. And it follows that in looking at her so fixedly, he became such "within"—that is, in the soul—as **GLAUCUS** became, who by eating the herb became a god. Thus it shows that his soul was deified. And certainly, through the contemplation of the divinity, we become divine and gods, as Boethius <note>original: *Boetio*</note> demonstrates at length. Glaucus, the son of Anthedon, was a fisherman. And placing the fish he had caught on the meadow so that the nets might dry, it happened that some of them, tasting a certain herb, regained their strength and jumped back into the water. Glaucus was stunned by the event and tasted the same herb himself; and seized by a sudden madness, he threw himself into the sea, and there from a man he became a sea god. **TRANSHUMANIZE**: that is, to transcend from human nature to divine.

The poet shows that he was rapt by the Holy Spirit, and by the sweetness of the song that he heard, and by the very great light that shone. Thus, his sight and taste were filled with ineffable joy. Wherefore, turning to the Holy Spirit, he speaks like a man now returned to the world: "O Holy Spirit who are Love, who governs the heavens: only when I was in such meditation was I that soul <note>Dante refers to himself as the "newly created" soul, the part of man created directly by God</note> which You created of me newly when You transformed me, You know it. Because You raised me with Your light," that is, You made me elevated to such contemplation with the light that You infused into my mind. And it shows here that there was in him that which the sacred letters affirm: that without the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, one does not come to such high speculations. **WHEN THE WHEEL**: because not only the heavens but all things created by God turn around with the desire they have to see Him. Therefore, "when the wheel"—that is, the revolution of the heavens which You, Holy Spirit, make eternal because every creature desires to enjoy God as much as its nature allows—"made me intent upon You," that is, made me...

<summary>This page covers Dante’s initial ascent from the Earthly Paradise, using the metaphor of the sun to represent divine truth and the myth of Glaucus to explain "transhumanization." The commentary emphasizes that through theology and the Holy Spirit, the human soul is "deified" and strengthened to behold things beyond earthly capacity.</summary>

# ATHENAGORAS,

## ATHENIAN, PHILOSOPHER

### CHRISTIAN,

->On the resurrection of the dead.<-

<note>A horizontal decorative printer's ornament features symmetrical floral and scrollwork patterns.</note>

IN ALL opinions and all arguments that approach the truth in human affairs, some falsehood arises. It arises not because it proceeds naturally either from the matter of the thing or from that form which gives it being, but from the study of those who welcome the wicked seed out of a desire to corrupt the truth. And that this is so, one can perceive primarily from those ancients who placed great care into the consideration of human affairs, and from the discordance of opinions that existed among them, their elders, and those who lived at that time.

<-*Dell'origine della Virtù.*->

**XL.** La virtù tiene la proprietà d'essere d'origine divina (1); conciossiachè queste tre sue parti tutte insieme costituiscono la vera virtù; e ciascuna di esse si trova sempre colle altre due congiunta. E in effetti nella prudenza avvi ancora la fortezza, in quantochè la mente nel ricercare il vero vi si travaglia e dura fatica, nè si ristà sino a che nol ritrovi; vi è anche la temperanza, essendo che è pur cosa savia l'ignorare talune cose. Nella temperanza poi si ritrova la prudenza, che ci consiglia a non trasandare le cose utili alla vita, per non riportarne detrimento; e perciò la Medicina è di origine divina, perchè dettata da questo vero eterno: vi è anche la fortezza, acciocchè sappia egli tenersi lungi dai piaceri. Infine nella fortezza si trova pure la prudenza per difendere l'onesto; vi è poi la temperanza, acciocchè i vincitori non vogliano distruggere i vinti, che possono senza danno serbare in vita.

<-*Della virtù vera.*->

**XLI.** Non avvi adunque virtù alcuna che stia sola, chè ove trovi veramente la virtù, sii certo che vi si trovano tutte le altre insieme riunite: poichè le virtù, che stiano isolate, meritano appena, secondo le parole di S. Agostino, il nome di virtù (2).

<-*Della Grazia divina.*->

**XLII.** Quella virtù poi, che sola dee dirsi vera, e come tale va innanzi a

(1) Cap. III.
(2) Epist. CLXVI; altrimenti XXIX ad Hieronymum, c. 3, n. 11, cap. 4, n. 14.

---

<-*Virtutis divinae origo.*->

**XL.** Virtus divinae originis proprietatem obtinet (1); namque hae tres ejus partes una sunt vera virtus; et quaeque earum semper est cum aliis duabus complicata. Etenim in prudentia et fortitudo inest, ut in vero vestigando laboret, nec in eo nisi explorato acquiescat; inest et temperantia, qua quaedam ignorare sapientia est. In temperantia et prudentia inest, ne quis ad exitium usque sui utilibus vitae rebus abstineat: quare Medicinae origo divina; nam ab hoc vero aeterno dictata: inest et fortitudo, ut sustineat a voluptatibus temperare. In fortitudine et prudentia inest, ut pro honesto pugnet; inest et temperantia, qua victores nolint perdere, quos possunt servare victus.

<-*Virtus vera.*->

**XLI.** Igitur nulla virtus solitaria, et ubi ex vero una ibi omnes Comites adsunt: solae enim virtutes vix est, ut cum Divo Augustino (2) loquar, ut nomen virtutum mereantur.

<-*Divina gratia.*->

**XLII.** Virtus autem, quae una vera, et quia vera, omnes virtutes praestat, non

(1) De qua Cap. III.

translation:
->*Of the origin of Virtue.*<-

**XL.** Virtue possesses the property of being of divine origin (1); for these three parts of it together constitute true virtue; and each of them is always found joined with the other two. Indeed, in prudence there is also fortitude, in that the mind, in searching for the truth, labors and endures fatigue, and does not rest until it finds it; there is also temperance, since it is a wise thing to be ignorant of certain things. In temperance, then, one finds prudence, which counsels us not to neglect things useful to life, so as not to suffer detriment; and therefore Medicine is of divine origin, because it was dictated by this eternal truth: there is also fortitude, so that one may know how to keep oneself far from pleasures. Finally, in fortitude, one also finds prudence to defend the honest; there is also temperance, so that the victors do not wish to destroy the vanquished whom they can keep alive without harm.

->*Of true virtue.*<-

**XLI.** There is, therefore, no virtue that stands alone, for where you truly find virtue, be certain that all the others are found united with it: since virtues that stand in isolation scarcely deserve, in the words of St. Augustine, the name of virtue (2).

->*Of divine Grace.*<-

**XLII.** That virtue, however, which alone must be called true, and as such goes before all others, is not proper to man, but rather belongs to God, and is called *Divine Grace*, which, by means of its light, makes it clearly seen by Christians what their duty is in this life; and it operates in such a way that with a single species of irremovable assent we assent both to the rational order, upon which our contemplation must dwell, and to the order of the facts that must be performed.
And in this way the principles of *Christian Morality* are considered demonstrated.
