# CANTO XXI OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

### THE NOBLE SUBJECT MATTER: and nobly treated in this twenty-first canto. In which he sets forth: how as they follow their path they were joined by a soul, from whom they learned the cause of the shaking of the mountain and of the song of the souls. And finally they recognized this man to have been a poet; nor without the greatest pleasure did Virgil recognize him.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A large historiated initial 'L' containing a scene with two figures in a landscape, representing the meeting of Dante and Virgil with the spirit of Statius. The initial is framed in a square border with decorative elements.</image-desc>

The natural thirst that is never satisfied
except with the water for which the young 
Samaritan woman <note>A reference to the woman at the well in John 4:1-42, who asks Jesus for "living water."</note> asked for grace
troubled me, and the haste pricked me
along the obstructed way behind my leader,
and I grieved for the just vengeance <note>The punishment of the souls on the terrace of Avarice.</note>.
And behold, just as Luke describes to us:
that Christ appeared to two who along the way
had already gone out from the sepulchral tomb,

nor were we aware of it until it spoke first,
saying: "My brothers, may God give you peace."
We turned suddenly, and Virgil
returned to him the sign that is appropriate for that.

<column-break/>

**THE NATURAL THIRST.** He shows us that there can be an innate thirst and desire in man to know. And because the knowledge of divine things is that through which we are blessed, we cannot have this perfectly through our own industry nor by natural ways unless we are illuminated by the Holy Spirit. Which Christ indicated in the Gospel of Saint John, Chapter IV, when asking for a drink from the Samaritan woman at the well of Jacob; and she denying it to him, alleging that the Jews do not associate with Samaritans. He added: "if you knew who it is who asks you for a drink, you would have asked him, and he would have given you to drink from a water of a fountain that springs up into eternal life." <note>original: "fons aquae salientis in vitam aeternam"</note> The young woman, then, after many words, asked for the grace, and Christ filled her with the Holy Spirit. Therefore, most wisely, the poet shows at present that the natural thirst—that is, the natural desire for knowing and understanding—is never satisfied except with the water. Wherefore the young Samaritan woman asked for grace—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. **IT TROUBLED ME.** <note>original: "mitravagliava"</note> This is a metaphor <term>translation: a figurative use of a word</term> from grain already threshed, which, so that it remains purged and clean, is "travailed"—that is, they make it pass from sieve to sieve <note>The commentator connects the word "travailed" (troubled) with "vagliare" (to sieve or winnow), suggesting a process of refinement.</note>; thus our soul, wishing to find the truth, goes on purging itself from time to time. **AND THE HASTE PRICKED ME** shows that at the same time the soul was eager to investigate the cause of the shaking of the mountain and the song of the souls, and the body had to hurry in following its journey. But Statius, arriving, explains that which neither Dante—that is, sensuality—nor Virgil—that is, human intellect, although illuminated by much learning—could understand by themselves. But Statius, who because of being accustomed to such things, explains them. And he puts Statius for the human intellect, which extends to comprehending that which cannot be understood by way of reason. And by comparison he shows, according to what Luke writes in the twenty-third chapter <note>The commentator likely means Luke 24, which describes Christ appearing to two disciples on the road to Emmaus.</note>.

<summary>This page introduces Canto XXI, where Dante and Virgil meet the spirit of the poet Statius, who is likened to the resurrected Christ appearing to disciples. The accompanying commentary explores the human "natural thirst" for divine knowledge, using the biblical figure of the Samaritan woman as an allegory for the soul's need for the Holy Spirit.</summary>
<keywords>Statius, natural thirst, Samaritan woman, Holy Spirit, divine knowledge, Virgil, Luke the Evangelist, winnowing metaphor</keywords>

# ON THE FINISHING OF ARTILLERY. 117

consideration or design, for it is enough for them that they hold the thing they fasten. Next to the bolt-work are the different types of bindings, which, as I have told you, some make in the manner of a **brace** <note>original: "braca"; a reinforcing strap or bracket.</note> that grips the reverse sides of the iron bands, and where they meet underneath, they are tied with a **twisted pin** <note>original: "chiaua-detta ritorta"</note>; and some fold them back into themselves. There are also those who make two instead of one, and at each end, and even in the middle of the iron band, they place one. All such things are a matter of the opinion and will of the masters. 

I also wish to warn you regarding the **timber** <note>original: "legname"</note> you must use for this purpose; be careful what kind it is. It must be dry and seasoned. For making the **carriage beds** <note>original: "li letti"</note>, the **hubs** <note>original: "li mozzi"</note>, and the **felloes** <note>original: "li gaui"; the curved wooden segments forming the rim of a wheel</note>, it should be of **elm** <note>original: "olmo"</note>. The **spokes** <note>original: "li razzi"</note> and the **axle** <note>original: "l'asse"</note> should be of **holm oak** <note>original: "leccio"</note> or **oak** <note>original: "quercia"</note>. I tell you again that it must be very well seasoned and dry; otherwise, in a short time or after a short journey, everything will come loose and be ruined, and you will have to make them all over again from the start. 

Now, according to the weight of the piece, one must think about putting it on its carriage, about which I could tell you of many types of screws and weight-lifters. But what is used by necessity is a **perforated lifting-jack** <note>original: "scaletta bucarata"; literally "holed little ladder," a frame used with a lever to ratchet up heavy weights.</note>, which, with an iron bolt, is used as a lever. First, let the piece be set into its bed on the ground without wheels. Then one side of the axle is raised and something is placed under it so it does not slip back; then the same is done on the other side. Thus, in two or three lifts, it is raised enough so that a wheel can fit onto the axle, and then the other is put on as well. With striking and with levers, they are brought to their proper places, and are secured with a **linchpin** <note>original: "chiaua-detta"</note> at the tip of the axle. 

Now, to be able to move it, you only need to arrange the **limbers** <note>original: "timoni"; the poles or shafts used for steering and pulling.</note>, which must be adapted according to what you wish to pull it with: whether with men, horses, oxen, or buffaloes. If with men, a small two-wheeled cart is placed underneath so that it holds the carriage suspended from the ground, and the **small rope** <note>original: "funichio"</note> is attached to the chain that you placed at the foot. With a bolt, the tail of the carriage is fixed onto the small cart, and the rope is pulled. If with oxen or buffaloes, a single pole is attached to the middle bolt, and at the tip of the pole, the first yoke is attached to the oxen, and the rest follow by being attached to the rope. And if with horses, two shafts are adapted, one on each side, and one horse goes in the middle. Then the cable is attached to a hook on the shaft and passes through the collar of the first horse, one by one or two by two; with this order, you can attach as many as you need so that they pull it easily. With these, more than 
->with any other animal, it is led with speed and ease to<-
->the place you desire. And let this be enough of what<-
->can properly be said of artillery. Of the<-
->powders, the balls, and the ways of using<-
->them, I will tell you in their proper places, when I<-
->speak to you of the batteries that are made.<-

they delighted more in one kind of harmony than another: because the Dorian harmony was named after the Dorians, who were its inventors; the Phrygian from the people who inhabited Phrygia; and the Lydian from those of Lydia, and so on for the others in order. It is certainly true that each of these had something unique in its song, and being accompanied by different <term>Numbers<note>In this context, "Numbers" (*Numeri*) refers to the rhythmic proportions and poetic meters that governed the movement of the music.</note></term>, they called some of them grave and severe; some bacchanalic and furious; some decent and religious; and others they named lascivious and warlike. Therefore, in this respect, they took great care in matching such Harmonies to the rhythmic Numbers, and this together with a purpose suited to the subject matter they expressed in Oratory or Speech, according to their nature. Taking all these things into consideration, they named their compositions according to the nature of the compound, such as, for example, the **Mournful Modes**, which are the Elegies: for they contain sad and mournful matters. This can be seen expressly in those two volumes (besides the almost infinite others by other authors) which Ovid wrote after he was sent into exile by Augustus; and also from what he writes in the *Epistle of Sappho to Phaon*, wanting to show that amorous things are mournful matters and that they suit the Elegy, saying:

> Perhaps you ask why my verses are in alternating meters,
> when I am better suited to lyric modes.
> My love is to be wept for. Elegy is a mournful song.
> No lyre is made for my tears.
> <note>Original Latin: *Forsitan & quare mea sint alterna requiris / Carmina, cùm lyricis sim magis apta modis. / Flendus amor meus est. Elegia flebile carmen. / Non facit ad lacrymas barbitos ulla meos.*</note>

Horace made mention of these Modes, saying:

> You always pursue with mournful modes
> the loss of Mystes.
> <note>Original Latin: *Tu semper urges flebilibus modis / Mysten ademptum.*</note>

And also Boethius in the third book of *The Consolation of Philosophy*:

> Once the Thracian bard <note>Referring to Orpheus.</note>,
> mourning his wife's death,
> after he had compelled the forests to run,
> and the swift rivers to stand still with mournful modes;
> <note>Original Latin: *Quondam funera coniugis / Vates thraicius gemens, / Postquàm flebilibus modis, / Syluas currere, mobiles / Amnes stare coegerat;*</note>

Just as Cicero also commemorated them in the *Tusculan Disputations*, when (mentioning the humble and low ones together) he said: *These things, when sung with low and mournful modes, bring sadness to entire theaters.* <note>Original Latin: *Hæc cum pressis & flebilibus modis, qui totis theatris moestitiam inferant, concinuntur.*</note> And in another place, mentioning the slow ones: *The same Roscius used to say that as he aged, he would make the modes of the flute player slower and the songs more relaxed.* <note>Original Latin: *Solet idem Roscius dicere, se quo plus ætatis sibi accederet, eo tardiores tibicinis modos, & cantus remissiores esse facturum.*</note>

Others named them **Lamenting Modes**, as can be seen in Apuleius, when he says: *And the sound of the wedding flute changes into the complaining Lydian mode.* <note>Original Latin: *Et sonus Tibiæ Zigiæ mutatur in quærulum Lydij modum.*</note> Some then called them **Sweet Modes**, as the same Horace shows us in another place, when he says:

> Now Thracian Chloe rules me,
> learned in sweet modes, and 
> skilled with the lyre.
> <note>Original Latin: *Me nunc Tressa Chloe regit, / Dulces docta modos, & / Citharæ sciens.*</note>

And Seneca also: *Let the flute pour out sweet modes for the sacrifice.* <note>Original Latin: *Sacrificas dulces tibia effundat modos.*</note> They also named some others **Sad Modes**, as can be seen from the authority of Boethius:

> I who once composed songs with flourishing zeal, 
> am now forced, alas, to enter into mournful modes of sadness;
> <note>Original Latin: *Carmina qui quondam studio florente peregi, / Flebilis heu mæstos cogor inire modos;*</note>

And some **Immodest Modes**, which Quintilian commemorates saying: *I think it must be stated more openly that I am not teaching this [music] which is now effeminate on stages and broken by immodest modes.* <note>Original Latin: *Apertius tamen profitendum puto, non hanc a me præcipi, quæ nunc in scenis effæminata, & impu dicis modis fracta.*</note> Others called them **Crude** or **Coarse Modes**, which Ovid demonstrates:

> And while the Tuscan flute player provides a crude mode,
> the Lydian strikes the leveled ground three times with his foot;
> <note>Original Latin: *Dumq; rudem præbente modum tibicine Tusco, / Lydius æquatam ter pede pulsat humum;*</note>

And others **Discordant Modes**; and of these Statius makes mention:

> I attempt discordant modes,
> and sobbing words.
> <note>Original Latin: *Discordesq; modos, & singultantia uerba / Molior.*</note>

Finally (leaving out many others for brevity), they universally called some compositions **Lyric Modes**, as can be understood from the authority of Ovid cited above. Such matters were not expressed by the voice alone, but were accompanied by the Harmony that arose from some instrument, whether it be the <term>Cittern<note>A wire-strung fretted instrument, popular in the Renaissance.</note></term>, or the Lyre, or the <term>Pipe<note>The "Piffero" or flute.</note></term>, or of any other sort. There was nonetheless a great difference between these Modes: since the people of one province used one manner of Verse and one Instrument, and those of another used another Instrument and another manner. And they were not different in these alone, but in the Harmonies as well: for one kind of harmony was used by one people and another by another; in such a way that they were also different in the rhythmic Numbers found in the verses. From this it arose later that the Modes were named after those peoples (as I have said above) who most

Met een groote troepenmacht bestormden zij de patihswoning, maar het eenige resultaat was, dat zij de patihsvrouw de zenuwen op het lijf joegen en de schuld er van waren, dat zij flauw viel. Gajah-Mada had namelijk, zonder dat iemand het bemerkt had, de kapatihan verlaten en zich naar het strand begeven. Daar knoopte hij een gesprek aan met varensgezellen (event. reizende kooplieden) en vernam, dat één (eenigen) van hen een stem had (den) gehoord, die zeide: „Mada, kom terug; ge hebt nu lang genoeg op aarde geheerscht en genoten”. De patih begreep nu, dat zijn tijd gekomen was. Hij verzocht een schipper hem midden op zee te brengen ¹), waarvoor hij hem als belooning zijn eigen uiterlijk zou schenken, dat hem in staat zou stellen bezit te nemen van de kapatihan en alle schatten, die zich daarin bevonden. Het voorstel werd aangenomen. Midden op zee verdween Gajah-Mada plotseling. De schipper ging, aan land teruggekeerd, naar de kapatihan, en daar hij inderdaad volkomen het uiterlijk van den patih gekregen had, bemerkte de patihsche niet eens, dat de man, die juist de kapatihan bereikte, toen de door den koning uitgezonden troepen weer vertrokken waren, Gajah-Mada niet zelf was, en begroette hem met vreugde. Zij en haar medevrouwen zorgden voor nieuwe kleeren, bloemen en waschwater en dienden een copieus maal op. Ofschoon de schipper, de pseudo-Gajah-Mada, zich in zijn nieuwe milieu geenszins op zijn gemak voelde, maakte hij vooral van den aangeboden drank zoo gretig gebruik, dat hij weldra in kennelijken staat was. Zoo ging het den geheelen dag door. Pas 's nachts ontdekte de patihsvrouw door zijn gedrag in het slaapvertrek, dat hij niet de echte Gajah-Mada was. Tot wanhoop gebracht door deze beproeving der goden ging zij zich in zee verdrinken.

# CAPUT TRIGESIMUM PRIMUM.

## *Chirotheca marina. Sarong tangan laut.*

Hæc quoque est planta spongiosa, ex angusto principio ample sese extendens in multos quasi digitos, inferius angustatos & conjunctos, superius latos, & foramine excavatos, concava porro est, & duplicis formæ.

Prima multos rotundos gerit digitos, quorum quidam haud crassiores sunt pollice, superne gerentes angustum & rotundum foraminulum.

Alii crassitiem habent brachii infantis, ampleque aperti sunt instar intestini, suntque porro interne concavi instar crateris vel instar abscissorum digitorum in chirothecis laneis, interne glabriores quam externe, substantiæ instar lanæ & spongiæ inter sese mixtæ, coloris ex gilvo cinerei instar aliarum spongiarum.

Sine notabili radice quibusvis insidet scopulis, inque digitorum cavitatibus pisciculi habitant & squillæ, in & extra natantes.

Altera forma longiores & superius acutiores gerit digitos, externe maxime spinulosos, sed spinulæ non duræ sunt, texturæ crassioris & latioris præcedente, magis ad spongiosam quam ad ligneam accedens naturam. Digiti interne quoque concavi & glabri funt, in quibus similes pisciculi & squillæ ludunt. Sunt autem fasciculi ultra pedem alti, multis digitis simul concretis, qui vili insident radici.

*Nomen.* Latine *Chirotheca marina*; Malaice *Sarong tangan laut.*

*Locus & Usus.* Hæ plantæ nulli inserviunt usui, sed instar priorum tanquam res raræ servantur.

In hac *Chirotheca marina* pisciculus habitat peculiaris naturæ & formæ, estque species *Ican batu*, formæ planæ & tenuis, coloris rubri cum nigricantibus annulis, atque hic pisciculus sub cavis etiam reperitur saxis, hosce autem inhabitat digitos, sed non constat, an hosce formet, pungit homines instar Gallinæ, si nimis prope accedunt, sed non dolet.

---

# CAPUT TRIGESIMUM SECUNDUM.

## *Barba marina.*

Binæ denique subsequuntur plantæ marinæ, quæ cum Zoophytis quoque conveniunt, sed magis ad saxosam accedunt naturam, ac proinde ad hunc pertinent librum.

Primo. *Barba marina*, videtur esse fasciculus albarum vel cinerearum firmarum fetarum, forma penicilli. Inferius vero locantur radici nodosæ, quæ formam fere gerit scroti, & composita est ex granis saxosis. Hisce fetæ insident, totumque penicillus ultra spithamam longus est, superne acuminatus instar coni, externe glaber & parum angulosus, tenui obductus substantia instar nebulæ linteæ *Tshjavoni* dictæ, sub qua multi oculi seu foraminula conspiciuntur. Hac nebula saxosa abstracta in conspectum modo veniunt albæ istæ seu griseæ fetæ crassitie Equiseti, rugosæ & acutæ, præfertim circa inferiorem partem, ubi & quodammodo lædunt. Tumque sese aperiunt capilli istius coni, & incomptam formant barbam, quæ tactu facile frangitur, frustaque cuti inhærent cum levi pruritu. Cætera coni pars sibi porro adhæret instar Capillitii, per sordes & lentes intricati. Sub aqua per nebulam mucosam vivere videtur, fed supra aquam nullum signum vitæ vel sensus in ea detegitur, excepto levi cutis pruritu.

*Nomen.* Latine *Barba marina*; Malaice vocari posset *Djangot* feu *Barba laut*. Aliis quoque *Penicillus marinus* dicitur, hujus enim species quoque reperitur in mari mediterraneo. Hisce in terris raro in conspectum venit, aliquando enim per piscatorum hamos modo adtrahitur, profunde in mare demissos. Nullum quoque huc usque notum habet usum, piscatores enim pro noxio habent producto, ac proinde in mare id mox iterum projiciunt.

# EEN EN DERTIGSTE HOOFDSTUK.

## *De Zee-Handschoen.*

Dit is ook een spongieus gewas, uit een smal begin zig ver uitbreidende in veele vingeren, beneden smal, en allegaar by malkander gevoegt, boven breed, en met een gat, voorts binnen hol, van tweederlei gedaante.

De eerste heeft veele ronde vingeren, zommige niet dikker, dan een duim, boven met een smal rond gaatje.

*Andere zyn zoo dik als een kinder arm, en wyd geopent als een darm. Voorts binnen hol als een bekertje, of gelyk afgesneede vingeren aan de wolle handschoen, binnen essener dan buiten, van substantie als wol en spongie door malkander gemengt, van couleur vaal-graauw als andere spongie.*

Het staat zonder kennelyke wortelen op alderhande klippen, en in de bolligheden van de vingeren woonen kleine Visjes en Garnaaltjes, daar uit en in-zwemmende.

*De tweede gedaante heeft langere en boven spitzere vingeren, van buiten heel steekelig, dog de doorens zyn niet hard, grover en breeder van weeweef dan het voorgaande, meer na de spongieuse dan houte natuur trekkende. Binnen zyn de vingeren mede hol en effen, daar diergelyke Visjes en Garnaaltjes in speelen. Het zyn bossen ruim een voet hoog, met veele vingeren nevens malkander gewassen, op een slegten wortel staande.*

Naam. In 't Latyn *Chirotheca marina*; in 't Maleits *Sarong tangan laut.*

Plaats en Gebruik. Deze gewaffen dienen tot niets, maar werden gelyk het voorgaande tot rariteit bewaart.

In deze *Chirotheca marina* woond een ander klein Visje van een byzondere aart en fatzoen, een slag van *Ican batu*, plat en dun, rood met zwartagtige banden, die men ook onder de holle stenen vindt, hy woond in deze vingeren, maar men weet egter niet, dat hy dezelve formeerd, hy pikt na de menschen als een Hoen, als men hem te na komt, dog zonder zeer te doen.

---

# TWEE EN DERTIGSTE HOOFDSTUK.

## *De Zee-Baart.*

Daar volgen nog twee zeldzame zeegewassen, die met de Zoopytis ook al mede gemeenschap hebben, dog de steenige natuur nog al nader zyn, en dierhalven in dit Boek behooren.

*1. Barba marina schynt een bondeltje te zyn, van witte of gryze, styve borsteltjes, in gedaante van een quast of grof Penseel. Beneden staan ze op een knobbelagtig wortel, geformeert schier als een klootzak, gemaakt van klein en steenig gruis. Hier in steeken de borstels, zynde de geheele quast ruim een span lank, boven spits toeloopende gelyk een kegel, van buiten effen, en wat hoekig, omgeven met een fyne substantie, gelyk het linnen Tshjavony genaamt, daar onder men veele oogjes of gaatjes ziet. Dit steenagtig linnen afgetrokken zynde, vertoonen baar eerst de witte of gryze borstels in de dikte van Paartshairen, ruig en scherp, inzonderheid omtrent het onderste, daar ze ook eenigzints snyden. Als dan open bun de hairen des kegels, en maken een verwerden baart, in 't aanraken ligt breekende, en de stukken kleeven aan de huid met een klein jeuken. De rest van de keegel kleeft nog al aan malkander gelyk een lok hairs, die door vuiligheid en neeten aan malkander hangt. Onder water schynt het met zyn slymeryg vel eenig gevoelen te vertoonen, maar boven water kan men geen teeken van leven nog beweeging daar aan gewaar werden, behalven een klein jeuken op de huid.*

Naam. In 't Latyn *Barba marina*; in 't Maleits mag men 't noemen *Djangot* of *Barba laut*. By anderen werd het ook *Penicillus marinus* genaamt, want een gedaante daar van ook in de Middellantse Zee gevonden werd. Hier te lande komt het zelden voor den dag, werdende maar somtyts opgehaalt met de Vissers hoeken, die wat diep in zee gelaten werden. Het heeft ook tot nog toe geen bekent gebruik, want de Viffers houden 't voor een schadelyk gewas, smytende het straks weder in zee.

# BOOK XII. CHAPTER XXXI. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-ONE.

## *The Sea Glove. Sarong tangan laut.*
<note>original: *Chirotheca marina*</note>

This is also a spongy plant. It expands from a narrow base into many fingers. These are narrow and joined at the bottom, but wide and hollowed out with a hole at the top. It is hollow inside and has two forms.

The first form has many round fingers. Some are no thicker than a thumb and have a small round hole at the top.

Others are as thick as a child's arm. They are wide open like an intestine. They are hollow inside like a small cup or like the severed fingers of a wool glove. The interior is smoother than the exterior. The substance is a mixture of wool and sponge. The color is a pale grayish-yellow, similar to other sponges.

It sits on various rocks without a visible root. Small fish and shrimp live in the hollows of the fingers, swimming in and out.

The second form has longer fingers that are sharper at the top. The exterior is very prickly, but the spines are not hard. The texture is coarser and wider than the previous kind. It is more spongy than woody in nature. The fingers are also hollow and smooth inside, where similar fish and shrimp play. These are clusters over a foot high with many fingers growing together from a simple root.

*Name.* In Latin, *Chirotheca marina*; in Malay, *Sarong tangan laut* <note>literally "sea hand-sleeve" or glove</note>.

*Place and Use.* These plants serve no practical purpose. Like the previous ones, they are kept as curiosities.

A specific fish of a peculiar nature and shape lives in this *Sea Glove*. It is a species of *Stone Fish* <note>original: *Ican batu*</note>. It is flat and thin. Its color is red with blackish rings. This fish is also found under hollow stones. It lives in these fingers, but it is not known if the fish forms them. It pecks at people like a hen if they come too close, but it does not cause pain.

---

# CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO.

## *The Sea Beard.*
<note>original: *Barba marina*</note>

Finally, two rare marine plants follow. These share characteristics with zoophytes <note>organisms that appear to be between plants and animals</note>, but they are closer to a stony nature. Therefore, they belong in this book.

First. The *Sea Beard* appears to be a bundle of white or gray stiff bristles in the shape of a brush or coarse paintbrush. At the bottom, they sit on a knotty root. This root is shaped almost like a scrotum and is made of stony grains. The bristles sit in this base. The entire brush is over a span long. It is pointed at the top like a cone. The exterior is smooth and somewhat angular. It is covered with a thin substance like the linen called *Tshjavoni*. Many small eyes or holes are visible beneath this. Once this stony linen is pulled away, the white or gray bristles appear. They are as thick as horsehair. They are rough and sharp, especially near the bottom, where they can cut. Then the hairs of the cone open up and form a messy beard. It breaks easily when touched. The pieces stick to the skin and cause a slight itch. The rest of the cone sticks together like a lock of hair tangled with dirt and lice. Under water, it seems to show some sensation through its slimy skin. Above water, no sign of life or feeling is detected, except for the slight itching on the skin.

*Name.* In Latin, *Barba marina*; in Malay, it could be called *Djangot* or *Barba laut* <note>Sea Beard</note>. Others also call it the *Sea Brush* <note>original: *Penicillus marinus*</note>. A species of this is also found in the Mediterranean Sea. In these lands, it rarely comes to light. It is sometimes pulled up by fishermen's hooks that have been lowered deep into the sea. It has no known use. Fishermen consider it a harmful growth and immediately throw it back into the sea.

<meta>catchword: Second.</meta>

<column-break/>

# CHAPTER THIRTY-ONE.

## *The Sea Glove.*

This is also a spongy growth. It expands from a narrow beginning into many fingers. It is narrow at the bottom where all parts are joined together. It is wide at the top with a hole. Furthermore, it is hollow inside and of two types.

The first has many round fingers. Some are no thicker than a thumb and have a narrow round hole at the top.

*Others are as thick as a child's arm and wide open like an intestine. Furthermore, they are hollow inside like a small cup, or like severed fingers on a wool glove. They are smoother inside than outside. The substance is like wool and sponge mixed together. The color is pale gray like other sponges.*

It stands without visible roots on all sorts of cliffs. Small fish and shrimp live in the hollows of the fingers, swimming in and out.

*The second form has longer and sharper fingers at the top. The outside is very prickly, though the thorns are not hard. It is coarser and wider in weave than the preceding one, leaning more toward a spongy than a woody nature. Inside, the fingers are also hollow and smooth, where similar fish and shrimp play. These are bunches over a foot high, with many fingers grown next to each other, standing on a simple root.*

Name. In Latin, *Chirotheca marina*; in Malay, *Sarong tangan laut.*

Place and Use. These growths serve no purpose, but like the previous ones, they are kept as rarities.

Another small fish of a special nature and shape lives in this *Chirotheca marina*. It is a type of *Stone Fish* <note>original: *Ican batu*</note>. It is flat and thin, red with blackish bands. It is also found under hollow stones. It lives in these fingers, but it is not known if it forms them. It pecks at people like a hen if one comes too close, though without causing pain.

There follow two more rare sea growths that have commonality with zoophytes. However, they are closer to a stony nature and therefore belong in this Book.

At the bottom, they stand on a knotty root, formed almost like a scrotum, made of small and stony grit. The bristles are stuck in this. The entire brush is over a span long and tapers at the top like a cone. It is smooth on the outside and somewhat angular. It is surrounded by a fine substance like the linen named Tshjavony. Underneath this, one sees many small eyes or holes. This stony linen being pulled away, the white or gray bristles first appear in the thickness of horsehairs. They are rough and sharp, especially around the bottom part, where they also cut somewhat. Then the hairs of the cone open up and make a tangled beard. It breaks easily upon touching, and the pieces stick to the skin with a slight itching. The rest of the cone still sticks together like a lock of hair that hangs together through filth and nits. Under water, it seems to show some feeling with its slimy skin. But above water, one can perceive no sign of life nor movement, except for a slight itching on the skin.*

Name. In Latin, *Barba marina*; in Malay, one may call it *Djangot* or *Barba laut*. By others, it was also named *Penicillus marinus*, for a form of it is also found in the Mediterranean Sea. In this country, it rarely appears. It is only sometimes pulled up with fishermen's hooks that were let deep into the sea. It has no known use to this day, for the fishermen consider it a harmful growth, throwing it back into the sea immediately.

After this operation, we sailed to the Island Canon or Cocles, to caulk the ships there and to provide ourselves with all necessities. While we were busy with this, we saw a ship at sea taking a course toward the Philippine Islands; we chased it, and having caught it, we robbed the merchant goods from it and let the ship go.

<margin>Drake considers departing for the Fatherland.</margin>
When Drake saw his operation had succeeded this far, and thinking back on his dangers and the inconveniences of the journey, and that he had sufficiently avenged the violence and insolence that his Queen had suffered from the Spanish King, he deliberated on which way he should turn his course back to England. But because he was worried that the Spaniards would try to intercept him everywhere, and because the great dangers he had already endured from the storm outside the Strait of Magellan on the south side deterred him, he finally took the decision to turn toward the Moluccan Islands, keeping the Portuguese course to set it via the Cape of Good Hope.

<margin>Turn toward the Moluccan Islands.</margin>
But when we had too much calm, we were forced to steer the Spanish course more northerly, from where we still had at least 600 miles to sail. We spent the time here from the sixteenth of April until the third of June. On the fifth of the same month, we arrived at 42 degrees north latitude, found it so cold there that it was barely endurable, and were therefore forced to seek land.

<margin>Arrive at 42 degrees, and endure great cold.</margin>
We then discovered low-lying land, but as it was entirely covered with snow, we did not land there. We sailed further to 38 degrees and found a beautiful harbor where we anchored.

<margin>38 degrees</margin>

*The Soul in meditation on the new Creature.*

When the little seed died in the earth's lap,
And seemed forgotten and lost,
Then the little flower turned green through that death,
And came forth as if born anew,
From dark earth into the beautiful light,
To bring forth scent and colors.
Greeted by the face of heaven,

So grows the new creature,
When one's own will goes into destruction,
In death and the grave, though it tastes sour,

Though none born blind to the world see it,
It stands before God and his Son,
And smells through all the angels' choirs.

A little flower on your <term>Roozenhoed</term> <gloss>hat or wreath of roses</gloss>,

dit Werk te vinden, alwaar wy ons zelven niets dan de ſtichting van den Chriſtelyken Leezer hebben voorgeſteld. 't Is dan genoeg dat men weete, dat het Evangelium, 't welk den naam van Markus draagt, zo wel als de drie andere, een voortbrengſel is van den H. Geeſt, die de hand en pen van deezen Evangeliſt heeft beſtierd. Dit alleen is het dat de voortreffelykheyd der Heylige Boeken maakt, en dat hen 't gezag geeft, dat zy hebben, van ons geloof aan zich te onderwerpen, en niet de naamen hunner Schryveren, hoe vermaard zy ook in de Kerke geweeft moogen zyn. Ten opzigt van de taal in welke Markus geſchreeven heeft, de eerſte Oudheyd heeft nooit getwyfeld, nóch ook anders gezegd, dan dat het de Griekſche geweeſt zy. In de völgende eeuwen waaren 'er eenige welke die eere aan de Latynſche hebben willen opdraagen; en dewyl het hart menigmaal eenige tédere belangen heeft, die 't gemoed in zyne party wikkelen, heeft men naa dien aardigen droom menſchen gevonden, die 'er eene Hiſtori van hebben willen maaken, en dezelve voor waar uitgeeven.

Dewyl 't gelooflyk is dat Markus zyn Evangelium niet geſchreeven heeft, dan toen dat van Mattheus, en waarſchynelyk dat van Lukas, het licht al gezien hadden, zo heeft hy niet, gelyk de twee eerſte, het geſlachtregiſter van Jeſus Chriſtus verhaald: het gene zy geſchreeven hadden was genoegzaam om te toonen, dat Jeſus, de zoon van Maria, waarlyk uyt David geſprooten was, völgens de voorzeggingen welke men daarvan in de Profeten ziet. Derhalve heeft Markus de Hiſtori des Evangeliums anders begonnen dan de twee eerſte Evangeliften, en hy heeft die van ſtonden aan op de Profecye van Maleachi, die het hek van 't Oude

<column-break/>

Teftament fluyt, willen laaten vólgen, gelyk als om dezelve met het boek van dien Profeet aan één te ſchákelen. Maleachi had zyne profecy aldus geëyndigd:
> *Ziet ik zend ulieden den Profeet Elias, eer dat die groote en die vreeflyke dag des HEEREN komen zal. Ende hy zal het hart der váderen tót de kinderen wederbrengen, en het hart der kinderen tót hunne vaders: opdat ik niet kome, en de aarde met den ban slaa.*

Deeze woorden betékenen klaarlyk Joannes den Dooper; daarop komt Markus vyfhonderd jaaren na Maleachi, en ſchákelende aan de voorzegginge haare vervúlling, maakt hy daarme de 't begin van zyn Evangelium.
> *Het begin, zegt hy, des Evangeliums van Jeſus Chriſtus des Zoons Góds; gelyk geſchreeven is in de Profeten, Ziet ik zend mynen Engel voor uw aangezigt.*

Hy vervólgt met weynige woorden van Joannes den Dooper te ſpreeken, en treedt voorts over, gelyk Mattheus en Lukas, tót den doop van Jeſus Chriſtus. Wyders houdt hy tót aan 't eynde toe bykans dezelfde órde als de eerſte, en 't ſchynt als óf hy niet gedaan hadde dan hem te verkorten, 't zy zulks inderdaad op veele plaatſen zyne meening geweeſt zy, om eenige andere wat meer uyt te breyden, óf dat de H. Geeſt, die hem met hetzelfde verſtand verlichtte als Mattheus, hem dikwils met denzelven heeft doen overeenkomen, gelyk eertyds Micha aan Jeſaia. Maar men behoeft daarom Markus niet aan te zien als eenen verkorter van Mattheus, dewyl zulks niet verheven genoeg ſchynt voor eenen aangeblaazen Schryver, die zelf een oorſpronglyke verhaalder is; behalve dat dit gevoelen klaarlyk wederſprooken wordt door een nauwkeurige vergelyking van 't één Evangelium met het ander.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the Gospel of Mark, specifically regarding its divine authority, its original language, and its relationship to the Prophet Malachi and the Gospel of Matthew. It then transitions into the life of the third Evangelist, Luke.</meta>

# HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

to find in this work, where we have intended nothing but the edification of the Christian reader. It is enough, then, that one knows that the Gospel which bears the name of Mark, as well as the three others, is a product of the Holy Spirit, who guided the hand and pen of this Evangelist. This alone is what constitutes the excellence of the Holy Books and gives them the authority they possess to subject our faith to them, and not the names of their authors, however famous they may have been in the Church. In regards to the language in which Mark wrote, the earliest antiquity <note>referring to the early Church Fathers and scholars of the first few centuries AD</note> never doubted, nor said otherwise, than that it was Greek. In following centuries, there were some who wished to award that honor to Latin; and because the heart often has certain tender interests that involve the mind in its cause, people have been found who, after that fanciful dream, wished to make a history of it and present it as truth.

Since it is likely that Mark did not write his Gospel until that of Matthew, and probably that of Luke, had already seen the light, he did not—as the first two did—recount the genealogy of Jesus Christ. What they had written was sufficient to show that Jesus, the son of Mary, was truly descended from David, according to the prophecies seen in the Prophets. Therefore, Mark began the History of the Gospel differently than the first two Evangelists, and he chose to have it follow immediately upon the prophecy of Malachi, which closes the gate of the Old

<column-break/>

Testament, as if to link it together with the book of that Prophet. Malachi had ended his prophecy thus:
> *Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD. And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and smite the earth with a curse.* <note>original: Malachi 4:5-6. The author uses the name 'Elias,' the Greek/Latin form of 'Elijah.'</note>

These words clearly signify John the Baptist; thereupon Mark comes five hundred years after Malachi, and linking the fulfillment to the prophecy, he makes it the beginning of his Gospel.
> *The beginning,* he says, *of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God; as it is written in the Prophets: Behold, I send my messenger before your face.* <note>Mark 1:1-2</note>

He continues by speaking briefly of John the Baptist, and then passes over, like Matthew and Luke, to the baptism of Jesus Christ. Furthermore, until the end, he maintains almost the same order as the first, and it seems as if he has done nothing but abridge him—whether that was indeed his intention in many places to expand somewhat more on others, or that the Holy Spirit, who enlightened him with the same understanding as Matthew, often caused him to agree with him, as Micah once did with Isaiah. <note>Micah 4 and Isaiah 2 contain nearly identical passages, a parallel the author uses to explain similarities between Gospels without assuming one simply copied the other.</note> But one need not view Mark as a mere abridger of Matthew, as such does not seem exalted enough for an inspired <term>inspired: "aangeblaazen," literally "breathed into," referring to divine inspiration</term> writer who is himself an original narrator; besides, this opinion is clearly contradicted by a close comparison of one Gospel with the other.

## *Thirteenth Scene.*

See how the Christians sit here in silence,
Listening attentively to the life-giving word,
Which, like a sharp sword, pierces the hard heart,
Or burns like a fire, to purify the conscience.

For one, the Scripture serves as comfort in adversity;
For another, it strengthens virtue through pure teaching;
It awakens another to penance and the conversion of the soul,
Or supports the wavering mind with strength.

Thus it serves as milk for this one, and solid food <note>original: "vaste spyze"</note> for that one,
Strengthening them from time to time in the pure faith,
Through which the Christian soul notices its transgressions,
And finds cause to praise God for His grace.

Give thanks, Christian, to your Lord for this precious treasure of salvation,
Far more powerful in brilliance than Aaron’s breastplate <note>A reference to the High Priest Aaron in the Old Testament, whose breastplate was set with twelve precious stones representing the tribes of Israel.</note>,

<meta>This page continues from the general introduction. Having established that painting is a form of "investigating things" akin to poetry, the text now transitions into a specific historical survey of flower and bird painting, beginning with the Tang Dynasty and moving through the transformative Song Dynasty.</meta>

# Simple Exposition on Woody Flowers, Volume One

The camellia <note>original: *cha* (茶), specifically the ornamental tea-flower or camellia</note> possesses a brilliance that rivals cinnabar. The sweet osmanthus <note>original: *yuegui* (月桂), the "moon laurel"</note> produces a fragrance like "golden grains" <term>jinsu: a poetic name for osmanthus blossoms based on their tiny, golden appearance</term>. Add to these the lofty purity of the willow and the *wutong* tree, or the vigorous, aged strength of the tall pine and the ancient cypress—when these are committed to a painting, they are quite enough to inspire a refined elegance in the viewer. Such art rivals the works of Nature <term>zaohua: the creative force of the universe</term> and can even shift the human spirit.

If we examine the history of this art, the Tang Dynasty masters of flowers and plants began with the "feathers and furs" <note>a traditional category for birds and mammals</note> style established by **Xue Ji** and **Bian Luan**. Later, masters like **Liang Guang**, **Yu Xi**, **Diao Guang**, **Zhou Huang**, and the brothers **Guo Qianhui** and **Guo Qianyou** emerged in succession; all were famous for their bird-and-flower paintings.

In the Five Dynasties period, **Teng Changyou**, **Zhong Yin**, and **Huang Quan** and his sons rose to prominence one after another. **Teng Changyou** possessed a lofty heart and a unique brush-and-ink style; he did not rely on the guidance of teachers. **Zhong Yin** followed the tradition of the Guo brothers. **Huang Quan** was exceptionally skilled at gathering the strengths of various schools: for flowers, he looked to **Teng Changyou**; for birds, he followed **Diao Guang**. Even for his dragons, cranes, trees, and rocks, each had a specific classical source. His sons, **Huang Jubao** and **Huang Jucai**, were able to carry on the family methods. Because of this, their reputation was immense in their own time, and their methods have been passed down for a thousand years—this is truly no exaggeration. Indeed, the painting styles of the early Song Dynasty were based entirely on the **Huang** father and sons as the standard.

When we reach the Song Dynasty, **Xu Xi** arose and uniquely transformed the old methods. He was truly unprecedented and has remained unsurpassed. Although he lived between the eras of **Huang Quan** and **Zhao Chang**, his divine subtlety was uniquely superior. He passed his legacy to his grandsons **Xu Chongsi** and **Xu Chongju**; their family learning was inherited so well that they could truly follow in their ancestor’s footsteps. 

The color application of **Zhao Chang** was also exquisitely fine; he did not merely capture the outward likeness of a form, but could directly convey its inner spirit. Some say that **Xu Xi**, **Huang Quan**, and **Zhao Chang** followed one another in excellence. However, it has been said that **Huang Quan’s** paintings have "spirit but lack subtlety," while **Zhao Chang’s** have "subtle beauty but lack spirit." <note>This refers to the *Four Classes* of painting excellence: "Divine" (shen), "Subtle/Wonderful" (miao), "Competent" (neng), and "Untrammeled" (yi)</note> Perhaps that is the case? 

Because of this, when the artist **Yi Yuanji** first mastered the art of painting and saw the work of **Zhao Chang**, he remarked: "The world does not lack for talented people, but one must break free from old habits and surpass the ancients to truly reach the peak of excellence." **Qiu Qingyu** first studied under **Zhao Chang**, but in his later years he surpassed his teacher and directly inherited the style of **Xu Xi**. Later, **Cui Bai**, **Cui Que**, **Ai Xuan**, **Ding Kuang**, **Ge Shouchang**, and **Wu Yuanyu** were all summoned to serve in the Imperial Painting Academy, and their reputations were heavy...

<summary>This page outlines the historical lineage of flower-and-bird painting, tracing the transition from the Tang and Five Dynasties masters to the defining styles of Huang Quan and Xu Xi in the Song Dynasty.</summary>
<keywords>Huang Quan, Xu Xi, Zhao Chang, Song Dynasty painting, bird-and-flower painting, lineage, Painting Academy, spirit-resonance, color application</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the strategic importance of using defectors and external intelligence. It moves from historical examples of great advisors who changed sides to the specific tactical methods for employing envoys and spies to dismantle an enemy from within.</meta>

To empty an enemy state, one uses "the stones from other mountains to polish one's own jade" <note>original: "他山之石可以攻玉" (tā shān zhī shí kě yǐ gōng yù). A classic idiom meaning that external resources, or even the faults of others, can be used to improve oneself or one's position.</note>. There are three ways to employ **envoys** <term>xingren</term> <note>Literally "travelers," this term historically refers to diplomats, envoys, and intelligence gatherers sent between states.</note> in this pursuit:

First: When people from the enemy state come to observe or praise us, we should bestow generous bribes upon them to induce them to subvert their own state's affairs.

Second: When scholars or officials from the enemy have committed offenses and flee to us, we should grant them high rank and generous salaries. We must carefully examine their words and verify the facts of their situation. If they are genuine, we employ them; if they are found to be false, we execute them. They are then used as guides for our high officials <term>qingdao</term> <note>Literally "ministers as guides," referring to high-ranking defectors who provide strategic directions for invading or undermining their former home.</note>.

Third: We send our own envoys to observe the enemy ruler’s inner circle and those in charge of affairs—noting who is worthy and who is foolish; which close ministers, whether within the court or without, are greedy and which are incorruptible; and which of the attendants or gatekeepers <term>yezhe</term> <note>Officials responsible for announcing guests and managing access to the ruler.</note> are gentlemen and which are "petty men" <term>xiaoren</term> <note>In Confucian thought, "petty men" are those who prioritize personal profit and ego over moral duty.</note>. Once we have grasped the true state of their affairs and act accordingly, our objectives will be achieved. 

Of all the vital components of the **Three Armies** <note>A traditional term for the entire military force of a state.</note>, none is more important than the envoy. Of all the secrets of the Three Armies, none are more sensitive than those of the envoy. If the envoy’s plans are leaked before they are executed, those who disclosed them must all be put to death. On the day the plan is set in motion, one must scrape away the drafts and burn the initial notes <note>This highlights the extreme security required in espionage; all written evidence of the plot must be destroyed as soon as it begins.</note>. Gold—

<summary>This page details three primary methods for using envoys to destabilize an enemy state: bribing visitors, vetting and employing defectors, and conducting deep-cover reconnaissance of the enemy's court hierarchy. It emphasizes that the diplomat/spy is the most critical and secretive element of military operations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ceremonial regalia, moving from the Golden Tallies used by envoys to the "Bone-Bud" (Guduo), a bulbous ceremonial mace carried by elite imperial guards. It provides an etymological explanation for the weapon's unusual name and describes its physical evolution across the Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties.</meta>

Page Thirty-one
# Thirty-one: Official [...]

According to the *Notebooks* of Song Qi <note>Song Qi (998–1061) was a renowned historian of the Song Dynasty and co-compiler of the *New History of the Tang*</note>, the current dynasty employs "Bone-Bud Bearers" <note>original: 骨朵子直 (Guduozi Zhi). These were elite guards who carried ceremonial maces</note> among the guards who attend closely to the Emperor. I once served in the compilation of the *Daily Records* <note>original: 日曆 (Rili). The official court chronicles</note> and investigated the meaning of this term.

The people of the Guanzhong region <note>The central plains of Shaanxi province, the historic heartland of several dynasties</note> refer to a large, protruding belly as a *Guzhun* <note>original: 胍肫</note>. Colloquially, because the head of certain ceremonial staffs was quite large, they also came to be called *Guzhun*. This was later corrupted into the name "Bone-Bud" <note>original: 骨朵 (Guduo). The name suggests a budding flower or a rounded bone joint</note>. *Guzhun* is pronounced similarly to *Gutu*. 

The *Classic of Military Affairs* <note>original: 武經 (Wujing). Likely referring to the *Wujing Zongyao*, a comprehensive military compendium</note> states that the Bone-Bud exists in two varieties: the "Caltrop" <note>original: 蒺藜 (Jili). Named for its resemblance to the spiny water caltrop plant, often featuring spikes</note> and the "Garlic Head" <note>original: 蒜頭 (Suantou). A smoother, bulbous shape resembling a head of garlic</note>. These feature a large head fashioned from either iron or wood. 

The system of the Yuan Dynasty <note>1271–1368</note> utilized a red-lacquered rod head pierced through with a copper mallet that had been coated in gold. There was also an "Engraved-Pattern Bone-Bud" <note>original: 刻絲骨朵 (Kesi Guduo)</note>, which was shaped like a standard Bone-Bud but featured additional twisted-silk patterns. 

The current system <note>The Ming Dynasty, during which this text was likely compiled</note> utilizes a red-lacquered pole as the handle, decorated with gold at the base, with a Bone-Bud mace head pierced through the top.

<summary>This page explains the etymology and design of the "Bone-Bud" (Guduo), a ceremonial mace used by imperial guards, tracing its name to a regional term for a large belly.</summary>
<keywords>Bone-Bud (Guduo), mace, imperial guards, Song Qi, military equipment, ceremonial regalia, Guanzhong dialect</keywords>

translation: Why is this so? The merits of the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss> are inconceivable. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present have all studied this <term>Prajnaparamita</term>, and thus they achieved auspiciousness. I say that one who can study the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> is, among all studies, the most supreme, the most honorable, the highest, the most subtle, the most wonderful, the superior, the unsurpassed, the vast, the immeasurable, and the boundless. Why is this? The merits of the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> are immeasurable and boundless. For this reason, the merits of the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> are immeasurable and boundless. Why is this? The merits of the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> are not things that can be measured. It is the victory of these immeasurable merits that the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> signifies. The venerable <term>Subhuti</term> said to the Buddha: "For what reason is the nature of the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> inexhaustible, and because it is far removed? The profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> knows that all Buddhas of the three periods have studied the <term>Prajnaparamita</term>, attained the ultimate and complete perfect enlightenment <note>original: Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi</note>, and expounded it for all sentient beings. Yet this <term>Prajnaparamita</term> is like empty space; it cannot be exhausted. Those who wish to exhaust the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> are like those who wish to exhaust empty space, which has no boundaries. For this reason, <term>Subhuti</term>, the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> is called inexhaustible. Because it is inexhaustible, it is called immeasurable." At that time, <term>Subhuti</term> again said to the Buddha: "How is the profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> said to be inexhaustible?" The Buddha told <term>Subhuti</term>: "The profound <term>Prajnaparamita</term> is like empty space; it cannot be exhausted." The venerable <term>Subhuti</term> again said to the Buddha: "How should a <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattva</term> <gloss>Great Bodhisattva</gloss> study the <term>Prajnaparamita</term>?" The Buddha told <term>Subhuti</term>: "All <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattvas</term> should contemplate all form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness as all being inexhaustible, and thus generate the <term>Prajnaparamita</term>. They should contemplate ignorance, and even up to old age and death, as all being inexhaustible, and thus generate the <term>Prajnaparamita</term>. In this way, <term>Subhuti</term>, all <term>Bodhisattva Mahasattvas</term>...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of monastic discipline (Vinaya), specifically focusing on the rules governing the Kaṭhina period—a time after the summer retreat when monks are granted special privileges regarding their robes.</meta>

# Pelliot chinois 3113

Regarding the equipment for luxury robes and the rules for **not losing the privilege of the robe** <note>During the Kaṭhina period, monks are permitted to be separated from their three robes without committing an offense. "Losing the robe" refers to the expiration of this special privilege.</note>. In the midst of water, if a few people draw water, even at night; or as some say, within the constant flow of a river, one must not stop or bury [the boundary]. 

The markers for the boundary are determined by eight trees, seven intervals, and sixty-two steps. These serve to partition the surface. If we discuss the **Pavāraṇā sheds** <note>Pavāraṇā (self-correction) is the ceremony held at the end of the rainy season retreat; "sheds" refers to the temporary structures or designated areas for this rite.</note>, there are fifteen types:

1.  Where the Sangha is absent, and the two times are not listed.
2.  Fruit trees, where the trees are interconnected; it is permitted for someone to guard them, and the interior is restricted by a screen.
3.  Where gaps are established by ten fingers' width <note>A traditional unit of measurement in the Vinaya.</note>, specifically screened; if in a place with fruit, it must be treated four times over.
4.  Where the establishment is constant.
5.  Where the middle is not yet reached.
6.  Where practitioners walk a great distance and return; the interior is double-screened. 
7.  If the area is insufficient, six types of boundaries are listed; the boundary is for the time of return and the location.
8.  A wooden boundary; "middle" refers to the markers of the fields where one stays.
9.  A screened boundary; after the screening, the time is fixed to the location.
10. A room boundary; a place where many scattered repairs are made.
11. A house boundary; where numbers are stored in six locations.
12. **An island boundary**; involving lakes or rivers; if one studies there, even if the time passes, one does not lose the robe privilege.
13. **A well boundary**; involving secret paths and irrigation; if one stays overnight and places their robe there, they do not lose the privilege during their stay.
14. [Missing in original sequence]
15. A boundary where there are many people, or a small sea, or the sands and stones of the south. <gloss>Bulrushes</gloss> A path through the surging waves. These two boundaries are established by name.

There are two types of "reaches" <note>likely referring to coastal or river reaches</note> at the boundary's edge. When people of three types arrive, seeking a common residence, they establish the **Kaushambi** <note>original: 憍薩彌 (Qiāosàmí). This likely refers to a legal precedent or specific tradition regarding the Kaṭhina robe from the city of Kosambi.</note> foundation. If there are people within the boundary together with the monastery, or if they are outside the boundary, or if they are not in order, the boundary may be large or slightly different. If they merge into one later, it follows the Kaushambi extension.

If within a large boundary there is a monastery, and the outside of the boundary is not confused and does not flow together, then later scriptures mention villages like Tangmai and Yicun. 

According to the **Vinaya** <term>Vinaya: The code of monastic discipline.</term>, if there is no established Law <note>Dharma-rule</note>, and one is within a village, the robe is protected. Because this matter is not yet according to the Law, the "Path" is considered the Law. It does not matter if there is a village or not; the Law of the Vinaya flows through. If a village existed first, one follows the Law and later establishes the unified "Golden Cloister." 

If an outsider has not yet entered, the rule states that the head of the teaching is not within the boundary. If one departs from the village, a new boundary path is made. If there is a village marker, and the village acts improperly, it is called an "Empty Kaṭhina." According to the meaning, one seeks the Kaṭhina through the village marker. If it is not a Kaṭhina, the robes are not yet relinquished. 

If a person enters and the robe is not under the Kaṭhina boundary, and they stay within the riverbed, the robes accumulate merit to the limits of the village. If the village is gone, or if the markers of the teaching are not established, it is not a robe boundary. This is fixed. Therefore, next we remove the robes and the deep Kaṭhina teachings. This is the ultimate discussion.

**Question:** When there is a village, can one borrow it first? How is the Kaṭhina removed?
**Answer:** According to the Vinaya, it does not matter if it exists or not. One first observes the surroundings, then relinquishes the robe. If the relinquishing of the robe follows the Law, one can first establish the Kaṭhina markers. If one speaks of the method of removal, and says it follows the previous village markers, the current Law is not the Kaṭhina. 

Regarding the **Taking of the Kaṭhina**: The Vinaya says if a village existed previously, first observe the surroundings and rely on the previous clothing. If one takes the Kaṭhina outside the boundary, that is the "True Kaṭhina." Because it is a new Law, it is called the "Path Kaṭhina Boundary." If it is doubled, it is a new name and does not depend on the boundary. Among those who follow the Law, the witnesses manage the matter. In harmony, they follow the Law to modify and fix the robes. If the various parts of the body are too short or mismatched, it is decided by the Law.

Between the Kaṭhina and the village boundaries: one follows the markers of the village. The village boundary is the Kaṭhina boundary. Furthermore, when many people divide the merit, they obtain the boundary. Regarding the village, if one enters the village against the flow: 
According to the Vinaya, at the very beginning, there is a gap of one Kaṭhina. The "Faithful Kaṭhina" robe follows the Law. Furthermore, if one acts as a boundary companion, and the place fully has the Kaṭhina, the boundary is within the path. 

**Question:** Regarding staying overnight with the Kaṭhina robe? 
**Answer:** One follows the Law. If there is a gap, one follows the Law. Whether it is Kaṭhina or not, if it is by a river or stream, and the boundary is scattered or the boundaries of the "Color Limit" are fallen, and people do not know the markers: if there are houses in the middle, the robe rule says one must know the method of steps. Whether it is Kaṭhina or not is determined by the "Kaṭhina of Faith." One follows the twelve steps and relies on the gap. If this single gap of the robe is not a village, the markers are few. One can name it the "Kaṭhina of Faith." If the houses are not mismatched, they share the same nature.

There are three types of "Staff Paths": 
1. Utilizing the robe boundary and releasing many.
4. The village path in two places, with Kaṭhina markers appearing to be exhausted.

One checks the numbers and followers, then later determines the **Natural Kaṭhina of Faith**. Those who are not following the Law refuse the boundary and the restricted path of the Kaṭhina. Using the name of the path to differentiate a single interval, the Kaṭhina boundary does not follow the Law. Because of this, within the Kaṭhina boundary, there is a Natural Kaṭhina boundary. 

The signs do not necessarily need to be six or seven. For instance, in a village, most are village boundaries. If they are fixed and established and do not rely on each other, or if they are divided according to the Law, then the markers are for the Buddha's Law. The Kaṭhina signs rely on themselves. Afterwards, one marker, once it receives the Kaṭhina, if it rises to refuse the Law, it is the Kaṭhina marker. 

Within the curves, one follows the "Bucket Kaṭhina Boundary" and trusts it. Secondly, following the Law, one trusts the Kaṭhina boundary. Because of this boundary Law, within the two, a natural faith arises. The power of the two boundaries is divided; each boundary naturally has a Kaṭhina robe boundary. Because the exterior place does not follow the Law's modification, there is power.

If it is not according to the Law, it is the "Correct Kaṭhina." This "Surging Shape" below creates the Kaṭhina robe markers. Below it creates the Law Kaṭhina, which is also a flowing robe. The judgment of the flow is exhausted by the teaching robe's minimal division. Facing the "Correct Kaṭhina," the Vinaya calls it the "Fixed Kaṭhina." Following the Law provides the strength of the Kaṭhina robe. 

The **Natural Kaṭhina Robe** has "Bridge Stones" upon which the strength is divided. There is an explanation of the markers, as there were errors previously. 
**Question:** Regarding the strength of the Natural Kaṭhina land? 
**Answer:** The robe can be separated like a breast-child <note>Meaning it can be legally separated from the monk's person</note>. If one seeks the division of strength, it is the restricted Law outside the village markers. If that village is not a village, the land outside the markers where the strength is divided is where the "Heart-Governing Stone" is located. The **Kaṭhina Stone Boundary** is a type of stone boundary. 

1. A Natural Kaṭhina that does not disappear. The Vinaya recites that one side has a "Face-Washing Marker." Half of the text says the "Initial Hair Screen." This is also it.
2. Kaṭhina Ponds, etc. Looking at the Kaṭhina's construction, they are shown together. The Kaṭhina exists only within the Kaṭhina; it is not outside. It is also named "Not-Nine." 
3. Regarding the markers, the robes must not be mismatched first. When the Kaṭhina is released, the Bhikkhu <note>monk</note> follows his inclination. When the Kaṭhina is descending, the robes are not... <unclear>loss of text</unclear>

<summary>This page details the complex legalities of the Kaṭhina period, listing fifteen types of boundaries (sima) where monks can maintain their robe privileges and discussing how village boundaries interact with monastic law.</summary>
<keywords>Kaṭhina, Sima, Vinaya, Robe Privileges, Pavāraṇā, Monastic Boundaries, Kosambi, Natural Boundaries, Buddhist Law</keywords>

夫針灸皆是節穴俞募之處。若病甚則風氣衝擊於瘡。凡血氣相隨而行。故風乘於氣而動於血。血從灸瘡處出。氣盛則血不止。名為發洪。

# Syndrome of Profuse Bleeding from Acupuncture and Moxibustion Sores

Acupuncture and moxibustion points are all located at the junctions of vessels, points, and collection sites <note>referring to *shu* and *mu* points</note>. If an illness is severe, wind-energy may strike the sore. Generally, blood and *qi* travel together, so wind hitches a ride on the *qi* and disturbs the blood. If blood issues from the moxibustion sore and the *qi* is flourishing, the bleeding will not stop; this is called "profuse bleeding."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Straight Pillars" (Zhi) from the previous page, specifically detailing how their colors and clarity determine the outcome of a minister's rebellion. It then transitions into "Intersections" (Jiao) and "Solar Mouths" (Kou), relating these atmospheric shapes to military victory, internal discord, and the political ambitions of regional lords.</meta>

# Treatise on Armament Technology, Volume 139
## Divination of the Sun (Part II)

### Page 9

...ent.

If the sun has **Yellow Straight Pillars** <term>original: *Zhi* (直); vertical atmospheric phenomena resembling pillars of light</term>, it indicates that the ruler is properly establishing his ministers. However, if the **Straight Pillars** appear blue or red, it signifies that ministers are attempting to establish themselves as independent rulers.

If a **Straight Pillar** is red in the center and blue on the outside, those seeking to declare independence will not succeed. However, if the phenomenon appears yellow or white and looks moist and lustrous, their bid for power will be successful.

When blue and red vapors take the shape of two straight lines intersecting—whether positioned above, below, to the left, or to the right of the sun—this is called an **Intersection** <term>original: *Jiao* (交)</term>. Such **Intersections** are omens of **Excess** <term>original: *Yin* (淫); referring to licentiousness, social imbalance, or transgressive behavior</term>.

This vapor primarily governs the presence of licentious actions. If intersecting red clouds appear beside the sun, there will be military conflict <note>literally "there are soldiers/weapons"</note> in the lands below.

If two vapors on either side of the sun intersect, pierce through one another, or face away from each other, it signifies that great armies will rise across the world. It also portends internal rebellion and discord within the military. Another interpretation states: if there is an **Intersection** beside the sun, the army that attacks from the direction of that intersection will emerge victorious.

When various vapors form the shape of the character for "mouth" <note>original: *kou* (口); a simple square shape in Chinese script</note> near the edge of the sun, it is called a **Solar Mouth**. The appearance of one or two such "mouths" indicates that treacherous and evil people are causing harm. If three, four, or five **Solar Mouths** appear, it signifies that princes and marquises are plotting to seize power and establish themselves as independent sovereigns.

<summary>This section details how vertical pillars and intersecting vapors around the sun predict the success of ministerial rebellions and the movement of great armies. It also introduces "Solar Mouths" as omens of political conspiracy by high-ranking lords.</summary>
<keywords>Straight Pillars (Zhi), Intersections (Jiao), Solar Mouth (Kou), rebellion, military victory, treacherous ministers, Wubizhi</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the conflict between the Later Liang and Jin dynasties during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. The previous page detailed the Jin forces' psychological warfare and their victory at the Battle of Baixiang, which sent shockwaves through the region north of the Yellow River.</meta>

# Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance
## Page 18

"Returning to them would be like throwing oneself into the mouths of tigers and wolves. I ask to go alone to try it." At night, he was lowered by rope <note>縋 (zhùi): A common siege tactic where a person is lowered from the city walls using a rope to avoid detection by the enemy below.</note> down the wall to surrender. He asked for Zhou Yi. When Zhou Yi summoned and questioned him, he replied: "It will not be easy to take the city within half a month." He then requested a sword, <gloss>born of</gloss> <gloss>faithful unto death</gloss> <gloss>perhaps</gloss> to dedicate his life. Zhou Yi did not allow it, but instead ordered him to carry shoulder-poles <note>荷擔: Performing manual labor as a camp follower.</note> and follow the army. 

Eventually, the man found an opportunity; he lifted his shoulder-pole and struck Zhou Yi's head. Zhou Yi fell to the ground, but rescue arrived and he escaped death. The Liang Emperor <note>Zhu Wen, the founding ruler of Later Liang.</note> became increasingly enraged and ordered Yang Shihou to attack urgently day and night, intending to massacre the inhabitants. 

Meanwhile, He Delun attacked Tiao. The Jin general Li Cunshen said to Shi Jiantang and Li Sigong: "Our King is currently occupied with affairs in the You-Ji region <note>Modern-day Beijing and northern Hebei.</note> and has no troops to spare for this location. If we allow the rebels to take Tiao, they will certainly invade westward into the Shen and Ji prefectures, and our troubles will only deepen. I must work with you gentlemen to defeat them using a clever plan." 

Li Cunshen then led his troops to block the Xiabo Bridge. He sent Shi Jiantang and Li Sigong on separate routes to capture those gathering wood and fodder <term>樵芻 (qiaochu): Soldiers or laborers sent out from a military camp to collect firewood and grass for horses.</term> for the Liang army. They captured several hundred people and killed them, but spared a few men, cutting off their arms and letting them go, saying: "Tell Lord Zhu for me, the Jin...."

<summary>This page describes an assassination attempt on the Liang general Zhou Yi by a fake defector and the subsequent strategic counter-moves by Jin generals to protect Tiao County through psychological warfare and resource denial.</summary>

<keywords>Zhou Yi, Later Liang, Jin Dynasty, Li Cunshen, Siege of Tiao, psychological warfare, military strategy, Five Dynasties period</keywords>

Upon investigating the forms of these vessels, we find that the **Gui** <term>Gui</term> <note>A ritual bronze vessel used for holding cooked grains like rice and millet, typically having a circular bowl on a square base or vice versa.</note> is square, whereas the **Pu** <term>Pu</term> <note>A tray-like ritual vessel with a perforated stand, used for dried fruits or meat.</note> is round. Furthermore, the **Pu** appears to have almost no discernible difference from the **Dou** or the **Deng** <term>Deng</term> <note>A vessel similar to the Dou, but often made of earthenware and used specifically for holding unseasoned meat broth.</note>. 

Because of these similarities, their inscriptions are often confusingly alike. A previous inscription stated, "The Lord made this **Pu** for nourishment," while the **Dou** vessel of Yisheng <note>Referring to the 'Yisheng Dou' (疑生豆), a specific famous bronze artifact.</note> also bears the inscription "Dou for nourishment." This indicates that the wording used in their inscriptions is nearly identical.

I suspect that the reason some vessels are inscribed with the name **Pu** is to evoke the meaning of "to arrange and display" <note>original: 鋪; *pū*. The word for the vessel is a homophone for the verb 'to spread out' or 'to display' offerings.</note> for the presentation of sacrificial offerings. However, in terms of the actual physical object, it is simply a **Dou**. For this reason, I have appended the discussion of the **Pu** to the end of the section on the **Dou**.

The following items are categorized:

| Vessel Type | Quantity | Period |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Gui** | One | **Zhou Dynasty** |
| **Gui** | Three | **Zhou Dynasty** |
| **Dou** | Four | **Zhou Dynasty** |
| **Dou** | Two | **Han Dynasty** |
| **Pu** | One | **Zhou Dynasty** |

Detailed illustrations of these vessels can be found in the *Illustrated Catalogue of Antique Curiosities* <note>original: 博古圖; *Bógǔtú*. A massive thirty-volume catalog of ancient bronzes compiled by Wang Fu during the Song Dynasty (11th century).</note>.

<summary>This page clarifies the classification of the Pu vessel, arguing that while it is inscribed differently to emphasize the act of "displaying" offerings, it is physically a variation of the Dou vessel. It concludes with an inventory of specific Zhou and Han dynasty vessels found in the Bogutu catalogue.</summary>

Having concluded the rites for Jupiter on the previous page, the manuscript now moves to the ritual installation (nyāsa) and meditation (dhyānam) for Venus (Shukra) and begins the sequence for Saturn (Shani). <margin>Na</margin> <note>Likely a folio marker or shorthand</note> Earth, Atmosphere, Heaven <note>original: "Bhūr-bhuvaḥ svaḥ"</note> — the hair-lock. Venus <note>original: "Shukra"</note> in my head. Then at the seat... My hymns in the sacrifice... in the eyes. In the nostrils... *Vashat!* <note>a ritual exclamation used when making an offering</note>. Like the sky on the arms... on the two ankles... on the heart... on the belly. On the joints... in the speech... in the pair of thighs... on the knees. Thus... on the feet. **Now, the ritual installation in the hands. Thus, the ritual installation in the feet.**

Om. The seer of this mantra for Venus is Bharadvāja, placed in the mouth; the meter is Trishṭup, placed in the heart.

### Now, the Meditation on the Arts

The all-knowing giver of subjects, the shaker of the gods. Subtle... like a goddess <note>original: "Shākinī," a class of female spirits or yoginis</note>. ॥ 1 ॥

The one art of Venus... known as the form of the head... teacher... of all the gods... may he destroy the sins through serpent-wisdom <note>original: "Nāgaviyo"</note>. ॥ 2 ॥ <margin>7</margin>

---

...through success, of balanced mind, having obtained special knowledge. The leader and guide of the sons of the demons <note>original: "Daityas"</note>. The one who calms the serpent-wisdom, the peaceful one. ॥ 3 ॥

<insert>Shukra</insert> <note>Added by a later scribe to clarify the subject</note>
The syllable "A," the supreme teacher of the demons. I bow to the one in the lineage of the serpents, the proclaimer of all scriptures. ॥ 4 ॥

### Thus ends the ritual installation of Venus. Now, the ritual installation of Saturn.

Om. Earth, Atmosphere, Heaven. **Salutations to the two thumbs.**
"May the fire be peaceful with its fires" — **to the two index fingers.**
"May the Sun burn peacefully for us" — **to the two middle fingers.**
"May the wind..." — **to the two ring fingers.**
"May the waters..." — **to the two little fingers.**
Reciting the entire mantra — **to the palms and the backs of the hands.**

### Now, the installation in the six limbs

Om. Earth, Atmosphere, Heaven — **Salutations to the heart.**
"May the fire be peaceful with its fires" — **Swāhā <note>an invocation used when offering to fire</note> to the head.**
"May the Sun burn peacefully for us" — **Vaṣat to the hair-lock.**
"The gift of rays..." — **Hum <note>a protective seed-syllable</note> to the armor.** <note>refers to the chest and torso</note>
"May the waters..." — **Vauṣat to the three eyes.**
Reciting the entire mantra — **Phat <note>a mantra used to dispel obstacles</note> to the "weapon" ritual gesture.**

### Now, the ritual installation in the feet

Om. Earth, Atmosphere...

### Top Leaf

To live well in this world, many auspicious matters must be achieved. To make the necessary arrangements for success, one should perform deeds with an auspicious intent on a fortunate and holy day. One should complete these auspicious tasks with the right timing and without delay. These deeds should be carried out in a proper manner, aligned with favorable astrological conjunctions. To finish these auspicious tasks successfully, they must be performed with auspicious conjunctions and in a state of holy blessing.

### Bottom Leaf

One should complete auspicious deeds with discernment. Following the rules and as is appropriate, perform auspicious matters with favorable conjunctions. On a holy and auspicious day, with auspicious intent, one should complete these deeds. Finishing these tasks properly, with the right conjunctions and in a holy manner, is essential. One must complete the auspicious deeds with favorable conjunctions and in a holy, auspicious way.
