The perfect Buddha is seen within their own [minds].

And:
Just as the reflection of the Buddha appears,
Just as the reflection of the gods' bodies appears,
Likewise, in the minds of the beings to be trained,
The reflection of the body of the Sage arises.

And:
This is just the appearance of one's own mind.
Ordinary beings do not know this.

And:
Because they arise and cease,
The Buddha-body appears to arise and cease.
Like Indra, the Sage's
Dharmakaya does not arise or cease.

Those who speak in such a way have not understood even a fraction, for they do not understand the meaning of those scriptures. If one follows their wishes, it would contradict the intention of the scriptures. Those scriptures explain that the Buddha, who is free from the emanations of the Dharmakaya...

Subhuti, if the Bodhisattva, the great being, practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, through skillful means, he manifests as complete and perfect buddhahood in unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Subhuti, furthermore, when the Bodhisattva, the great being, practices the perfection of wisdom, he practices the perfection of patience, yet he does not apprehend the patience or the one possessing patience. If he does not practice otherwise than those two dharmas, then at that time, the Bodhisattva, the great being, attains the path of enlightenment. Subhuti, if the Bodhisattva, the great being, practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, through skillful means, he manifests as complete and perfect buddhahood in unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Subhuti, furthermore, when the Bodhisattva, the great being, practices the perfection of wisdom, he practices the perfection of diligence, yet he does not apprehend the diligence or the one exerting diligence. If he does not practice otherwise than those two dharmas, then at that time, the Bodhisattva, the great being, attains the path of enlightenment. Subhuti, if the Bodhisattva, the great being, practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, through skillful means...

...practices the perfection, he practices up to the eighteen unshared Buddha-qualities, yet he does not apprehend the unshared Buddha-qualities or the one meditating on them. If he does not practice otherwise than those two dharmas, then at that time, the Bodhisattva, the great being, attains the path of enlightenment. Subhuti, if the Bodhisattva, the great being, practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, through skillful means, he manifests as complete and perfect buddhahood in unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Then the venerable Sariputra said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, how does the Bodhisattva, the great being, exert himself on the path of enlightenment while practicing the perfection of wisdom?" The Blessed One replied, "Sariputra, in this regard, when the Bodhisattva, the great being, practices the perfection of wisdom, through skillful means, he does not attach to or separate from form. Why? Because there is no intrinsic nature in the form to be attached to or separated from. He does not attach to or separate from feelings, perceptions, volitional formations, and consciousness. Why? Because there is no intrinsic nature in the consciousness to be attached to or separated from. The sense bases..."

translation:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
because of the <term>emptiness of that which has passed beyond limits</term> <gloss>atyanta-śūnyatā</gloss> and the <term>emptiness of that which has no beginning or end</term> <gloss>anavarāgra-śūnyatā</gloss>.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, because the self is entirely infinite, the <term>emptiness of nature</term> <gloss>prakṛti-śūnyatā</gloss> is entirely infinite.

The Blessed One replied: Subhuti, it is because of utter purity.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, why is it that because the self is entirely infinite, the purity of the emptiness of nature is entirely infinite?

The Blessed One replied: It is because of the emptiness of that which has passed beyond limits and the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, because the self is entirely infinite, the <term>emptiness of all phenomena</term> <gloss>sarva-dharma-śūnyatā</gloss> is entirely infinite, and the purity of the emptiness of all phenomena is entirely infinite.

The Blessed One replied: Because the self is entirely infinite, it is because of the utter purity of the emptiness of all phenomena.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One?

The Blessed One replied: It is because of the emptiness of that which has passed beyond limits and the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, in the same way the Blessed One replied, and the Blessed One replied, because it is entirely infinite, the purity of the <term>emptiness of non-existence</term> <gloss>abhāva-śūnyatā</gloss> is entirely infinite.

The Blessed One replied: It is because of the emptiness of that which has passed beyond limits and the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, Blessed One, Blessed One.

The Blessed One replied: Blessed One, why is it that <note>the transcription appears repetitive or corrupted here</note> because it is entirely infinite?

The Blessed One replied: Subhuti, it is because of utter purity.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, why is it that there is the emptiness and the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end?

The Blessed One replied: Subhuti, because the self is entirely infinite, the <term>emptiness of its own marks</term> <gloss>svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā</gloss> is entirely infinite.

The Blessed One replied: Subhuti, it is because of utter purity.

Subhuti asked: The Blessed One replied, the Blessed One spoke, and the Blessed One asked, it is because of the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.

Subhuti asked: The Blessed One replied, Blessed One, why is the <term>emptiness of essence</term> <gloss>svabhāva-śūnyatā</gloss> itself without beginning or end?

The Blessed One replied: It is because of the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, the self is without beginning or end, and the Blessed One replied, the Blessed One is without beginning or end.

The Blessed One replied: Blessed One, the Blessed One replied: Subhuti, it is because of utter purity.

Subhuti asked: It was spoken, it is entirely without beginning or end, it was spoken.

<summary>This page contains repetitive dialectical exchanges between Subhuti and the Buddha concerning the emptiness of nature, all phenomena, non-existence, and own-marks. The text emphasizes that these various forms of emptiness are infinite and pure because they transcend temporal beginnings and endings.</summary>

translation:
...that son of the gods remembered his former state and came very quickly to offer worship to the Blessed One to repay his kindness. Because the Dharma was taught to him, he obtained the fruit of Stream-entry. At that time, the buffalo herders saw the appearance of the great light and were filled with doubt. They went to the Blessed One and asked, "Who was it that made such a great light last night?" 

When the Buddha told the story of how the buffalo was reborn as a god, the buffalo herders were filled with wonder and thought, "If even one born in an animal state can achieve such a result, why should we not obtain something special?" They satisfied the Blessed One and the Sangha with excellent food, then took ordination and, through great diligence, manifested the state of an Arhat <note>original: "Dgra bcom pa"</note>.

Again, at one time when the Blessed One was staying in Jetavana, King Prasenajit was preparing to make offerings to the Blessed One. The King of Panchala sent five hundred geese as a gift to King Prasenajit of Kosala, who then offered those geese to the Jetavana grove. Whenever the Buddha and the Sangha were taking their meals, the geese would go to the Blessed One. The Blessed One and the great disciples would give them scraps of food; the geese would eat, be satisfied, and their faculties would become clear. 

The majority of those who heard the Blessed One's Dharma became weary <note>of samsara</note>. Then Utpala prostrated with her head at the Blessed One's feet and requested, "Please teach me the Dharma so that I may be completely liberated from this body of pus and blood through a small amount of merit." 

When the Blessed One taught the Dharma, some of the assembly obtained the fruit of Stream-entry <note>original: "Rgyun du zhugs pa"</note>. Some obtained the fruit of Once-returner <note>original: "Phyir 'ongs pa"</note>. Some obtained the fruit of Non-returner <note>original: "Phyir mi 'ongs pa"</note>. Some obtained the state of an Arhat. Utpala also found faith in the Buddha, was ordained, and through great diligence in practice, manifested the state of an Arhat. Those dancers also manifested the state of an Arhat.

Again, when the Blessed One was staying in the forest called Kachangala, an old woman named Kachangala lived in that country. She took a jar and went to a well for water. The Blessed One said to Ananda, "Go and ask that old woman to give some water to the Blessed One for his thirst." Ananda went and told her this, and she replied, "I will come myself to serve the Noble One."

The distinction between the phenomena of virtue is as follows: They are the phenomena that produce benefit and happiness for the mind. These include the three roots of virtue, the six <term>perfections</term> <gloss>paramitas</gloss>, the eightfold path, <term>pristine wisdom</term> <gloss>jnana</gloss>, and the phenomena of the <term>two accumulations</term> <gloss>the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of wisdom</gloss>. Phenomena other than these are the phenomena that produce harm and suffering for the mind. These include the three roots of non-virtue, the six <term>afflictions</term> <gloss>kleshas</gloss>, the twenty secondary afflictions, and the phenomena of wandering in <term>cyclic existence</term> <gloss>samsara</gloss> under the power of karma and afflictions.

<summary>This page defines virtuous phenomena as those producing happiness and lists specific Buddhist paths, while non-virtuous phenomena are those causing suffering within cyclic existence.</summary>

入人衣秋生庾園鷄歸少客到高樓蛺語多等恥杜瀾微亭難高岑未少處

The teaching of poetry in the Eastern Country <note>original: "Dongguk," referring to Korea</note> is different from the Middle Province <note>original: "Jungju," referring to China</note>. In the Middle Province, current trends are followed, and the style flows daily toward detailed craftsmanship and delicate ornamentation. In the Eastern Country, we still value the ancient methods. Although there may be times when the tones do not harmonize perfectly or the choice of words feels forced, the natural spirit is so overflowing that it does not harm its excellence. 

In the Gyeongja year <note>likely 1840</note>, I met with the brothers Li Chunkye and Nianzhai to discuss this and composed a book. Now, Buyuan <note>the author's nickname, Ch'oe Hyang-wŏn</note> has brought and shown me this collection. Its sentiment is transcendent and vast. It is what one might call a spirit that emerges with ancient singularity and extraordinary charm. From time to time, it reveals a crisp and refreshing posture that is enough to startle one's eyes. Knowing what he possesses in his heart, one cannot help but feel there is no one else like him in this generation. Is Buyuan's rise not different from ordinary men? If the state of Lu had no gentlemen, where could he have acquired such qualities? Truly, the Eastern Country has many worthies! 

Holding this volume and adjusting it, I cannot bear to let it go. It is truly as the saying goes: by the time one finishes reading new poems, the blue mountains have already turned to dusk. Yet, like the colors of floating clouds and trees, or the sound of the setting sun on the Jialing River, his charm is boundless. The old masters like Master Yu in the past wrote of "the frost of the fifth watch entering one's clothes" or "autumn rising in the Yu garden." Lines such as "few guests arrive at the high tower" or "many butterflies speak" are so fine they would make even Du Fu <note>original: "Du Lan"</note> or the poets of the High Tang feel humble.

<summary>A preface comparing Korean and Chinese poetic styles, praising the author Ch'oe Hyang-wŏn for maintaining ancient standards and natural spirit.</summary>

translation:
# The Ministers of Song Congratulate the Appointment of Zhang Jun and Zhao Ding as Chancellors, Recruiting Talented Men and Proclaiming it the "Minor Yuanyou" Era

<margin>Look to your illustrious ancestors and do not be idle in admiring the beauty of great revitalization. Together acting for the Son of Heaven to obtain men, the name of "Minor Yuanyou" <note>referring to the virtuous Yuanyou era of the Northern Song</note> is spread abroad.</margin>
Excellent scholars all gather. Great fortune opens again. Reverently, the Zhou nation flourishes again. The ten generations of Han's hardship are over.
<margin>Remembering the achievements of the Philosophic Temple <note>Emperor Zhezong</note> in achieving Great Peace. Relying on worthy ministers to help the fragrant scent of the virtuous classes.</margin>
Sitting in the high halls, eight out of nine parts of the land are recovered; thus, the old evils of the Xi and Feng eras are reformed. In the bright court, the most outstanding men of the age are listed, able to restore the grand regulations of the Jia-you era.
<margin>Unfortunatley, a single mistake led people to be employed. We quickly restore the governance of the nine-year period.</margin>
Now, throughout the historical records of the dynasties, this is the third time great transformation has ascended. Amidst the national fortune, the danger has stopped, and we mourned that the prosperous times would not return.
<margin>Fortunately, in these days of rebuilding from the grass and mud. There is the beauty of selecting the worthy through divination.</margin>
Harmonizing two men <note>Zhang Jun and Zhao Ding</note> to be upright together; they do not shame the long-held reputation of the monarch's clan. Drawing many talents to stand side-by-side; are these not the remaining talents of the caliber of Tao, Han, and Wei?
<margin>Indeed, the sincere heart of the people's praise. It reaches the level of the governance in the first year of the Respectful Tomb <note>Emperor Zhezong</note>.</margin>
We rejoice that the group of worthy men assists together; all say the former fragrance will increase. We celebrate the harmony and prosperity of the new transformation; all claim that the auspicious fortune is seen again.
<margin>This is what is called having the same path as governance. Who says the sunlight of the eras is different?</margin>
Because the good chancellors are at court, many scholars have the joy of "dusting off their caps" <note>preparing for office</note>. Therefore, the people's hearts look up to the transformation, as if it were the time when Empress Xuanren held the court.
<margin>Sighing for the remains of the Jingkang decline, which no longer had the old form. Who would have said that in the days of the new Jian-yan creation, we would see the Great Peace of the previous dynasty again?</margin>
Can the congratulations ever end? We think the present is just like the past.

<column-break/>

<margin>The prohibition on the Cheng Yi school of learning is lifted, and worthy scholars flourish; the historical slanders of Cai Jing are cleansed, and ancestral glory shines again.</margin>
Relying on a generation of great men, we still speak of the virtuous influence of the former Empresses. Achieving the governance of Yao and Shun for a thousand years, this is the most prosperous period of our Song dynasty.
<margin>The gentlemen obtain the expected period of cooperation, unlike the atmosphere of the Jingguo era. The Pure Court relies on the transformation of "adjusting the candle," still following the scale of the Shaosheng era.</margin>
The figures of the Eastern Capital <note>Kaifeng</note> are not inferior to the high officials of the Western Han. Between the governance of the Yuan and Zhiping eras, there is the elegant style of the Zhenguan era.
<margin>Following the fragrance of the former cultivated and talented men, how could it be only the joint maintenance of the chancellor's work? Treading the path of the former kings in employing the worthy, we look up to the identical signs of sacred transformation.</margin>

For in truth, whoever takes [the credit or goods] does not fail to lose credit unless they are very well established in property <term>hazienda: an individual's wealth, estate, or total assets</term>. But certainly, they [the lenders] do not have the same license as others to purchase it back. This is quite clear, for to the common people themselves, without much philosophy but by the light of nature alone, it seems very wrong for the lender to take the goods back, and they hold them in poor regard—while they do not condemn or reprove any others who might buy those same goods. This should be an argument to them that the practice is not lawful for everyone. Such a negotiation is an affront <note>original: "da en rostro" — literally "hits one in the face," meaning it is a shameful or offensive sight</note>; it has a very bad appearance and, perhaps, bad substance as well. I mean that, inside and out, it has nothing healthy or proper about it. 

Also (as we said above), one of the things that validates these *baratas* <term>barata: a predatory credit transaction where goods are sold at high prices on credit and then resold for immediate cash at a loss</term> is when the goods are sold in public, and many people are aware of it, so that more buyers attend and the items can be sold for better prices—and not just known to the broker and the retailer <term>regatón: a petty merchant or reseller, often viewed as a middleman who drives up prices</term>. 

Thus, I say in conclusion that this business is very shameful, because it is generally forbidden for the same person who gives the clothing to take it back. This is especially true when they have not actually delivered the merchandise, but rather everything happens only in words; this is not a true sale, but rather a real and manifest usury, and as such it is condemned. If it should happen that, having sold his clothing, a merchant sees it later in a shop or at an auction <term>almoneda: a public sale or auction of goods</term> exposed for sale—with no secret agreement involved, and without fear of infamy—he may well buy it just like any other person at the price others pay. He will not be at fault, unless he was at fault in the initial sale he made by charging more than it was worth simply because he was selling it on credit. 

Although the best thing is to abandon the practice entirely, due to the great evils mixed within it. BY useful plants, I understand those that, besides giving something to eat at home, bring money to their owner. ...is lost. We could also add, as a final cause, the harsh and rigorous cold, which usually burns and scorches <note>original: "quemar y abrassar." The author uses "burn" here to describe the effect of extreme frost on foliage.</note> the tender and delicate leaves, flowers, and sprouts (as the common people say). This happens by quenching the natural heat with which the said leaf and plant live and are preserved.

All of this being assumed, it is easy to satisfy the question asked in the problem; and so, responding in order, I say that the trees of this land never lose their leaves, because none of the causes we mentioned above are enough to dry them out and make them fall. Firstly, they cannot fall during the winter because, since we are and live within the <term>Torrid Zone: the tropical region of the Earth between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, which was once thought by some ancient philosophers to be too hot for human habitation.</term>, the sun moves very little away from us during the winter. Thus, we cannot call such a time "winter," but rather a perpetual summer, since the sun is always near us. Furthermore, since these trees of the land are always raised in hot lands, they are never abandoned by the heat, which is what gives life and preserves the plant.

The <term>Indian trees: trees native to the Americas, referred to at the time as the West Indies.</term> are even less likely to lose their leaves or dry out due to a lack of moisture, because in the summer there is an abundance of moisture from the rains, and in the winter there is the moisture that descends from the mountain ranges to water these hot lands where we have said the fruit trees of the Indies grow. Moreover, the burning heat of the summer is even less able to dry the leaves of the trees because, since the rains occur in the summer, their moisture blunts and restrains the great force of the heat. Thus, we can truly say that in the Indies, more heat reigns during the spring than during the summer, because the rains that temper the summer heat have not yet begun in the spring.

As for extreme cold that might scorch the leaves of the trees, such a thing was never seen in the very hot lands of the Indies. And so, for all the aforementioned reasons, the trees of the land do not lose their leaves at any time. All of this is aided by the fact that the trees of the land are wild and untamed, and consequently sturdy and very tough; thus, they forcefully resist any opposition from cold or heat, which, as I have said, are not very strong in the hot lands of the Indies.

And if I were told that the <term>capulin: a type of black cherry native to North and Central America (*Prunus salicifolia*).</term> and the <term>manzanillo called xocote: referring to the Jocote or Mexican plum (*Spondias purpurea*); "xocote" comes from the Nahuatl word for sour fruit.</term>, despite being trees of the Indies, do lose their leaves, I respond that these two trees are more like those of Spain than those of the Indies, since the *xocote* is directly a species of medlar, and the *capulin* is a species of cherry.

Among these latter ones, the *Piüres* are notable—*Pyura gen. nov.* (1)—as much for their shape as for the manner in which they house themselves. These living beings, barely worthy of such a name, are shaped like a pear about an inch in diameter; or rather, they are nothing more than a small, fleshy, conical sac filled internally with a reddish, brackish water. They are provided with two trunks <note>original: *trompas*; Molina is describing the siphons used by the animal to filter water</note> at the top, one of which serves as a mouth and the other as an anus, in the same way as occurs with the *Tethys* <note>original: *Tetias*; a genus of sea slugs or nudibranchs</note>, and in the middle of these are seen two tiny, shiny black dots, which one must believe to be the eyes.
